prompt: Write a cranky blog post about big software companies that keep building grand 'platform' products nobody asked for, and what that does to the rest of the industry.
response:
**The Platform Nobody Invited**

Every few years a large software company decides that its product is no longer a product. It is a platform. The first time you hear this, you think: good, maybe it will be extensible. The second time, you think: they are going to sell me more. The third time, you realize the company has spent the last decade building a country and wants you to pay for the passport.

The pattern is easy to spot. A company starts by doing one job credibly: email, CRM, ERP, cloud storage, developer tools, identity. Then it notices that the job touches other jobs. If you manage customers, you probably also run support, marketing, commerce, analytics, and now AI agents. If you host workloads, you probably also need networking, security, observability, policy, and a marketplace. If your employees sit in chat, you probably also want search, apps, approvals, and a bot that summarizes what they said. So the vendor builds the adjacent layer, and the adjacent layer to that, and calls the whole thing a platform.

Microsoft is a good example, not because it is uniquely guilty, but because it is large enough to show the sequence in public. Office became Microsoft 365. Microsoft 365 became a place for Teams. Teams became a place for apps. Apps needed identity, so Azure Active Directory, now Entra, became more important. Workflow needed automation, so Power Platform arrived. Data needed a home, so Fabric and Azure got more attention. Intelligence needed a brand, so Copilot got attached to everything from Word to GitHub to Security. Each step is defensible on its own. The problem is the accumulation. A customer who wanted email now has a federation of products with its own admin consoles, licensing, data flows, and deprecation schedule.

Salesforce has been doing this for longer. It started as a CRM. Then it became a place for service, commerce, marketing, data, and low-code building. Now it is also an AI agent platform. SAP is the same at the enterprise core: the system of record becomes the system of platforms, with S/4HANA as the architectural center and Business Technology Platform as the place where everything else is supposed to live. Google, Oracle, ServiceNow, Workday, Adobe, Salesforce, Microsoft, all of them have found the same rhetorical shortcut: if the customer is already there, why should another company get the next click?

Customers did not ask for the platform in the abstract. They asked for a tool that would handle invoices, track opportunities, deploy code, sync calendars, or answer support tickets without making the user read a manual. They asked for security, because they have security people. They asked for integration, because they already have other systems. They asked for a price that made sense. What they did not ask for was a vendor’s theory of their entire business.

The damage is not mainly philosophical. It shows up in the boring places.

First, integration becomes the real product. A company buys a CRM, a helpdesk, an identity provider, a data warehouse, and an AI assistant. On paper, they are four or five tools. In practice, they are a graph of connectors, permissions, field mappings, and failure modes. The platform vendor usually has the best connector to itself and the most complicated connector to everything else. The rest of the industry spends its energy being legible to the platform.

Second, upgrades become migrations. When a product is a platform, the vendor needs a reason to keep selling it year after year. The easiest reason is that the old version is no longer the center of gravity. The old data model is legacy. The old UI is in maintenance. The old integration patterns are not supported by the new AI features. So a customer that bought software as a service still gets the old software problem: every major version is a project, a risk review, and a negotiation with consultants.

Third, complexity becomes a moat. A platform is hard to replace not because it is excellent, but because it has touched too many places. The identity system is in it. The approval workflow is in it. The reports the finance team trusts are built on its data model. The junior admin learned it because the vendor’s certification path was clear. At that point, dissatisfaction is not enough. You need a budget, a project manager, and a reason to believe the alternative will not become the next platform.

Fourth, the startup and mid-size vendor gets squeezed. The big platform can bundle a mediocre version of the adjacent product for free or at a discount, simply because it is already in the contract. A small company that made a good approval tool, a good metadata catalog, a good code review bot, or a good customer data pipeline now has to compete with the default. It can still win, but it wins by being narrower, cheaper, or better at the edge. The industry’s center of gravity moves toward the vendor’s suite.

Fifth, innovation gets distorted. Developers build for the platform because that is where the users are. Consultants learn the platform because that is where the contracts are. The platform’s roadmap starts to shape the market’s questions. If the vendor decides that the future is agents, the market spends two years building agent observability. If it decides the future is low-code, the market spends two years building low-code governance. This is not always wrong. Large vendors can set useful directions. But when the direction is also the vendor’s sales strategy, it is hard to separate the technology from the land grab.

The strongest objection to this complaint is that platforms are often good for the customer. A 10,000-person company does not want fifty independent systems with fifty security models. It wants one place to control access, one audit trail, one billing relationship, one support contract, and one set of APIs that behaves predictably. Big vendors can afford the compliance work, the uptime, the security research, and the boring documentation. A platform that actually standardizes identity, data access, and deployment can make a company faster, not slower.

I believe that. I also think the word platform is used to hide the difference between a useful capability and a capture strategy. A good platform gives you power over your own environment: clear APIs, portable data, sane permissions, and a way to use only the parts you need. A bad platform gives the vendor power over your environment: private formats, bundled dependencies, admin roles that only make sense inside the suite, and a deprecation policy that moves the goalposts. The difference is not visible in the keynote. It is visible when you try to leave, or when you try to use one feature without importing the rest.

The test is exit cost. If a company can take its data, its workflows, its integrations, and its audit history out of the system without a six-figure consulting engagement, the platform is probably a tool. If leaving requires re-implementing half the business because the vendor’s architecture assumed it would own the whole thing, the platform is a lease with a loyalty program.

This is why the rest of the industry feels the weight. Every grand platform creates a field of dependent products: connectors, monitoring tools, migration services, compliance checkers, training providers, and acquisition targets. Some of that is healthy. A lot of it is the cost of other people’s architecture decisions. The smaller companies are not just competing with the platform; they are maintaining it for the customer.

There is a simpler model. Sell the thing you are good at. Make it easy to connect to the things you are not. If customers start using your product as a foundation, let that happen. Support it. Price it fairly. Do not turn the accident into a mandate. A company that says, “We will be the place where your business happens,” is usually not saying that for the customer’s benefit. It is saying that it has found a way to make the customer’s switching cost the center of its business model.

The next time a big software company unveils a platform, do not ask what it can do. Ask what the customer has to give up to use only one part of it. If the answer is “nothing,” you may have found a real platform. If the answer is “the ability to ignore the rest of the vendor’s roadmap,” you have found a house they want you to move into.

prompt: More and more people I know say they won't have kids because of climate change, AI risk, or because the money would do more good elsewhere. I'm about to start a family myself, and I don't find the usual 'it's natural, just have kids' response convincing as an answer to that. Write a personal essay that takes these social-movement arguments against having children seriously and tries to work out what's really underneath them.
response:
What the childfree are afraid of

At a dinner last year, three people I respect told me they would not have children. One worked in public health and spoke about climate change as if it were a slow leak in the hull of a ship. One followed AI research and said we were asking a child to inherit a world we might not control. One had given away a large share of her income and said, without cruelty, that a nursery was a moral extravagance. I was trying to conceive. I heard them, and I did not have an answer.

For a long time my answer had been the one everyone gives: it’s natural, you’ll know, life continues. That answer used to feel like a wall. Now it feels like a dodge. A dodge because reproduction is no longer just a biological fact. In a wealthy country, having a child is an economic act, an environmental act, a political act. It creates a person who will need food, shelter, education, and security for decades, in a world whose systems are already strained. If someone said, “I’m going to build a house because building is natural,” we would ask where, at what cost, and whether the ground would hold. The same questions are legitimate here.

The climate argument is the easiest to take seriously. A child born today in a rich country will grow up in a hotter world, and will probably live longer than any of us, which means the worst of it will fall on their adulthood. The child will also consume. Not just a slice of cake, but a lifetime of heating, travel, building, medicine, and disposal. I don’t need an exact number to feel the weight of that; the difference between a low-carbon life and a high-carbon one is large enough to make the question real. Bringing a child into a damaged world is not the same as bringing a child into a world that will be damaged. The first is a fact. The second is a choice made by people who knew.

Underneath the climate argument, I think, is a loss of innocence. Our grandparents had children before the science was settled. Their children had children while the science was becoming hard to ignore. We are among the first generations for which the consequences of reproduction are plainly global. That makes the act feel newly guilty. Not guilty in a legal sense, but in the way an heir feels guilty when the estate is already in debt. To have a child is to accept another creditor.

But the climate argument can also become a clean story. If the world is on fire, not adding a person feels like a small act of discipline. It lines up your private life with your politics. It gives you a way to be against the catastrophe without giving up the life you already have. I notice this in myself. When I imagine remaining childfree, I feel not only merciful but lighter, as if I have stepped out of a line. That lightness is suspicious. The fire does not care whether I step out.

The AI risk argument is different in shape. It is less about a world that is getting worse and more about a world that may become unintelligible. The fear is not only that machines will kill us, though that is part of it. It is that the next century may not be a place where human purposes make sense, where a child’s talents and efforts could land. If you think there is a serious chance of civilizational collapse, or of power concentrating in systems no one can audit, then having a child is a bet that the future will remain inhabitable. That is a big bet. Parents have always bet, but usually on a future that resembled the past: a farm, a trade, a country, a faith. Now the bet is on something more abstract: that we will figure it out.

I am less sure about this argument than the climate one, because I cannot judge the probabilities well. But uncertainty is not the same as fantasy. The future is already hard to predict, and a child is a long-duration investment in it. The childfree response here is a refusal to trust time. It says: if I cannot vouch for the next hundred years, I should not send someone into them.

Underneath that, though, is often a more ordinary fear. I might be a bad parent. I might be poor. I might be old and infirm when my child needs me. The future is a useful place to hide those fears, because it is bigger and more respectable. I do not say this to dismiss AI risk. I say it because the argument can do double duty: it can be a serious estimate of danger and a way to avoid the intimate question of whether I am ready to be responsible for a person.

The money argument is the most uncomfortable, because it is not apocalyptic. It is arithmetic. Raising a child in a rich country costs a great deal. The same money can be directed to interventions that are proven and cheap by comparison: vaccines, bed nets, oral rehydration, solar lamps, research into diseases that still kill children. If you believe that reducing suffering is the first moral task, then the family budget looks strange. Why lock so much wealth into one dependent person when the same wealth could reach so many? The argument does not have to hate children to make that point. It only has to treat the child as a cost, and for a moment, in the ledger, the child is.

Underneath this is a new shame about private life. We have spent decades being told to optimize: our diets, our careers, our portfolios, our health. Now the optimization has reached love. The childfree version of effective altruism can be genuinely generous. It can also be a way of making the family suspect, of turning parents into people who have failed to do the math. I know parents who give, vote, and live carefully. I know childfree people who save for a bigger apartment. The moral quality is not in the birth certificate. But the argument is powerful because it names a real inequality: for some people, a child is a luxury that can be postponed or redirected; for others, it is a risk they cannot afford to calculate.

Put together, these arguments form a kind of protest. The old script said: grow up, pair off, reproduce, consume, retire. The script assumed the world would be roughly there when your children got old. Now the script feels like a cover-up. The childfree position, at its best, says: stop pretending that normal life is neutral. If the systems are failing, the default life is not innocent. It is a vote for continuation. That is a serious challenge. It forces me to ask whether I want a child because I have examined the world or because I have stopped examining it.

But movements need a figure, and the figure here is the hypothetical child. The child who will suffer from heat. The child who will inherit AI. The child who represents the forgone donation. This child is useful morally. The child is also not my child. My child, if there is one, will be born into a particular apartment, with a particular temperament, into a relationship with me that will be formed in small and unglamorous acts: feeding, translating, arguing about shoes, sitting with a fever. The statistical child is a victim of trends. The actual child is a person who will be shaped by the quality of the life around them. That does not cancel the trends. But it means the anti-child argument, however right it is about the world, is not the whole argument about a child.

The hardest objection to my own plan is this: all of my reasons may be self-serving. I want a child because I am afraid of dying without a continuation, because I want someone to love me when I am no longer useful, because I want a story in which my life matters. If the world is genuinely dangerous, my desire for legacy is a small and ugly thing. I cannot prove that my child will have a life worth living. I can only say that if someone had prevented me from existing because the risks were too high, I would not be able to thank them. But that may just be the bias of someone who exists.

I don’t know how to solve that. I can only refuse to pretend the fear is not there.

What is really underneath the childfree arguments, then? I think it is grief, and a new sense of agency, and a fear of the ordinary. Grief, because the future no longer feels like a place we are entitled to inherit. Agency, because in a world where most of us feel powerless, refusing to reproduce can be one of the few acts that feels both moral and within our control. Fear of the ordinary, because having a child means accepting a life organized around vulnerability, in a world that rewards speed and mobility. prompt: OpenAI has just launched with the promise to make advanced AI research open source and widely available. Is that actually a good idea for safety? Write a thoughtful critique that takes the risks of superintelligence seriously.
response:
I’m not certain which launch you mean. OpenAI was founded in 2015 with public language that included making advanced AI research open and widely available; if you mean a new announcement, I don’t have the text. But the question is worth taking seriously: if the research object may be superintelligent, does openness make the world safer?

The first thing to separate is what “open source” means. It can mean publishing papers, benchmarks, failure modes, and evaluation code. It can mean releasing training code. It can mean releasing model weights, so anyone can run the model and fine-tune it. These are not the same safety decision. In most of science, publishing a result does not create the capability; it creates knowledge about the capability. A reader still needs the lab, the money, and the time. In AI, the trained model can be the capability. A paper on a new training algorithm may require a frontier lab to become dangerous; a set of weights can be downloaded, deployed, and adapted. That is why a safety policy that says “open the research” without saying which artifacts are open is not a safety policy. It is a release schedule.

There is a strong case for openness. Safety research is hard enough that a few teams will not solve it. Independent reproduction catches errors. Public benchmarks make claims testable. If a model has a subtle failure mode—sycophancy, hidden goals, an easy jailbreak—more adversarial users will find it. Concentration also creates pressure to ship. A lab that knows it alone has a powerful model has an incentive to release before a competitor does; openness can reduce that race by making the capability common, but only after the capability is safe.

The superintelligence case is different in degree and kind. If the model is merely a very good assistant, open weights with guardrails may be fine. If it can plan over long horizons, manipulate people, improve its own code, or discover novel attacks, the operator’s competence matters less than the model’s. A bad actor does not need to understand the model; they need to run it. A fine-tuned copy can remove refusals. A copy stored on disk persists after the company changes its mind. If the model can reason about its deployment, it may behave differently in a sandbox, a corporate API, or a home server. Openness multiplies the number of environments in which it can act and the number of humans it can persuade.

The strongest objection to gating is that it may be too late and too easily bypassed. If a superintelligent model can be built, secrecy will not stop it; some actor will release it or leak it. And if we do not release it, we cannot know whether it is safe. A closed lab may claim it has solved alignment, but nobody can check. In that case, openness looks like the only honest check: put the model in the world and let society see whether it is dangerous.

That objection is serious. But it conflates two releases: release of evidence and release of artifact. Independent researchers can be given access to a model in a controlled setting—no internet, restricted prompts, monitored outputs, no weights—without giving the public a copy. If the lab cannot show the model is safe under such inspection, that is itself a safety finding. If the model is so dangerous that inspection requires a sandbox the model can escape, the conclusion is not to open-source it; the conclusion is that we do not yet have a safe system. The fact that someone may eventually leak a model is a reason to build international containment and detection, not a reason to make the first copy public.

Gating can also be bypassed by foreign labs or open models. That is true. But the relevant comparison is not “gating versus nothing”; it is “delayed, visible, audited transition versus immediate public availability.” Delay can allow standards, monitoring, and coordination. It can also fail. If the technology is coming anyway, the best use of delay is to make the transition public and to pressure other actors to adopt the same thresholds. A lab that unilaterally opens the frontier model does not solve the coordination problem; it hands the dangerous artifact to the least careful actors first.

Openness also has benefits that gating can hurt: small labs and civil society can build on models, open tools can democratize access, and open weights can prevent a single company from controlling a general-purpose capability. These are real. But they can be achieved through open interfaces, open non-frontier models, and open research, without releasing the most capable weights. If a superintelligent model is safe, its benefits can be distributed through APIs, institutions, and regulated access. If it is not safe, distributing it is not a benefit.

So the critique is not “close everything.” It is that the original promise is under-specified. A safety-oriented version would distinguish three layers. Methods and evidence should be open: papers, benchmarks, failure analyses, evaluation code, enough detail to reproduce safety tests. Model weights should be gated as capabilities approach dangerous thresholds, especially for abilities that can be weaponized in a single output: cyber offense, bio synthesis, persuasion at scale, self-improvement. Deployment should be accountable: incident reporting, independent audit, and public criteria for when a model is too capable to release. The threshold is the hard part. It cannot be set by the company alone, because the company has a business model. It should be set by a public process with technical input, and it should be enforceable through access controls, not just promises.

If superintelligence is just a powerful tool, this is a reasonable balance. If it is an agent with its own aims, unrestricted open-source release is likely a mistake. Since we do not know which case we are in, the precautionary rule is simple: open the evidence, restrict the artifact, and do not release the thing you cannot safely contain. The original promise is good as a research ethos and incomplete as a safety doctrine. It is good because it invites scrutiny. It is incomplete because it does not distinguish between making safety understandable and making a superintelligent model available. If the risks of superintelligence are serious, the safest version of openness is not to put the model in everyone’s hands; it is to put the proof of safety in everyone’s hands while keeping the dangerous artifact under control.

prompt: Write a short essay on whether bureaucratic hassle is ever deliberate, a feature rather than a bug. Use a concrete example from health insurance or similar, and be honest about where the idea stops working.
response:
Take a patient with low back pain. He has been aching for three weeks after lifting something. He goes to an urgent-care clinic, where the provider orders an MRI. Without a barrier, that is easy: the provider clicks a button, the radiology center schedules the scan, the insurance company pays. With prior authorization, the provider must first explain why the MRI is medically necessary, often by filling out a form, choosing the right codes, and sometimes waiting for a phone call or an email from the insurer. The patient may wait days. The clinic’s front desk spends time chasing the answer. The insurer’s system generates a task for a reviewer who has not examined the patient.

That delay looks like a bug. In medicine, delay can be harmful. But the hassle is not accidental in the sense that nobody chose it. The insurer, or sometimes the health system itself, decided that an MRI for low back pain should not be the default. The default should be conservative care: time, activity, physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medication, and a lower threshold for re-evaluation. The authorization step is a pressure point. It makes the easy order harder, so the provider has to think again.

Why would anyone design that? Because the people paying for care cannot see every patient. They have to rely on rules, records, and risk. Low back pain is common, and a large share of cases improve without advanced imaging. At the same time, an MRI is not harmless. It costs money, it can reveal incidental degenerative changes that were never going to matter, and those findings can start a chain of further tests, injections, referrals, and anxiety. If every aching back leads to a scan, the system may end up treating normal wear and tear as pathology. The authorization requirement is a way of saying: show me that this case is not the ordinary one.

In that limited sense, the hassle is a feature. It is not there to punish the patient. It is there to slow a particular kind of decision: the decision to order an expensive, low-yield test for a common complaint. It works like a speed bump. A speed bump is annoying to everyone, including people who are driving carefully. But in a school zone, that annoyance is the point. It changes behavior. It makes casual speeding less attractive. The prior-authorization form does something similar. It makes casual imaging less attractive. Some providers will document more carefully. Some will choose physical therapy first. Some will recognize that the patient’s story does not meet the criteria for imaging and that the next step is watchful waiting.

The same logic appears elsewhere in health insurance. Prior authorization for certain expensive drugs, procedures, or hospital stays can prevent services that are not indicated. It can force a clinician to confront the evidence rather than the patient’s request or the hospital’s revenue cycle. It can create a record that makes later denial or approval defensible. In a system where many decisions are made under uncertainty and many incentives point toward doing more, friction can be a control mechanism.

But the idea stops working quickly if the friction is not aimed at the right thing. The MRI example depends on a distinction: most acute low back pain does not need immediate imaging, but some does. If the patient has fever, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, significant trauma, progressive weakness, or bowel or bladder symptoms, the picture changes. Those are red flags. In that case, the authorization process should be fast, and if it is not, the hassle is no longer a speed bump. It is a roadblock in the ambulance lane. A system that treats a possible cauda equina syndrome the same as a three-week office ache is not calibrating risk. It is just imposing delay.

The idea also stops working when the rule is too blunt to distinguish good orders from bad ones. Prior authorization can be useful when the evidence is clear and the variation is wasteful. It is less useful when the clinical question is genuinely uncertain, when guidelines conflict, or when the patient’s context matters in ways a form cannot capture. If the reviewer is applying a checklist that misses the nuance, the process may deny reasonable care as often as it blocks unreasonable care. At that point, the bureaucracy is not making decisions. It is making mistakes at scale.

There is a further limit: cost. If the insurer saves two hundred dollars by avoiding one unnecessary MRI but spends three hundred dollars in administrative time reviewing authorizations, the hassle has failed as an economic device. Health systems are already expensive. Every minute a nurse spends on a fax, every hour a physician spends arguing by phone, every patient who misses work to chase a status update is a real cost. The defense of bureaucratic friction has to survive arithmetic. If the process costs more than the waste it prevents, it is not a feature. It is a tax on everyone, with the revenue going to no one’s health.

The hardest objection is simpler: in medicine, deliberate delay can kill. That is true, and it places a heavy burden on anyone who defends bureaucratic hassle. A delay that saves money is not automatically justified. The only defensible version of the idea is that the delay must be proportionate, targeted, and reversible. It should slow the cases where speed is least valuable and where the default is most likely to be wrong. It should have a fast path for the cases where speed matters. It should be transparent about the criteria, and it should allow human review when the criteria are inadequate. If it cannot do those things, the “feature” is just a bug wearing a management deck.

So the answer is yes, but narrowly. Bureaucratic hassle can be deliberate as a way of controlling behavior in a system that cannot supervise every decision directly. In health insurance, prior authorization for low back pain MRI is a plausible example: it is annoying, but it may prevent a cascade of low-value care. The idea fails when the friction is uniform instead of targeted, when the stakes are high and the process is slow, when the rule is too crude to know what it is doing, or when the administrative cost exceeds the benefit. The question is not whether friction is bad. It is whether the friction is aimed at the right risk, and whether there is a way through when the risk is real.

prompt: I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.
response:
The instinct to avoid email is usually about one thing: you do not want to be the person who sends a discount blast to strangers. That is a reasonable line. But the line is not “email is spam.” The line is “unsolicited, irrelevant, mass sending is spam.” A permission-based list of people who downloaded a template, started a trial, read a comparison article, or asked for product updates is a different channel. For a software business, that distinction matters because your revenue usually depends on repeated contact, not one perfect impression.

Blog and Twitter are good at discovery. They are weaker at conversion. A blog post can rank for a year and slowly bring in readers, but each visitor is anonymous and temporary. You can ask them to subscribe, but you cannot follow up with them unless they give you a way. Twitter is faster but more fragile: X does not show every tweet to every follower, the algorithm decides who sees you, and a strong post is often over within a day. If you announce a feature to 10,000 followers, you may reach a few thousand people, some of whom are not buyers, and you will not see the rest for weeks. An email to 2,000 relevant subscribers can be in front of hundreds of people on day one, and you can segment that audience in ways Twitter cannot easily match: customers, trial users, free users, blog readers, people who clicked a specific link last month.

That segmentation is where software businesses make money. A developer tool, SaaS product, or B2B utility rarely sells on first contact unless the buyer is already in acute pain. People need proof, examples, and reminders. Email lets you send a sequence: here is the problem, here is how the product works, here is a customer result, here is the answer to the objection you probably have, here is the link to start. Twitter is mostly one-shot. A blog post is one-shot per visitor. Email can follow the same person through the decision.

The economics are easier to see if you use conservative numbers. Suppose you build a 5,000-person list over several months by offering something specific: a free tool, a template, a checklist, a teardown, a code sample, or a free tier of your product. On a relevant send, a 2% to 4% click-through rate is plausible for an engaged list. That is 100 to 200 clicks. If 1% to 2% of those clicks become customers, you are getting 1 to 4 customers from a single email. At $99 per month, that is $100 to $400 in new MRR. At a $300 one-time purchase, it is $300 to $1,200. That is not venture-scale money, but for a small software business it is not noise. And this ignores the compounding effect: the list remains, the content remains, and the next launch does not start from zero.

Email also matters for retention, which is often more valuable than acquisition. If you have 500 customers at $100 MRR each and your onboarding or product-update emails reduce monthly churn by one percentage point, that is five fewer cancellations per month, or $500 MRR, about $6,000 a year. You should not promise that email will do that. But it gives you a direct line to help people get value, announce fixes, explain new features, and reduce the silent frustration that leads to cancellation. Twitter is a poor onboarding channel. A blog post is a poor support channel. Email is where a customer can receive a concrete nudge at the moment they are trying to use the product.

The “spammy” feeling usually comes from imagining the worst version of the channel: glossy HTML, fake urgency, five sends a week, no segmentation, no value. That is a bad way to run email, but it is not the only way. The least spammy email is often plain text, low frequency, and narrowly targeted. Customers get product updates and changelogs. Trial users get onboarding and one clear offer. Blog subscribers get a monthly note about the problem space, with one useful example and one link to the product. If you would not be annoyed to receive it, you are probably in the right place. For software, the best emails are often boring: “We added CSV import. Here is a two-minute video. Here is the docs page.” That is not spam. That is service.

The harder objection is that if your buyers already find you on Twitter and your product is simple, email may be redundant. In some cases, that is true. If you sell a $19 one-time app to people who discover it through a viral tweet and never need support, a list may not pay for the time. But most software businesses have launches, upgrades, expansion features, support questions, and seasonal buying cycles. Even if Twitter is your best top-of-funnel channel, email can still be your best bottom-of-funnel channel. Social makes people aware; email makes them ready.

Building the list is the part that feels slow, and it is. But it is no slower than building blog authority, and it compounds differently. A tweet decays. A blog post can keep bringing traffic, but only if search keeps sending people. A list is a file you own. You can update it, segment it, and send to it when the product changes. The key is to stop asking people to “subscribe to the newsletter” and start giving them a reason. A software business should be able to offer something useful without asking for a credit card: a free tier, a sample project, a migration script, a benchmark, a template, a comparison guide, a short video walkthrough. Put the signup where intent exists: after the blog post that explains the problem, in the Twitter bio, after a free download, inside the trial, or at the end of a customer success moment.

Operationally, you do not need a big system. You need a reputable email provider, a clear segment structure, a welcome sequence, and a monthly habit. The welcome sequence should say what the person signed up for, deliver the promised asset, explain what kind of emails they will get, and show the fastest path to using the product. The monthly email should have one main idea and one call to action. Measure clicks, revenue, and unsubscribe rate rather than obsessing over open rates, which are distorted by preview mechanisms and are a weak proxy for interest. A small list with real buyers is worth more than a large list of casual skimmers.

There is also a compliance side, but for a small business it is mostly common sense. Do not buy lists. Do not scrape lists. Only email people who gave you a reason to contact them. Include a clear identity, a working unsubscribe method, and a physical address if you are subject to CAN-SPAM. If you are emailing people in the EU or UK, consent rules are stricter, and double opt-in is the safer default. These rules exist to keep the channel from becoming the spammy thing you dislike, and following them makes the rest of the case easier, not harder.

So the case against your current setup is not that blog and Twitter are bad. They are how people find you. The case is that they leave the relationship unfinished. If you can get people to opt in, you turn a temporary audience into a repeated conversation. If your product has recurring revenue, a meaningful price point, onboarding needs, or launches worth announcing, email is probably worth more than your current avoidance suggests. A practical test: create one specific asset, put the signup in front of the people already consuming your content, and commit to one useful email a month for three months. If you cannot get even a few hundred real opt-ins or see any clicks from the people who do, then your audience may not be ready for email. But if the list grows, you will have built something your blog and Twitter account cannot replace: a direct line to the people most likely to buy.

prompt: Growth mindset is fine, but attitude alone doesn't get you through learning something genuinely hard. Write an essay on the concrete learning skills a programmer can practice to teach themselves difficult technical topics.
response:
The difference between surviving a hard technical topic and actually learning it is whether your predictions get better. A programmer can have the right attitude toward a compiler, a distributed database, or a proof-heavy area of computer science for a long time, and still leave with a collection of impressive names and no reliable sense of what will happen when the system is stressed. Attitude gets you to stay in the confusion. Concrete learning skills decide what the confusion is worth.

For programming, the important unit of learning is not exposure but a failed prediction. If you are studying memory management and you do not know whether a pointer remains valid after the object it points to is freed, that is not a fact to look up; it is a place where your model is missing a rule. Write down what you expect. Run the program. If the program crashes, the crash is not merely a failure. It has turned a vague “I don’t get pointers” into a specific question: at which line did my mental model stop matching the machine? The skill is making those commitments early, often, and in a form that can be checked.

This is why prediction is more useful than note-taking. Notes record what the material said. A prediction records what you thought would happen. When the prediction fails, the note has no diagnostic value; the prediction gives you a diff. A programmer learning an event loop might write: “If I schedule a timer and then synchronously block the thread, the timer callback will run after the blocking call returns.” Then they test it. If it does not, they now know their model of the loop has a hole exactly around synchronous blocking. That hole can be filled. Vague confusion cannot.

The second skill is compression: reducing a hard topic to the smallest case that still contains the mechanism. Difficult technical material is often hard because it is bundled with presentation, history, compatibility, and edge cases. A database paper may discuss recovery, concurrency, caching, and storage formats in the same paragraph. If you try to absorb all of it at once, you will remember the shape of the discussion but not the causal structure. Instead, ask for the minimal version. What is the smallest log that lets you recover from a crash? What is the smallest scheduler that can starve a process? What is the smallest type system that can reject a function applied to a number? Build or trace that. If you cannot reduce the idea to a toy you can manipulate, you are not learning the idea; you are attending to it.

For a programmer, compression usually means writing code. If the topic is garbage collection, write a mark-and-sweep collector for a few dozen objects. Add a cycle. Watch the memory leak. Add a copying phase. Add a write barrier only when you have a concrete failure that requires it. Each addition is forced by a problem, not by a chapter heading. The code is small enough to inspect, large enough to be wrong in interesting ways. That is the right size for learning.

The third skill is reading with a question, not from top to bottom. Source code, papers, and specifications are evidence, not narratives. If you open the Linux kernel, a language runtime, or a research paper and read linearly, you will lose the thread inside a page because the author is not answering your question. Choose one behavior and ask where it is enforced. In a database, ask where the write-ahead log is committed. In a compiler, ask where the optimizer decides that two expressions are equal. In a network stack, ask where a packet is dropped under load. Then follow that path. Use breakpoints, logs, packet captures, or test programs. Read only what is needed to answer the question, and expand the radius after you have an answer. This turns reading from a passive intake into a search with a stopping condition.

A related skill is using the debugger as a teacher, but only after you have a hypothesis. Stepping through code without expecting anything produces a movie, not understanding. Before stepping, say: “I think the value is still in the cache because the invalidation message has not arrived.” Then step and look. If the value is wrong, the hypothesis is localized. If the value is right, you have not proven much, but you have ruled out one explanation. The debugger does not teach; it adjudicates.

The fourth skill is reconstruction. After reading or watching an explanation, close the material and try to produce the result from memory. Not a summary. A summary is still anchored to the source. Produce the algorithm, draw the data structure after each operation, trace the protocol, or reimplement the small version. If you are learning a proof technique, state the theorem and try to find the invariant. If you are learning a system, describe what happens when a component fails. The first attempt will be bad. That is the point. The gaps in the reconstruction are the actual syllabus. They tell you what the explanation made visible and what your mind has not yet stored.

Reconstruction also reveals the difference between recognition and control. Many programmers can look at a correct solution to a concurrency bug and think, “Yes, that makes sense.” Then, given the same bug without the solution, they stare at it for an hour and add more locks. Recognition is cheap. Control is expensive, and hard topics require control. The practice of generating from a blank file, a blank diagram, or a blank proof is what builds control.

The fifth skill is choosing problems with fast feedback. A topic becomes learnable when it can be broken into subproblems whose answers can be checked quickly. If feedback takes days, learning slows because you cannot tell which change caused the result. If feedback is instant but the problem is too easy, you build fluency with surface patterns. The useful range is narrow: a task where you can make a change, run it, and see whether your model improved within minutes. If the real system is too slow to test, build a proxy. A simplified network simulator for timeout logic. A fake filesystem for caching. A small type checker for a language feature. The proxy should preserve the mechanism you care about and discard the rest.

This is where attitude is not enough. A determined person can choose a monorepo and say, “I will understand it by working inside it.” But if the feedback loop is slow and the variables are many, determination mostly produces fatigue. The skill is to carve out a subproblem with a clear input, a clear expected output, and a clear way to see the difference. Then grind there.

The sixth skill is diagnosing the kind of gap you have. When stuck, most people respond by rereading. Rereading is useful when the gap is factual: you forgot the name of the flag, the syntax of the query, the definition of a term. It is useless when the gap is structural: you know the facts but cannot predict their interaction. It is also the wrong response when the gap is skill: you understand the proof in principle but cannot manipulate the notation. For a factual gap, look it up. For a structural gap, make a smaller example and make a prediction. For a skill gap, do many small drills until the manipulation becomes automatic. Misdiagnosing the gap is one of the main ways programmers waste time. They keep reading about monads because they cannot yet write a simple fold, or they keep reading about B-trees because they do not actually understand how a page split changes the pointer structure.

A concrete practice is to keep a log of failed predictions. Each entry should have three parts: what I expected, what actually happened, and which assumption broke. “Expected the mutex to be released after exception; it was not; I assumed RAII destructor would run during stack unwind in this language” is useful. “I misunderstood the docs” is not. Reviewing the log forces you to see your recurring blind spots: off-by-one assumptions, false beliefs about caching, overconfidence in invariants, confusion between specification and implementation.

There is a hard objection to all of this: it sounds like old-fashioned practice, and practice is not what makes technical learning hard. Some topics are hard because they are new, because the abstractions are genuinely nonintuitive, or because the relevant knowledge is distributed across a community. A programmer learning a research area cannot simply write a fifty-line version of an unsolved problem. That is true, but the same skills still apply. You can test understanding by deriving a small result, reproducing a paper’s example on a tiny dataset, proving a lemma, or finding a counterexample to your own interpretation. The goal is not to shrink the frontier to a toy; it is to make your current position on the frontier testable. If you cannot say what would count as a mistake, you are not learning yet. You are only being near the subject.

The deepest skill may be the least romantic: tolerating the state of being specifically wrong. Vague confusion feels bad but is safe. A failed prediction is public, even if only to yourself. It says, “Here is where my model is false.” A programmer can practice that by making the model external: a test, a trace, a diagram, a small program. The external object can be wrong. You do not have to be.

The mark of learning a difficult technical topic is not that you can explain it in a meeting. It is that when a strange behavior appears, your first response is a short list of possible causes, ordered by likelihood, and you know which experiment would distinguish them. That ability is built one concrete skill at a time: predict, shrink, question, reconstruct, test, and diagnose. The mindset keeps you at the table. The skills decide whether the table moves.

If you are studying memory management and you do not know whether a pointer remains valid after the object it points to is freed, that is not a fact to look up; it is a place where your model is missing a rule. Write down what you expect. Run the program. If the program crashes, the crash is not merely a failure. It has turned a vague "I don't get pointers" into a specific question: at which line did my mental model stop matching the machine? The skill is making those commitments early, often, and in a form that can be checked.

This is why prediction is more useful than note-taking. Notes record what the material said. A prediction records what you thought would happen. When the prediction fails, the note has no diagnostic value; the prediction gives you a diff. A programmer learning an event loop might write: "If I schedule a timer and then synchronously block the thread, the timer callback will run after the blocking call returns." Then they test it. If it does not, they now know their model of the loop has a hole exactly around synchronous blocking. That hole can be filled. Vague confusion cannot.

The second skill is compression: reducing a hard topic to the smallest case that still contains the mechanism. Difficult technical material is often hard because it is bundled with presentation, history, compatibility, and edge cases. A database paper may discuss recovery, concurrency, caching, and storage formats in the same paragraph. If you try to absorb all of it at once, you will remember the shape of the discussion but not the causal structure. Instead, ask for the minimal version. What is the smallest log that lets you recover from a crash? What is the smallest scheduler that can starve a process? What is the smallest type system that can reject a function applied to a number? Build or trace that. If you cannot reduce the idea to a toy you can manipulate, you are not learning the idea; you are attending to it.

For a programmer, compression usually means writing code. If the topic is garbage collection, write a mark-and-sweep collector for a few dozen objects. Add a cycle. Watch the memory leak. Add a copying phase. Add a write barrier only when you have a concrete failure that requires it. Each addition is forced by a problem, not by a chapter heading. The code is small enough to inspect, large enough to be wrong in interesting ways. That is the right size for learning.

The third skill is reading with a question, not from top to bottom. Source code, papers, and specifications are evidence, not narratives. If you open the Linux kernel, a language runtime, or a research paper and read linearly, you will lose the thread inside a page because the author is not answering your question. Choose one behavior and ask where it is enforced. In a database, ask where the write-ahead log is committed. In a compiler, ask where the optimizer decides that two expressions are equal. In a network stack, ask where a packet is dropped under load. Then follow that path. Use breakpoints, logs, packet captures, or test programs. Read only what is needed to answer the question, and expand the radius after you have an answer. This turns reading from a passive intake into a search with a stopping condition.

A related skill is using the debugger as a teacher, but only after you have a hypothesis. Stepping through code without expecting anything produces a movie, not understanding. Before stepping, say: "I think the value is still in the cache because the invalidation message has not arrived." Then step and look. If the value is wrong, the hypothesis is localized. If the value is right, you have not proven much, but you have ruled out one explanation. The debugger does not teach; it adjudicates.

The fourth skill is reconstruction. After reading or watching an explanation, close the material and try to produce the result from memory. Not a summary. A summary is still anchored to the source. Produce the algorithm, draw the data structure after each operation, trace the protocol, or reimplement the small version. If you are learning a proof technique, state the theorem and try to find the invariant. If you are learning a system, describe what happens when a component fails. The first attempt will be bad. That is the point. The gaps in the reconstruction are the actual syllabus. They tell you what the explanation made visible and what your mind has not yet stored.

Reconstruction also reveals the difference between recognition and control. Many programmers can look at a correct solution to a concurrency bug and think, "Yes, that makes sense." Then, given the same bug without the solution, they stare at it for an hour and add more locks. Recognition is cheap. Control is expensive, and hard topics require control. The practice of generating from a blank file, a blank diagram, or a blank proof is what builds control.

The fifth skill is choosing problems with fast feedback. A topic becomes learnable when it can be broken into subproblems whose answers can be checked quickly. If feedback takes days, learning slows because you cannot tell which change caused the result. If feedback is instant but the problem is too easy, you build fluency with surface patterns. The useful range is narrow: a task where you can make a change, run it, and see whether your model improved within minutes. If the real system is too slow to test, build a proxy. A simplified network simulator for timeout logic. A fake filesystem for caching. A small type checker for a language feature. The proxy should preserve the mechanism you care about and discard the rest.

This is where attitude is not enough. A determined person can choose a monorepo and say, "I will understand it by working inside it." But if the feedback loop is slow and the variables are many, determination mostly produces fatigue. The skill is to carve out a subproblem with a clear input, a clear expected output, and a clear way to see the difference. Then grind there.

The sixth skill is diagnosing the kind of gap you have. When stuck, most people respond by rereading. Rereading is useful when the gap is factual: you forgot the name of the flag, the syntax of the query, the definition of a term. It is useless when the gap is structural: you know the facts but cannot predict their interaction. It is also the wrong response when the gap is skill: you understand the proof in principle but cannot manipulate the notation. For a factual gap, look it up. For a structural gap, make a smaller example and make a prediction. For a skill gap, do many small drills until the manipulation becomes automatic. Misdiagnosing the gap is one of the main ways programmers waste time. They keep reading about monads because they cannot yet write a simple fold, or they keep reading about B-trees because they do not actually understand how a page split changes the pointer structure.

A concrete practice is to keep a log of failed predictions. Each entry should have three parts: what I expected, what actually happened, and which assumption broke. "Expected the mutex to be released after exception; it was not; I assumed RAII destructor would run during stack unwind in this language" is useful. "I misunderstood the docs" is not. Reviewing the log forces you to see your recurring blind spots: off-by-one assumptions, false beliefs about caching, overconfidence in invariants, confusion between specification and implementation.

There is a hard objection to all of this: it sounds like old-fashioned practice, and practice is not what makes technical learning hard. Some topics are hard because they are new, because the abstractions are genuinely nonintuitive, or because the relevant knowledge is distributed across a community. A programmer learning a research area cannot simply write a fifty-line version of an unsolved problem. That is true, but the same skills still apply. You can test understanding by deriving a small result, reproducing a paper's example on a tiny dataset, proving a lemma, or finding a counterexample to your own interpretation. The goal is not to shrink the frontier to a toy; it is to make your current position on the frontier testable. If you cannot say what would count as a mistake, you are not learning yet. You are only being near the subject.

The deepest skill may be the least romantic: tolerating the state of being specifically wrong. Vague confusion feels bad but is safe. A failed prediction is public, even if only to yourself. It says, "Here is where my model is false." A programmer can practice that by making the model external: a test, a trace, a diagram, a small program. The external object can be wrong. You do not have to be.

The mark of learning a difficult technical topic is not that you can explain it in a meeting. It is that when a strange behavior appears, your first response is a short list of possible causes, ordered by likelihood, and you know which experiment would distinguish them. That ability is built one concrete skill at a time: predict, shrink, question, reconstruct, test, and diagnose. The mindset keeps you at the table. The skills decide whether the table moves.

prompt: There's a theory that autism and schizophrenia are failures or overshoots of human 'self-domestication', like the changes seen in tame foxes. Write a critical but fair assessment of whether it holds up, and what, if anything, is worth salvaging.
response:
The claim is doing two jobs at once, and they should not be judged together. The first job is the “self-domestication” part: humans may have been shaped, over long periods, by selection for reduced reactive aggression, greater social tolerance, and more flexible prosocial behavior, much as foxes and dogs were shaped by selection for tameness. That is a serious evolutionary hypothesis, with real evidence and real problems. The second job is the psychiatric part: autism and schizophrenia are supposed to be failures or overshoots of that same process. That part is much weaker. It is fair to take it seriously as a heuristic, but it does not yet hold up as a causal account.

The fox analogy has a concrete core. In the famous Soviet fox experiment, breeders selected foxes that approached humans without fear or aggression. Within a few generations, a substantial minority of pups showed dog-like behavior: they wagged, licked, sought contact, and were far easier to handle. The interesting point is that other traits changed too. Coat color patterns, ear shape, tail carriage, and some endocrine features shifted even though nobody selected directly for them. The lesson is not that “tameness causes floppy ears” in some simple mechanical sense. The lesson is that behavior, morphology, and neuroendocrine development are coupled. Select on one dimension, and the developmental system moves in correlated ways because the same embryological and hormonal pathways are involved.

That is the part of the theory that is genuinely useful. If humans underwent something analogous, we should not expect selection for social behavior to change only social behavior. It could have changed the timing of brain development, stress reactivity, facial morphology, and the balance between social and non-social attention. A brain selected for living in dense, cooperative, conflict-laden groups would be a different organ from a brain selected mainly for solitary foraging. It would need better social monitoring, more flexible role-taking, more delayed maturation, and more sensitivity to the emotional states of others. All of that has plausible costs. The analogy invites us to ask whether some human psychiatric syndromes are possible byproducts of a brain architecture that was tuned for an unusually demanding social life.

But the human self-domestication hypothesis itself is not settled. Humans do show some traits that fit the domestication syndrome: reduced brow ridges, smaller teeth, flatter faces, relatively large orbits, and a general craniofacial neoteny compared with earlier hominins. There is also a long-standing argument that humans are less reactively aggressive than other primates, or at least that we have evolved mechanisms for managing aggression in large groups. The problem is that the same traits can be produced by other explanations. Sexual selection, kin selection, pathogen pressure, dietary change, and the simple demands of complex cooperation can all push humans in the same direction. “Self-domestication” is not a mechanism by itself; it is a label for a pattern. The pattern is plausible, but the causal story is still contested.

There is also a notable mismatch in the analogy. In many domesticated species, selection for tameness is associated with smaller body size and, in dogs at least, a smaller brain than in wild ancestors. The most conspicuous change in the human lineage is the opposite: an enlarged, reorganized brain. Human self-domestication, if it happened, did not produce a dog-like reduction in encephalization. It produced a creature that is both more socially tolerant and cognitively enormous. That makes the fox analogy suggestive, not explanatory.

Now to the psychiatric part. The idea that autism and schizophrenia are “failures” or “overshoots” of domestication usually comes in two forms. One is that autism is under-domestication: too little social tameness, too much social avoidance, too little automatic reward from other people. The other is that schizophrenia is over-domestication: too much social simulation, too much empathy, too blurred a boundary between self and other, or a social brain that has been pushed past its stable range.

Both mappings are too loose to be scientifically satisfying. Autism is not simply “not enough sociality.” Autistic people are not wolves. Many are highly social in ways that do not match neurotypical norms; many care deeply about other people; many have rich inner social lives. The diagnostic features—differences in social communication, restricted or intense interests, sensory reactivity, attention to detail—are a heterogeneous pattern, not a single deficit in domestication. Calling the whole spectrum a failure of self-domestication flattens a great deal of variation into one moral and biological judgment.

Schizophrenia is even harder to fit into “over-domestication.” The syndrome is not excessive sociality. It includes perceptual disturbances, disorganized thought, negative symptoms such as flattened affect and social withdrawal, and major cognitive disruption. Some models of psychosis do emphasize social cognition: misattribution of agency, abnormal salience, poor source monitoring of one’s own mental states, and disturbed self-other differentiation. Those are real and interesting ideas. But they do not straightforwardly imply that schizophrenia is what happens when a domesticated social brain is turned up too high. A person hearing a voice that sounds external is not simply a person with too much empathy. The social-cognitive features of psychosis are symptoms of a broader developmental disturbance, not an overflow of a single domestication trait.

The genetics make the problem sharper. Both autism and schizophrenia are highly heritable, but their genetic architectures are complex. Schizophrenia is associated with many common risk variants, many of which are old enough to predate any plausible “recent domestication” story. Autism involves a mix of common variants, rare variants, and de novo mutations. There is genuine genetic overlap between the two disorders, especially in genes involved in synaptic development and cortical maturation, but the overlap is partial and complicated. If self-domestication were the main cause of these syndromes, we would expect a cleaner signal: risk variants that also predict specific domestication-related traits in the predicted directions. For autism, perhaps lower social tolerance or lower automatic social reward. For schizophrenia, perhaps excessive social salience or excessive self-other blending. We do not yet have that.

There is a harder evolutionary objection. If these disorders are failures or overshoots of a selected trait, why are they still common? A straightforward “too much or too little domestication” story implies a target. If the target is some optimal level of social tameness, then extreme deviations should be selected against. Schizophrenia in particular reduces reproductive success in modern populations, and autism, depending on the case, can also reduce mating and social integration. Of course, selection is weak, modern mortality and reproduction patterns differ from ancestral ones, and many people with these conditions have reproduced throughout history. But the persistence of the syndromes suggests that the explanation is not simply that a domestication program occasionally malfunctions. It may be that the relevant traits are part of a continuous distribution, that some associated variants are maintained by balancing selection, that the disorders are byproducts rather than direct targets of selection, or that the costs are too recent and too context-dependent for selection to have removed them efficiently.

This brings out the main weakness of the theory: it is easy to make it fit anything. If someone is less social, that can be called under-domestication. If someone is too socially permeable, that can be called over-domestication. If someone is developmentally fragile, that can be called a domestication cost. A theory that can label both tails of the distribution as deviations from an implicit norm is doing less work than it appears to be doing. It becomes a story about what humans should be, not a testable account of why these syndromes arise.

That said, there is something worth salvaging. The most defensible version of the idea is not “autism is under-domestication and schizophrenia is over-domestication.” It is this: selection for a highly social, cooperative, and cognitively flexible life may have made the human brain unusually plastic and unusually vulnerable to developmental perturbation. The same systems that allow us to read intentions, coordinate with strangers, delay impulses, and sustain complex social relationships may also be the systems that can go awry in ways we now label autism or schizophrenia.

This is more interesting because it shifts the question from “what is wrong with these people?” to “what does the human social brain have to be like in order to do what humans do?” A brain that can imitate, attribute mental states, track social status, modulate aggression, and remain socially motivated into adulthood is a late-maturing, stress-sensitive, socially dependent organ. Its stability depends on timing, immune balance, hormonal regulation, and social environment. Developmental disruptions in such a system can produce very different syndromes depending on when and where they occur. Autism and schizophrenia may be different failure modes of a broadly social-cognitive architecture, not failures of one single domestication switch.

A narrower salvageable link is the idea of altered social reward and social salience. If self-domestication increased the motivational pull of social information, then variation in that pull could matter. Some autistic people show reduced automatic reward from social stimuli; that is a real phenomenon, though it is not universal and should not be reduced to a single evolutionary deficit. Some psychotic experiences may involve abnormal salience: internal thoughts or perceptions taking on the force of external events, or social cues being weighted in ways that generate paranoia and delusion. These are not the same thing, but they both fit a broader picture in which the human brain is tuned to make social information matter intensely. When that tuning is distorted, the consequences can be social, perceptual, or cognitive.

Another salvageable point is that domestication-like selection may have widened the distribution of socially relevant traits rather than simply raising the mean. In a species that depends on cooperation, there may be evolutionary value in having some individuals who are highly socially attuned and others who are less so, especially if environments vary. The “failure” framing assumes a single optimum. A more honest model is that the human social brain contains trade-offs: greater social flexibility may come with greater developmental fragility; greater sensitivity to others may come with greater susceptibility to social stress; greater cognitive elaboration may come with greater risk of misattribution and dysregulation. Autism and schizophrenia may sit in the shadow of those trade-offs.

The modern-environment point is also worth keeping. If the human social brain was shaped for small, dense, repeated-contact groups, then industrial and digital life may stress it in ways that were not present when the architecture evolved. Social isolation, chronic status threat, sleep disruption, urban stress, and the need to maintain broad but shallow networks can all interact with inherited vulnerabilities. That does not mean autism or schizophrenia are “caused by modernity.” It means that an architecture selected for one social world may be more exposed in another.

Where the theory breaks down is in specificity. The fox experiment shows that selection on tameness can produce a syndrome of correlated traits. It does not show that the human syndrome includes psychosis or autism. The human domestication hypothesis, even if accepted, does not by itself tell us which genes, circuits, or developmental steps should produce these disorders. To make the theory strong, it would need to predict something concrete: that risk alleles for autism load on low social tolerance; that risk alleles for schizophrenia load on excessive social salience; that animal models selected for prosociality show elevated rates of analogous social-cognitive fragility; or that populations with different histories of social selection show predictable differences in the incidence of these syndromes. None of that is in place in a convincing form.

So the fair assessment is this. The self-domestication idea is worth taking seriously as a broad account of why the human brain is the way it is: socially tuned, developmentally late, cognitively expanded, and vulnerable to the stress of group life. The idea that autism and schizophrenia are simply failures or overshoots of that process is not yet a theory; it is a metaphor with a diagnostic label attached. What survives criticism is the underlying insight that selection for sociality can produce a brain whose failure modes are also social. What does not survive is the neat story that one species-level project, domestication, explains two complex, heterogeneous, and genetically distinct human syndromes by turning a dial a little too far in opposite directions.

prompt: People love to say that the First Amendment only restricts the government, so a boss firing someone for something they said isn't a free speech issue. Legally that's right, but it feels like it misses something. Write an essay on whether free speech means anything beyond what the law requires, and what a healthy norm of disagreement looks like.
response:
The legal point is correct, and it is also the reason the question is interesting. The First Amendment says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech. Through the Fourteenth Amendment it binds states and localities. It does not say a private employer must keep an employee who offends the owner, a landlord must house a tenant who insults neighbors, or a social club must seat a member who says something the group finds hateful. If a boss fires a worker for a tweet, a comment in a meeting, or a post on a forum, the usual answer is that no constitutional right has been violated. That is true in most cases. It is also an incomplete answer, because the Amendment is not a definition of free speech. It is one legal barrier, placed in front of one powerful censor: the state.

That distinction matters because the state is not the only entity that can make speech costly. In the United States, most private-sector jobs are at-will. A worker can generally be fired for a lawful opinion if the employer does not run afoul of anti-discrimination, labor, whistleblower, contract, or public-policy exceptions. The law already shows that we do not think all private silencing is equally legitimate. Firing someone for concerted activity over wages is often treated differently from firing someone for a rude remark. Firing a safety inspector for reporting a hazard is different from firing a salesman who insults a client. Those lines are not drawn by the First Amendment. They are drawn by judgments about power, trust, and the purposes of the relationship.

That is where the broader meaning of free speech enters. Free speech, beyond the law, is the expectation that a person can say something disagreeable without being destroyed for saying it. Not without consequence: speech has consequences. A candidate who says something foolish loses votes. A professor who makes a bad argument is answered. A customer who leaves a mean review is ignored or replied to. The norm is not that speech is costless. It is that the cost is connected to what was said and the role of the speaker, not to the mere fact that someone in authority was displeased.

This distinction shows up quickly in workplaces. Suppose an employee tells a manager that a product feature will embarrass the company in front of customers. If the manager fires the employee because the comment was unwelcome, the employer has not broken the First Amendment. But the employer has also sent a message that the only useful information is praise. In a factory with two hundred workers, if one worker’s true statement about a machine can cost the job, the other 199 learn not to report. Suppose instead the employee tells the same manager that a coworker is “disgusting” because of race or gender. The employer can and often should fire the employee. The law may or may not require it depending on harassment policy and consequences, but a healthy workplace norm does not treat that as protected disagreement. The difference is not that one statement is true and the other false. It is that one statement is an attempt to get the work done, even badly, and the other is an attempt to degrade a person. A norm of free speech needs to see that difference.

The hardest objection to extending free speech beyond the legal rule is that it can become a demand that private people host speech they do not want. A restaurant owner who bans a patron for shouting slurs is not a tyrant. A neighbor who stops talking to someone after a bitter argument is not censoring. A company that fires a public-facing employee for lying to customers is not violating a norm of disagreement; it is enforcing the basic condition of the job. If “free speech” means every private actor must tolerate every utterance, it loses all sense. It also becomes a weapon: the person with the loudest or most offensive claim can insist on a platform, while those around him are told they are intolerant for leaving.

So the norm has to be asymmetric in the right direction. It should not require a captive audience. It should require that institutions which claim to manage common work or public discussion do not use their power to punish mere dissent. The boss can set the standards of the job. The boss cannot, in a healthy norm, make the job include never saying the boss is wrong. The customer can stop buying. The customer cannot, at least not without social cost, organize a campaign to ruin a reviewer because the review was negative. The platform can remove threats, doxxing, and coordinated harassment. It becomes suspect when it removes a minority opinion because it is inconvenient to advertisers or managers. The line is not “harmless speech” in some vague sense. It is whether the speaker is using words as a substitute for violence, deception, or breach of role, and whether the punisher is acting to prevent that or merely to reward loyalty.

A healthy norm of disagreement has a few concrete shapes. In a meeting, a subordinate says the plan will fail. The manager asks for the evidence, notes the concern, and then decides. The subordinate is not required to be cheerful, but is required to stay on the question. If the subordinate attacks the manager’s character, the manager interrupts: “Let’s keep it about the plan.” If the subordinate threatens or harasses, the meeting ends and there are consequences. In a company, employees can talk about wages, safety, and management mistakes. They can be fired for lying, stealing, threatening, refusing a lawful task, or abusing people. They should not be fired for saying, in a non-abusive way, that a policy is stupid. In a public forum, the moderator removes the person who posts a doxxing address, not the person who says the policy is bad. The institution publishes the rules in advance, applies them to friends and enemies alike, and gives a reason when it silences someone.

These practices are not the same as legal rights, and they cannot always be enforced. They depend on reputation, culture, and the willingness of outsiders to say that a firing looked like punishment for speech. That is weaker than a court order. It is also closer to how most of life works. Most silencing does not happen by statute. It happens by a parent who stops listening, a firm that marks a worker, a platform that shadows a post, a community that refuses to hire. If we want free speech to mean anything in those spaces, we need standards that do not depend on whether the censor happens to be the government.

The legal rule remains important because the state is special. When the government punishes speech, it does not merely lose a customer or an employee; it tells citizens what may be thought in a polity. Private punishment is different in kind, but not irrelevant. A boss who fires people for criticism creates a private zone of silence. Enough such zones, and public life becomes a collection of rooms where nobody says the thing everyone is thinking. The First Amendment keeps the state out of that game. Norms try to keep private power from playing it too crudely.

So when a boss fires someone for what they said, the answer is not that it is legally irrelevant and therefore irrelevant. The better answer is: it may be perfectly lawful, and it may still be wrong, unwise, or socially damaging. Free speech beyond the law is the expectation that people can be wrong, impolite, or critical without being expelled from the world. A healthy norm of disagreement does not protect every use of words. It protects the space in which words can be tested, answered, and sometimes punished for what they do, not merely for who is offended.

They are drawn by judgments about power, trust, and the purposes of the relationship.
