Not without consequence: speech has consequences. A candidate who says something foolish loses votes. A professor who makes a bad argument is answered. A customer who leaves a mean review is ignored or replied to. The norm is not that speech is costless. It is that the cost is connected to what was said and the role of the speaker, not to the mere fact that someone in authority was displeased.

This distinction shows up quickly in workplaces. Suppose an employee tells a manager that a product feature will embarrass the company in front of customers. If the manager fires the employee because the comment was unwelcome, the employer has not broken the First Amendment. But the employer has also sent a message that the only useful information is praise. In a firm with hundreds of people, that message is expensive. The people closest to the problem stop describing it. Suppose instead the employee tells the same manager that a coworker is "disgusting" because of race or gender. The employer can and often should fire the employee. The law may or may not require it depending on harassment policy and consequences, but a healthy workplace norm does not treat that as protected disagreement. The difference is not that one statement is true and the other false. It is that one statement is an attempt to get the work done, even badly, and the other is an attempt to degrade a person. A norm of free speech needs to see that difference.

A restaurant owner who bans a patron for shouting slurs is not a tyrant. A neighbor who stops talking to someone after a bitter argument is not censoring. A company that fires a public-facing employee for lies to customers is not violating a norm of disagreement; it is enforcing the basic condition of the job. If "free speech" means every private actor must tolerate every utterance, it loses all sense. It also becomes a weapon: the person with the loudest or most offensive claim can insist on a platform, while those around him are told they are intolerant for leaving.

So the norm has to be asymmetric in the right direction. It should not require a captive audience. It should require that institutions which claim to manage common work or public discussion do not use their power to punish mere dissent. The boss can set the standards of the job. The boss cannot, in a healthy norm, make the job include never saying the boss is wrong. The customer can stop buying. The customer cannot, at least not without social cost, organize a campaign to ruin a reviewer because the review was negative. The platform can remove threats, doxxing, and coordinated harassment. It becomes suspect when it removes a minority opinion because it is inconvenient to advertisers or managers. The line is not "harmless speech" in some vague sense. It is whether the speaker is using words as a substitute for violence, deception, or breach of role, and whether the punisher is acting to prevent that or merely to reward loyalty.

A healthy norm of disagreement has a few concrete shapes. In a meeting, a subordinate says the plan will fail. The manager asks for the evidence, notes the concern, and then decides. The subordinate is not required to be cheerful, but is required to stay on the question. If the subordinate attacks the manager's character, the manager interrupts: "Let's keep it about the plan." If the subordinate threatens or harasses, the meeting ends and there are consequences. In a company, employees can talk about wages, safety, and management mistakes. They can be fired for lying, stealing, threatening, refusing a lawful task, or abusing people. They should not be fired for saying, in a non-abusive way, that a policy is stupid. In a public forum, the moderator removes the person who posts a doxxing address, not the person who says the policy is bad. The institution publishes the rules in advance, applies them to friends and enemies alike, and gives a reason when it silences someone.

These practices are not the same as legal rights, and they cannot always be enforced. They depend on reputation, culture, and the willingness of outsiders to say that a firing looked like punishment for speech. That is weaker than a court order. It is also closer to how most of life works. Most silencing does not happen by statute. It happens by a parent who stops listening, a firm that marks a worker, a platform that shadows a post, a community that refuses to hire. If we want free speech to mean anything in those spaces, we need standards that do not depend on whether the censor happens to be the government.

The legal rule remains important because the state is special. When the government punishes speech, it does not merely lose a customer or a employee; it tells citizens what may be thought in a polity. Private punishment is different in kind, but not irrelevant. A boss who fires people for criticism creates a private zone of silence. Enough such zones, and public life becomes a collection of rooms where nobody says the thing everyone is thinking. The First Amendment keeps the state out of that game. Norms try to keep private power from playing it too crudely.

So when a boss fires someone for what they said, the answer is not "that is not a First Amendment issue, end of story." The better answer is: it may be perfectly lawful, and it may still be wrong, unwise, or socially damaging. Free speech beyond the law is the expectation that people can be wrong, impolite, or critical without being expelled from the world. A healthy norm of disagreement does not protect every use of words. It protects the space in which words can be tested, answered, and sometimes punished for what they do, not merely for who is offended.

prompt: Write an essay, from the point of view of a working software engineer who gets plenty of recruiter emails, on why some job pitches get a reply and others don't, and what that suggests about how teams should think about recruiting.
response:
My inbox has a simple physics: most recruiter emails are archived before I finish the second sentence. A few get a reply. Not because they are flattering, and not because they promise a bigger title. They get a reply because they make it possible to spend two minutes thinking about a job as a problem rather than a brand.

A pitch that usually works says something like this: “We’re hiring a senior backend engineer for the team that owns merchant payouts. The hard part is that our settlement job has grown into a large Python service with hidden state, and we want to split it into smaller services without breaking reconciliation. The team is five engineers, the stack is Go, Postgres, and Kafka, and the comp band is $240k to $290k. Would a thirty-minute conversation be useful?”

I can answer that. I know what I would be talking about, what I would be evaluating, and whether the money clears my threshold. I can also guess whether the problem is my kind of problem. If I have spent the last three years doing exactly this and it has become dull, I will not reply. If I have been doing adjacent work and want to go deeper, I might. Either way, the email gave me something to think about.

A pitch that usually does not work says: “Hi, I came across your profile and was impressed by your experience with backend systems. I’m hiring for a senior software engineer role at a high-growth company with a mission-driven culture. If you’re open to opportunities, I’d love to connect.”

There is no question in that email that I can answer without first giving up an hour of my life. The only next step is to talk to a human and discover what the job actually is. That is a worse deal than ignoring the sender. I have seen that sentence, with small variations, so many times that it has become a kind of white noise. It tells me that someone needs to fill a role and has not yet formed a clear picture of what the role requires.

The reason this matters is that a candidate is not deciding whether to like a company. A candidate is deciding whether to spend scarce attention on a possible tradeoff. I already have a job. It has known costs and known benefits. Maybe the code is bad. Maybe the manager is good. Maybe the compensation is fine but the work is no longer interesting. Maybe I am unhappy in a way I have not fully named yet. To even consider moving, the expected value of exploring has to exceed the cost of exploring. A vague pitch raises the cost and does nothing to raise the value. It says, “Trust us, then find out.” A specific pitch lowers the uncertainty enough that the next step feels reasonable.

That does not mean the email has to sell me. I do not want to be sold. I want to know whether this is a real thing. When a recruiter writes “fast-paced environment,” I assume the team is either under-resourced or incapable of describing the work. When a hiring manager writes “the service has a nasty failure mode around retries and we need someone who has lived with that kind of system,” I know what they are looking for and whether I have lived with it. The first phrase is a mood. The second is a test.

The hardest objection to all of this is that replies are noisy. Sometimes I reply because I am bored that week. Sometimes I reply because the company is famous. Sometimes I reply because the comp is high enough that I will listen to almost anything. Sometimes I do not reply to a great opportunity because I am in the middle of a release and I am being lazy. If pitch quality were the only variable, recruiting would be easy. It is not.

But if pitch quality did not matter, teams could solve hiring by volume. They could send ten thousand vague messages and wait for the market to select the desperate, the curious, or the unemployed. In practice, that produces a pipeline full of people who are looking for a job, not people who are looking for this job. Those candidates are more expensive to filter, more likely to bounce, and more likely to accept an offer from the first team that appears serious. A specific pitch does not guarantee a better candidate, but it changes the population you are talking to. It tends to attract people for whom the problem itself is a reason to pay attention. That is a cheaper and more durable pool.

This suggests that teams should stop thinking of recruiting as interest generation. The first email is not an advertisement. It is a hypothesis: “This person might find this problem worth their time.” If the team cannot state that hypothesis clearly, the problem is not the recruiter’s writing skill. The problem is that the team has not yet worked out what it is hiring for.

Hiring managers often write job descriptions as wish lists. They include “strong ownership,” “excellent communication,” “experience with distributed systems,” and “bias toward action.” Those are not descriptions; they are hopes. A candidate reading them learns the minimum bar and nothing about the actual work. The first outreach message should be closer to a short design doc: what is broken, what constraints exist, what success looks like, what the team does not yet know, and what the person would own in the first year.

“Fast-paced” is not a constraint. “We ship weekly, but two legacy payment providers make rollback annoying” is a constraint. “Ownership” is not a problem. “You would be the second backend engineer on the team and would own the API surface” is a problem. “Modern stack” is not information. “Most of the service is in Go, but the batch layer is old Scala and we are not sure whether to rewrite it” is information. The candidate can evaluate that. They can also decide whether they want to be the person making that decision.

Recruiters should not be the only voice in that conversation, at least not for technical roles. Recruiters are good at logistics, screening, and keeping the process from falling apart. But the technical hook should come from someone who has touched the code. A recruiter who can say, “We need to reduce p99 latency on search results from eight hundred milliseconds to two hundred without adding another cache layer,” is useful. A recruiter who can only say, “We need a strong IC who can hit the ground running,” is asking the candidate to do the hiring manager’s job.

Compensation belongs in the pitch, too, where local rules allow. If I cannot rule out a lowball offer, I will not spend time finding out. “Competitive package” is not a number. It is a request for faith. If the comp is the main reason I should listen, say so plainly. “We can offer a higher base than most teams your size” is a reason. “Total rewards are market-aligned” is a sentence written by someone who has never had to explain why a good engineer should leave a stable job.

Honesty matters for the same reason. Candidates are not stupid. We have read the public postmortems, the layoff threads, the anonymous reviews, and the GitHub activity. If a team hides the bad parts, we assume the bad parts are worse than they are. If a recruiter says, “The codebase is old and the on-call load is real, but the problem is interesting and the team is stable,” I believe them more than I believe a person who says, “It’s a great place with a strong engineering culture.” The first sounds like a human describing a situation. The second sounds like a brochure protecting a decision.

There is also a difference between being complete and being closed. The best pitch is complete enough to be credible but open enough to invite a question. If it says, “We are solving X, the hard part is Y, and we have not figured out Z,” I can reply with a question about Z. If it answers every possible objection in four paragraphs, it starts to sound like a landing page. If it answers nothing, it sounds like spam. The goal is to give the candidate a seam they can pull on.

Teams should also measure the early part of the funnel as seriously as the late part. Applications tell you how many people saw the role. Replies tell you how many people thought the role was worth considering. Interviews tell you how many people survived contact with the real thing. Offers tell you how many people wanted it after the uncertainty was removed. If reply rates are low, the role may be poorly defined, the market may not need it, or the first message may be too generic. If replies are high but interviews fail, the pitch overpromised. If interviews pass but offers decline, the problem may be comp, brand, or process. The inbox is an instrument. Most teams ignore it until after they have already hurt themselves.

What I am saying is not that recruiters should become engineers. They should not. They should become translators of engineering problems, not gatekeepers of company mystique. The candidate is not trying to impress the company. The candidate is trying to avoid making a bad decision. A job pitch gets a reply when it respects that. It says, “Here is a real situation, here is what is hard about it, here is what it pays, and here is a small next step if you want to think about it.” That is enough to make a working engineer stop triaging and start considering.

prompt: Everyone is using a ridiculous overpriced startup product as proof that Silicon Valley is vapid and shallow. Write a blog post giving a reality check on that: is the stereotype fair, and why does it feel so true to so many people?
response:
## The ridiculous product is not the whole valley

There is a reliable genre of internet argument that begins with a photo of a product and a price tag. The product is usually a thing you already own, made slightly smoother, slightly louder, and five times more expensive. A water bottle that tracks hydration. A coffee maker that needs an app. A mattress that tells you slept badly. A kitchen gadget whose main innovation is that it is matte black. The comments do the rest: “This is Silicon Valley.”

The joke lands because the product is easy to mock, and because “Silicon Valley” has stopped being a place and become a personality type: overconfident, under-explained, willing to charge you a premium for the feeling that life has been optimized. The stereotype is that this is what the industry is really about, not just what it sometimes makes.

That is where the reality check begins. The stereotype is not fair if it means Silicon Valley is mostly vapid and shallow. It is fair if it means the most visible, most celebrated, most photogenic layer of tech is often vapid and shallow. Those are different claims, and the difference explains why the argument feels so true while still being badly overgeneralized.

Most of what the technology industry actually does is boring. The internet runs on chips, networking, storage, security, payment rails, compilers, databases, cloud infrastructure, logistics software, industrial controls, medical devices, and a great deal of unglamorous maintenance work. A lot of that work happens in and around Silicon Valley, and a lot of it is hard. A company that makes a new kind of memory, a safer payment protocol, a better database index, a chip that uses less power, or a system that keeps a factory from stopping is doing serious engineering. But none of those achievements produces a good social media post. You can make a fifteen-second video about a $300 water bottle. It is much harder to make a viral clip about a twelve percent improvement in inference cost, and even if you could, the audience would not know why it mattered.

So the serious work is invisible by default. The shallow work is visible by design.

Consumer products have to be legible instantly. They are sold to people who do not want to read a white paper. They need a name, a color, an unboxing experience, a founder story, a lifestyle association. If the product is infrastructure, the surface can be a login page. If the product is a status object, the surface is the whole point. That is why the most memeable tech products tend to live in areas where identity and convenience already overlap: fitness, sleep, beauty, coffee, parenting, home, productivity, wellness, self-improvement. These are categories where people already pay for the feeling of being better, and a tech brand can charge extra for making that feeling frictionless.

The money reinforces the pattern. Venture capital is not a neutral fund for good ideas. It is a financial structure that needs outliers. A company that sells a better industrial pump may be profitable, respectable, and technically interesting, but it may not offer the kind of return that justifies a venture bet. A company that can own a consumer habit, a demographic, or a lifestyle category can raise money at absurd valuations and then spend that money making the category more visible. The system overproduces things that look like personal upgrades because personal upgrades can be scaled into platforms, subscriptions, and data networks.

That does not mean every expensive startup product is fraud. High prices can reflect low volume, good materials, strong support, real convenience, or the fact that early adopters are paying for risk reduction and identity. Sometimes the $400 version is genuinely better than the $40 version. But when the performance gap is small and the price gap is large, the extra cost is usually not paying for function. It is paying for brand, taste, belonging, or the pleasure of being early. That is a real market. It is just not a market that requires much engineering.

The culture makes it worse. Tech has developed a style: clean, minimal, fast, personal, slightly mystical. The language borrows the grammar of deep work without always doing the work. Products are “seamless,” “ambient,” “intelligent,” “effortless.” Founders talk about “changing how humans experience” ordinary activities. Investors talk about “owning the category.” The result is that a technically mediocre product can feel advanced if the onboarding is smooth and the website is quiet. Polish gets mistaken for substance. A nice interface becomes evidence of a new paradigm.

This is the hardest part to argue against, because the vibe is not an accident. It is often the strategy. The overpriced consumer product is not a bug in an otherwise serious industry; it is a rational response to incentives that reward brand, margin, attention, and behavioral lock-in. Serious engineers often end up at those companies anyway because the money is excellent. The industry’s public face is shaped by the people who are best paid, best funded, and best at telling their own story. If that face looks shallow, it is not only because outsiders are caricaturing it. The industry has selected for the things that look well in public.

That is also why the stereotype feels so true to so many people. The evidence is concrete. You can hold the object. You can see the price. You can compare it to the cheaper version and ask what you are actually getting. Abstract claims about “infrastructure” or “AI” are harder to test. A smart water bottle is a small, tangible artifact of a set of incentives: people with capital, talent, and media access chose to make this, and they chose to make it expensive. It feels like proof because it is proof, just proof about the wrong population.

There is also a class resentment built into the joke. Tech has become associated with outsized wealth, remote-work flexibility, real estate pressure, performative progressivism, and a confidence that can sound like entitlement. The ridiculous product gives that resentment a handle. It is not only about the product. It is about who gets to define convenience, who pays for it, and who profits from the gap between what something costs to make and what a brand can charge for it. The product is small enough to mock and large enough to stand in for a whole economy of taste and money.

So is the stereotype fair? As a description of the field, no. Silicon Valley is bigger, dirtier, and more technical than the joke allows. There are people there doing important work that will never trend. There are companies making things that matter to factories, hospitals, banks, grids, developers, and scientists. The industry is not a single mindset wearing a black T-shirt.

As a diagnosis of what gets celebrated, yes. The center of gravity in tech publicity is skewed toward consumer behavior, personal identity, and lifestyle optimization. The most impressive things the industry makes are often the least visible, and the most visible things are often the least impressive. The stereotype survives because the industry keeps handing it new evidence.

That is the actual reality check. The ridiculous product is not the whole valley, but it is not a random flaw either. It is a symptom of what gets rewarded, what gets photographed, and what gets turned into a story. Until the most admired things in tech are boring, the stereotype will keep winning the marketing war.

prompt: Write a personal, funny-but-sincere essay from the point of view of a husband whose wife and he spent six years on unexplained infertility, about how they used an AI chatbot during treatment and what came of it. Include some honest ambivalence about AI more broadly.
response:
The first time I asked an artificial intelligence about my wife’s body, I was sitting on the closed toilet lid in the downstairs bathroom because the upstairs one creaked. It was 1:13 a.m. Mara had taken the pregnancy test at the kitchen counter, the digital one she said was kinder, though it was never kinder. It said negative. She had not cried. She had put the test in the drawer with the others, a small white museum of almosts, and gone to bed. I sat on the lid and opened the app I usually used to fix spreadsheets.

I typed: My wife and I have been trying for six years. All tests are normal. She just got another negative. What should I do?

The first line of the answer was about validating her feelings. I thought: I can validate. I have been validating for six years. But the fourth bullet point said to consider whether there were unanswered medical questions. That was the one that made me sit up.

Unexplained infertility is a phrase that sounds like a weather report for a place you cannot leave. Unexplained means the doctors looked and found no fault. prompt: For a decade you ran your own small software businesses, then four years ago you joined a payments company that has been growing extremely fast the whole time. Write a reflective essay on what that experience has taught you: what hypergrowth actually does to an organization and the people in it, how your own work changed, and where your old mental model of the company turned out to be wrong.
response:
For ten years I ran software companies small enough that the whole thing fit behind my eyes. I knew the customers, the code, the invoice that had not been paid, and the one employee who was carrying too much. When I joined a payments company four years ago, it was about 110 people. It is now roughly 2,800, and the payment volume we move is more than fifteen times what it was when I arrived. The easy version of this story is that I learned to scale. That is true, but it misses the point. The deeper thing I learned is that hypergrowth does not make a company a larger version of itself. It changes the kind of object the company is.

In a small software business, the unit of work is a thing you can finish. A feature, a fix, a migration, a sales call. You can stand next to the output and see whether it is good. In a fast-growing payments company, the unit of work becomes an interface. Most of my time is no longer spent making a particular feature correct. It is spent making it safe for one team to change something that another team depends on, without a third team noticing until the books do not balance.

I learned that from a refund bug. A product change allowed refunds to be issued before the original capture had fully settled at the bank. In test, it looked like a latency improvement. In production, a batch of refunds landed in a settlement run that had already closed. Finance saw a negative balance in a subledger and called it an incident. Three teams spent a day arguing about whose bug it was. Product said risk had not blocked the refund. Risk said treasury had not defined the settlement window. Treasury said engineering had written a state transition that no one had asked for. The fix was smaller than the argument: a refund had to reference a settlement batch, and if the batch was closed, the refund had to be rejected or routed to a later batch. But the real bug was not the code. The real bug was that three systems had different definitions of “closed,” and growth had made the difference between those definitions expensive.

That kind of gap is not a sign of incompetence. It is a natural product of speed. In a twenty-person company, “settled” means the same thing to everyone because everyone has seen the bank file. In a 2,000-person company, “settled” is a word that has to be maintained. It lives in a document, a schema, a test, a runbook, and the memory of whoever was on call last month. Hypergrowth is the process by which shared memory turns into shared infrastructure. If you do not build the infrastructure, you get shared confusion.

This is where the organization changes. A small company can be held together by attention. The founder looks at the work and notices the gap. A hypergrowth company cannot be held together by attention because no one can see enough. It has to be held together by contracts: ownership boundaries, definitions, error budgets, escalation paths, and boring ceremonies that sound like bureaucracy until you need them. I used to think meetings and documentation were the tax you pay for size. Now I think they are the size. The meeting is where the interface is negotiated. The document is where the company stores its assumptions so that a new hire does not have to extract them from a person’s head.

We felt this during a hiring surge. We added about sixty engineers in one quarter. They were smart, but they made assumptions that would have been obvious in a smaller company: which service owned a payment method token, whether a dispute could be reopened after a certain date, what “posted” actually meant to the issuing bank. At first, we answered by pulling people into meetings. That made things worse, because the answer depended on who was in the room and what they had recently broken. We started treating onboarding as a product. We built a map of ownership, a glossary of payment states, and a list of places where new code should not be sent. The map was never complete. But it reduced the number of questions that required a human, and that mattered more than any individual feature we shipped.

People change too, and not always in a way that feels good. Hypergrowth selects for people who can stay calm while their role changes underneath them. Last year, an engineer’s job was to make the checkout flow faster. This year it is to define which service owns a payment method token. The person who excels is not necessarily the one who misses the old work least. It is the one who can treat the old work as a clue, not an identity. I have watched strong engineers burn out not because they were overloaded, But because they were repeatedly asked to become someone else before they had finished becoming the previous someone. Some of them are mismatched with the company, and that is not a tragedy to be solved by better management. A company growing this fast cannot keep every role stable. It has to change people or replace them, and it should say that plainly.

But there is a cost that is easy to romanticize away. When roles churn, institutional knowledge leaves in small pieces. A new manager does not know why a particular bank integration has a weird retry rule. A new product lead does not know that a seemingly harmless field in a dispute payload is actually used by finance to reconcile a legacy merchant. The company pays for that later, usually in an incident. I have sat in incident reviews where the root cause was not a bad deploy but a missing sentence: nobody had written down why the exception existed. In a small company, the exception lives in the founder’s head. In a fast-growing one, it has to live somewhere durable or it becomes a landmine.

My own work changed more than I expected. I came in expecting to build and ship. I still do, but the valuable work has moved upstream. I spend more time deciding what we will not do, what we will not support, and what we will not change without a migration plan. In payments, those decisions are not caution for its own sake. They are where the product is made.

A good example was instant payouts. The product ask was simple: let workers get paid immediately instead of waiting for a batch. The engineering estimate for the button was small. The real work was elsewhere. Instant payouts changed our fraud exposure because we would be moving money before some signals had matured. It changed treasury because we had to hold more liquidity overnight. It changed legal and risk because issuer agreements and consumer disclosures had to cover the new timing. It changed support because the first customer who was paid by mistake and then reversed would not understand why. The feature took months, not because engineers were slow, but because the company had to decide what kind of payments business it wanted to be: one that optimizes for worker speed at the edge of fraud loss, or one that keeps a larger buffer and explains the delay.

That decision could not be made by the team closest to the code. It had to be made by people who could see the balance sheet, the regulatory posture, and the customer promise at the same time. My job was not to have the answer. It was to make the tradeoff visible enough that the right people could disagree without pretending the issue was technical. I stopped judging my work by what I shipped and started judging it by how much future work my decisions created. A change that saves a day in engineering but creates a month of reconciliation pain is not fast. It is slow work scheduled later.

That is where my old mental model broke. I used to think a company was a plan being executed by a group of smart people. The plan was the product roadmap, the hiring plan, the budget. If the people were good and the plan was sound, the company would move. At small scale, that is mostly true. At hypergrowth scale, the plan is less important than the feedback loop. A company is a set of constraints that force decisions. The question is not whether the plan is elegant. The question is whether the organization can discover a bad assumption before the assumption becomes a customer complaint, a bank rejection, a regulatory report, or a chargeback.

I also used to think culture was a set of values. We had values, like most companies. They were not useless, but they did not explain much. Culture is what happens when two teams disagree about a deadline and no one senior is in the room. It is what happens when an incident crosses from engineering into finance at six in the evening and someone has to decide whether to page a controller. It is what happens when growth is missing and a manager has to tell a team that the project they love is dead. In a fast-growing payments company, culture is the default behavior under pressure. You can see it in the incident review: do people look for the smallest true explanation, or the safest person to blame? Do they write down what they learned, or do they close the ticket because the metric is green?

The hardest part of this learning is that it can sound like a complaint about scale. Of course a 2,800-person company is slower to turn than an eight-person one. Of course it has more meetings, more policy, more friction. If the only lesson were that small is nicer, I would not have spent four years inside the machine. Scale is where a payments company creates most of its value. The company can absorb more merchants, more workers, more banks, more edge cases, more regulatory scrutiny. It can hire specialists who would never join a tiny startup because the problem is too narrow. It can build redundancy so that one bad actor or one bad day does not destroy trust. The mess is not an argument against growth. It is the material from which the company has to build something durable.

The mistake is to treat that material as free. Hypergrowth creates organizational debt the way fast code creates technical debt. You can move quickly if you are willing to patch, special-case, and defer decisions. For a while, that feels like speed. Eventually, the patches become the system. The special cases become the product requirements. The deferred decisions become the reason three teams are arguing in a room while a merchant’s payouts are late. I have seen this in payments more than in any small software business: the debt does not show up as a bug report. It shows up as a bank partner losing confidence, a finance close that takes too long, a risk model that no one fully trusts, or a support team that has learned to apologize before explaining.

I am less certain now about clean stories, and I do not know how much of our speed came from good institutions and how much from the fact that the market was large enough to forgive some of them. I do not think the company would have been better if it had grown slower, though it would have been easier to understand. I do not think the people who left were all wrong for the company, nor were all the people who stayed automatically right. I do think the old model was wrong: a company is not a mind that gets bigger. It is a system for turning uncertainty into action. The job of leadership, at least at this speed, is not to remove uncertainty. It is to decide where the company can afford to be uncertain, where it must be rigid, and what it will pay to find out when it has gotten the answer wrong.

In a small company, you make things. In a fast-growing company, you make the conditions under which other people can make things safely. In a payments company, those conditions are the product. The customer is not buying a dashboard or an API. The customer is buying the certainty that money will move when it is supposed to move, that a dispute will be handled according to a rule, that the books will balance, and that the company will still be there when the settlement window closes. Hypergrowth tests whether an organization can extend that certainty to more people without diluting it.

For ten years I ran software companies small enough that the whole thing fit behind my eyes. I knew the customers, the code, the invoice that had not been paid, and the one employee who was carrying too much. When I joined a payments company four years ago, it was about 110 people. It is now roughly 2,800, and the payment volume we move is more than fifteen times what it was when I arrived. The obvious story is that I learned to scale. That is true, but it is too clean. The deeper thing I learned is that hypergrowth does not make a company a larger version of itself. It changes the kind of object the company is.

In a small software business, the unit of work is a thing you can finish. A feature, a fix, a migration, a sales call. You can stand next to the output and see whether it is good. In a fast-growing payments company, the unit of work becomes an interface. Most of my time is no longer spent making a particular feature correct. It is spent making it safe for one team to change something that another team depends on, without a third team noticing until the books do not balance.

I learned that from a refund bug... [detailed]

That bug was not unusual because anyone was careless. It was usual because growth had increased the distance between the people who named a state and the people who acted on it. In a twenty-person company, "settled" means the same thing to everyone because everyone has seen the bank file. In a 2,000-person company, "settled" is a word that has to be maintained. It lives in a document, a schema, a test, a runbook, and the memory of whoever was on call last month. Hypergrowth is the process by which shared memory turns into shared infrastructure. If you do not build the infrastructure, you get shared confusion.

This is where the organization changes. A small company can be held together by attention. The founder looks at the work and notices the gap. A hypergrowth company cannot be held together by attention because no one can see enough. It has to be held together by contracts: ownership boundaries, definitions, error budgets, escalation paths, and boring ceremonies that sound like bureaucracy until you need them. I used to think meetings and documentation were the tax you pay for size. Now I think they are the size. The meeting is where the interface is negotiated. The document is the place where the company stores its assumptions so that a new hire does not have to extract them from a person's head.

People change too, and not always in a way that feels good. Hypergrowth selects for people who can stay calm while their role changes underneath them. Last year, an engineer's job was to make the checkout flow faster. This year it is to define which service owns a payment method token. The person who excels is not necessarily the one who misses the old work least. It is the one who can treat the old work as a clue, not an identity. I have watched strong engineers burn out not because they were overloaded, but because they were repeatedly asked to become someone else before they had finished becoming the previous someone. Some of them are mismatched with the company, and that is not a tragedy to be solved by better management. A company growing this fast cannot keep every role stable. It has to change people or replace them, and it should say that plainly.

But there is a cost that is easy to romanticize away. When roles churn, institutional knowledge leaves in small pieces. A new manager does not know why a particular bank integration has a weird retry rule. A new product lead does not know that a seemingly harmless field in a dispute payload is actually used by finance to reconcile a legacy merchant. The company pays for that later, usually in an incident. I have sat in incident reviews where the root cause was not a bad deploy but a missing sentence: nobody had written down why the exception existed. In a small company, the exception lives in the founder's head. In a fast-growing one, it has to live somewhere durable or it becomes a landmine.

My own work changed more than I expected. I came in expecting to build and ship. I still do, but the valuable work has moved upstream. I spend more time deciding what we will not do, what we will not support, and what we will not change without a migration plan. In payments, those decisions are not caution for its own sake. They are where the product is made.

A good example was instant payouts. The product ask was simple: let workers get paid immediately instead of waiting for a batch. The engineering estimate for the button was small. The real work was elsewhere. Instant payouts changed our fraud exposure because we would be moving money before some signals had matured. It changed treasury because we had to hold more liquidity overnight. It changed legal and risk because issuer agreements and consumer disclosures had to cover the new timing. It changed support because the first customer who was paid by mistake and then reversed would not understand why. The feature took months, not because engineers were slow, but because the company had to decide what kind of payments business it wanted to be. A business that optimizes for worker happiness at the edge of fraud loss, or one that keeps a larger buffer and explains the delay.

That decision could not be made by the team closest to the code. It had to be made by people who could see the balance sheet, the regulatory posture, and the customer promise at the same time. My job was not to have the answer. It was to make the tradeoff visible enough that the right people could disagree without pretending the issue was technical.

That is where my old mental model broke. I used to think a company was a plan being executed by a group of smart people. The plan was the product roadmap, the hiring plan, the budget. If the people were good and the plan was sound, the company would move. At small scale, that is mostly true. At hypergrowth scale, the plan is less important than the feedback loop. A company is a set of constraints that force decisions. The question is not whether the plan is elegant. The question is whether the organization can discover a bad assumption before the assumption becomes a customer complaint, a bank rejection, a regulatory report, or a chargeback.

I also used to think culture was a set of values. We had values, like most companies. They were not useless, but they did not explain much. Culture is what happens when two teams disagree about a deadline and no one senior is in the room. It is what happens when an incident crosses from engineering into finance at 6 p.m. and someone has to decide whether to page a controller. It is what happens when growth is missing and a manager has to tell a team that the project they love is dead. In a fast-growing payments company, culture is the default behavior under pressure. You can see it in the incident review: do people look for the smallest true explanation, or the safest person to blame? Do they write down what they learned, or do they close the ticket because the metric is green?

The hardest part of this learning is that it can sound like a complaint about scale. Of course a 2,800-person company is slower to turn than an 8-person one. Of course it has more meetings, more policy, more friction. If the only lesson were that small is nicer, I would not have spent four years inside the machine. Scale is where a payments company creates most of its value. The company can absorb more merchants, more workers, more banks, more edge cases, more regulatory scrutiny. It can hire specialists who would never join a tiny startup because the problem is too narrow. It can build redundancy so that one bad actor or one bad day does not destroy trust. The mess is not an argument against growth. It is the material from which the company has to build something durable.

The mistake is to treat that material as free. Hypergrowth creates organizational debt the way fast code creates technical debt. You can move quickly if you are willing to patch, special-case, and defer decisions. For a while, that feels like speed. Eventually, the patches become the system. The special cases become the product requirements. The deferred decisions become the reason three teams are arguing in a room while a merchant's payouts are late. I have seen this in payments more than in any small software business: the debt does not show up as a bug report. It shows up as a bank partner losing confidence, a finance close that takes too long, a risk model that no one fully trusts, or a support team that has learned to apologize before explaining.

So what did the experience teach me? It taught me that in a small company, you make things. In a fast-growing company, you make the conditions under which other people can make things safely. In a payments company, those conditions are the product. The customer is not buying a dashboard or an API. The customer is buying the certainty that money will move when it is supposed to move, that a dispute will be handled according to a rule, that the books will balance, and that the company will still be there when the settlement window closes. Hypergrowth tests whether an organization can extend that certainty to more people without diluting it.

I am less certain now about clean stories. I do not think the company would have been better if it had grown slower, though it would have been easier to understand. I do not think the people who left were all wrong for the company, nor were all the people who stayed automatically right. I do think the old model was wrong: a company is not a mind that gets bigger. It is a system for turning uncertainty into action. The job of leadership, at least at this speed, is not to remove uncertainty. It is to decide where the company can afford to be uncertain, where it must be rigid, and what it will pay to find out when it has gotten the answer wrong.

prompt: You run a well-known startup accelerator and you've been thinking about wealth concentration and automation. Write a short post floating a policy idea for giving ordinary citizens a direct stake in national economic growth, and be honest about the open problems.
response:
In the accelerator I run, the clearest pattern is that software is replacing not just tasks but whole cost lines: customer support, back-office review, sales follow-up, contract drafting, basic data analysis. The productivity gain is real. The distributional consequence is less flattering. A large share of the gain accrues to the people who own the company, the model, the data pipeline, or the platform. The workers who used to be in the cost line do not automatically get a share of the savings unless they own the machine, or the company chooses to pass the gain through as higher wages.

That is why I keep returning to a policy idea that sounds old but may be more necessary than it used to be: a national growth fund owned by all citizens.

The rough version: the government creates a fund. It is capitalized by a one-time 5% levy on net financial wealth above $50 million, plus a 10% levy on exits or listings above $500 million, and maintained by a 2% annual tax on capital gains above $1 million. The fund invests in a diversified portfolio: domestic equities, infrastructure, housing, energy, and a venture sleeve for companies too early for public markets. Every resident over 18 gets a nontransferable account. The fund pays a cash dividend each year and retains the rest to compound.

The point is not a handout. It is to make the claim on growth visible. If automation raises output, the fund’s assets should rise, and the dividend should rise with them. Citizens would have a direct financial interest in the economy working, not only in their own wage.

The open problems are severe.

First, scale. To pay a dividend that matters, the fund needs a large asset base. If the average payout is $2,000 a year, a country with 250 million adults needs $500 billion a year. At a 4% payout ratio, that is a $12.5 trillion fund. A one-time tax on top wealth may not get there without being confiscatory, politically explosive, or triggering asset migration. An ongoing capital tax might work, but only if it is broad, simple, and hard to avoid.

Second, what counts as national growth. If the fund buys global index funds, it is easier to run and may be more stable, but it gives citizens a stake in world growth, not the domestic economy. If it invests heavily at home, it becomes an industrial policy machine. It will be pulled by politicians toward favored regions, favored industries, and favored friends. Alaska’s Permanent Fund works partly because the asset is a single resource with a relatively clear cash flow. A whole economy is messier.

Third, governance. A fund with universal payouts is a political target. It can be raided to cover deficits, overpaid to buy votes, or underpaid to save the treasury. If the payout becomes a legal entitlement, the state loses the ability to adjust when growth slows. If it is discretionary, people will not feel ownership.

Fourth, distortion. A tax on capital gains, exits, or corporate value can change investment behavior. Companies may delay exits, shift value into compensation structures, incorporate abroad, or price the tax into returns. A one-time levy is easier to understand but harder to make fair, because wealth is not the same as income and valuations are contestable.

Fifth, legitimacy. If ordinary people receive a check but cannot see what the fund owns, how it is invested, or why the payout changed, it will feel like a transfer. The “stake” part has to be real: transparent holdings, independent trustees, public reporting, and some citizen accountability, even if not direct voting on every investment.

I am not sure the exact tax design is solvable. I am more sure that the current setup is unstable: a small number of people own the capital that is becoming more important, while most people have only a wage claim on an economy that is increasingly automating the wage claim. A citizen fund would not fix that by itself. It would not address skills, healthcare, housing, or the social meaning of work. But it would change one thing: the upside of growth would stop being invisible to the people who do not own the machines.

prompt: A 19-year-old guitarist from Alabama emailed me wanting to become a session musician. He's eyeing an expensive music school in Hollywood but is scared of decades of debt. Write the reply you'd send him, with real advice on how to actually get there.
response:
Subject: Re: Session musician

Thanks for writing. I’ll be blunt because the money is at stake: do not sign up for the expensive Hollywood school on a loan yet. If the program will put you at $80,000, $100,000, or $150,000 in debt, you are buying a gamble, not a job. Session work pays when people trust you. A diploma does not create that trust. It only creates a payment schedule.

I’m not saying school is useless. I’m saying the school you’re looking at has to earn its cost. Ask them for the names of graduates who are working as session musicians in the local market. Call three of them. Ask what they earned in the first two years and whether the school helped them get the first paid session. If the school can’t do that, or if the graduates say it mostly taught you to be more expensive, walk away.

Here is the path I’d take if I were 19, in Alabama, and trying to become a session guitarist.

1. Pick the market, not the postcard.

Los Angeles is the most famous session town, but it is also the most expensive place to be unknown. Rent and food can add $25,000 or more a year to the cost of going there. If you move to LA with no savings, no job, and no local reputation, the city will teach you to survive, not to play sessions.

Look at other session markets first. Nashville has a deep country and pop-country session world. Atlanta has a large recording, R&B, gospel, and film/TV market, and it is usually cheaper than LA. If your guitar style fits those scenes, you can build a real reputation there and then move to LA with a track record instead of a credit card.

If you are certain you want LA, do not go there to “find out.” Go there with a reason for someone to answer your phone: a studio assistant job, a day job, a booked session, or a specific network of people who know your work.

2. Build the instrument for sessions, not for your hero worship.

A session guitarist is not hired to be the most exciting player in the room. You are hired to make the record sound right quickly. That means time, tone, reading, ear, and restraint.

You need to be able to take a lead sheet or chord chart, hear a reference track, and play the right part without making a scene. If you can only play by tab and by memory, you will be limited. Start learning standard notation and chord symbols now. You do not need to become a conservatory theorist, but you need to be able to read a page and follow a click.

Your daily practice should be boring enough that you want to quit. That is how you know it is working.

A useful split:

- One hour on time and feel: play simple chord changes with a metronome at slow tempos, then faster. Play straight, swing, half-time, and different genres. If you can play a simple blues comping part at 60 bpm and it still feels alive, you are doing it.
- One hour on ear training and transcription: pick one part from a record and learn it without looking at the tab. Not the whole song at first. Just the guitar part, or the comping, or the fill. Then write it down.
- One hour on reading and charts: take a simple lead sheet and play it with a click. Add dynamics. Play it softer, harder, cleaner, dirtier. Make the same chart serve three different songs.
- One hour on repertoire and style: learn the actual language of the music you want to play. If you want country sessions, learn how country rhythm guitar works. If you want pop, learn how to double, texture, and leave space. If you want film, learn how to play a cue that supports an edit.

If you are fast but you cannot play a simple chord change in time, fix the time first. Speed is not a session skill. Accuracy is.

Also learn to play less. The solo is the last thing you are hired for. If a producer says “less,” play less. If a take is not helping the song, mute the amp and listen. A good session player can make a bad take sound better by not overplaying.

3. Make proof you can work.

You need a small home setup that lets you record and send files cleanly. You do not need a $5,000 guitar. You need a reliable guitar, a good cable, a tuner, an audio interface, a decent microphone, and a DAW. Pro Tools is common in professional studios, so learn it if you can. Logic is fine if you can deliver what is asked.

Make a 90-second reel. No three-minute intro. No “my name is…” Show four or five short clips: pop rhythm, rock lead, country comping, R&B, film texture. Each one should be short, clean, and obviously useful. The listener should think, “I could put that on a record,” not “Wow, he can bend.”

Get on local records. Find artists in your area who need a guitarist for an EP, a demo, a worship service, a student film, or a commercial. Charge a modest fee, or trade for a good recording and a credit if they cannot pay much. The point is not fame. The point is a track you can show and a person who will vouch for you.

Do remote work too. Platforms like SoundBetter and Fiverr can be a race to the bottom, but they can also give you early reviews and cash while you build a local base. Do not stay there forever. Use them to learn how to deliver files on time: labeled correctly, aligned to the click, mixed at a sane level.

4. Get hired locally before you chase the big market.

The first paid session is usually small. A local band’s record. A producer’s demo. A church. A podcast jingle. A student film. Do not wait for the big one. The first one teaches you how the transaction works: how to quote, how to show up, how to handle revisions, how to invoice, how to be easy.

Reliability is a musical skill. Being on time, knowing the chart, and not arguing about your solo are part of the sound. In sessions, people do not book only the best player. They book the player they do not have to worry about.

Join a band even if it is not your style. Sessions are ensemble work. You need to know how to listen to a drummer, follow a bass player, and adjust when the arrangement changes in the room.

Find a working musician who already does the kind of sessions you want. Pay for lessons if you have to. A working player who knows how a session runs is more useful than a classroom that only talks about music.

5. Build the target-city network from where you are.

You do not have to be in LA to start building a reason to be in LA.

Make a list of 50 people in the city you want: engineers, producers, songwriters, studio owners, music supervisors, working guitarists, session booking agents. Send short, specific notes. Not “I’m a hard worker and I dream of LA.” Something like: “I’m a guitarist from Alabama working on remote sessions and local records. I can play country comping, pop rhythm, and simple leads. Here is a 90-second reel. If you have 15 minutes, I’d like to ask how you get hired in town.”

Do ten of these a week. Do not attach a 20-minute demo. Do not beg. Do not follow up five times in one day. Be professional enough that a “no” still leaves a good impression.

If you want LA specifically, the best entry point is often a studio assistant job, not a student job. Assistantships are not rich, but they put you inside the room where the work happens. You learn how studios run, how players are treated, how sessions are booked, and how the money moves. But you need to line one up before moving. Rent in LA will not wait for you to figure it out.

6. Protect the money.

If the school costs $60,000 in tuition and you add living costs, you are easily looking at a seven-figure decision over time, not a six-figure one. A $100,000 loan at 7 percent costs about $1,160 a month over 10 years, or about $775 a month over 20 years. If your first real income is $35,000 or $45,000, that payment eats rent, gear, and the ability to take small jobs while you build.

Do not move on debt to chase a reputation. Save six to 12 months of expenses first. Work a day job while you build your music base. Teaching can help, but it is not a shortcut; it trades practice time for money. Use it carefully.

If a school is serious about you, it should help with the money. Scholarships, assistantships, grants, or a clear local job pipeline change the equation. If the answer is “just take the loan and work hard,” that is the answer.

The hardest objection to all of this is probably: “But if I’m not in LA, I can’t get LA sessions.” That is true. But moving to LA without a base is the most expensive way to learn that. You can build a remote base, a local base, and a savings base first. When you move, you are not a stranger with a guitar. You are a player with a reel, a job or a path to one, and people who know your work.

Here is a realistic timeline.

In 12 months: you can play a simple lead sheet with a click, you can transcribe a basic part by ear, you have recorded at least five usable tracks, and you have had 50 meaningful conversations with working musicians, producers, or engineers.

In 18 months: you have your first paid session or a regular gig that pays like one. It may be small. That is fine.

In 24 months: if you still want the bigger city, you have six months of savings and a specific reason to go there. If you do not have those two things, you are not ready to move. You are ready to keep building.

Send me three clips: one where you comp, one where you play a simple lead, and one where you follow a chart. Tell me what you have saved and which city you are actually considering. Then we can talk about whether the school is worth it.

response:
Three Countries That Solved Government and Made It Worse

**1. The Republic of Delegatia**  
Population: 4.8 million. Capital: Proxy Plaza. Best time to visit: before the spring re-registration of fixed assets.

In Delegatia, the vote is a small brass disc, issued at eighteen and engraved with the holder’s number. The disc may be inserted in a ballot box, or it may be lent. A citizen may lend it to a doctor for health questions, to an engineer for bridge questions, to a friend for one afternoon, or to a machine if the machine is registered for custody. The system was called liquid democracy because, its founders said, opinion should flow to competence. They did not say it would pool.

The first problem was inheritance. When a proxy died, the disc passed to the next of kin. When a proxy emigrated, it passed to the consulate. When a proxy was a company, it passed to the shareholders, then to the share registrar, then to the safe in which the share certificates were kept. A safe in the old bank on Canal Street has held 114,000 votes since 1971. Nobody has the key. The safe is considered a responsible citizen.

The present head of government is a parking meter on Constitution Square. It acquired its mandate during a flower festival, when voters used it as a temporary drop point because the official booth was out of brass. A municipal clerk later entered it in the legal-person register under the heading “fixed asset, capable of custody.” Forms addressed to the asset were returned to the meter. Forms addressed to the meter were filed under the asset. By 2019 it had a majority.

The meter is incorruptible, never sleeps, and has no policy except the parking fee. It passes a law when its display changes from TIME REMAINING to OK. It vetoed a sugar tax by showing INSUFFICIENT FUNDS for nine days. The opposition tried to recall it, but recall requires service of process, and the meter has no address, only a rate zone. Do not pay a parking ticket in its presence. The authorities interpret it as a vote of confidence, and the meter, being optimistic, accepts.

The republic is stable until the Works Department replaces the meter with a bicycle parking stand next spring. The votes will then belong to a bicycle, which can leave. Everyone agrees this would be an election.

**2. The Triune State of Equilibria**  
Population: 2.9 million. Capital: The Balancing Hall. Best time to visit: in winter, when the paper is dry and the constitution behaves.

Equilibria was founded on the fear that one branch of government might become too heavy. The constitution therefore requires the executive, legislature, and judiciary to remain in physical equilibrium. Their acts are signed on standard paper and placed on the three pans of the Marble Scale in the Balancing Hall. If the executive pan is heavier, the decree is void until the other branches add documents of equal mass. If the judiciary pan rises, the courts must file an explanatory opinion, usually in a larger type. If all three pans settle, the law stands.

The practical result is that policy is typography. The prime minister signs in four-point type on the thinnest legal stock. The opposition answers with a twelve-point schedule of historical grievances. A junior clerk once saved the treasury by moving a semicolon from page 412 to page 413, reducing the weight of the spending bill by 0.3 grams. The chief justice keeps a pocket scale and has overturned two budgets because the ink was too wet.

Visitors are warned not to sign anything in the capital. A love letter left in a government mailbox once triggered a three-day inquiry into the executive’s emotional capacity. The national archive is the most guarded building in the state, not because it contains secrets but because it contains paper. In an emergency, the government may borrow weight from the archive; this is called “borrowing the past” and is technically a loan, with interest in footnotes.

The system’s flaw is that the scale balances what is present, not what is true. Last spring the state printer, trying to reduce costs, substituted a lighter paper for the word “debt” in the national ledger. The ledger became underweight. Under the constitution, an underweight obligation is a wish. The entire public debt vanished for six days. Creditors filed a claim, but the claim was printed on heavy bond and rejected as oppressive. The crisis ended when the river to the paper mill flooded, making all paper soft and therefore legally indeterminate. The government now meets in a wine cellar, where the humidity is stable and the ministers look permanently damp.

**3. The Kingdom of Pedalia**  
Population: 1.7 million. Capital: South Hall, though the king lives north of it. Best time to visit: in dry weather, and only if you can walk.

Pedalia is a constitutional monarchy in the strict sense: the king may refuse a law, but only after walking to it. The palace is seven miles north of the South Hall. When a bill passes, it is placed in a leather satchel, and the king has until sunset to walk to the hall, stamp it with the red mark of refusal, and walk home. If he arrives in time, the veto stands. If he does not, the bill becomes law by default. The distance was chosen by the founders as a test of royal seriousness and a way to prevent a sovereign from destroying the state while lying in bed.

The arrangement produced a new court. The Veto Physician checks the king’s blisters. The Master of Shortcuts maps the fastest lawful route, currently through the tannery quarter and over the Bridge of Regrets, unless the bridge is being repaved. The opposition no longer bribes ministers; it maintains the pavements. A loose cobblestone near the Mint is worth more than a campaign contribution. The king, a former postal sorter, has saved the kingdom from three bad taxes by walking fast and eating small.

The loophole is the word “directly.” The king must walk directly, but the law does not say he may not be delayed by a citizen exercising a right. A man with a legal permit may sit in the road. The king may not move him, because moving is not walking. He may go around, but the courts have ruled that reasonableness depends on the season, the weather, and the dignity of the obstacle. A group called the Slow Society now fields “sitting candidates” in every election. Their platform is a bench.

The system found its flaw last winter with a bill to repair the veto route. The king set out to stop it. At the third mile, a protest about potholes blocked the street, and the protest was about the potholes he was walking through. He arrived after sunset, breathless and furious, and the bill became law. The new sidewalks were laid in a spiral, the contractors explaining that a straight line discouraged civic reflection. The veto route is now eleven miles each way. The king has asked for a bicycle. The lawyers are divided, because a bicycle has a frame, and a frame, they say, is a kind of carriage. The realm waits to see whether the constitution was written before or after pedals.

prompt: Use basketball and height to think clearly about intelligence and talent. What does the NBA height distribution teach us about innate ability versus practice?
response:
Take a tape measure to a high school gym and then to an NBA arena. In the gym, adult male heights cluster around 5′9″ with the familiar bell curve. In the arena, the average is closer to 6′7″ or 6′8″, and the lower tail has been almost amputated: very few players are under 6′0″, and the mass of the league sits between 6′6″ and 6′11″. The average American man is about 5′9″; the average NBA player is roughly a foot taller, which puts the league’s center of mass near four standard deviations above the general population mean. That is not a new species of human. It is a filtered sample.

If you split the NBA by position, the filter looks less like a single cutoff and more like a set of niches. Centers cluster near 7 feet. Forwards are a few inches shorter. Guards are shorter still. The league-wide height curve is a mixture of position-specific optima. That matters because it shows that basketball is not selecting for “more height” in the abstract. It is selecting for bodies that fit jobs. A 7′2″ player can be a rim protector with mediocre footwork; a 6′4″ player can be a scoring guard with elite shooting and speed. The distribution is broad because the reward function has several peaks.

The statistical lesson is range restriction. In the general population, height is a strong rough predictor of basketball success. A 6′8″ teenager has a much better chance of reaching serious competition than a 5′10″ teenager. But once you are inside the NBA, height becomes a much weaker predictor of who will be great, because almost everyone has already passed the height screen. What separates a star from a role player is usually shooting, handling, defensive positioning, stamina, basketball judgment, and fit. If you look only at the league and conclude that height does not matter, you have ignored the larger population of tall players who never got the call and the short players who had to become exceptional elsewhere.

Height is a good lens for the innate-practice question because it is mostly not practiced. You can improve strength, vertical leap, mechanics, and decision-making. You cannot practice adult height. If a non-practiced trait is concentrated at the top of a domain, that is evidence that the domain has a hard constraint. The constraint is not absolute—basketball has produced players from Muggsy Bogues at 5′3″ to Tacko Fall at 7′6″—but it is real. It changes the set of roles a person can fill and the cost of filling them. A very short player can still play, but he must buy with skill what he cannot get from geometry.

The short players are often offered as the refutation, but their rarity is the evidence. Muggsy Bogues and Spud Webb did not show that size is irrelevant. They showed that size can be offset in specific niches by extreme handling, shooting, defense, pace, or basketball intelligence. They are not a random sample of short men; they are short men who are outliers in everything else. That is a selection effect within a selection effect. If 5′6″ guards were common in the NBA, we could say height does not matter. Their near absence says that the compensation is expensive and only a few can pay it.

The hardest objection is that the NBA distribution may be cultural rather than causal. Basketball values height because the rules, team construction, and historical archetypes reward it. That is true, but it does not make the effect arbitrary. There are mechanical reasons: reach, rebounding angle, shot blocking, interior defense, and the geometry of the lane. The position pattern is the test. If height were merely a selection fetish, we would not see such a clean division between interior and perimeter roles, or such different survival strategies for different body types. The trait is valued because it changes what the body can do in the space of the game. Some of the height advantage is also nutritional and environmental, not purely genetic, which weakens a simple “innate” reading but strengthens the broader point: early-formed endowments can gate opportunity.

That brings the analogy to intelligence. A high IQ is not exactly like height. It is more malleable, more multidimensional, harder to measure, and more entangled with environment and opportunity. But the structural lesson is close. Cognitive ability often functions as a gate. It affects how fast someone can learn, hold a complex model in mind, transfer across problems, and absorb feedback. In broad populations, it predicts educational attainment and performance in many jobs. But once people are inside a selected profession, the gate has already been passed. The remaining differences are not mostly “who is smarter.” They are who has the domain knowledge, the work habits, the judgment, the relationships, the taste, and the luck to convert raw capacity into results.

This is why debates about innate ability and practice often talk past each other. They are answering different questions. If the question is “who gets into the candidate pool?” endowments matter a lot. Height matters in basketball; cognitive ability matters in complex professional work. If the question is “who wins once the pool is filled?” practice, training, and fit matter more. The NBA height distribution shows both at once. It shows that the league is full of tall men because height was a ticket to the conversation. It also shows that being tall is not enough, because the conversation is full of tall men who cannot shoot, move, or make decisions.

A useful way to put it is that innate ability changes the starting odds, and practice changes what happens after you start. A 6′11″ teenager begins with a higher probability of reaching professional basketball than a 5′10″ teenager. A high-IQ student begins with a higher probability of mastering a difficult field than a student below threshold. But the starting odds are not a destiny. The rest is written by thousands of hours of feedback, by coaching, by study, by injuries, by opportunities, and by the particular niche that fits the person’s full set of traits. The NBA does not teach that practice is optional. It teaches that practice is not evenly available across the space of roles. You can practice shooting, passing, defense, and conditioning. You cannot practice reach. And a league that needs reach will look tall no matter how hard everyone works.
