Take a tape measure to a high school gym and then to an NBA arena. In the gym, men's heights cluster around 5'9" with a familiar bell curve. In the arena, the average is closer to 6'7" or 6'8", and the left tail is almost gone: there are a handful of guards under 6'0", but the mass of the league sits between 6'6" and 6'11". That shift is not a new biology of human beings. It is a selection effect. The NBA is not a random sample of tall men; it is a sample of men who are tall enough, skilled enough, fast enough, and useful enough to survive a sequence of cuts.

The first thing the distribution teaches is that you must ask which population you are looking at. In the general population, height is an excellent rough predictor of basketball success. A 6'8" teenager has a much better chance of reaching college ball than a 5'10" teenager. But inside the NBA, height becomes a much worse predictor of who will be great. Everyone is already tall. What separates a star from a role player is usually shooting, handling, defensive positioning, stamina, basketball judgment, and fit. If you use the NBA to argue that height does not matter, you have already thrown away the cases where it mattered most: all the tall players who never got the call, and the shorter players who had to become exceptional elsewhere.

This is the statistical idea of range restriction. When you select on a variable, the correlation between that variable and the outcome shrinks. It is not that the cause disappeared; the variation disappeared. A similar pattern appears in many selected groups. In a general labor market, cognitive ability predicts productivity and training outcomes. In a top law firm or research lab, everyone has already cleared the intelligence threshold, so the spread in IQ is smaller and other traits—judgment, persistence, taste, social skill, domain expertise—do more of the explaining. The gate and the race are not the same thing.

Height is useful as a thought experiment because it is mostly not practiced. You can improve posture, strength, vertical leap, and skill, but you cannot practice your way from 5'9" to 6'9" after puberty. If a non-practiced trait is concentrated at the top of a domain, that is evidence that the domain has a hard constraint. A 7'2" player can be a terrible basketball player; a 5'10" player can be a star. But the set of roles available to them is different. The 7'2" player can be a rim protector even with mediocre footwork; the 5'10" player cannot. The 5'10" player can be a scoring guard if his shooting and speed are elite. The league's height distribution is a shadow of those role constraints. It is not one peak but several: centers are tall, forwards are a bit shorter, guards shorter still. The distribution is broad because basketball has multiple niches, not because height is irrelevant.

The short players are often presented as the refutation: Muggsy Bogues at 5'3", Spud Webb at 5'7", a handful of guards who have played at a high level. But their rarity is the evidence. They did not disprove the value of size; they found ways to make size less relevant to their specific jobs. They became elite in handling, shooting, defense, decision-making, or pace. If 5'5" players were common in the NBA, we could say height does not matter. Their absence says that the compensation required is expensive, and only a few can pay it.

The hardest objection is that the NBA distribution may reflect culture rather than causation. Basketball values height because the rules, team construction, and historical archetypes reward it. That is true, but it does not make the effect arbitrary. There are mechanical reasons: reach, rebounding angle, shot blocking, interior defense, and the geometry of the lane. The position pattern is the test. If height were merely a selection fetish, we would not see such a clean division between interior and perimeter roles. We would not see 7' players struggling to survive as perimeter defenders or 6'0" players thriving as playmakers. The trait is valued because it changes what the body can do in the space of the game.

That brings the analogy to intelligence. A high IQ is not exactly like height. It is more malleable, more multidimensional, harder to measure, and more entangled with environment and opportunity. But the structural lesson is close. Cognitive ability often functions as a gate. It affects how fast someone can learn, hold a complex model in mind, transfer across problems, and absorb feedback. In broad populations, it predicts educational attainment and performance in many jobs. But once people are inside a selected profession, the gate has already been passed. The remaining differences are not mostly "who is smarter." They are who has the domain knowledge, the work habits, the judgment, the relationships, the taste, and the luck to convert raw capacity into results.

This is why debates about innate ability and practice often talk past each other. They are answering different questions. If the question is "who gets into the candidate pool?" endowments matter a lot. Height matters in basketball; cognitive ability matters in complex professional work. If the question is "who wins once the pool is filled?" practice, training, and fit matter more. The NBA height distribution shows both at once. It shows that the league is full of tall men because height was a ticket to the conversation. It also shows that being tall is not enough, because the conversation is full of tall men who cannot shoot, move, or make decisions.

A useful way to say it is that innate ability changes the prior, and practice changes the posterior. A 6'11" teenager starts with a higher prior probability of reaching professional basketball than a 5'10" teenager. A high-IQ student starts with a higher prior probability of mastering a difficult field than a student below threshold. But the prior is not a destiny. The posterior is written by thousands of hours of feedback, by coaching, by study, by injuries, by opportunities, by the particular niche that fits the person's full set of traits. The NBA does not teach that practice is optional. It teaches that practice is not evenly available across the space of roles. You can practice shooting, passing, defense, and conditioning. You cannot practice reach. And a league that needs reach will look tall no matter how hard everyone works.

prompt: Fred Brooks's 'No Silver Bullet' still gets quoted constantly to argue that most of the difficulty in programming is essential and that tools and languages can only buy us a small constant factor. I'm skeptical. Write an essay taking that argument on, looking back at it with the benefit of everything that's happened in software since 1986.
response:
The sentence usually attributed to Brooks is not the one he wrote. He did not say that software is doomed to be expensive. He said that no single technology or management trick would, by 1990, produce the tenfold gains the industry kept promising. That is a narrower and more defensible claim. The damage comes from turning a prediction about single technologies into a law about all technologies, and from treating the essential complexity of a system as if it were the whole cost of building it.

Brooks’s real point was that software has an irreducible conceptual core. A compiler must transform programs. A bank must keep ledgers consistent. A distributed system must decide what happens when messages fail. No editor, language, or framework can remove the need to understand those things. But between that core and the programmer’s keyboard there has always been a large amount of other work: managing memory, drawing windows, talking to disks, moving bytes, testing, deploying, keeping the thing alive. If tools reduce that other work, the total time falls by whatever fraction it occupied. That fraction has not been constant.

Let total work be `T = E + A`, where `E` is the essential conceptual work and `A` is everything else. A tenfold reduction in `A` changes `T` from `E + A` to `E + A/10`. If `A` is a quarter of the work, the project becomes about 20 percent faster. If `A` is four fifths, it becomes about five times faster. The “small constant factor” reading assumes `E` is always the big term. History says that is not true for most new software.

Consider data. In the 1970s and 1980s, a large share of application code was bookkeeping for records: opening files, finding rows, maintaining indexes, recovering from crashes. The relational database moved that into a component. A programmer who can write a query and trust ACID semantics is not merely typing faster; the programmer is not carrying the concept of the storage engine. The complexity has not vanished. It is paid for by the database vendor and amortized over millions of programs. That is a structural change, not a constant factor.

Consider distribution. In 1986, a networked application meant writing protocol code, handling byte order, timeouts, retries, and the slow discovery that the other machine had died. Today the default stack gives you HTTP, TLS, JSON, load balancers, queues, and managed databases. The hard problem of consistency remains. But the cost of getting a message from one process to another has fallen so far that products which were once departmental projects are now weekend prototypes.

Consider interfaces. GUI toolkits, then the web, then mobile frameworks absorbed the work of drawing and event handling. A 1986 team building a desktop app had to think about widgets, fonts, window managers, and input devices. A modern team can spend that time on the domain model and let a browser or operating system handle the surface. The surface still leaks—every web developer knows—but the baseline cost is lower.

The most underrated change is not writing code but changing it. In 1986, a change to a large system was an event: rebuild, integrate, test, hope. Unit testing, mocking, continuous integration, and version control made change routine. Brooks’s immutability factor—the idea that maintenance is really a rewrite—still describes the conceptual work, but the mechanical fear has been reduced. A team that can test a module in seconds can afford to refactor it. That changes what architecture is possible.

The cleanest evidence against a universal constant factor is the existence of software that would not have been economic in 1986. Real-time collaborative editors, global SaaS, mobile commerce, video conferencing at scale, personalized recommendation systems, ride-hailing platforms. Each has a hard essential core. Collaboration needs conflict resolution. Commerce needs payment consistency. Video needs synchronization. But the surrounding cost—networking, distribution, UI, deployment, payments, maps, notifications—was absorbed by platforms. A small company can now build on top of Stripe, Twilio, AWS, and the app stores. In 1986 those capabilities were not available as off-the-shelf components; they were projects.

None of this makes the hard part easy. The systems that still fail spectacularly are usually the ones where the essential complexity is large and the organization is not aligned with it. Building a correct compiler, an operating system kernel, a consensus protocol, a global payments system, or a medical device remains a research-scale problem. LLMs can write the function; they do not remove the need to know whether the function belongs in the service, whether the state should be replicated, or whether the requirement was misunderstood.

The strongest objection to the revisionist view is that large software is still large, late, and over budget. If tenfold gains had arrived, we would not still struggle to replace a mainframe or integrate an ERP system. Scope also expands until it eats the gains. A 1986 word processor edited text; today’s editor has cloud sync, collaboration, AI, plugins, and telemetry. Measured by total capability, cost per feature may look modest.

This is real, but it proves a different point. Gains in accidental complexity are usually reinvested in more features, more users, more platforms, and more change. The test is not whether the total cost of a mature product has fallen; it is whether the marginal cost of building and changing a class of system has fallen. It has. The 1986 word processor was not a smaller version of today’s; it was a different product made possible by different costs.

Languages deserve the same local treatment. A language is not a magic multiplier. It is a contract with an ecosystem. Each can be a tenfold improvement for the problems it targets and a nuisance for others. Brooks’s conservation-of-complexity idea is often used to dismiss abstractions: the complexity goes somewhere, so the programmer will pay it eventually. That is only half true. A load balancer’s scheduling is complex, but a developer can use it without understanding the algorithm. Good platforms make the common path simple and the failure path legible. Bad ones make both hard.

The newest tool fits the pattern. Language models are excellent at the translation layer: turning a known requirement into boilerplate, tests, regexes, configuration, or a plausible first draft. They can be a large constant factor for greenfield code and for navigation in unfamiliar code. They are much weaker at the essential layer: deciding the data model, choosing the boundary between services, interpreting a stakeholder’s real need, or proving that the system is safe. I am less sure how far they will push the boundary, because the technology is young and the productivity metrics are noisy. The benefit of hindsight is that the essential complexity has not stayed still. In 1986, part of the essential work in a business application was managing files and terminals. Today that work is inside the platform. The essential work has moved outward: multi-tenancy, privacy, API compatibility, global scale, model evaluation, supply-chain security. Each abstraction lowers one floor and raises another. The total cost of a system is not a fixed sum of eternal concepts; it is a moving target set by the current platform.

So the fair verdict is not that Brooks was wrong, but that his warning was overgeneralized. He correctly identified the part of software that cannot be bought away: the need to form and test a coherent concept of a complex system. He was wrong, if his argument is read as a ceiling, because the part that can be bought away has often been the larger part. Since 1986, the industry has had many small silver bullets—databases, networks, browsers, tests, packages, clouds, type systems, mobile platforms—and their combined effect has been to make entire categories of software cheap enough to build, change, and abandon. The essential complexity is still there. It is just no longer the only thing on the bill.

prompt: Write an essay about the word "racism". People use it to mean very different things, and I suspect that muddle is part of why political arguments get so nasty. Open with some puzzling hypothetical cases if that helps, and take your time getting to a view about what we should do differently.
response:
Suppose a bank denies a loan to a Black applicant because the officer says, in the privacy of his mind, that he does not want that kind of person in the neighborhood. Suppose another bank denies a loan to an applicant from a census tract with a low median income, a tract that is mostly Black because of decisions made forty years ago. The second bank uses a formula. It claims to be colorblind. Now suppose a white resident says, “I am not racist; I have Black friends,” while voting against a plan that would integrate a school two miles from his house. And suppose a Black man says, “White people cannot be trusted.” Are all four racist? The answer depends on whether you are checking a heart, an act, a machine, or a social position. That is where the trouble begins.

The word racism is not a mistake. It did necessary work. It grew up around a real evil: the idea that human beings come in natural ranks, and that some ranks deserve to rule. Slavery, colonial exclusion, segregation, and scientific ranking all fed on that idea. To call a practice racist was to say that it was not merely unfair, but that it treated race as a moral fact. The word’s strength was its simplicity. Its danger is the same simplicity.

In current use, racism can mean a belief, an act, a structure, or a position. A belief: this group is inferior, lazy, dangerous, or less entitled to respect. An act: I will not hire, house, teach, or protect you because of your race. A structure: a set of rules produces different outcomes for racial groups, and the people who control the rules leave it that way. A position: you belong to the group that has, on the whole, used race to dominate others. These are connected. Beliefs can justify acts, acts can build structures, structures can protect positions. But they are not the same claim, and they do not fall or stand together.

Political arguments get nasty because the word lets a speaker move among those claims without saying so. If I say “you are racist” and you answer “I don’t hate Black people,” I can say I meant your vote, not your heart. If you answer “the disparity is economic,” I can say I meant the system, not the budget line. Each reply is true, and neither answers the question that was actually asked. The charge also lands on identity. To be called racist is not to be called wrong; it is to be sorted into a kind of person. Once that happens, the person being accused has a strong incentive to deny everything, and the accuser has a strong incentive to treat the denial as proof of bad faith. The policy becomes a side issue.

The hardest objection to untangling the word is that the muddle has a politics. If we insist that racism requires a racist heart, we give a pass to institutions that were built by racism and still operate in racial patterns. A credit score, a school boundary, a police stop, a hiring test may be neutral in the moment and poisonous in the aggregate. To call the result “bias” or “inefficiency” is to drain it of its history. The people who suffer the outcome are not the people who define the word. So any proposal that sounds like “let’s stop calling systems racist” deserves suspicion.

That objection is right, and it shows where the fix should go. We should not stop calling institutions racist. We should make the claim specific enough to be tested. A bank is racist if it sorts customers by race. It is also racist, in a defensible sense, if it uses a proxy that it knows functions as a racial sort and refuses to correct it. A school district is racist if it maintains boundaries that reproduce segregation after being told what those boundaries do. This is not the same as saying every statistical difference is racism. Race is a social category, and many inequalities attach to it for complex reasons. But when a known racial pattern is left in place by people who could change it, the word racism is not an insult. It is a description of what the institution is for.

The position sense needs different handling. It is true that race is not only a set of individual opinions; it is a distribution of power. A white person in a country with a history of white supremacy occupies a different social position from a Black person, whether or not they hold hateful views. That fact matters. But if “you are racist” means only “you are in that position,” the statement is no longer an accusation that can be answered. It is a coordinate. It may be true, but it tells the person little they can do except change their ancestry. For argument, we need claims that involve agency: you benefit from this arrangement, you defend it, you stay silent when it is challenged, you vote to keep it. Those claims can be true or false, and they point toward action.

So the practical change is not to retire the word but to stop using it bare in serious disagreement. When someone says “that is racist,” ask which sense is at work: a belief, an act, an institution, or a position. And when you make the charge, say which one. “I think you are prejudiced” is a claim about your mind. “I think your act discriminates” is a claim about your conduct. “I think this institution is racist” is a claim about rules, outcomes, and maintenance. “You have the social position of the dominant group” is a claim about location, not character. The first two can be complicated by good intentions; the third can be true even when everyone in the room is personally decent; the fourth can be true even when the person is fighting the system. Keeping them separate does not weaken the charge. It makes the charge harder to dodge and easier to prove.

Go back to the cases. The officer who does not want Black people in the neighborhood is racist in belief and act. The formula may be colorblind on paper, but if the bank knows it re-creates old exclusion and leaves it running, the bank is racist in structure. The resident with Black friends may have no hatred in his heart, yet his vote against integration can still be a racist act if its effect is to keep schools separate by race. The Black man who says white people cannot be trusted is expressing a prejudice, perhaps one formed by real treatment, but it is not the same kind of claim as the power-backed hierarchy that has shaped the other three. If we can say that much, the argument can begin. The word racism will still carry weight. It should. The point is to make the weight land on something that can be examined, changed, or refuted, instead of on a person’s whole self.

prompt: I keep hearing about William Carlos Williams but find modernist poetry intimidating. Write a funny, opinionated review of his early book Kora in Hell for a general reader: what it is, how it was written, and whether you need a literary critic to enjoy it.
response:
If modernist poetry has made you feel like you are being asked to admire a locked room from the outside, *Kora in Hell* is the odd comfort. If you know Williams from the red wheelbarrow, this is earlier and stranger. It is not a collection of poems. It is a small 1920 prose book, subtitled *A Discourse on Music*. You can open it without a key because the sentences are in prose. The trouble is that Williams uses prose the way a drummer uses a snare: the words are there, but the point is the hit. It reads like a doctor’s fever chart for a patient named Rhythm.

The book is a manifesto, a rant, and a tune-up all at once. Williams is trying to explain what the new American poem should sound like, and he keeps getting distracted by the fact that the old poem sounds like a dead language. To him, meter is not a neutral tool. It is an inheritance, a habit, a way of making the present speak in a costume. He wants poetry to have the phrase, not the foot; the breath, not the rule; the street, not the drawing room. The result is a book that talks about rhythm while trying to become one.

How was it written? In the manner of a man who had a day job, a strong opinion, and no patience for ceremony. Williams was a physician, and the prose has that diagnostic snap: no, not that; yes, this; again, but faster. It is full of fragments, dashes, false starts, and sudden declarations. That is not a flaw to be corrected. It is the argument. If he insists that the new verse should be made of phrases, he writes in phrases. If he believes the old forms are stiff, the sentences stiffen only to be broken. Read a page and you will see a mind that has decided to stop polishing and start playing.

This is where the book can be funny, if you are willing to laugh at its confidence. Williams is not a subtle explainer. He is a converter. He will tell you what a poem is not, as if negation were a genre. He will pile up musical terms, American terms, urgent terms, and then land on a point that seems obvious only after he has shouted it. There is a lot of posturing. There are passages where the energy outruns the idea, where the man is clearly more excited about the new thing than the reader is yet. I have put the book down for this. I have picked it up because the next page started to sound like a band finding a tempo.

That tempo is the real subject. The title sounds like a Gothic novel, a little character study of someone in damnation, but the book is not about hell in any way that will comfort a theology student. I do not think the title is a riddle you have to solve before entering. The name is a door with a strange sign on it. Behind it is a room full of music: jazz, the new American idiom, the idea that a poem can be built from the way a phrase lands rather than the way a foot marches. Williams is not saying poetry should be nonsense. He is saying it should be alive in the mouth, and that the mouth is American, and that America has a new music, so why keep marching in iambic pentameter like a man in a funeral parade?

Do you need a literary critic? No. You need a little context, and the context fits in a sentence: Williams is trying to make American poetry sound like American speech and American music, and he is impatient with the old forms. A critic can add the genealogy—Pound, Europe, the postwar mood, the desire to make it new—but the book does not depend on the genealogy. It depends on your ear. If you read it slowly, treating every fragment as a clue, it becomes a puzzle. If you read it at its own speed, it becomes a character. The best method is to read a page, then another, then stop when it gets tedious, then come back when you are annoyed. The annoyance is useful. It means you are listening.

I would not recommend it as a first exposure to modernist poetry if what you want is a single beautiful poem to sit in your pocket. It is not that. It is a book about the making of poems, and its own making is part of the show. But it is a better first exposure than most anthologies, because it names the problem instead of hiding in it. Modernist poetry often asks you to trust a surface. *Kora in Hell* asks you to trust a rhythm. That is not the same thing, and it is much less frightening. Buy the cheap edition. Read it in an afternoon. If you finish it wondering whether the man was brilliant or merely loud, you have read it correctly.

prompt: Write a short, punchy blog post defending nitpicking: why it's worth correcting small exaggerations and falsehoods even when they're on your own side's talking points, and when it isn't. Include caveats.
response:
**In Defense of Nitpicking**

The most useful correction often starts with “Yes—and also not quite.”

When your side says “the data prove it,” and the data only suggest it, correcting that is not pedantry. It is maintenance. A movement that lies a little teaches everyone that its truths are negotiable. A policy debate that rounds by a billion can become a debate about a different policy. A campaign that says “everyone agrees” when a minority agrees has made the minority invisible.

Small falsehoods are not small because they are small. They are small only until they become the version people repeat. “Almost all” becomes “all.” “Most years” becomes “always.” “It was worse then” becomes “progress is impossible.” Once the inflated claim is the baseline, the honest claim sounds like a defense.

This matters most when the exaggeration is on your side. Allies can be sloppy because they expect you to cover for them. If you don’t correct the cover story, you own it. Not morally, maybe, but practically: the public will remember the claim, not the footnote.

But nitpicking has a failure mode. The worst kind treats language as the only thing that matters. You can be exact about a statistic while missing that the person is frightened. You can win a word and lose the room. You can make your side look bloodless, more concerned with sounding right than doing good.

So the test is not “Is this technically false?” It is: “Does the inaccuracy change what someone would do, believe, or feel?”

If a friend says, “This law is a disaster,” and the law is actually a mixed bag with one serious problem, correct it. The mixed bag is more true and more useful.

If a supporter says, “The other side doesn’t care about people,” maybe don’t. That may be a feeling, not a census. If it’s clearly hyperbole, let it be hyperbole. If the forum is a comment section, maybe don’t. If the person is trying to be heard, maybe don’t. If the correction will be read as a loyalty test, maybe don’t. If the real issue is power and you are polishing adjectives, don’t.

And if the exaggeration is load-bearing—if the whole argument depends on “always” or “everyone”—then it isn’t a nitpick. It’s the point. Challenge it plainly.

The good nitpick is quiet about itself. It does not say “actually” with a smile full of knives. It says: “I want to say the same thing, but I don’t want to say it too fast.”

That is the version worth keeping.

prompt: I keep seeing a particular kind of bad argument in debates where someone who says 'we should do some of Y too' gets treated as though they claim 'only Y matters.' Can you write a short blog post naming and explaining this pattern, with several examples and some sympathy for why it happens?
response:
**The “Only Y Matters” Strawman**

There is a common move in policy debates that goes like this:

Person A says, “We should do more of Y.”  
Person B replies, “So you think only Y matters?”

Person A did not say that. Person A said that Y is currently underweighted, or that it has been ignored too long, or that the present mix of priorities is badly skewed. Person B has turned that into a claim of exclusivity: if Y gets any room, everything else must vanish.

The pattern shows up everywhere.

Someone says, “We should spend more on public transit.” The reply is, “You want to ban cars and end the economy.” Someone says, “We should put more money into AI interpretability.” The reply is, “You want to stop building AI.” Someone says, “We should enforce existing labor laws more consistently.” The reply is, “You want to destroy small businesses.” Someone says, “Vaccines are important, but ventilation matters too.” The reply is, “You think vaccines don’t work.”

In each case, the original point was about relative priority. The response treats it as a zero-sum demand: either Y gets everything, or Y gets nothing.

This is not always done in bad faith. There are understandable reasons it happens.

First, debates reward clear positions. “I want a better mix” is harder to dramatize than “they want to sacrifice everything else.” A person who says “we should also do Y” is making a comparative claim, and comparative claims are less satisfying to argue against. It is easier to build a caricature: the transit person hates cars, the safety person hates progress, the enforcement person hates enterprise.

Second, there is a fear of concession. If one side admits that the other side’s concern has some weight, the next question is how much weight. That can feel dangerous. If you are defending the current arrangement, even a modest shift can look like a foothold. So the rationalizing move is to treat any demand for change as a demand for replacement.

Third, the person making the original point may not be precise enough. “We should do some of Y too” is often too thin to defend. It does not say how much Y, what gets displaced, or whether Y is a complement or a substitute. If someone says “we need more testing” without saying whether that means taking money from treatment, hiring from another department, or finding new revenue, the listener is invited to assume the worst.

But inviting a bad inference is not the same as making the bad inference correct.

The real question is never whether Y matters at all. In most serious debates, everyone already agrees that Y matters. The question is how much Y matters relative to the other things on the table. If someone says, “We should raise Y’s priority,” the honest reply is not, “You’re a Y maximalist.” The honest reply is: “How much higher? What are you willing to give up? And is that tradeoff worth it?”

That is a harder conversation, but it is the actual one.

## The Busiest People Have the Clearest Priorities

A man in a clinic chair told me he couldn’t do the program. He had a job, a kid, no car, no money. I believed him. Then he pulled out his phone and showed me a text: a friend offering him twenty bucks if he would pick something up from a shop across town. He said, “I can do that tomorrow.”

Tomorrow he did not come to session. Tomorrow he went to the shop.

I don’t tell this to be cruel. I tell it because it keeps happening. People who cannot find fifteen minutes for a promise, a parent, a treatment plan, a bill, a relationship that is slowly dying will find three hours for the thing they love. The father who misses the recital but checks the fantasy football league every night. The woman who can’t manage the bus fare to her appointment but can manage the fare to the bar, the phone, the person, the machine.

We call this a time problem. It is not. Time is the least interesting part.

Money is usually clearer. A person may be broke in a real way: rent is high, wages are low, the system is stacked. But if the same person can produce $20 for a drug, $50 for a ticket, $100 for a gift to someone they want to impress, the scarcity is not total. It is selective. The wallet is doing what the calendar does. It is revealing what the person has already decided matters.

The hard objection is obvious: depression, trauma, chaos, poverty, disability, bad luck. These things can make obligations genuinely impossible. I do not think every missed appointment is a moral choice. But in the pattern I’m describing, the missed thing is not just hard. It is specific. It is the promise that would require them to be reliable, sober, present, accountable, or loving in a way that feels like a cost. The thing they love is not necessarily easier. It may be risky, expensive, and bad for them. But it is a place where they feel wanted, skilled, free, or like themselves.

That is the key. Obligations often ask a person to be responsible. The thing they love often lets them be themselves.

Responsibility is a strange demand. It says, “Show up for someone else’s world, before you feel ready, before you enjoy it, before you are sure it will go well.” For people who have been punished for needing, failed by institutions, or spent years being used, responsibility can feel like a trap. The thing they love, even if it is destructive, can feel like a home. It does not ask them to be mature. It asks them to be there, and it rewards them for it. A game rewards you. A substance rewards you. A certain person rewards you with the feeling that you matter. A habit rewards you with the feeling that you are still in control of something.

Addiction makes this sharper because it does not just compete with the good life. It becomes the good life, at least for the next hour. The next dose, the next hand, the next contact, the next hit is not a small item on the schedule. It is the center of gravity. Everything else becomes background noise. When the brain has decided that one thing is urgent, the rest of life starts to look like chores.

This is why shaming the “too busy” person usually fails. If I say, “You just don’t care,” I am right about the behavior and useless about the cause. The person may care in the abstract. They may know the obligation is good. They may even say they want to do it. But wanting is not the same as being moved. A person can know that treatment is important and still reach for the thing that makes the present moment bearable.

The useful question is not, “Why can’t they find time?” It is, “What is the thing they love actually giving them?” And, “What would have to be true for the obligation to feel less like a debt and more like a life?”

A promise that is only a demand will lose. It will lose to the phone, the bottle, the game, the person, the fantasy, the next easy relief. But if the obligation can become something the person wants to be part of—something where they are respected, where the cost is fair, where they can be honest about what they can do—then the calendar changes without a single lecture about priorities.

People do not run out of time. They run out of reasons to be the kind of person who keeps the promise. The thing they love is the place where they still feel like they have a reason to be themselves. Recovery, or a relationship, or a life, only starts when the other place begins to offer something like that too.

prompt: 'It's all who you know' always felt like a door slammed in my face. Write an essay that looks at that saying differently, from the point of view of someone who started with no connections.
response:
For years I heard “It’s all who you know” as a sentence with a period. If it were all who you know, then the contest was over before I entered it. My parents had jobs, but their work did not touch the work I wanted. I went to schools where nobody was going to inherit a practice, and the word referral entered my life only as something a doctor did to another doctor. So when adults said the line, I heard it as a gate closing: you are late, and you do not have the key.

The saying is cruel as a theory of life, but accurate as a description of risk. Most people cannot evaluate a stranger quickly. A hiring manager, a landlord, a contractor, a journal editor, a union steward, a client all face the same problem: they must decide before they fully know. They lean on people they already trust. A network is not a mystical club. It is a reputation system, a way of answering the question: if this person fails, who will hear about it?

Starting with no connections meant I had no reputation system. I was a name on an application, and names are cheap. The first job I got was not glamorous. I answered an advertisement, showed up, and was given work that tested whether I could be trusted with small things. I misfiled reports, forgot passwords, asked questions that made coworkers sigh. I also corrected course: I stayed late to fix mistakes, wrote down the procedure so the next person would not have to ask, and told the truth when I messed up. Nobody was impressed. That was the point. I was becoming a known quantity.

In the first two years, I probably had forty people who could place my face, maybe five who would say my name to a stranger, and only one or two who would put their own credibility behind it. The difference mattered. The first group knew I existed. The second group could describe me in a hallway. The third group could say, in effect, I would not be embarrassed to recommend this person. I did not have many of them, but I had stopped being a pure unknown.

A position opened that I wanted. I did not have a sponsor. But a temporary employee from another department, someone I had covered for once and whose reports I had learned to sort the way she liked, mentioned to a supervisor that I was steady. The supervisor did not know me. Her sentence did the work a credential sometimes does: it gave my name a context. I got the interview. I got the job partly because I was competent, but also because the competence had been witnessed. The saying had not disappeared. It had changed scale. I no longer had zero people who knew me; I had a few who had a reason to say something true.

What surprised me later was that the most useful introductions rarely came from my closest friends. They came from the loose ring of people I had touched briefly: a contractor, a classmate from one seminar, a vendor, a former temp. Close friends are valuable, but they often live in the same world you do. They can vouch for your character, but they may not know about the opening, the company, the unspoken requirement. Acquaintances sit at edges. They have seen you do one thing well, and they belong to another room. When they pass your name along, they carry a small piece of your reputation across a border you could not cross alone. Sociologists have a phrase for this, the strength of weak ties, but the experience is simpler: the people you know a little are often the ones who know other people.

This is where the old sting returns, and it should. If opportunities travel through trust, and trust is built through shared spaces, then the system favors people who start in the right spaces. A kid whose parent works in an industry hears about jobs before they are posted. A student at a rich school meets recruiters in dining halls. A person with money can afford to go a year without pay. A person without those advantages is not just less connected; they are less visible, and less visible people are often easier to pass over. The saying can become a polite way of saying: the game was loaded.

I do not want to answer that with a smile and a tip about attending mixers. The unfairness is not a misunderstanding. Some doors are locked by prejudice, geography, disability, bad luck, or the simple fact that no one in the room has ever seen someone like you. Blaming the locked-out person for not networking enough is cruel. But if I make every door a fortress, I stop moving. The person who started with no connections cannot usually buy a family name, but can often do the slower work of becoming legible. That means showing up where the work happens, not just where the titles gather. It means asking specific questions instead of broad ones. It means doing a small task so well that someone can later describe it: she understood the spreadsheet, he called the client before the problem blew up, they remembered the name of the supplier. What a network stores is not names but evidence: short descriptions a person can offer to someone else.

There is a difference between knowing someone and being known by them. The first is information in your phone. The second is a file in someone’s mind. I sent dozens of cold emails in those early years. Most got no answer. A few got polite no’s. One or two got a reply because the ask was small, relevant, and easy. I was not asking for a job; once, for example, I asked whether a woman at a company I admired had ever cleaned up a spreadsheet that three departments had ruined. That kind of request costs the other person little and still opens a crack. Through the crack comes not favor, exactly, but attention. Attention can be repeated.

Later, a better door opened because of a chain I could not have planned. A former coworker moved to another company. A year after that, a mutual acquaintance mentioned my name in a conversation about a project. I had not asked for either step. I had only made it true that, if someone thought of me, the thought would be useful. That is not the same as having a patron. It is more fragile and more earned. It depends on my continuing to be someone worth mentioning.

So I now hear the saying differently. It is not a declaration that birth decides everything. It is a description of how information moves among people who must take risks. It is also a warning: if you are unknown, you are a higher risk, and people will often choose the lower risk even when the difference is small. The answer to that is not to pretend risk does not matter. The answer is to reduce it, one witnessed act at a time.

The door that used to feel slammed was not the only entrance. It was a door that opened from the inside by someone who had a reason to trust the knock. I did not start with a network. I started by becoming the kind of person a network could hold: present, useful, and not a risk to mention. That sounds less romantic than talent, but it is what actually carried me through.

prompt: I work in tech and, like most people around me, I've been pretty cynical about universities. Someone told me I should look at what Arizona State has done under Michael Crow before writing academia off. Can you write a long blog post walking through ASU's reform model, how it's organized, what it changed, and whether the results hold up or it's mostly marketing? Write it from the point of view of a tech person who is interested in research but wary of academia.
response:
I have spent enough time in tech to believe that most institutions are easier to run than to transform, and that most transformation stories are partly real and partly brand. So when someone told me I should look at Arizona State University under Michael Crow before writing academia off, I took it seriously, but not uncritically. ASU is one of the few cases where a university has changed shape visibly over two decades: bigger, more online, more interdisciplinary, more research-funded, and more aggressively managed. It is also a case where the legend has outrun the evidence in some directions and understated the evidence in others.

The short version is this: ASU did not invent a new way of doing science or teaching. It applied a fairly conventional corporate operating model to a large public university at a moment when its circumstances allowed that model to pay off. That is enough to matter. It is not enough to prove that all universities are broken or that a president with a strategy deck can fix research.

Crow became ASU’s president in 2002, after already spending time as provost. He was not an outsider parachuted in from Silicon Valley. He was a scientist who had been inside the system long enough to know where the leverage points were. That matters, because the ASU story is often told as if a visionary CEO walked into a dying university and rewired it. The more accurate story is that a capable institutional operator took a large, underappreciated state university in a growing state, flattened some of its politics, made units justify themselves, and pushed the place toward scale and visibility.

The first thing to understand is that ASU was not a blank slate. It was already a public research university with a real engineering program, a business school, a medical ecosystem in the Phoenix metro, and a student body that included many working adults. What it was not, in the early 2000s, was a national powerhouse. It had potential, but it did not have the brand momentum of, say, University of Arizona, its in-state rival, or the older research universities everyone already assumes are serious. Crow’s job was less to create value from nothing than to convert existing assets into a more coherent machine.

The core of the reform model is what ASU often calls performance management. Every major unit is supposed to have a strategic plan. Those plans are not just internal documents; they are tied to performance measures, and they are reviewed by external peers. In practice, that means a department, school, institute, or center has to say what it is for, what it does better than comparable units elsewhere, and what it will be measured on. The president’s office can then allocate money, create new units, or let old ones shrink.

From a tech point of view, this is the part that looks familiar. It is OKRs with peer review and a budget attached. The units are product teams. The strategic plan is the roadmap. The external review is the audit. The performance metrics are the dashboard. The difference is that in a company, the “customer” is usually easier to define. In a university, the customer is students, the state, donors, faculty, researchers, employers, and the public all at once, and those customers often want contradictory things.

That is where the ASU model gets more interesting than the slogan version. The slogan version is: kill tenure, fire bad professors, put everything on a spreadsheet. The real version is: make the institution’s center of gravity move from departmental autonomy to strategic alignment, and make the president’s office the place where resources follow priorities.

Departmental autonomy is one of the oldest features of American universities. Departments have their own cultures, their own hiring lists, their own ideas of what matters, and a fair amount of inertia. That is good for intellectual diversity. It is bad if you want the whole institution to move in a coordinated direction. ASU did not abolish departments. It made them less self-sufficient. If a department wants resources, it has to fit into a larger strategic story. If an institute can do the job better, the department may lose relevance even if the discipline survives.

That is a big deal. Most universities talk about interdisciplinarity, but the money and the tenure lines usually still sit in departments. ASU tried to put more weight on cross-cutting units. Institutes and schools became more than side projects. They became places where the administration could concentrate faculty, funding, and brand around a theme.

The institute model is the clearest example. Take Biodesign. It is not a traditional department. It is an interdisciplinary research hub built around the idea of designing solutions to biological and medical problems, with translational ambition and industry-facing energy. That kind of unit is hard to create inside a conventional departmental structure, because departments optimize for disciplinary depth, not for the messy project of turning ideas into devices, companies, or clinical tools. ASU gave that kind of unit room to grow.

The same logic shows up in sustainability, design, innovation, and other theme-based units. Some of these are serious. Some are trend-chasing. The model does not automatically tell you which is which. What it does do is let the institution create new organizational containers quickly, which is something older universities are usually bad at.

The “no tenure” line is the part I would handle carefully. It is one of the most repeated claims in the ASU legend, and it is also one of the least precise. ASU has changed the tenure conversation. It uses performance reviews, unit-level strategic accountability, and reappointment decisions in ways that make faculty status more contingent on institutional priorities than at many older research universities. Whether you call that no tenure, tenure-lite, or just aggressive performance management depends on the contract, the era, and how much you trust administrative power. The practical point is not that ASU eliminated a legal status in one clean stroke. The practical point is that the old buffer between a department and the central administration got thinner.

That matters because tenure is not just a benefit. It is a governance mechanism. It gives faculty a floor of security that lets them survive bad deans, bad politics, and bad fashions. It also lets institutions keep people who are valuable but not currently fashionable. If you weaken that buffer too much, you get a more responsive workforce and a more anxious one. In tech, we know this tradeoff well. Performance culture can raise the ceiling and lower the tolerance for slow work.

So the first honest verdict on ASU is that it became more like a managed organization. Whether that is good depends on what you want a university for. If you want a place that can pivot, scale, and point itself at market-relevant problems, the model has real advantages. If you want a place where a small number of people can work on obscure questions for decades without having to justify them to a strategic plan, the model is less friendly.

The second thing ASU changed is scale. This is the part that is easiest to see and easiest to overrate. Enrollment grew from roughly 45,000 students in the early 2000s to well over 80,000 full-time-equivalent students today, with a much larger headcount if you include part-time and non-traditional students. That is not a small change. It changes the institution’s revenue base, its political weight, its hiring power, and its ability to fund new units.

A lot of that growth came from online education. ASU was an early mover in online degree programs and built a large online operation. Tens of thousands of students now take courses online. From a product standpoint, this is obvious: the marginal cost of another student is low, the addressable market is huge, and the format fits working adults. From an academic standpoint, it is more complicated. Online scale can improve access, but it can also make the institution more of a content-delivery machine. It can increase completion problems. It can make the brand broader without making it deeper.

I am less sure about the long-run educational value of ASU’s online growth than I am about its financial and strategic value. The public data on student outcomes are messy, and completion rates at large public universities are often lower than people want to admit. If you are a tech person, that should bother you. A product can have impressive top-line numbers and still have a churn problem. A university can have impressive enrollment and still be underdelivering on what students actually paid for: a credential that changes their life.

The third thing ASU changed is research posture. It is an R1 institution now in a very real sense. It has grown research expenditures to several hundred million dollars a year, and it has built out centers and institutes that are visible enough to attract grants, industry partners, and faculty. It shows up in patent counts, startup formation, and applied research activity in ways that make it more interesting than its national rankings suggest.

That is an important caveat, because rankings are not the only thing that matters. ASU is not a top-20 university in the way people usually mean that phrase. It is not the place you go if you want the maximum possible prestige signal from a faculty name. But if you are a researcher who cares about applied work, interdisciplinary teams, engineering, health, sustainability, data-intensive problems, or the ability to move an idea toward a prototype, ASU is more worth taking seriously than its brand reputation might suggest.

This is where the tech comparison gets useful. A university is not a lab. It is a lab plus a school plus a hospital plus a housing authority plus a media company plus a political creature. Research is one of its outputs, not its whole identity. ASU’s model is especially good at making the research side look like part of a larger innovation engine: institutes, industry partnerships, technology transfer, student entrepreneurship, branded programs. That is attractive if you want research with a path to application. It is less attractive if you want research that is allowed to be strange for a long time.

The fourth thing ASU changed is brand. This is the part the cynics latch onto, and they are not entirely wrong. ASU has a very strong institutional narrative. It tells you that it is the “New American University,” that it is performance-driven, globally connected, accessible, and built for the future. Some of that is self-congratulatory. Some of it is marketing. But brand is not separate from operations. In higher ed, brand affects recruiting, donations, faculty hiring, and partnerships. A university that can tell a coherent story and then deliver enough evidence to back it up has a real advantage.

The marketing question is not whether ASU markets itself. It does, obviously. The question is whether the marketing is attached to a durable asset base. In ASU’s case, I think it is, but only to a point. The enrollment is real. The research dollars are real. The institutes are real. The online operation is real. The brand is not just paint. But the brand also creates expectations that the institution may not fully meet. A marketing narrative can make a university seem more elite than its faculty, more innovative than its curriculum, or more mission-driven than its financial incentives.

That brings us to the hardest objection. If ASU’s model works so well, why is it not everywhere?

There are a few answers, and none of them is flattering to the people who want a simple playbook.

First, ASU’s context matters. It is a large public university in a fast-growing metropolitan region with a tech corridor, a large working-adult population, and a state politics environment that has tolerated aggressive growth. That is not the same as running a small liberal arts college, a state flagship with a huge legacy, or a private research university with a different governance structure. The model is more transferable than people admit, but less transferable than the brand suggests.

Second, Crow’s tenure matters. In the literal sense. Institutional transformation usually requires a long runway and a central leader who can absorb political pain. ASU had both. That is rare. Most universities do not get a president with that combination of ambition, institutional knowledge, and staying power. If the model depends heavily on one operator, it is not as robust as the mythology implies.

Third, the model has costs. It creates bureaucracy. It creates metric pressure. It can make faculty feel like employees in a portfolio rather than members of a scholarly community. It can reward visible outputs over slow ones. It can make the institution better at doing what it already thinks is important and worse at discovering what it should start caring about. That is the classic failure mode of any performance system, and it is not unique to higher ed.

Fourth, and this is the one I think people miss, the model is better at improving certain kinds of output than others. It is good at scale, coordination, applied research, industry engagement, and brand. It is less clearly good at the kind of research that changes the base assumptions of a field. That kind of work is hard to forecast, hard to benchmark, and often produced by small groups with unusual freedom. A university can build a system that makes applied excellence more likely. It cannot simply OKR its way into intellectual surprise.

So does the result hold up? Partly.

The parts that hold up are the operational ones. ASU became larger, more research-intensive, more interdisciplinary, and more globally visible. It built a real online business. It created units that did not exist before and gave them enough weight to matter. It turned a mid-tier public university into a place that national employers, researchers, and students take seriously. If someone says ASU is “mostly marketing,” they are ignoring the balance sheet and the research infrastructure.

The parts that do not hold up as cleanly are the aspirational ones. ASU is still not the kind of university that defines the frontier in the way the top research universities do. Its brand is strong, but not elite in the old-money academic sense. Its online scale is impressive, but it raises real questions about learning and completion. Its performance model is powerful, but it also creates the same pathologies you see in any large organization that has learned to manage itself through metrics.

I think the best way to think about ASU is not as a proof that academia is salvageable, but as a proof that university management is real. People in tech often treat universities as if they are naturally inefficient because they are old. That is lazy. Some institutions are inefficient because their incentives are bad. Others are inefficient because the work is hard and the feedback loops are slow. ASU shows what happens when you take a large public university and treat it like an organization with a strategy, a performance system, and a brand to protect. It gets better at many things. It does not become a different species.

For a tech person interested in research, the takeaway is narrower than the cult version suggests. ASU is worth watching if you care about applied, interdisciplinary, industry-connected work. It is less compelling if you care about the purest possible forms of academic prestige or the most protected possible forms of intellectual freedom. The university did not solve the basic tension in higher education: it is supposed to be both a public institution and a competitive enterprise, both a place of inquiry and a place of credentialing, both a community of scholars and a customer-facing organization. It just managed that tension better than most.

That is a more modest claim than “ASU is the future of higher ed,” and a more useful one. The future of higher ed is not one model. It is a set of constraints. ASU is a good example of what one set of constraints, plus one strong operator, can produce. It is not a universal cure. But if your prior is that universities are too stupid to change, ASU is a serious counterexample. If your prior is that one clever president can turn any university into a research rocket ship, ASU is also a warning.

prompt: I'm asexual and polyamorous, and a lot of what I value in relationships is physical closeness that isn't sex. Write a personal blog post about cuddling, why it matters, and whether whole communities can make it normal.
response:
**Cuddling Is Not a Warm-Up**

The first time I asked a partner to cuddle, plainly and without preamble, they went quiet. Not offended, exactly, but uncertain, as if I had changed the genre of the evening. I am asexual, and I am polyamorous. A lot of what I want from relationships is physical closeness that is not sex: being on a couch with someone, a hand on the small of my back, the weight of a body across my lap. I have learned to ask for it carefully, which means I have learned to ask for it rarely. That feels wrong.

Cuddling matters because it is one of the few ways a relationship can accumulate evidence. A grand gesture is memorable, but it is also expensive and therefore scarce. Cuddling is cheap. It can happen after dinner, during a bad episode, while watching something neither of us is interested in. Each time, someone is making a small decision: I will be soft with you, I will not use this proximity to escalate, I am available for a minute longer. Over months, that becomes a kind of knowledge. You know that a person can be near you without wanting something from you. You know your own body is allowed to relax in front of them. That is not a small thing.

In a culture that treats touch as a ladder toward sex, non-sexual closeness has no stable category. A hug is either friendly or not. Holding hands is either innocent or foreplay. Cuddling is either a prelude or a consolation prize for people who can’t manage the real thing. For an asexual person, that framework is not just incomplete; it is a dead end. If sex is the summit, then I am stuck in the foothills, and everyone assumes I am climbing. But the foothills are where I live. I need a vocabulary that says: this is not a substitute. This is not a lesser form of intimacy because it is missing the most famous part. This is the part I was looking for.

Polyamory makes the problem sharper because it multiplies the bodies involved. I do not expect one person to be all of my touch needs, and I do not want them to be. One partner may be good for long, silent cuddles. Another may be good for quick hugs and a hand in the pocket while we walk. Another may prefer close conversation with no physical contact at all. None of these arrangements is less committed than the others. But they require a level of specificity that monogamous scripts rarely reward. “I love you” is not enough. “I like being touched” is not enough. You have to say: I need ten minutes on the couch before I can do my evening. I need someone to sleep near me. I need a hand on my shoulder when I’m anxious, not a solution. I need you to ask before you pull me in.

That sounds logistical, and it is. But logistics are what make love possible when desire is not automatic.

Can whole communities make cuddling normal? I think they can, but only up to a point, and only if “normal” is defined carefully. A community makes a behavior normal when enough people can do it without being treated as an exception. If I ask for a cuddle and the response is curiosity or simple consent, the behavior is available. If the response is laughter, pity, or a long explanation of why I must be lonely, the behavior is available only at the cost of my dignity. Communities change that cost. A friend group with a comfortable couch and a history of people sitting close together is not the same as a friend group where anyone who initiates touch is immediately interpreted as making a move. The difference is not the furniture. It is the script.

Asexual and queer communities are especially well placed to do this, because they are already working on a different set of possibilities. We already have to explain that romance does not require sex. We already have to invent forms of relationship that the default narrative does not name. Cuddling fits naturally into that work. A “cuddle relationship” is not a failed sexual relationship; it is a relationship whose center is non-sexual physical closeness. A community that takes that seriously gives asexual people something rare: a model in which our bodies are not problems to be managed, but participants in intimacy.

But here is the objection I keep coming back to. If a community makes cuddling normal, can it also make it expected? The two are easy to confuse. Some people do not like being touched. Some people have trauma histories that make closeness dangerous. Some people have chronic pain, sensory differences, cultural backgrounds, or simply a temperament that finds unsolicited affection intrusive. A community that celebrates cuddling can quietly become a place where people who do not cuddle are seen as cold, broken, or unsocial. That would be bad. It would replace one pressure with another: the pressure to want sex, with the pressure to want touch.

So the goal is not universal participation. It is universal respect for the ask. Cuddling becomes normal when a person can say “yes” without being read as available for more, and when another person can say “no” without being read as rejecting the relationship. It is normal when a man in his forties can ask for a hug and not be mocked. It is normal when a teenager can pull away and not be punished. It is normal when “I’m not up for touch tonight” is as boring and acceptable as “I’m not hungry tonight.” That is a much lower bar than making everyone a cuddler, and a much higher one than leaving every person to negotiate touch from scratch in a world that assumes sex is the point.

Communities can build the lower bar in concrete ways. They can model asking: “Can I sit close?” “Do you want a hug?” “I’m going to put my feet on your legs; tell me if that’s annoying.” They can make refusal uneventful. They can create spaces where touch is explicitly optional—cuddle parties, if they are run with strict consent, are one example, though they are not the only one. They can stop treating public non-sexual affection as suspicious. They can let couples hold hands in a park without turning it into a story. In polyamorous contexts, they can encourage agreements that name non-sexual touch directly: who is expected to provide it, how often, what forms count, what happens when needs change.

I do not think a community can make bodies want what they do not want. It cannot make a person who flinches from touch feel safe simply by declaring touch wholesome. It cannot make a person who needs distance feel held simply by surrounding them with people who are hugging. The body is not a policy problem. What communities can do is reduce the social cost of saying what the body needs. If asking for closeness is expensive—because it might be sexualized, infantilized, or dismissed—people will not ask. They will go home and sit on their own couch, and the absence will look like contentment.

What I want, in the end, is not a world where everyone cuddles. I want a world where I can say “sit with me” and people understand that I am not being coy. I want non-sexual closeness to be a recognized currency of love, not a leftover from a love that failed. I want my partners to know that a hand on my back can be a complete sentence. If communities can make that ordinary, even in small rooms and small groups, they will have done something that no amount of theory can: they will have made it possible to be near another person and mean nothing more than that.

prompt: A newspaper article claims an old doomsday forecast has been vindicated because the data have tracked its predictions for forty years. Write a critical essay about whether that kind of track record is actually evidence, bringing in some philosophy.
response:
A forty-year track record sounds like the kind of thing that settles a dispute. A doomsday forecast made in 1985 says the world will run out of something, or heat up, or pass a threshold; in 2025 a chart shows the line has bent the way the forecaster said. The newspaper calls this vindication. It may be, but the word is doing too much work. The question is not whether the data came after the prediction. It is whether the prediction was in a position to be wrong. A track record is evidence only if it is a record of surviving risks, not a record of time passing.

Karl Popper’s lesson is easy to state and easy to forget: a claim is not made strong by the fact that it is still standing; it is made strong because it could have fallen. “There will be trouble ahead” is still standing after forty years, but it has not been tested, because almost every history contains trouble ahead. “The concentration of X will pass level Y by date Z” has been tested every year after the prediction, and it has a failure condition. If the doomsday forecast’s terms are elastic—“scarcity,” “stress,” “consequences,” “a turning point”—then the data can be made to track it by choosing which consequences count. That is not confirmation. It is the logical position of a sentence that has no possible refutation.

Bayesian reasoning makes the point sharper. The support a datum gives a hypothesis is not a matter of how dramatic the hypothesis is or how long we have waited. It is a matter of likelihood ratios: how probable the observed data would be if the doomsday forecast were true, compared with how probable they would be if a rival explanation were true. If the forecast says “resource use will keep rising” and the rival says “resource use will also keep rising, because population and income are rising,” the data are not very discriminating. If the forecast says “per capita copper use will fall after 2000 because substitution will kick in” and the rival says “it will continue to rise with GDP,” then a fall in per capita copper is evidence. The forty years matter only insofar as they contain moments when the forecast was exposed: a deadline, a threshold, a quantity, a place, a time. If the deadline is still in the future, forty years of tracking is an interim report, not a verdict.

There is a second problem hidden in the plural “predictions.” Many old doomsday forecasts are not single bets; they are portfolios. A 1970s resource model may predict population growth, industrial expansion, pollution, depletion of several minerals, and social unrest. Some lines will bend one way, some another. A journalist can select the line that looks like the chart and call the model vindicated. This is the multiple-comparisons problem in narrative form. If a forecaster makes twenty predictions and one is partly right, the probability of at least one hit may be high even if the forecaster is bad. We need the hit rate, not the highlight reel. The 1972 *Limits to Growth* is a useful case. Its World3 model did not issue one neat prophecy; it produced a family of possible trajectories. Later defenders can therefore choose the trajectory whose resource or pollution line resembles the data, while the model’s more dramatic demographic and industrial peaks did not arrive in the form needed to confirm the whole model. A track record built from selected variables is a track record of selection.

Even when a prediction is specific, the data are not innocent witnesses. They depend on definitions, units, baselines, and aggregation. The Duhem-Quine thesis, in its everyday form, says that a prediction is never tested alone; it is tested together with a bundle of auxiliary assumptions. Suppose a forecast says “the world will run out of oil.” What counts as oil? Conventional oil? Oil sands? Shale? Liquid fuels? If the forecaster begins with conventional oil and, when production rises, switches to a broader category, the apparent track record is partly a track record of redefinition. If “collapse” means a thirty percent fall in GDP, the data may not track; if it means rising inequality, stagnant wages, or a refugee crisis, they may. A forecast can be made unfalsifiable by making its target movable. Philosophy calls this underdetermination: the same observations can fit different theories if we are allowed to adjust the connecting assumptions. In journalism, it looks like a line graph that always ends up in the right place.

Base rates matter too. Doomsday forecasts are common, and the world has long-term trends. If a thousand writers in 1985 say some form of environmental or economic stress will increase, and stress increases, the fact that one of them said it is weak evidence for his insight. We also have survivorship bias in memory. The forecasts that miss are forgotten or reinterpreted; the forecasts that hit are printed with charts. A fair test would compare the old forecast with what other forecasts said, and with the prior probability that a vague doomsday claim would accidentally be borne out. “It was right” is not the same as “it was more right than the alternatives.”

The strongest objection to this skepticism is that some old forecasts really are corroborated in a way that matters. The ozone hole is one. Chemists did not merely say the atmosphere would get worse; they identified chlorine compounds, a stratospheric transport mechanism, polar chemistry, and a seasonal pattern. When satellite and ground data showed springtime ozone depletion over Antarctica, the match was not a vague moral. It was a specific physical story that could have been wrong. Climate science is another, though with more complexity: models predicted not only that the planet would warm but where and how—faster warming in the Arctic, a particular vertical temperature profile, longer heat waves, sea-level rise consistent with thermal expansion and ice loss. When those patterns appear, they are evidence because rival explanations predicted different patterns. The difference is not that these forecasts are old; it is that they were risky. They specified what would count against them.

So the newspaper article’s claim is not automatically false, but it is under-argued. “The data have tracked its predictions for forty years” is a conclusion presented as a description. To make it evidence, the article should say: the forecast, made in year X, predicted quantity Y by date Z; the measurement is W; the rival expectation was V; the observed value is U; and the forecast was not revised in the intervening decades, and the data were not chosen after the fact.
