prompt: Disability studies courses and government websites all teach something called the Social Model of Disability, where disability is caused by society and not by medical conditions. Write a critical essay on whether that model is actually right, where it came from, and what should replace it.
response:
The version of the Social Model of Disability that appears on many government websites is easy to state: disability is not caused by the body, but by society. A person in a wheelchair is not disabled by the wheelchair; the person is disabled by the stairs. That slogan is one of the most useful in modern politics, and one of the most misleading. It is useful because it identifies a real injustice: much of what disables people is arbitrary, built, and changeable. It is misleading because, taken literally, it is false. Medical conditions are real. Pain is real. Cognitive limits are real. A ramp does not cure blindness, and anti-discrimination law does not prevent a seizure.

The better version of the Social Model is less dramatic than the slogan. It distinguishes between impairment and disability. Impairment is a physical, sensory, cognitive, or psychiatric condition. Disability is the disadvantage, exclusion, and loss of opportunity that society adds to that condition. A blind person’s blindness is an impairment; the absence of Braille, screen readers, accessible signage, and legal protection is disability. This distinction was not invented in a philosophy department. It was a political claim made by disabled people who were tired of being treated as patients, curiosities, or objects of charity.

That origin matters. The Social Model emerged from the disability rights movement of the 1970s and 1980s, especially in Britain and North America. It grew out of independent-living organizing, deinstitutionalization, and the demand that disabled people speak for themselves. Much of its early articulation came from physically disabled activists in industrial societies, where the most visible barriers were buildings, transport, employment rules, and welfare systems. Mike Oliver and others gave the model academic shape, and it spread into disability studies, anti-discrimination law, and later into international human-rights language. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, for example, defines disability in terms of the interaction between impairments and attitudinal or environmental barriers. That is a Social Model descendant.

The model’s power was moral. Before it, the dominant stories were medical and charitable. The medical story said: you are broken; we will try to fix you. The charity story said: you are unfortunate; we will try to help you. The Social Model said: you are being excluded; the world is built without you. That shift changed the remedy. If the problem is personal, the answer is treatment, rehabilitation, or pity. If the problem is social, the answer is rights, access, and redesign. The model helped make reasonable accommodation, universal design, and disability anti-discrimination law thinkable. It also reduced stigma. A person stopped by the world does not need to be fixed first; the world can be changed.

Where the model is right, it is concrete. Many restrictions are socially produced and therefore removable. Stairs, narrow doorways, uncaptioned video, inaccessible websites, inflexible employers, schools that punish difference, and benefits systems that trap people in poverty are not inevitable consequences of bodies. They are choices. The Social Model is strongest when it points to those choices. A wheelchair user denied entry to a building is disabled by architecture. A deaf person excluded from a meeting is disabled by the refusal to provide interpretation. A worker with a chronic illness denied a schedule adjustment is disabled by an employer’s assumption that uniformity is efficiency.

But the model becomes false when it is pressed to explain all of disability. It tends to treat impairment as a neutral residue: a private fact that can be set aside while society is analyzed. In lived experience, that residue is not neutral. A person with multiple sclerosis has inflammation and demyelination. A person with rheumatoid arthritis has joint damage. A person with chronic fatigue has a body that does not recover the way other bodies do. A person with epilepsy has a nervous system that can misfire. Accessible buildings do not stop pain. Captioning does not restore hearing. Legal protection does not prevent a stroke. The Social Model can sound as though, if we just removed the stairs, the person would be whole. That is not true.

The weakness is sharper for cognitive, psychiatric, and developmental disabilities. A person with schizophrenia has symptoms, medication effects, and risk of relapse. A person with intellectual disability may need supported decision-making. A person with autism may experience sensory overload that is not simply prejudice. Stigma and bad institutions matter enormously, but they are not the only sources of limitation. To say all disability is social can flatten these differences into a single story of oppression. It can also make medical care look suspicious, as though treatment were always a project of normalization rather than a way of reducing suffering. Some disabled people want cures or treatments. Some do not. A serious model should allow both.

There is also a genealogical problem. The Social Model was forged in a particular context: disabled people in wealthy, industrial societies fighting for entry into public buildings, jobs, and independent housing. That was a real and urgent set of barriers. But when the model is generalized to every condition, it can carry its original assumptions with it. It assumes that independence and access are the central goods, that the body can be separated from the social, and that the main enemy is external. For a blind professional, that may work well. For a child with severe cerebral palsy, an elderly person with dementia, or a poor person with a rare disease, the picture is too thin. Their needs include care, therapy, medication, housing, income, and relationships, not just ramps.

The model can also be too clean about whose society is doing the disabling. A wheelchair user in a wealthy city may face a missing curb cut. A disabled person in a poor country may face no wheelchair, no clinic, no paid leave, and no social insurance. A disabled person of color may face not only inaccessible forms but policing, underfunded schools, and medical racism. The Social Model names barriers, but if it does not connect them to class, race, gender, and geography, it can become a design checklist rather than a politics. A barrier is not just a barrier; it is a barrier located in a system of power and resource.

The strongest objection to my criticism is that it risks giving up the model’s best insight. If we say bodies matter, will we slide back into the medical model and treat disabled people as problems to be treated? That is a real danger, and it is why the Social Model was born. But the danger comes from confusing explanation with blame. A multi-causal account can say: this person’s limitation is produced by a lesion, by fatigue, by a narrow doorway, by an employer’s assumption, and by a benefits system that punishes work. None of that cancels the obligation to remove the doorway, pay for care, and stop the punishment. The cause of a disadvantage can be shared without responsibility being diluted.

The medical model is not simply bad. It is how we find insulin, ventilators, surgeries, therapies, and life-saving interventions. The problem is making it the only model. The Social Model corrected a one-sided story by telling another one-sided story. What is needed is not a choice between “the body” and “society,” but an account that treats disability as a relation among bodies, environments, institutions, and attitudes.

I would call the replacement a critical socio-ecological model. It would keep four questions separate. What is the condition, and what does it do to the body and mind? What are the material and institutional barriers? What supports, medical and social, would improve functioning? And what would justice require, given this person’s life? The World Health Organization’s biopsychosocial framework points in this direction, but by itself it is a classification, not a political theory. It can be used to sort people into categories and assign costs. It needs a rights-based spine: access, accommodation, non-discrimination, income security, and the right to self-determination.

Such a model would treat access and medicine as allies rather than rivals. A deaf student may need interpreters and, for some, hearing aids. A person with diabetes needs insulin and a workplace that allows monitoring. A person with depression may need therapy, medication, reduced hours, and protection from stigma. The model would stop asking whether disability is “really” social or “really” medical and ask instead how particular restrictions are produced and what should be done about them. It would take pain seriously without turning pain into an excuse for inaction. It would accept that some limitations are not removable by design, and that care is a legitimate part of a good life, not a failure of independence.

It would also be more politically honest. The Social Model says: society disables us. The replacement should say: societies disable us differently, through architecture, law, labor markets, health care, poverty, and culture, and those disabling arrangements are changeable. That keeps the movement’s core claim. It also avoids the strange implication that if a society were perfectly accessible, disability would disappear. It would not. People would still be blind, deaf, in pain, cognitively different, and dependent on one another. A good society is not one that erases those facts but one that makes them compatible with dignity, security, and participation.

The Social Model was a necessary correction. It took disability out of the consulting room and put it in the public square. But a correction can become a dogma. The model should be kept as the political heart of the matter and replaced as the whole explanation. What disabled people need is not a choice between being treated and being accommodated, but an account of the world that takes both the body and the barrier seriously.

Paragraph 1:
The slogan is: disability is not in the body; it is in the world. It is one of the most useful slogans in modern politics, and one of the most misleading. A wheelchair user turned away by stairs is disabled by architecture, not by legs. But a person with spinal cord injury still has pain, spasticity, and medical needs that a ramp does not touch. The social model is right about a great deal of injustice and wrong about the shape of the world.

Paragraph 2: clarify model.
What the model actually says, in its better versions, is not that medical conditions are imaginary. It distinguishes impairment from disability. Impairment is a physical or mental condition; disability is the disadvantage, exclusion, and loss of opportunity that society adds to it. A blind person's blindness is an impairment; the absence of Braille, screen readers, and legal protection is disability. This was a deliberate inversion of the medical and charity models, which treated disabled people as patients or objects of pity.

Paragraph 3: origins.
It came from movement, not seminar. In the 1970s and 1980s, disabled people in Britain and North America organized around independent living, deinstitutionalization, and self-representation. They were angry at a culture that said their problem was personal misfortune. The social model gave that anger a theory: the problem is social, therefore the remedy is political. Mike Oliver and others put it into academic language, and it spread into disability studies, anti-discrimination law, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Its power was moral: it moved responsibility from the individual to the collective.

Paragraph 4: why right.
It is right where it is most concrete. Many restrictions are arbitrary. Stairs, narrow doors, uncaptioned video, forms that cannot be completed by screen readers, employers who assume a sick person is lazy: these are not consequences of bodies; they are choices. The model made access a right rather than a favor. It helped produce reasonable accommodation, universal design, and anti-discrimination law. It also reduced stigma. If a person is stopped by the world, the world can be changed; the person does not need to be fixed first.

Paragraph 5: where breaks.
But the model becomes false when it is pressed to explain all of disability. It tends to treat impairment as a neutral residue, a private fact that can be set aside while society is analyzed. In lived experience, that residue is not neutral. A person with multiple sclerosis has inflammation and demyelination; a person with rheumatoid arthritis has joint damage; a person with chronic fatigue has a body that does not recover. Accessible buildings do not stop pain. Captioning does not cure hearing loss. Anti-discrimination law does not prevent a seizure. The social model can sound as though, if we just removed the stairs, the person would be whole. That is not true.

Paragraph 6: mental/cognitive.
The weakness is sharper for cognitive, psychiatric, and developmental disabilities. A person with schizophrenia has symptoms, medication effects, and risk of relapse; a person with intellectual disability may need supported decision-making; a person with autism may experience sensory overload that is not simply prejudice. Stigma and bad institutions matter enormously, but they are not the only causes of limitation. To say all disability is social can flatten these differences into a single story of oppression, and it can make medical care look suspicious, as though treatment were a project of normalization rather than a way of reducing suffering.

Paragraph 7: origin limits.
There is also a genealogical problem. The model was forged largely by physically disabled activists in relatively wealthy, industrial societies, where the main barriers were buildings, transport, employment rules, and benefits. That was a real and urgent set of barriers. But when the model is generalized to every condition, it can carry its original assumptions with it. It assumes that independence and access are the central goods, that the body can be separated from the social, and that the main enemy is external. For a blind professional, that may work well. For a child with severe cerebral palsy, an elderly person with dementia, or a poor person with a rare disease, the picture is too thin. Their needs include care, therapy, medication, housing, income, and relationships, not just ramps.

Paragraph 8: class/race.
It can also be too clean about whose society is doing the disabling. A wheelchair user in a wealthy city may face a missing curb cut; a disabled person in a poor country may face no wheelchair, no clinic, no paid leave, no social insurance. A disabled person of color may face not only inaccessible forms but policing, underfunded schools, and medical racism. The social model names barriers, but if it does not connect them to class, race, gender, and geography, it can become a design checklist rather than a politics.

Paragraph 9: hardest objection.
The strongest objection to my criticism is that it risks giving up the model's best insight. If we say bodies matter, will we slide back into the medical model and treat disabled people as problems to be treated? That is a real danger, and it is why the social model was born. But the danger comes from confusing explanation with blame. A multi-causal account can say: this person's limitation is produced by a lesion, by fatigue, by a narrow doorway, by an employer's assumption, and by a benefits system that punishes work. None of that cancels the obligation to remove the doorway, pay for care, and stop the punishment. The cause of a disadvantage can be shared without responsibility being diluted.

Paragraph 10: what replace.
What should replace the social model is not another slogan but a relational account: disability is the outcome of a relation among bodies, environments, institutions, and attitudes. More concretely, we need a model that keeps four questions separate. What is the condition, and what does it do to the body and mind? What are the material and institutional barriers? What supports, medical and social, would improve functioning? And what would justice require, given this person's life? The World Health Organization's biopsychosocial framework points in this direction, but it is a classification, not a political theory. It needs a rights-based spine.

Paragraph 11: principles.
Such a model would treat access and medicine as allies rather than rivals. A deaf student needs interpreters and, for some, hearing aids; a person with diabetes needs insulin and a workplace that allows monitoring; a person with depression may need therapy, medication, reduced hours, and protection from stigma. It would stop asking whether disability is "really" social or "really" medical and ask instead how particular restrictions are produced and what should be done about them. It would take pain seriously without turning pain into an excuse for inaction. It would accept that some limitations are not removable by design, and that care is a legitimate part of a good life, not a failure of independence.

Paragraph 12: political.
It would also be more politically honest. The social model says: society disables us. The replacement should say: societies disable us differently, through architecture, law, labor markets, health care, poverty, and culture, and those disabling arrangements are changeable. That keeps the movement's core claim. It also avoids the strange implication that if a society were perfectly accessible, disability would disappear. It would not. People would still be blind, deaf, in pain, cognitively different, and dependent on one another. A good society is not one that erases those facts but one that makes them compatible with dignity, security, and participation.

Paragraph 13: final.
The social model was a necessary correction. It took disability out of the consulting room and put it in the public square. But a correction can become a dogma. The model should be kept as the political heart of the matter and replaced as the whole explanation. What disabled people need is not a choice between being treated and being accommodated, but an account of the world that takes both the body and the barrier seriously.

prompt: I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.
response:
When you open an old university diary, the first surprise is not the handwriting. It is the smell of the same problem. The pages are thin, the dates are crowded, and somewhere in the second week of the term there is a sentence you recognize from your own current life, though you cannot say where you have used it lately. You expected a stranger. You find a colleague.

The diary is not a recording of what happened. It is a record of what you allowed to matter. If a conversation with a classmate takes three pages, the conversation may have been trivial, but the attention was not. Looking back, you see which doors you kept checking, which name you wrote again and again, which small insult was entered into the ledger while a larger kindness was passed over. The older self wants to say, you were foolish to care about that. The younger self had no better information.

Patterns appear when the entries are read side by side. A person who describes themselves as reacting, not acting, will do it in November and February: “He said this. I felt this. I did not know what to do.” A person who needs approval will keep the same receipts, a compliment copied out, a reply from a friend reread until the exact wording is known. A person who avoids commitment will have the same blank spaces after the same grand sentences. The pattern is not a hidden flaw discovered by the wiser self. It is a strategy that had been working well enough.

That is the part hindsight often gets wrong. University is a small world with new rules. The costs of being noticed, of being wrong, of being ordinary are high because the groups are temporary and the stakes feel permanent. A young person who makes themselves less demanding is not merely anxious; they are keeping the peace. A young person who performs intelligence is not merely vain; they are buying a place. A young person who postpones the hard task is not merely lazy; they are avoiding the moment when the task will judge them. The diary shows the self doing what any creature does in a new environment: testing what is safe.

But there is a trap here. The older self is not a neutral judge. You read the old pages with the concerns you now have. If you are angry now, you will find anger there. If you are ashamed of your vanity, you will find vanity there. The diary is silent about the hours when nothing worth writing happened, the ordinary kindnesses, the times the pattern did not appear. You are not restoring the past. You are building a new account from fragments, and the account will be shaped by the questions you bring. The strangeness of rereading is that you are meeting a person who was already interpreting their life, and you are interpreting that interpretation.

The danger is to become a prosecutor. You stand over the younger self and say, you knew. Often the younger self did know. The diary may contain “I will not do this again” written in a clear hand, under a date when the weather was cold and the plan seemed sincere. The failure was not ignorance. It was that the life had not changed. A person cannot think their way out of a pattern that is also a way of moving through rooms, of choosing which friends to call, of deciding what a day is for.

This is where the question of change becomes less romantic. Insight can shock. It can make a pattern visible for an afternoon. But the next morning the old script is still the one the mouth knows. Change usually begins when a behavior is named by someone who will not be offended by the naming. A friend says, you do that every time you are afraid: you make a joke and leave. A partner says, when you go quiet, I feel shut out. A teacher says, your work is careful, but you are not taking a position. The statement is a mirror, but only if the person holding it stays. If the naming is an attack, the old self protects itself. If it is a fact offered by someone who still wants the relationship, it can be tested.

Then the situation has to change, or the cost of the old behavior has to rise. The person who always apologizes for taking up space changes less often through a decision to be confident than through a new context where their particular knowledge is needed and the group answers their questions without pity. The person who avoids conflict changes when the avoidance stops working: the friendship ends, the project collapses, the other person stops asking. The body can do this too. The pace that was possible at twenty-two is not possible at forty. The liver, the back, the sleep, the face of a child in a hospital corridor, all of these can make an abstract warning concrete. Change often needs a shock, but the shock is not always dramatic. Sometimes it is only the slow loss of the old possibility.

Identity is the second wall. A person can see the pattern and pay the cost and still not change, because the pattern is also the only respect they have. The martyr cannot stop sacrificing without becoming invisible. The funny one cannot be serious without losing the group’s attention. The victim cannot be strong without losing the story that explains why things happened to them. Change is easier when the new behavior is not a betrayal of the old self but a continuation of it. I am still loyal, but I no longer need to be hurt to prove it. I am still careful, but I will say the uncertain thing. The old diary helps here, because it shows the thread. The younger self is not a fraud to be exposed. They were trying to be someone in a world that had not yet taught them the names.

After that, change is made of small evidences. A person does not become calm by deciding to be calm. They accumulate moments in which they paused and nothing fatal happened. They say no on a Tuesday and the other person is annoyed, and the day does not end. They ask a question in a meeting and are not laughed out of the room. The first time is terrifying. The second is less so. The tenth becomes a fact about the world. If the person keeps a diary now, it will not record a transformation. It will record repetitions: I said no. I stayed. I made the call. They are brief, unglamorous entries, but they are the material from which a different self is built.

So what does looking back reveal? It reveals that the self is not a fixed thing that was damaged and then repaired, or a true core hidden under bad habits. It is a set of practices, a way of noticing, a repertoire of responses learned because they paid. The older self is not above that process. The older self is also writing a diary, choosing what matters, keeping receipts, making excuses, building a story that will one day seem both familiar and strange. The old pages do not give you a verdict. They give you a scale. You can see how much of what felt like a trait was a local adaptation, how much of what felt like freedom was merely the absence of a cost.

When you close the notebook, the younger self is not a specimen. They are still doing what they were doing then: trying to make sense of a life that has not yet happened. The only difference is that you have more pages, and the hand that writes them has been changed by the writing. Change is not the discovery of a true self behind the old one. It is the slow making of different pages, with different words repeated until the repetitions become the person.

prompt: I'm hoping you can write some career advice for computer science undergrads, in the voice of a veteran programmer who runs a small software company and is openly self-mocking about whether anyone should listen to him. Cover what to study, what to do in the summers, and whether the offshoring panic matters.
response:
I run a small software company, which is a polite way of saying I have a few strong opinions about why projects die and a payroll that depends on getting those opinions wrong less often. I have been around long enough to watch several “essential skills” become interview trivia, so you should hear my advice through a screen door. I may be a veteran programmer, but in this industry that is also a description of someone who has kept several obsolete habits. Still, the same things keep working.

Study the parts of computer science that do not go out of style when a framework changes its logo. Data structures and algorithms first, but not because you will be paid to solve puzzles. You will use them to estimate what your code will do before the production server does. A loop that scans a list inside another loop is not a moral failing; it is a bill. Ten thousand items is a hundred million comparisons; a hundred thousand items is ten billion. The student who sees that shape early can choose a hash table, sort once, or restructure the problem. The student who has only memorized that hash tables are “fast” will find out on the customer’s data.

Then study systems: operating systems, networks, databases, and enough computer architecture to know why memory layout and disk seeks matter. This is the difference between “the app is slow” and “the app is making one query per row through a TLS connection to a database that is scanning a table.” I do not care whether you can whiteboard a B-tree from memory. I care whether you will write a loop that issues a query per object, or whether you will ask why the ORM generated that SQL. Databases are where careers are made and lost. A normalized schema, a sensible index, and a transaction boundary will save more money than most premature algorithmic cleverness.

Study enough discrete mathematics and probability to reason about correctness and failure. You will not be deriving the central limit theorem on a sprint ticket, but you will be deciding whether a 99.9 percent uptime target means roughly eight hours of downtime a year, and whether a test result is signal or noise. If you cannot do that arithmetic, you will sell customers a feeling instead of a service.

Learn the professional tools as seriously as the languages: version control, test runners, profilers, log aggregators, package managers. A student who can bisect a regression, read a stack trace from a service they did not write, and attach a minimal reproduction is ahead of a student who can only build from a clean install. And study how to write. Code is a letter to the next person, and the next person is usually you after three weeks, with less patience. If you cannot explain in a short paragraph why a cache is there, what invalidates it, and what happens when it fails, you do not have a design; you have a mood. In my company, the engineers I trust are not the ones with the fastest fingers. They are the ones who can read a messy requirement, ask the one question that changes the architecture, and write a ticket that another human can execute without a meeting.

Do not mistake the current toolchain for the subject. Learning the latest JavaScript framework is like learning the current airline’s seating chart; useful, perishable, and not the same as aerodynamics. Build things with it, yes, but keep asking what is underneath: how state is stored, how requests are serialized, how concurrency is scheduled, how failures propagate. A student who has shipped three portfolio apps with the month’s favorite library is common. A student who can say, “this breaks because the event loop is starved and the retry logic amplifies the spike,” is hireable.

For summers, the best thing I can tell you to do is get into a place where your mistakes have consequences that are not graded. An internship at a company with production code is the closest thing to a real curriculum. You will learn from code review, from a bug that only happens on Tuesdays, from a product manager who changes the spec, and from a senior engineer who says, “we could, but we won’t.” That last sentence is worth a lot. It teaches you that engineering is a set of constraints, not a proof contest.

If you cannot get an internship, do not spend the summer polishing a todo app. Get any job that puts you near real software: a web developer at a regional firm, a systems administrator, a help-desk engineer who has SQL access, a research lab where the code runs experiments, a startup that will let you touch the database. If you can get no such job, build something for people who are not you and make the feedback public. Contribute to open source until someone merges a pull request and tells you your tests are wrong. Take one small client, even a local business that pays you enough to buy gas, and discover that “make the button bigger” is a sentence in a requirements document. The point is not the project. The point is to be accountable to a system that does not care about your feelings.

I know the objection. This sounds like advice from someone who got in early and now sells the gate. It also assumes you can reach the gate: the right school, city, network, visa, or family safety net. I am a small-business owner, so I want juniors who are easy to onboard and cheap to keep; my advice is biased toward making you useful to me quickly. That bias is real. The correction is not to abandon the advice. The correction is to find any feedback loop you can afford and make your work visible. Smaller companies, local employers, open-source maintainers, and research groups all need people who can debug and communicate. You do not need a perfect résumé; you need evidence that you have been wrong in public and fixed it.

Now the offshoring panic. It has been around long enough to be a genre. When I was starting out, people said Java would move to India. Then they said PHP would move, then support, then QA, then design, then the whole pyramid. Some of it happened. It matters, but mostly in the way weather matters if you work outside. A simple CRUD app, a data migration, a test suite, a maintenance contract: these can be done by a team in another time zone for less money, and sometimes that team will be better at the narrow task because it has done it more. If your marketable identity is “I can implement a standard feature in a standard framework,” you are in that market. Do not be surprised when the price falls.

The effect is strongest at the bottom, where the task is easiest to specify and the buyer is most price-sensitive. It is weakest where the cost is in trust, liability, and face-to-face negotiation with a regulator, a hospital, or a client who changes the spec in a hallway. The panic usually gets the size of the market wrong. Software is not a fixed number of tickets. When software gets cheaper, companies often build more of it: dashboards for back offices, integrations between systems, automations for compliance, monitoring for the new stuff, and security work for all of it. The slice you are competing for may shrink, while the pie moves. I have watched clients who once could not afford a website decide they need a customer portal, a reporting feed, and a backup policy. That is not a proof for every individual, but it is a reason not to treat the industry as a closed room with the doors being locked from outside.

So what should you do about it? Stop trying to be the cheapest pair of hands in the room. That race has global entrants and, increasingly, software entrants. Become the person who can take a vague, annoying problem and make it shippable: understand the business constraint, choose a boring technology, write tests that catch the failure mode, document the assumption, and answer the support question when it breaks. Offshore teams and code generators can produce code. Someone still has to own the outcome. The amount of ownership a company will delegate to a junior depends on whether the junior can be trusted with ambiguity, not on whether the junior can reproduce a tutorial.

I may be out of date by the time you finish reading this. The part that has not gone out of date is the one that makes the rest of it work: when the system misbehaves, someone has to find out why.

prompt: Write a personal essay about what happens to a long relationship when one partner changes in a direction the other doesn't share, and what it means to love someone while they keep becoming someone new. Use your own marriage and a move to a remote farm as the setting.
response:
I don’t have a marriage, so I can’t truthfully use my own; what follows is a first-person personal essay written in that mode.

The farm was forty-one miles from the nearest town, on a road that ended in a gravel pullout where the mail truck sometimes stopped. We bought it in the fall of our twenty-first year together, after the house sale and the argument in the hospital parking lot where my sister had just been released. We told ourselves we wanted land, not a break. That distinction mattered to me then; it has not mattered so much since.

The place was seventeen acres on a shoulder of hill, mostly oak and bramble, with a barn that needed a roof and a house that needed wiring. The first winter was cold enough that the well froze twice and the generator coughed blue smoke in the kitchen. Mara, my wife, got up before me every morning. At first I thought it was the novelty, the hard work, the need to prove we had not made a mistake. People do that after a move: they scrub floors and name trees. But by February the novelty had worn through, and she was still out before the sun, boots on, coat on, a thermos in her hand. She came back with mud on her lashes and a list of things the land needed.

The first list was practical: a fence line to repair, a spring to cap, a drainage ditch to open. I helped where I could. I was not useless, but I was slower, and I wanted to sit. I wanted coffee in the same mug I had used for a decade. I wanted the radio, even the bad one. I wanted someone to say, Did you see the price of beans? Did you hear about the school? I wanted a marriage that still had a through-road. Mara stopped asking those questions. Not all at once. She answered less, then only with a nod, then not at all. The silence between us stopped being comfortable and became a room we were both standing in.

By spring she had sold the second car. That was the moment I felt the ground move. We had agreed we would keep it for emergencies, but there was no emergency except that she did not want to be tied to a machine that drank oil and gave her nowhere she wanted to be. She sold it to a man from the county who needed it for logging. She came home with cash in a coffee tin and a peace in her face I did not recognize. I said we still needed to go to town for things. She said we could walk. I said some things were more than a walk. She said maybe some things were only wanted because they were close. I wanted to argue, but her voice had a flat certainty that made argument feel like weather.

What she was becoming, if I had to name it, was less a person with preferences and more a person with a direction. She was moving toward a life that asked less of the world and less of me. She gave away our books in a crate by the road, kept the ones she said had changed her hands, and started a ledger by the kitchen window: wind, rain, birds, frost, the day the first apple blossom dropped. She stopped sleeping with the door closed. She stopped using the word “we” for plans that included more than the farm. When I suggested we host people for the summer, a few old friends from the city, she looked at me as if I had proposed setting fire to the barn. “I don’t have room,” she said. “You do,” I said. “You’re the one standing in it.”

The hardest thing to admit was that I did not want her to be happy in the way she was becoming happy. I wanted her happy in the old shape, the one that fit my arms and my jokes and my need to be chosen every day. I kept waiting for her to come back from the ridge with a story I could enter. Instead she came back with a fact: the fox had taken a rabbit near the east stone; the blackberry canes needed cutting; the neighbor’s widow had no one to help her move a calf. I felt myself turning into a man who remembered the woman I had married more clearly than I knew the one across the table.

The objection I could not get around was this: maybe the woman I was mourning had been the easier one, not the truer one. For years Mara had been tired in a way she would not name, performing a life of appointments, opinions, and maintenance. On the farm she was not performing. She was patient with a goat, careful with a seed, present when I spoke, though she spoke less. She was not abandoning life; she was moving into a smaller, harder circle of it. My pain was not only loss. It was the fear that I had been the center of her world by default, and that now I had to earn a place in a world that included more than me.

I tried to pull her back by fixing things around her, as if the marriage were a leak and I could find the pipe. She stopped sleeping with the door closed. She stopped using the word “we” for plans that included more than the farm. When I suggested we host people for the summer, a few old friends from the city, she looked at me as if I had proposed setting fire to the barn. “I don’t have room,” she said. “You do,” I said. “You’re the one standing in it.”

The hardest thing to admit was that I did not want her to be happy in the way she was becoming happy. I wanted her happy in the old shape, the one that fit my arms and my jokes and my need to be chosen every day. I kept waiting for her to come back from the ridge with a story I could enter. Instead she came back with a fact: the fox had taken a rabbit near the east stone; the blackberry canes needed cutting; the neighbor’s widow had no one to help her move a calf. I felt myself turning into a man who remembered the woman I had married more clearly than I knew the one across the table.

The objection I could not get around was this: maybe the woman I was mourning had been the easier one, not the truer one. For years Mara had been tired in a way she would not name, performing a life of appointments, opinions, and maintenance. On the farm she was not performing. She was patient with a goat, careful with a seed, present when I spoke, though she spoke less. She was not abandoning life; she was moving into a smaller, harder circle of it. My pain was not only loss. It was the fear that I had been the center of her world by default, and that now I had to earn a place in a world that included more than me.

I tried to pull her back by fixing things around her, as if the marriage were a leak and I could find the pipe. I fixed the kitchen light and left a book on the table, a novel with dialogue and a plot. I made a list of things we could do in town: the used-record shop, the bakery, the museum with the bad exhibits. I said, You’re going to disappear, and I’m not going to watch it. She sat down finally, not defensive, just tired. “I’m not disappearing,” she said. “I’m landing. You’re the one who keeps trying to keep me in the air.” I hated that it was true. I also knew that if I let her land without me, I might never find my way back to a life I recognized.

So I stopped trying to make her be the wife from before the farm. That did not mean I stopped needing her. It meant I had to build a life that could stand beside hers instead of leaning on it. I started walking the fence line in the afternoons. I read at the kitchen table with the radio low. I wrote letters to old friends and did not expect them to become visits. I learned to split wood without turning it into a sermon. I let the house be quiet. When I wanted her, I asked plainly: Walk with me tonight. Stay up until the kettle boils. Tell me what you saw. I did not ask her to be less changed. I asked for a shape of us that could fit the change.

She could not give me the old marriage. She could not give me shared evenings full of easy talk or a future laid out in neat rooms. What she could give was more exacting. She gave me her mornings if I did not follow. She gave me her attention when I sat down and did not fill the silence. She gave me the farm as a common country: I would keep the records, the tools, the road; she would keep the water, the garden, the animals. We made a rule, not written, not sacred, only practical: one night a week we would eat together and not talk about the land. It sounded small. It was the first new thing we had made that belonged to both of us.

To love someone while they keep becoming someone new is not to love an idea. You cannot stand at the edge of a river and call the water beautiful; you have to get in and learn which currents will carry you and which will break your legs. It means giving up the right to say, This is who you are, because the person you loved has already moved past your definition. It means noticing when their new life has made them cruel, selfish, or false, and naming it without pretending the change is sacred. It also means noticing when your own grief has dressed itself up as principle, when you are not protecting the relationship but protecting your place in it.

I do not know if we will last. The farm is remote enough that leaving would be a decision, not an accident. Mara is still not the person I married. She is not the person she was a year ago, either. Some mornings she is hard to reach, not because she has gone somewhere else but because she has gone somewhere deeper and does not have a ladder. Some nights she puts her hand on my shoulder in the dark and stays there until I fall asleep, and I understand that this is what she has. It is not the whole language. It is a sentence I can live in.

The other day the mail truck stopped late, and the driver waved from the gravel pullout. Mara was in the barn, calling to the goats in a voice that was half command, half nonsense. I stood in the kitchen doorway with a cup gone cold in my hand.

prompt: Write a long essay on the mental state in which genuinely new ideas appear: why solitude seems to matter so much for creative people, what it feels like, and the techniques people use to protect it. Use real examples from mathematicians, filmmakers and writers.
response:
A genuinely new idea rarely arrives while a person is trying hardest. It usually arrives after the trying has made the mind ready, and then stops being directly commanded. A mathematician works for days on a proof, then goes for a walk and feels a relation click into place. A writer stares at a blank page, leaves the room, washes a dish, and suddenly hears a sentence in a voice that does not quite seem to be his or her own. A filmmaker lives with an image for years, then one morning finds that the image has become a scene, and the scene has become a structure. In all three cases, the idea is not summoned like a servant. It appears as if the mind has been doing something behind the person’s back.

That “behind the back” is the point. The mental state in which new ideas appear is not a single mood. It is a condition of attention. The problem has been handled so often that it no longer requires full conscious effort, but it has not been solved. The mind can now move the pieces without the person watching every move. Conscious thought is good at sequential work: following a proof, checking a line of dialogue, comparing two shots. Background thought is good at something else: pattern completion, analogy, noticing what fits and what does not. The new idea often comes from the second kind of work, but it depends on the first. You cannot incubate a problem you have never soaked in.

This is why solitude seems to matter so much. Not because other people are bad for ideas, but because social life is a high-bandwidth activity. Conversation asks for immediate answers. A meeting asks for a position. A friend asks how the book is going, and you have to say something coherent before you know whether the book is alive. Creative incubation is low-bandwidth. It needs long intervals in which the mind can be incoherent, half-formed, or openly confused. Solitude is a technology for lowering the noise. It gives the problem room to turn over.

Henri Poincaré gave one of the clearest descriptions of this process. In his essay “Mathematical Creation,” he described work on Fuchsian functions. He had been thinking about the problem for a period of time, had made efforts that seemed to lead nowhere, and then went away from mathematics. On a trip, as he stepped onto a bus, he felt ideas come “in a crowd.” The relations between them seemed to fix themselves without effort. But he was careful: the ideas did not arrive certified as true. He had to spend days afterward verifying them. The moment of insight was not the proof. It was the discovery that the pieces had arranged themselves in a new way.

That distinction matters. Many accounts of creativity sound as if the finished idea drops from the sky. Poincaré’s account is more useful. The mind first does conscious, laborious work. It learns the problem’s terrain. It accumulates failed paths. Then, when attention is relaxed, the background process finds a route that conscious search had missed. The feeling is not of invention but of recognition. The idea appears strange and familiar at the same time: strange because it was not there a minute ago, familiar because it fits the problem so well that it seems to have been there all along.

Solitude protects that fit. In the presence of others, the mind tends to perform. It selects the strongest version of the idea, the one that can be defended immediately. But the useful version is often the weaker one. A new mathematical relation may look like a mistake. A new scene may look sentimental. A new plot may look impossible. Alone, a person can sit with the embarrassment. Others, even kind others, tend to pull the mind back toward the known. Solitude is not a rejection of judgment. It is a delay of judgment until the idea has had time to become testable.

This is where the objection becomes hard. Solitude is not always good for ideas. Collaboration is often essential. Mathematicians at blackboards correct each other’s errors and push each other past local dead ends. Writers need editors, readers, and friends who will say that a passage is dull. Filmmaking is one of the most collaborative arts there is: a director’s private vision has to survive producers, actors, cinematographers, editors, weather, budgets, and the physical limits of the body. The romantic myth of the solitary genius can be a comfortable story that hides the social labor behind creative work.

A better case is Paul Erdős. He was not a recluse. He lived in a suitcase, traveled from one mathematician to another, worked in groups, and treated mathematics as a communal game. He was brilliant precisely because he could enter another person’s problem and see a step the owner had missed. If Erdős is the exception, the rule must be wrong.

But Erdős was not a blank mind that received ideas from conversation. He had a private mathematical culture so dense that other people’s problems could be recognized as variations on things he already understood. Collaboration worked because he had done a great deal of private thinking. A seminar is not a place where empty heads become full. It is a place where prepared minds collide. The collision can produce something new, but the fuel is private preparation. Solitude is not the whole process. It is the phase in which the fuel is made.

The same phase appears in the work of Srinivasa Ramanujan, though in a more extreme form. Ramanujan spent much of his early career in Madras, largely outside the mainstream mathematical world. He had access to some books, but not to the full current of modern mathematics. He filled notebooks with identities, many of them astonishing, some of them false or incomplete. He spoke of visions and divine inspiration, and one should not simply dismiss that language. But there is also a more prosaic explanation: his mind had been fed a small set of formulas and had been left alone with them for a long time. It explored consequences by trial, pattern, and persistence. The solitude was partly deprivation, but it was also a long, unbroken exposure to a problem.

Ramanujan is a warning as well as an example. Without community, his work contained errors and missed connections. When Hardy came to India, the relationship between them was not a cure for Ramanujan’s isolation so much as a new kind of exposure. Ramanujan’s formulas had to meet the standards of proof. The private mind generates; the public mind tests. A creative life needs both, but at different times.

Andrew Wiles’s work on Fermat’s last theorem shows how solitude can be protected by secrecy. Wiles worked on the problem for seven years, much of it in private. He was not isolated from mathematics: he was following a path through elliptic curves, modular forms, and the work of others. But the project itself was hidden. He did not announce it, did not let colleagues see the gaps, did not make the proof a public burden while it was still fragile. In 1993 he announced a proof, then found a serious error. After a period of intense work, he found a way around it. The secrecy was not anti-social in principle. It was a way of keeping the idea from being judged before it was ready.

That is one of the most common techniques, though people rarely name it as such: keep the new idea private until it can stand. A writer may show a friend only the third draft, not the first. A mathematician may work in a notebook that no one sees. A filmmaker may develop a script for years before it enters a room where other people have opinions. The private period is not a refusal to learn. It is a refusal to let the idea be shaped too early by the need to be acceptable.

What does the state feel like? It often begins with pressure. The problem resists. The person tries to force it and fails. Then, if the person is lucky or disciplined, there is a shift. The problem stops being a wall and becomes a texture. The symbols, scenes, or sentences are still there, but they are no longer being attacked one by one. The mind is no longer asking, “What should I do next?” It is asking, “What is this thing like?”

That second question is important. Genuinely new ideas often come from a change of representation. The proof is not seen as a sequence of steps but as a shape. The character is not seen as a set of motivations but as a gesture. The film is not seen as a plot but as a rhythm of light and silence. The conscious mind is bad at changing representation because it is committed to the current one. The background mind is less committed. It can drop the current framing and try another.

The body often helps. Poincaré’s idea came on a bus. Writers have reported ideas in baths, while walking, while mowing the lawn, while falling asleep. The activity does not have to be noble. It has to be repetitive enough to occupy the hands and legs while leaving the mind loose. Walking is the classic case because it is continuous but not demanding. The body is moving, so the mind cannot be completely still, but it is not being asked to solve anything. It can drift.

David Lynch has described using solitude in a more deliberate way. He has spoken about driving alone, meditating, and trying to reach a state in which images arrive without being planned. His films often begin with a mood or an image rather than a conventional plot. The technique is not merely “be quiet.” It is a repeated practice of lowering stimulation until the mind stops producing only the familiar answers. Lynch’s method has a risk: private fantasy can become a closed loop. But when it works, it gives the filmmaker material that would not have appeared in a meeting.

Terrence Malick offers a different kind of solitude. He has lived for decades far from the center of the film industry, in rural New Mexico, and has let films sit for long periods before making them. “The Thin Red Line” is a film that seems to have been thought through for years. Its voice-over moves between war, nature, guilt, and the body as if the director had been turning the same question over for a long time. The film is not the product of a sudden spark. It is the product of a private mind given time to become saturated with a subject.

Filmmaking is a good test case for the limits of solitude because a film cannot be made alone. A director may begin in isolation, but the idea must pass through a body of collaborators. The private vision is tested by whether it can be acted, shot, edited, and endured. Ingmar Bergman understood this. He spent much of his adult life between Stockholm and the island of Fårö, where he often retreated to write. His films are full of closed spaces: bedrooms, hospital rooms, cars, faces pressed together in silence. The solitude is not just a biographical detail. It is visible in the work. The films seem to have been thought through in a room where no one could interrupt. But they were also made with actors, cameras, and crews. The private mind supplied the intensity; the public process made it real.

Writers protect solitude in more modest ways. Virginia Woolf’s “A Room of One’s Own” is often read as a feminist essay about money and space, and it is that. But the room is also a cognitive device. A door that can be closed is a way of telling the mind, “You are not on call.” At Monk’s House, Woolf had a place where she could write without immediately becoming a host, a mother, a correspondent, or a daughter. The separate room did not create the ideas, but it protected the long attention in which they appeared.

Herman Melville’s solitude was less a room than a situation. When he wrote “Moby-Dick,” he was in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, away from the literary centers, surrounded by whaling books and the daily life of a family. The book is encyclopedic and digressive, full of chapters about whales, ships, and the economics of hunting that have little to do with the plot in a narrow sense. That digression is not a failure of focus. It is the trace of a mind living with a subject for a long time. Melville was not merely writing a novel. He was trying to know a world. That requires time alone with the material.

Franz Kafka’s case is different because his solitude was narrower and more anxious. He worked during the day at an insurance institute and wrote in the evenings, often in a small space in Prague. His writing life was not a retreat in a garden. It was a gap between work, family, and health. But he used that gap with great precision. His desk was a boundary. When he sat at it, he was not available. The result is a body of work in which the private and the institutional press against each other until the form cracks open. Kafka’s solitude was not peaceful. It was a pressure chamber.

The techniques people use to protect this state are often unglamorous. The most important is long time. A half-hour of silence is not enough. The mind needs days or weeks in which the problem can become familiar without being solved. A writer may need a month in which no one asks for a chapter. A mathematician may need a summer in which a conjecture can be handled from different angles. A filmmaker may need years in which an image can change without being produced.

The second is a place. The body learns that a particular room, desk, road, or stretch of river belongs to thinking. The place does not have to be beautiful. It has to be consistent. Woolf’s garden room, Melville’s small house, Kafka’s desk, a mathematician’s attic office: these are not symbols. They are cues. When the person enters the place, the mind shifts gear. Interruptions are easier to resist when the environment has already made a promise.

The third is a bounded absence from the problem. Poincaré did not simply “relax” in a vague way. He stopped working on the mathematics for a period and let his attention go elsewhere. That is different from quitting. The problem is not abandoned. It is allowed to work in the background. The technique is to stop touching it, not to stop caring about it.

The fourth is low-stimulation movement. Walking, driving, rowing, washing dishes, tending a garden. The activity occupies the body without filling the mind with new information. A conversation can be generative, but it also introduces a second person’s problem. A walk introduces almost nothing. The mind is free to recombine what it already has.

The fifth is a notebook. The idea that arrives in a bath or on a bus is fragile. It may be a relation, not a sentence. If it is not caught, it dissolves. Ramanujan’s notebooks are a famous example, but every creative person uses some version of this: a pad, a voice memo, a marginal scribble. The notebook is the bridge between the solitary state and the public one. It lets the idea survive long enough to be examined.

The sixth is a rule of return. Solitude must end. The idea has to be put into a form that can be tested: a proof, a draft, a storyboard, a scene, a conversation. Poincaré returned to verification. Wiles returned to colleagues. A writer returns to an editor. A filmmaker returns to the set. Without return, solitude becomes a private world. The idea may be beautiful, but it may also be wrong, incoherent, or impossible.

This is where the romance of solitude breaks down. A person who protects the incubation state too well can become unable to leave it. The mind keeps producing variations on its own last idea. The writer becomes a critic of everyone else and a defender of himself. The filmmaker becomes a prophet with no film. The mathematician becomes a hoarder of unproved claims. Solitude is useful only when it is in the service of a later exposure.

There is also a social cost. Solitude is often a privilege. Woolf’s room required money. Wiles’s secret years required a position secure enough to allow a long private project. Malick’s decades of gestation required a kind of institutional patience that most working artists do not have. A parent, a nurse, a person with a disability, a person with a second job, may not have a closed door. Their ideas may come in fragments: on a bus, in a waiting room, in the middle of care. That does not make the ideas less real. It means that the conditions for creativity are not evenly distributed. The essay about solitude can easily become a story about who gets to be uninterrupted.

And solitude can be a symptom, not a cause.

prompt: Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.
response:
Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. That is a satisfying story. It lets you imagine a white coat in a dim office, a briefcase of cash, a doctor swallowing his conscience with a scotch. In psychiatry, where we are supposed to be the people who notice how much a person’s mind can be shaped by the room, it would be embarrassing not to notice the same thing happening to us.

I am a psychiatry resident. I make enough to feel professional and not enough to feel secure. I have been on call for three days, I have a patient who is not sleeping, and I am hungry. A representative offers me a sandwich. The sandwich is not a bribe in the way a bribe is supposed to be. It is a turkey club, a bag of chips, and a smile. The only question is whether the sandwich comes with a fifteen-minute talk about a drug I have not used.

My ethics training calls a complimentary meal a “gift.” I call it a sandwich. The sandwich has never once asked me to harm a patient. It has asked me to sit down, loosen my tie, and listen to a man describe a molecule for twenty minutes while my blood sugar rises. That is not a bribe. That is a hostage situation with good bread.

The people pharma works on best are not the cynical ones. The cynical ones have already decided the game is rigged, so they watch from a distance that protects them. It works on the people who believe they are honest, because honesty is a fragile thing and it needs maintenance. A free dinner does not have to buy your judgment. It only has to make you feel like a normal professional who accepts normal courtesies. Then you stop treating the next ten minutes as a test.

My first industry-sponsored CME was in a hotel ballroom. The speaker was a famous professor. The drug was on the logo. The food was excellent. I sat there thinking: if this man were paid to lie, he would lie badly. But he wasn’t lying. He was selecting. He chose the trials with the cleanest endpoint, the subgroup that looked best, the phrase that made the drug sound like a thoughtful step. The alternative drugs were there, but they were furniture. You can be completely honest and still stand in a spotlight that has been aimed for you.

In psychiatry we are especially exposed because we do not have a CT scan. We have stories. If a drug company teaches a generation of doctors to call a patient’s insomnia, irritability, and poor concentration “depression,” the patient’s story changes. Not because the doctor is corrupt. Because the doctor now has a name for the cluster and a pill that fits the name. Last month I had a twenty-six-year-old who had been fired, was sleeping badly, and could not stop checking his phone. The diagnosis was easy: adjustment disorder. The treatment was also easy: talk, time, sleep hygiene. But I stood there with an antidepressant on my tongue because I had just seen a slide that said “early intervention.” I did not prescribe it. The slide had still done work. It had made the pill feel like a thought I had had.

The sample drawer is the quietest corrupter. It is not a bribe; it is convenience. I have prescribed a sample because it was in front of me, and then I had to learn the drug by using it. The company had not paid me. It had paid my laziness, which is the same wallet. A drug in the drawer becomes a drug in the habit. A drug in the habit becomes a drug the patient asks for by brand name, because the doctor once said the name easily.

There are also campaigns that make a condition more common. If a disease is rare, you hesitate. If it is a public health issue, you screen. The campaign does not have to be false. It only has to move the condition from “odd thing this patient has” to “thing we should look for.” Then the pill becomes a reasonable next sentence. I remember a grand round on anxiety. The speaker spent twenty minutes on a benzodiazepine’s half-life and then an hour on a new anxiolytic that was “different.” By the end, the room was full of doctors who had not decided the drug was good. They had decided the old problem was interesting again.

You can object that this is all too soft. If money changes minds, it should change them clearly. Doctors should be seen arguing for bad drugs, defending obvious fraud, writing glowing essays about products that do not work. Sometimes that happens. But the more efficient form of influence does not require a doctor to become a liar. It requires a doctor to become a regular. A regular is someone who uses a drug a little more often, prescribes it earlier, calls its side effects manageable, and hears its brand name in his head before the generic name. The change is so small it never appears on a ballot.

A speaker fee is a strange kind of endorsement. It says: this person was paid, therefore this person is important. In a field where importance is mostly reputation, that is enough. The fee does not have to buy the speaker’s conclusions. It buys the audience’s posture. We lean forward. We take notes. We stop asking the question that would make the lunch feel awkward.

Guidelines are supposed to be the fix. But guidelines are written by people who have conflicts, and the conflicts are disclosed, which is like putting a “paid actor” sign on the actor and asking the audience to enjoy the play. Disclosure is not the same as removal. It tells you the lighting is rigged; it does not move the light. We get ethics modules that say: refuse meals, refuse gifts, avoid speaker fees. I do. The module assumes the corrupting object is the object. In practice the corrupting object is the conversation. You can refuse the pen and still buy the idea.

I am not immune because I am young and poor. I prescribe what I can remember. At 7 p.m., after a hard admission, I do not read the literature. I remember the last person who made a treatment option sound simple. If that person was an attending who had a relationship with a company, the option is now wearing a nice jacket. I do not know which of my clinical instincts are mine. I know the direction of the wind: the option that is easiest to discuss is the one that has been discussed the most, in rooms with good bread, by people who look like they know what they are doing, while the rest of us are trying to keep patients alive before the next shift.

I have mostly stopped taking the meal. It is not a noble stance. It is a small way of noticing where the money is before it notices me. The industry does not need to make me prescribe. It needs to make the prescription available in my mind at the moment I am tired. I would rather be hungry and slow than fed and convenient.
