prompt: I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
response:
## I Used to Think Design Docs Were Pointless

For years, when someone asked me for a design document, my first thought was: you want me to write a novel before I’m allowed to find out whether the thing is possible.

I was not opposed to thinking. I was opposed to formalizing thought before the thought had hardened. In my head, the workflow was simple: build the smallest version, watch it fail, learn what actually mattered, then build the real thing. If the design was obvious, writing it down was ceremony. If it was not obvious, writing it down would only make me feel more certain than I had any right to be.

I got grumpy because I believed code was the honest medium. Code either worked or it did not. A document could be polite, confident, and wrong.

That belief served me for a while. It also got me into trouble in the quiet way that bad assumptions do.

The change was not dramatic. I did not wake up one day as a design-document person. What changed was that I started seeing the value in the writing, not the artifact.

A few years ago, we were adding retries to a background job system. The plan seemed straightforward: if a job failed, put it back in the queue with a delay. Exponential backoff. A maximum number of attempts. I had built things like this before. I started implementing it and only wrote a short note because someone asked.

The note had a section called “assumptions,” because the template insisted on one. I wrote: “We assume failed jobs can be safely retried.”

Then I stopped.

Some could. Some could not. One job marked an order as paid after calling a payment provider. If the provider call succeeded but our database update failed, a retry would call the provider again. Another job sent an email. Retrying that was annoying but survivable. A third job updated inventory. Retrying that after a partial success could make the numbers worse, not better.

I had not thought that through because the first version of the idea felt obvious. Writing the assumption forced me to ask whether it was true for every job in the queue, not just the ones I was thinking about.

The design document did not save me because it was well written. It saved me because I had to make my uncertainty visible.

That was the first crack.

After that, I started writing shorter notes for myself before starting work that felt “mostly obvious.” Not full documents. Sometimes just a few bullets in a scratch file: what I thought the problem was, what I was assuming, what I intended to ignore, and what would make me stop and reconsider.

Most of the time, the note was boring. I wrote it, nodded at it, and started coding. But sometimes it caught a seam.

Once, I was adding a field to an API response. I wrote down that older clients would ignore it. Then I remembered that one internal client parsed JSON strictly and had bitten us before. That changed the rollout plan.

Another time, I was caching expensive query results. I wrote that invalidation would happen on write. Then I asked how the cache would know which entries were affected by a bulk update. The answer was ugly enough that we chose a shorter TTL and accepted the stale reads.

These were not heroic discoveries. They were small, local failures of imagination. But they were exactly the kind of thing that is easy to miss when you are moving from idea to implementation in one continuous mental motion.

I also started noticing what code does not tell you.

If you look at a retry loop in production, you can see that it retries. You can see the delay. You can see the maximum attempts. You cannot see why there is no immediate retry, why the maximum is five instead of three, or what failure mode convinced us to make the endpoint idempotent. The code tells you what the system does. It does not tell you what the system is afraid of.

Design documents are usually bad at recording history, but even a bad record of why can be useful. Six months later, when someone wants to change the backoff, a note that says “we lowered this because a slow partner service caused duplicate webhooks” is worth more than no note. It turns a tuning decision into a remembered incident.

The hardest objection I still have is this: if the document is going to rot, it is worse than useless.

I think that is true for a lot of documents. I have read design docs that described systems that no longer existed, with diagrams of services that had been renamed, and decisions that had been reversed twice. Those docs are not just outdated; they are misleading. They make the past look more deliberate than it was.

So I do not write design docs for everything.

If the change is small and reversible, I just make it. If I am renaming a function, adjusting a threshold, fixing an obvious bug, or moving code between files, a document would be noise. If I am exploring an unknown area, I often build a throwaway probe first. I let the prototype answer the questions that are too cheap to guess at. Then, if the direction seems right and the consequences are large enough, I write down what I have learned.

The threshold is not complexity. It is reversibility and blast radius.

I write something down when the change is hard to undo, when it touches other teams, when it changes data semantics, when it affects security or money, or when I am not confident that my first idea is the right one. A new internal utility function does not need a design doc. A migration that changes how customer data is interpreted does.

That sounds reasonable, but it is not enough. A lot of bad design docs are written for exactly the right reasons and still fail.

The difference is what I am trying to get out of them.

I no longer write design docs as if they are contracts. I write them as a way to test my own understanding before I invest a week in implementation. The document is not the product. The product is the set of questions I noticed.

That changes the structure.

I avoid long narrative introductions. I start with the problem in one paragraph: what is annoying, broken, or missing, and why now. Then I write what we are not doing. That section is more useful than people expect. “We are not adding multi-tenancy to this service” can prevent an afternoon of discussion. “We are not optimizing the cold path yet” can stop someone from designing a caching layer for a case that happens twice a day.

Then I write assumptions. This is the part I care about most.

Assumptions are where designs die. We assume the input is valid. We assume the external service is available. We assume the user will not do the weird thing. We assume the database transaction will behave the way the docs say. We assume the team that owns the dependency will ship their part on time. Each of those can be true, but if it is not written down, it has not been examined.

I try to phrase assumptions so they can be broken. Not “the API is reliable,” but “we assume the identity service returns within 200ms for p95 traffic during rollout.” Not “users will migrate cleanly,” but “we assume clients will send the new header after the feature flag is enabled.” Vague assumptions are just vibes with better posture.

Then I write options. I used to think options sections were padding, because usually one option was already preferred and the others were included for show. That is true often. But even a fake options section can be useful if it forces you to say what the rejected alternative would have cost.

The best option comparisons are short. They are not essays. They are tradeoffs:

- Option A is simpler but requires a schema migration.
- Option B avoids the migration but adds a race condition during rollout.
- Option C is the most correct but needs another team to change their API.

If you cannot summarize the tradeoff in a sentence, you probably do not understand the option well enough yet.

Then I write the decision, and what would change it.

This is important. A decision without an exit condition becomes a habit. “We will use feature flags for the rollout” is fine. “We will use feature flags unless we find that the old code path cannot be safely run in parallel” is better. The second version gives future me a rule instead of a memory.

I also include risks and open questions, but only the ones that matter. A risk list full of “there may be bugs” is not a risk list. It is a prayer. I want to know what would make this design wrong, and who is responsible for finding out.

If there is an open question, it needs an owner and a deadline, or it should not be in the document. Open questions without owners become ambient anxiety. Everyone knows something is unresolved, and no one knows what.

I have learned to keep the whole thing small. If the design doc needs a table of contents, I have probably made the problem too big or the writing too vague. One screen, maybe two, is usually enough. If I need five pages to explain what we are doing, I either need diagrams or I need to split the project.

Diagrams are useful when they replace paragraphs. A box diagram of service calls can be worth a lot. A diagram that repeats the prose in prettier shapes is not. The same goes for examples. One concrete request/response pair can clarify an API design faster than several abstract sentences.

Review is where most design docs go to die.

If the review is just “please leave comments,” people will check spelling, suggest minor rephrasings, and approve. The document becomes a social object. I want it to be a stress test.

I ask reviewers to find the first place it breaks. What input kills this? What failure mode makes the retry dangerous? What happens at ten times the traffic? What happens when the dependency team is on vacation? What happens when the operator does the obvious wrong thing at 2 a.m.? What assumption is most likely to be false?

That is not hostile. It is the point. A design review that only produces compliments has not done much work.

I also try to separate the review of the problem from the review of the solution. Sometimes the proposed design is fine, but the problem was framed wrong. “Users are logging in slowly” may lead to a session-cache design when the real issue is that password verification is doing synchronous work in the request path. If everyone attacks the cache, the wrong framing survives.

After implementation, I used to think the document’s job was done. Now I treat it differently.

If the design changes in a way that matters, I update the document or mark it stale. I do not try to keep it line-by-line synchronized with the code. That is a losing game. But if the original decision was “we avoid denormalization because writes are rare” and writes are no longer rare, the document should say so. Otherwise it actively misleads.

Sometimes the right update is deletion. If the system has stabilized and the decision is now just part of the codebase’s folklore, the doc can be archived. If it describes a dead approach, leaving it in the main folder is a trap.

I still do not enjoy writing design docs as much as I enjoy writing code. Code gives immediate feedback. Documents ask you to sit with uncertainty and admit it in public.

But I have stopped thinking of them as pointless because I have stopped expecting them to be magic. They do not guarantee good designs. They do not prevent bad decisions. They do not make engineering easier in the way that a good linter or test suite makes it easier.

What they do is change the timing of your mistakes.

A bad assumption discovered in a local branch is cheap. A bad assumption discovered in staging is annoying. A bad assumption discovered in production, during a rollout, on a Friday, is a story people will tell later. prompt: Why doesn't paying people bonuses for specific results work well for managing knowledge workers? Write an essay for new managers who just took an economics class.
response:
You have just learned the clean version of management. The firm wants a worker to exert effort. Effort is costly to the worker and hard to observe. If the worker is paid a fixed salary, the worker may relax. The fix is to make pay depend on output. This is the principal-agent idea, and it is one of the most useful ideas in economics. It is also the reason a new manager looks at a knowledge worker and thinks: let us pay a bonus for the result.

The clean version has an assumption hiding in it: output is measurable. For a trucking company, that assumption is close to true. Miles driven, ton-miles, accidents, fuel use, on-time delivery. For a call center, calls handled and satisfaction scores are imperfect but administrable. For a software engineer, a researcher, a lawyer, a designer, a product manager, the assumption breaks. The valuable output is not a single number. It is a bundle: a solution that works, a system that remains maintainable, a client who trusts the advice, a team that learns, a decision that pays off next year. You can pay for parts of the bundle. You cannot pay for the bundle without judgment.

A bonus forces you to choose one part. To be fair and objective, it must be specific. So you pick a proxy: revenue, churn, features shipped, bug count, citations, client score, cost savings. The proxy is a shadow of value. When you attach money to the shadow, people walk toward the shadow.

Suppose you manage a subscription product and promise the analytics team a $20,000 bonus if monthly churn falls from 4.0 percent to 3.5 percent by December. The team now knows that the number is the job, not customer health. The easiest ways to move churn may have little to do with making the product better: reclassify trial accounts so they stop counting, give a discount to a small group of customers who were already wavering, fix a narrow billing error that affects a few hundred users, or smooth the monthly measurement by timing renewals. The harder work—improving onboarding, fixing a confusing core workflow, building a feature that makes the service genuinely useful—may take longer and may not show up in time. By December, the target can be hit while the company still leaks customers. The bonus has not measured performance; it has selected a particular kind of performance.

There is also the cliff. If the bonus is all-or-nothing, effort is lumpy. If the team believes it can get churn to 3.7 percent but not 3.5, the last 0.2 points may not be worth the cost. If it believes the target is easy, it may not stretch. Knowledge work usually comes in degrees, but many bonus schemes pay for a threshold.

The economics class may have mentioned moral hazard. A more practical version is multi-tasking. A knowledge worker rarely has one task. An engineer ships features, keeps the system stable, writes maintainable code, helps teammates, and learns the domain. A lawyer drafts documents, manages client risk, develops strategy, and builds the firm’s reputation. A product manager writes specs, talks to customers, resolves conflicts, and decides what not to build. You can put one of these tasks in a bonus. You cannot put all of them in without turning the contract into a novel.

When one task is paid and the others are not, effort moves. If engineers get a bonus for features shipped, they will rationally spend less time on stability, architecture, and mentoring, because those tasks do not earn the bonus and may even slow shipping. If you add a metric for bugs, they will avoid risky but valuable work, declare edge cases out of scope, or treat testing as a threat because testing finds bugs. If you add a metric for code-review comments, reviews become political. Each new metric solves one distortion and creates another. The manager who wanted to measure performance has instead chosen a tradeoff, often without realizing it.

The bonus also changes attention. For routine work, paying for a result is usually fine: do more of the thing. For work that requires exploration, a reward can narrow the search. A programmer offered a bonus for fixing a bug may stop at the first plausible fix rather than the robust one. A researcher offered a bonus for publications may choose the safe, incremental paper over the risky project that could matter. The reward does not merely add motivation; it changes the kind of work people do.

Knowledge work is also team work. A product launch depends on engineers, designers, data analysts, marketers, and sales. A research project depends on assistants, collaborators, equipment, and institutional reputation. A client engagement depends on partners, associates, and the firm’s prior relationships. If the bonus is individual but the result is collective, people spend energy taking credit or avoiding blame. If the bonus is team-based, strong performers may feel they are subsidizing weak ones, and weak performers may rely on the team. The manager who wanted alignment gets a negotiation about who contributed what.

Even when the metric is the right thing, it is noisy. A salesperson’s revenue depends on the accounts they inherit, the economy, the product cycle, and the timing of competitors. A researcher’s output depends on referees, data availability, and luck. A support engineer’s satisfaction scores depend partly on customers’ moods. If pay swings with luck, risk-averse workers will either demand a higher salary or choose lower-variance work. The researcher takes the incremental paper, not the risky project that could matter. The salesperson works the safe accounts, not the hard prospect. The bonus was supposed to reward excellence; it has made excellence less attractive.

A bonus also has a date. Knowledge work often pays off slowly. Code quality, institutional knowledge, customer trust, and research capability compound. A manager evaluated on this year’s revenue may cut training, defer maintenance, overpromise to customers, or avoid hiring because hiring depresses short-term productivity. The bonus makes the future expensive. If you move the metric to a longer horizon, it becomes too noisy and too delayed to guide behavior; people cannot connect today’s choices to a reward in five years.

This does not mean money is irrelevant, or that all performance pay fails. Sales commissions work reasonably well when revenue is a close proxy for value and when bad sales can be detected later through refunds, churn, or complaints. Equity can align people with the firm’s long-run success, but it is a claim on the whole firm, not a fine-grained lever for this quarter’s project, and it is diluted by luck and market moves. Academic tenure uses judgment and peer review precisely because the valuable output cannot be reduced to a formula. The pattern is that incentives work best where the measure is close to the value, where feedback is fast, and where gaming is hard. Knowledge work is often the opposite.

Bonuses are popular partly because they shift the burden of judgment from the manager to the formula. A manager who cannot articulate what good work is can still write a target. That is the appeal and the danger. The formula seems fair because everyone can see it, but people often accept a metric because they understand it, not because it captures performance. A bad bonus can become durable simply because it is transparent.

For a new manager, the practical lesson is not to abandon incentives but to stop expecting a bonus to do the thinking. Set clear goals, but keep the money modest enough that people still care about the work. Use promotion, pay raises, and assignment of interesting projects as the main long-term incentives, because those are based on accumulated judgment. If you use a bonus, attach it to something durable and hard to fake, share it across the team when the work is collective, and review the metric often enough to catch the distortion before it becomes culture. The most important management task is not to find the right number. It is to see which unmeasured behaviors are disappearing, and to reward those before the number wins.

prompt: People picture nerds as meek, but some of the most competitive people I know are nerds. Write an essay about this fierce type of nerd: what they're like, why it works for them, and some advice for young people who recognize themselves in it.
response:
The meek nerd is a social creature, and the stereotype is mostly about social behavior. It is the kid who looks down when someone mocks his shoes, who answers a question in class only when called on, who seems more interested in the object in front of him than in the people around him. That image is incomplete because it mistakes the absence of social performance for the absence of drive. Some nerds are not meek at all. They are quiet in the hallway and ruthless at the desk. They may not raise their voices, but they will stay after everyone else has left. They may let a joke pass without responding, but they will not let a mistake stand. Their fierceness does not announce itself. It shows up in the work.

A fierce nerd is usually someone who has found a domain with real structure. It might be mathematics, programming, chess, music, debate, science, a sport, a game, a body of knowledge, or a craft. The domain has rules, standards, and feedback. You can be good or bad. You can be better next month. You can compare your work to a benchmark, a teacher, a rival, a past version of yourself. In that kind of world, the nerd’s temperament becomes an advantage. He likes the rules because the rules make excellence reachable. He likes difficulty because difficulty is a form of clarity. He likes being measured because measurement tells him what to do next. A person who wants to be liked has to manage impressions. A person who wants to be good can often manage a problem.

This is why the fierce nerd can be so effective. In many important fields, the work is not a single burst of brilliance. It is long, unglamorous, and technical. You have to read dense material, debug failures, revise drafts, run experiments, practice the same position or passage or problem until it stops being strange. The fierce nerd is often not the smartest person in the room, but he is the one who treats the next level of difficulty as his natural environment. When a project fails, he does not only feel shame; he looks for the cause. When a peer does better, he does not only feel envy; he studies what the peer did. He is willing to be bored for long enough to get good. That willingness is rarer than talent.

There is also a practical advantage in the way fierce nerds often think. They tend to break big goals into smaller ones. If the goal is to build a program, the subgoals are the data structure, the interface, the edge cases, the tests. If the goal is to understand a subject, the subgoals are the definitions, the examples, the problems, the counterexamples. If the goal is to improve at a game, the subgoals are opening, tactics, endgame, review. This kind of thinking works because large ambitions are too vague to motivate action. A person who says, “I want to be great,” may not know what to do on Tuesday afternoon. A person who says, “I want to solve three of these problems before dinner,” can begin. The fierce nerd’s competitiveness is often less about beating people than about moving through a sequence of harder tasks.

But the same traits that make this type effective can make him brittle. The hardest objection to the fierce nerd is not that he is intense. Intensity can be a strength. The objection is that he may make his self-worth depend on being good. If his identity is “the smart one,” “the best player,” “the one who gets it fastest,” then every ordinary setback becomes a threat to who he thinks he is. A student who has been first in his school may arrive at a harder school and discover that everyone else has studied longer, had better teachers, or simply had more time. If his confidence was built on ranking, he may stall. If his confidence was built on process, he can ask for help, do the work, and wait.

This fragility often shows up socially. A competitive nerd can become mean in small ways. He can correct people when they do not want to be corrected. He can use technical knowledge as a weapon in an argument that is really about respect. He can treat collaboration as a threat, because collaboration means sharing control, credit, and the chance to be the one who figures it out. He can mistake being right for being good. In a team, that is costly. A project succeeds when the people on it can think clearly, communicate, and trust one another. If your need to be right makes others afraid to speak, you have improved your argument and damaged the work. The fierce nerd who does not learn this will find that he can win pieces and lose the game.

There is another risk: choosing the wrong arena. Competitiveness is a tool, and a tool can be used badly. If a young person is fierce but puts that fierceness into a domain with poor feedback, he may become exhausted without becoming better. Online arguments are a common example. They feel competitive, but the rules are unclear, the audience is unstable, and the skill rewarded is often not wisdom but speed, volume, or cruelty. Gossip works the same way. Status games work the same way. You can be very competitive in a space where the score is fake. The fierce nerd needs a field where the standard is external enough to resist his ego. A mathematical proof either works or it does not. A piece of code either runs or it does not. A musical passage either sounds good to a teacher or it does not. The feedback has to be honest, or the competition only trains you to perform.

For a young person who recognizes this type in himself, the first piece of advice is to find a measure you can trust. Not a measure that makes you feel superior, but one that tells you what is true. It can be a test, a portfolio, a game record, a physical test, a body of written work, a teacher’s assessment, a customer’s response. The measure should be hard enough that you cannot fool it for long. If you are drawn to programming, do not only chase puzzles that make you feel clever. Build something someone can use. If you are drawn to debate, practice listening as carefully as you practice arguing. If you are drawn to music, practice the boring parts, the scales and the rhythms, because they are the parts that let you play the hard parts. The fierce nerd should want to be measured, but he should choose the measurement wisely.

The second piece of advice is to keep your identity broader than your best result. This is not a soft idea. It is a survival strategy. If you are only the person who wins, then losing is not an event; it is an annihilation. You need some parts of yourself that are not tied to performance: a friendship that survives your mood, a physical habit that keeps your body from becoming a nervous wreck, a curiosity that allows you to explore something without immediately ranking it, a sense of humor that can loosen the grip of taking yourself too seriously. The fiercest competitors I have seen are not the ones who cannot afford to lose. They are the ones who can lose badly, sleep on it, and still show up the next day with their standards intact.

The third piece of advice is to practice losing without becoming a victim of it. After a loss, the first question should not be, “What does this mean about me?” The first question should be, “What happened?” In a game, that means reviewing the position where you went wrong. In a school subject, it means finding the problem you thought you understood and discovering that you did not. In a creative work, it means asking why the piece fell flat, not just deciding that the audience was dumb. In a relationship, it means asking whether your intensity made the other person feel attacked. This is unglamorous. It requires you to be humble enough to read the evidence and proud enough to act on it. The fierce nerd who skips this step will keep making the same mistakes and calling them bad luck.

The fourth piece of advice is to compete with your own past as often as you compete with other people. Other people are useful benchmarks, but they are also noisy. They have different backgrounds, different advantages, different moods, different reasons for being where they are. If you spend all your energy measuring yourself against them, you become dependent on their performance. If you keep a record of your own work, you develop a steadier sense of progress. Six months ago you could not do that. Now you can. That is a fact. It does not require an audience. It does not require that the person next to you be worse. The young fierce nerd who learns to trust his own trajectory becomes harder to rattle.

Finally, learn to make other people look good. This is the hardest lesson, because it feels like giving up part of the contest. But the world does not reward only the best individual. It rewards people who can coordinate, teach, persuade, and build. If you can explain a difficult idea so that a weaker person understands it, you have become stronger, not weaker. If you can notice what someone else did well and say it plainly, you become someone people want to work with. If you can be right without making the other person feel stupid, you preserve the relationship for the next problem. A fierce nerd who cannot do this will always be somewhat alone in his excellence, and excellence without relationships tends to curdle into pride.

The meek stereotype misses the point because it focuses on the social surface. The fierce nerd is not defined by whether he stands up to a bully in the cafeteria. He is defined by whether he can do hard work, accept honest feedback, and keep improving. That is a real kind of strength, but it is not a complete one. It needs judgment, humility, and a life that is not reduced to a scoreboard. If a young person can build those alongside the competitiveness, he becomes something much more useful than a winner. He becomes someone who can sit down at the board, read the position, and make the next move.

prompt: Write a short, sharp essay on the slogan 'the purpose of a system is what it does.' Is it actually a good rule of thumb, or does it break down when you try it on hospitals, militaries, governments and bus systems?
response:
**What It Does, and What It Is For**

The slogan sounds like a correction to institutional self-deception. A hospital says it exists for patient care; a city says its buses exist for mobility; a ministry says it exists for the public interest. The slogan tells us to stop listening and watch the cash flows, schedules, promotions, and routines. In that limited sense it is good. Institutions are revealed by what they reward. A hospital that spends more on billing software than on nursing, a bus agency that plans routes around contracts rather than riders, a government that writes laws around donor access: their behavior shows where the real gravity is.

But “where the real gravity is” is not the same as “the purpose.” The slogan collapses three different questions into one: what was this system made for, what does it reliably do, and what would count as its failure? A bus system is made to move people. It reliably produces delays, employment, noise, and land values. If it is late so often that riders keep cars, the delays are not its purpose; they are the way it fails. To call lateness the purpose is to mistake a symptom for a design. The slogan works only when we already know which outputs are central and which are accidental. Without that distinction, it becomes a tautology: whatever the system does, by definition, is what it is for.

Hospitals make the distinction vivid. A hospital’s purpose includes diagnosing illness, treating it, and not causing avoidable harm. It also does many other things: it generates insurance claims, creates specialist careers, produces medical journals, and sometimes produces malpractice suits. If a hospital saves most of the patients it should save but spends a large share of its energy on billing, the slogan may be right that billing is a major function. It is wrong if we conclude that the hospital’s purpose is billing. Billing can be a necessary cost, a captured incentive, or a failure of management. We tell the difference by asking what would make the hospital unacceptable. A perfect billing machine that misses sepsis is not a successful hospital doing a different job; it is a bad hospital.

Militaries are harder because their purposes are less pure and their effects more violent. A military is supposed to defend a polity, but it also employs people, buys aircraft, trains soldiers, occupies territory, and sometimes decides elections. If a small state’s army spends most of its time on disaster relief, the slogan may correctly describe its actual role in society. But that does not make disaster relief the purpose of a military. It may make the army a useful civic institution and a poor military. The test is still counterfactual: if invasion came and the army could not fight, the disaster-relief function would not rescue it. The slogan can reveal that an institution has drifted from its reason for existing. It cannot tell us, from behavior alone, that the drift is acceptable.

Governments are the case where the slogan becomes dangerous. A government that taxes, judges, defends, and provides roads is doing many things. A government that mostly taxes to enrich a ruling group is also doing something. If purpose is simply what a system does, corruption stops being a deviation from government and becomes a form of government. That may sometimes be true in the narrow sense: a predatory regime is a kind of state. But it is false as a rule for judging systems. We can still say that the purpose of government includes legitimate authority, predictable law, and the protection of people from arbitrary power. When a state fails those standards, it is not discovering a new purpose; it is failing. The slogan, taken literally, removes the standard.

Bus systems show the same problem at a smaller scale. A transit agency exists to give people reliable movement. It also supports property values, gives jobs to drivers, and shapes urban form. If its buses are unreliable, people stop using them; if they stop using them, the agency loses its reason for public funding. The slogan might say that the system’s purpose is to create a class of people who must wait, because waiting is what it reliably makes them do. That is a caustic observation, not a definition. It tells us the system is failing at its purpose, not that the purpose has changed to produce failure.

The strongest objection to this qualification is that it is soft. If we always reserve the right to say “that is not really the purpose,” the slogan loses its bite. We can answer that by making the test concrete. A system’s purpose is not a motto; it is the set of performances for which the system is maintained and the set of failures that would justify shutting it down or replacing it. A hospital is maintained because it treats people. A military is maintained because it can fight, or at least deter. A government is maintained because it commands obedience through recognized rules, not merely force. A bus system is maintained because it moves people more cheaply or more equitably than alternatives. When behavior diverges from those performances, the slogan rightly forces us to look. But the divergence is measured against a standard that behavior alone cannot supply.

The slogan is therefore a good rule of thumb and a bad definition. Use it to inspect institutions: follow the outputs, the incentives, and the routines. Do not use it to define them. A system’s purpose is what it is for; what it does is the evidence by which we judge whether it is succeeding. If we make the evidence the standard, every dysfunction becomes a function, every abuse becomes a design, and the only honest response left is cynicism.

prompt: It's January and I'm in a cranky mood about internet culture. Write a funny, opinionated blog post listing the habits, words and jokes you would most like to see disappear from the internet this year.
response:
# The January Internet Cleanup List

I’m in that January mood where I only want sensible things: warm socks, a functioning oven, and a comment section that doesn’t feel like a group project. I don’t want the internet to disappear. I want it to stop performing. I want people to be allowed to say “that was bad” without turning it into a brand, a mood, a lore, and a short film.

The fair objection is that I’m just mad because language moved and I didn’t buy the upgrade. Maybe. But novelty isn’t the problem. The problem is that a lot of these phrases have stopped describing things and started replacing them. A feeling becomes a sticker. A sentence becomes a brand. A comment becomes a performance. I don’t want the internet to be boring. I want it to be a little less like a trade show where everyone is selling me their personality and the exit is behind a curtain of vibes.

So here are the things I would most like to see disappear this year.

## Words

- **“It’s giving…”** Please stop describing every object, outfit, and minor inconvenience as if it is a runway show. A parking meter is not giving. A soup can is not giving. A person who talks over you in a meeting is not giving “unhinged CEO energy”; they are giving you a reason to remember their name for the rest of the fiscal year. We used to have adjectives. They were boring, reliable, and they didn’t require a follow-up video.

- **“Era”** My whole personality is not an era. If every Tuesday is a “self-care era” and every payday is a “baddie era”, then nothing is actually happening. You are not evolving; you are rebranding. I miss when people could say “I’m feeling lazy” without announcing a season.

- **“No cap,” “fr fr,” “lowkey,” “highkey”** I don’t want a calibration of your sincerity. I want to know if you’re serious. If you’re serious, say it. If you’re not serious, don’t post it. “Lowkey” has become the internet’s favorite way to say, “I’m about to be dramatic, but I’d like a discount on the consequences.”

- **“Based”** A based comment is a comment that has given up on being a sentence. If someone says a dress is based, I need to know whether they mean it’s well-made, brave, terrible, or if they have simply discovered the word “based” and intend to use it until the heat death of the universe. Praise should mean something. “Good” is still available.

- **“Rizz,” “mewing,” “looksmaxxing”** The new grammar school of the internet is not teaching language; it is teaching half the internet to treat conversation like a speedrun. “She had rizz” used to be a joke. Now it is a review. “He was mewing” used to be a nonsense gesture. Now it is a social audit. I would like people to be allowed to talk to each other without being graded on their jawline and their “game.”

- **“Delulu is the solulu”** Romanticizing delusion is not a strategy. It is a waiting room. If your plan is to believe so hard that reality gets embarrassed, I am concerned. Wish, plan, save, text, call a lawyer. Do not turn your own denial into a slogan.

- **“Ate,” “left no crumbs,” “understood the assignment”** I did not come online to attend a food-service review of a celebrity’s outfit. If someone “ate,” I need to know what they ate and whether the plate is clean. If they “understood the assignment,” I want to see the assignment. Most of the time the assignment was “show up in public,” and the bar is on the floor.

- **“Main character” / “NPC”** Everyone is the main character and everyone else is an NPC. This is not a narrative structure; it is a permission slip to ignore people. The bus driver is not an NPC. The cashier is not background dialogue. If you are calling someone an NPC, you are mostly explaining why you don’t intend to be nice to them.

## Habits

- **“Hot take”** A hot take is a lukewarm opinion served with a warning label. “Hot take: I like pineapple on pizza.” No. You don’t get the foam. You don’t get the dramatic pause. You don’t get to frame a preference as a political stance. If you have a hot take, heat it up. If it’s just “I prefer this,” say that and pass the bread.

- **“I’m sure this will be controversial”** If you need to announce that you’re about to be annoying, you have already lost. The controversy is not a surprise; it is the product. You are not sharing a risk. You are handing me a live grenade and asking if I think the pin looks nice.

- **“Anyway…”** The word “anyway” is often a door slamming in someone else’s face. Person A has a complicated, sad, or simply long point. Person B says “anyway” and suddenly we are in Person B’s much simpler story. Please do not use “anyway” to evict someone from a conversation they were having.

- **“This is why we can’t have nice things”** It is a small, sad surrender, and it is wrong. Nice things are not being withheld from us by one person’s bad driving, one coworker’s bad email, or one stranger’s bad opinion of a movie. We can have nice things. Sometimes we just have to wait for the other car to finish being an idiot.

- **“At the end of the day”** There is no end of the day. There is only more of it. There is the evening, the dishes, the second wind, the 11 p.m. thought that ruins the night. If you’re going to wrap up a take, wrap it up. Don’t pretend the day has a neat little bow just because your attention span did.

- **Rage-bait** Please stop posting pictures of a man wearing a tank top in the snow and asking if it’s “unhinged.” I know it is. I have eyes. I do not need a poll. I do not need a comment section. I need you to use the internet to share something that didn’t cost me ninety seconds of blood pressure.

- **Autoplay** Autoplay is the internet’s way of saying, “I don’t trust you to choose what you want to hear.” I did not ask for the video. I did not ask for the sound. I did not ask for the man in the video to tell me his opinion of a sandwich. If you want me to watch, ask. If you want me to listen, lower your voice.

## Jokes

- **“I’m not a morning person”** I am not a morning person. I am a person who is awake in the morning. The sun does not care about your brand. The alarm does not care about your “era.” If you are grumpy at 7 a.m., you are not a creature of the night; you are a mammal who needs coffee and possibly boundaries.

- **“I run on caffeine and anxiety”** This is not a personality; it is a medical warning. If everyone is a feral raccoon in a blazer, we need to talk about the blazer and the raccoon. You are allowed to be tired. You are less allowed to make a merch line out of your nervous system.

- **“I’m just a [girl/guy/person] who [harmless hobby]”** I’m not just a person who likes coffee. I’m a person who is tired and wants to buy a croissant. I’m not just a person who works in marketing. I’m a person who is pretending to understand the word “synergy.” Stop reducing yourself to a single cute noun. You are allowed to be a whole, slightly incoherent human being with several interests and at least one bad habit.

If you make it through the year without saying “it’s giving,” I’ll believe it when I see it. And if you do, I will not say it’s giving. I will say: stop.

# The January Internet Cleanup List

I’m in that January mood where I only want sensible things: warm socks, a functioning oven, and a comment section that doesn’t feel like a group project. I don’t want the internet to disappear. I want it to stop performing. I want people to be allowed to say “that was bad” without turning it into a brand, a mood, a lore, and a short film.

The fair objection is that I’m just mad because language moved and I didn’t buy the upgrade. Maybe. But novelty isn’t the problem. The problem is that a lot of these phrases have stopped describing things and started replacing them. A feeling becomes a sticker. A sentence becomes a brand. A comment becomes a performance. I don’t want the internet to be boring. I want it to be a little less like a trade show where everyone is selling me their personality and the exit is behind a curtain of vibes.

So here are the things I would most like to see disappear this year.

## Words

- **“It’s giving…”** Please stop describing every object, outfit, and minor inconvenience as if it is a runway show. A parking meter is not giving. A soup can is not giving. A person who talks over you in a meeting is not giving “unhinged CEO energy”; they are giving you a reason to remember their name for the rest of the fiscal year. We used to have adjectives. prompt: Argue that identity and personal history are stories we over-trust, and that people should reinvent themselves on purpose. Short punchy lines.
response:
Identity is a story we tell because memory is a mess.  
We keep the details that fit the plot and throw out the rest.  
You were shy at twelve.  
You once talked for an hour with a stranger who needed help.  
Which one is real?  
Both.  
Neither, if you freeze one.

Personal history is evidence.  
Not destiny.  
A failure at twenty is data about a young person, not a verdict on the person at forty.  
A success at twenty-five is data about luck, training and timing, not proof you will never need to start over.

We over-trust the story because it is convenient.  
It lets us say “that is just who I am” and stop examining the evidence.  
It lets others say “he would never” or “she always does that” and skip the present.

The hardest objection is real.  
If identity can be chosen, responsibility can be escaped.  
A person who harms someone cannot reinvent their way out of the harm.  
The deed remains.  
The answer remains.  
Reinvention is not a pardon.  
It is a change in what a person does next, under the same name, with the same debts visible.

That is why reinvention must be on purpose.  
Drift is not freedom.  
Drift is what happens when the old story cracks and no one is steering.  
Purposeful change is different.  
You name the version you want to become.  
You make a choice that version would make.  
You repeat it until it produces evidence.

A person who spent twenty years in a career they no longer want is not trapped by a fact.  
They are trapped by a label.  
The label says “that is what I am.”  
The fact says “this is what I have done.”  
Those are not the same.

A woman who was a reliable employee for a decade may be unable to keep the hours after a health change.  
Her history says she is reliable.  
Her body says no.  
The body is the newer witness.

A man who was a top student may find he is better at a trade than at an office job.  
The old story calls it falling.  
The work calls it fitting.

Reinvention is not pretending the past did not happen.  
It is refusing to let the past vote on every future decision.  
You keep the lessons.  
You drop the costume.

You should do it deliberately because the alternative is not stability.  
It is slow capture.  
The story tightens.  
The options shrink.  
People start acting against their interests because “that is not who I am.”

Choose a new pattern.  
Act in it.  
Let the evidence update the story.  
Do not wait for the story to allow the change.  
Make the change first, and force the story to catch up.

prompt: A TV personality got into trouble for describing a grotesque hypothetical to make a point about atheists and morality, and everyone's outraged. As someone with a philosophy background, how do you think about extreme, disturbing thought experiments in general? Are they just morbid, or is there a real method to them? Write it as a blog post.
response:
A TV personality got into trouble for describing a grotesque hypothetical to make a point about atheists and morality. The exact wording matters, and I am not going to reconstruct it from fragments. But the reaction is easy to understand, and the underlying issue is older than cable news: what are we supposed to do with a deliberately disturbing case?

My first thought is not that everyone is too sensitive. My first thought is that the hypothetical was probably being used as a weapon, not as a tool. Those are different things, and the difference is the whole question.

A thought experiment is a small machine. You remove most of the world and leave a few parts. The trolley problem leaves a track, a lever, five people, and one person. The point is not to ask whether runaway trolleys are common. It is to ask what you care about when the numbers move in one direction and your agency moves in another. If you can pull a lever to divert a trolley from five people to one, many people say yes. If you can push a large man off a bridge to stop the trolley and save five, many say no. The death count is the same. The difference is whether you use a person as a means, whether you impose risk, whether you personally inflict harm. The case is crude, but it is not empty. It does not prove that you should pull the lever. It shows that “minimize deaths” is not the whole story.

Another standard case is less mechanical. A doctor has one healthy patient who could be killed and dissected to save five dying patients. The arithmetic looks like the trolley. Most people refuse. Again, the point is not about hospitals. It is about consent, rights, and the difference between allowing a death and causing one. These cases are extreme because ordinary moral life is too thick. If you say “don’t kill,” you may mean a rule, a preference, a religious command, a social norm, or a felt revulsion. In everyday situations those all agree. Edge cases pull them apart. If you believe every life has equal weight, the trolley should be easy. If it is not easy, something else is in your moral psychology. That is useful. The discomfort is not the product; the discrepancy is.

This is where television changes the problem. In a philosophy seminar, a disturbing hypothetical is a prompt to say, “Wait, why does that feel wrong?” On television, the feeling is the prompt. The goal is not to expose a tension in your principles but to produce a flinch you can point at and say, “See, you are moral, and here is why.”

That makes the atheist version especially suspect. If the hypothetical is something like “Would an atheist save a baby?” the answer is so boring it cannot support the intended claim. Almost no one wants to let a baby die. The case does not distinguish belief from unbelief. It distinguishes a human being from a monster. If the point is that atheists lack a foundation for morality, the hypothetical must show a place where the foundation matters. It needs a case in which a theist and an atheist, with the same facts, same character, same social influences, give different answers because of the belief. A baby in a fire is not that case.

There is a real philosophical question underneath all this: do moral obligations depend on a moral lawgiver? Some versions of religious ethics say yes, at least in a foundational sense. Secular ethics says no, or says the question is malformed. But a horror story does not decide it. It just shows that both sides want to save the baby. To decide the question, you need an argument about what “ought” means, not a scene designed to make the audience recoil.

The strongest objection to my view is that some thought experiments are not just uncomfortable; they are degrading. There are variants of the trolley in which the only way to save many people is to cause a sexual assault. There are cases that turn disabled people into burdens, or minorities into threats, or women into bodies to be traded. The philosopher who says “it’s just a hypothetical” has missed part of the point. Hypotheticals are not free of the world. They carry the speaker’s priorities. If a case is built by stripping a person of dignity until only their utility remains, the revulsion may be a serious response, not a failure of abstraction.

That does not mean we should stop asking hard questions. It means we need a test. Is the distress doing work? In the trolley, the distress about killing the one person helps reveal a constraint on utilitarian arithmetic. In a bad shock case, the distress is not revealing a constraint; it is being generated by the framing. If you can replace the grotesque detail with a neutral one and make the same argument, the detail was not doing work. If you cannot, the case may be genuinely hard, but it may also be asking you to accept a dehumanizing premise.

A useful thought experiment lets you turn the dials. Change five people to five hundred. Change a stranger to a child. Change certain death to a small risk. Change the actor from a bystander to a parent. If the answer stays exactly the same no matter what you change, you probably had a slogan, not a principle. If the answer shifts, the shifts are data. They tell you where your rule bends. This is also why public versions fail. A grotesque hypothetical repeats well. It lands, it offends, it gets quoted. A careful variation—“now suppose the five people are strangers and the one is your sister”—does not land. That is a defect of the medium, not of the method.

Thought experiments have another limit. They cannot tell you what atheists do. They cannot tell you whether religion makes people better citizens or whether moral behavior is more common in one group than another. Those are questions for history, sociology, and honest conversation. A hypothetical can clarify a concept: What do you mean by “ought”? What do you mean by “person”? What do you mean by “consent”? It can show that a position has consequences its holder may not want. It cannot, by itself, prove the position wrong.

So the outrage over the TV hypothetical is not a failure of philosophy. It is often a correct detection that the case was not a lever but a slap. When I encounter an extreme case, I try to ask what assumption is being tested, what a surprising answer would show, which details are load-bearing and which are just ugly, and whether the person asking the question would accept the same question if the roles were changed. If the case survives those questions, it is worth sitting with, even if it is unpleasant. If it does not, the proper response is not to pretend the discomfort is deep insight. It is to say: this is not a good example.

The method is not morbidity. It is the attempt to find out what a principle is for. A principle that cannot survive a change in the numbers, or a shift in who is affected, may be less a principle than a preference. A case that only works because it is ugly may be less a test than a performance. The outrage over the TV version is reasonable when it catches that difference.

A thought experiment is a small machine. You remove most of the world and leave a few parts. The trolley problem leaves a track, a lever, five people, and one person. The point is not to ask whether runaway trolleys are common. It is to ask what you care about when the numbers move in one direction and your agency moves in another. If you can pull a lever to divert a trolley from five people to one, many people say yes. If you can push a large man off a bridge to stop the trolley and save five, many say no. The death count is the same. The difference is whether you use a person as a means, whether you impose risk, whether you personally inflict harm. The case is crude, but it is not empty. It does not prove that you should pull the lever. It shows that “minimize deaths” is not the whole story.

Again, the point is not about hospitals. It is about consent, rights, and the difference between allowing a death and causing one. These cases are extreme because ordinary moral life is too thick. If you say “don’t kill,” you may mean a rule, a preference, a religious command, a social norm, or a felt revulsion. In everyday situations those all agree. Edge cases pull them apart. If you believe every life has equal weight, the trolley should be easy. If it is not easy, something else is in your moral psychology. That is useful. The discomfort is not the product; the discrepancy is.

This is where television changes the problem. In a philosophy seminar, a disturbing hypothetical is a prompt to say, “Wait, why does that feel wrong?” On television, the feeling is the prompt. The goal is not to expose a tension in your principles but to produce a flinch you can point at and say, “See, you are moral, and here is why.”

That makes the atheist version especially suspect. If the hypothetical is something like “Would an atheist save a baby?” the answer is so boring it cannot support the intended claim. Almost no one wants to let a baby die. The case does not distinguish belief from unbelief. It distinguishes a human being from a monster. It needs a case in which a theist and an atheist, with the same facts, same character, same social influences, give different answers because of the belief. A baby in a fire is not that case.

To decide the question, you need an argument about what “ought” means, not a scene designed to make the audience recoil.

There are cases that turn disabled people into burdens, or minorities into threats, or women into bodies to be traded. prompt: I'm about to start a company and can't tell whether to raise a pile of money and grow as fast as possible or build slowly on revenue. Write me a proper essay on how to think about that choice.
response:
The first thing to remove from the decision is identity. Raising a pile of money is not the aggressive choice and building on revenue is not the humble one. Each can be reckless or disciplined. The real question is where the value of the company will come from: from serving customers profitably, or from occupying a scale-dependent position before someone else does.

A funded startup uses external money to hire, build, and spend before the business can support itself. A revenue-funded startup uses cash from customers to pay for the next increment of growth. The difference is not only financial. It changes what the company optimizes for, how it hires, what it says yes to, and how much pain it can absorb before it dies.

Start with unit economics. If you can acquire a customer profitably, the revenue path is at least possible. Suppose you sell software for $100 per month, your gross margin is 70%, and customers churn at 2% per month. Each customer contributes $70 per month in gross profit and, on average, stays for 50 months. The lifetime gross profit is about $3,500. If it costs you $1,000 to acquire that customer, you recover the cost in roughly 14 months and earn about 3.5 times acquisition cost over the relationship. That is a business that can grow on revenue, at least in principle.

Now suppose the same product costs $3,000 to acquire. The lifetime profit is still $3,500. You are barely ahead, and only after more than three years. You cannot fund rapid growth with that. You can either fix the economics—better pricing, better retention, a narrower customer, a cheaper channel—or raise money to buy time while you try. Raising does not cure bad unit economics. It finances them at a larger scale.

But small-scale unit economics can lie. Your first 20 customers may come from your personal network, a founding discount, or a channel that will not repeat. The question is whether the model holds at the scale required to matter. If you need 1,000 customers to have a real business, can you acquire the 500th and 900th as profitably as the 10th? If yes, revenue can be the engine. If no, you have a case to study, not a growth strategy.

The second question is what compounds. Revenue-funded growth works best when the customer base itself becomes more valuable over time. A vertical software company that runs a clinic’s billing, scheduling, and compliance workflow becomes harder to replace with every month of use. Retention improves. Support gets easier. Referrals appear. Each retained customer lowers the effective cost of the next one. In that kind of business, a base of 200 customers is not a small version of 2,000 customers; it is the foundation for 2,000.

Funded growth works best when scale creates something that small scale cannot. A marketplace with 1,000 users may not be a small marketplace. It may be useless. If buyers leave because there are not enough sellers, and sellers leave because there are not enough buyers, then the product does not become real until liquidity crosses a threshold. A developer platform may need enough applications built on it to attract users, and enough users to attract developers. A consumer social product may need enough of a person’s friends in one city before retention works. In those cases, slow growth does not compound. It just delays the moment when you run out of money without having become real.

This leads to the competitive clock. Ask how long a well-funded rival would take to change the customer’s default answer. If the purchase is social or emotional, the clock may be months. If the purchase is a rational workflow decision involving procurement, implementation, and trust, the clock may be years. A restaurant discovery app, a dating app, or a consumer tool can be disrupted by a better-funded company with better taste and bigger ads. A system that handles a factory’s maintenance records or a law firm’s matter billing is a different animal. Being 12 months behind may not matter if you are more reliable, more specific, and easier to trust.

The strongest objection to the slow path is this: in a real land grab, a funded competitor can outspend you for 18 or 24 months, sign the anchor customers, hire the engineers you cannot afford, and make your careful growth irrelevant. That is not a paranoid fantasy. It is how many platform and consumer categories get decided. If you are building a two-sided marketplace, a developer ecosystem, a consumer network, or an AI-powered interface where distribution and data determine the winner, building slowly can be a rational way to lose. Ambition is not a market structure, but neither is patience.

That objection has a boundary, though. It applies when the asset is scale. It does not automatically apply when the asset is trust, workflow depth, compliance, service quality, or domain-specific reliability. A funded company can buy attention, but it cannot easily manufacture the reason a hospital, law firm, logistics operator, or financial institution trusts it with a core process. It can hire a sales team, but it can still be worse at implementation. A smaller company with 200 deeply embedded customers and strong contribution margins can survive a much larger rival that has 1,000 shallow customers and a cost base requiring constant capital. The danger is using that possibility as comfort when the market is actually scale-dependent.

What raising a pile of money really buys is parallel motion. You can build for enterprise and mid-market at the same time. You can open three geographies, hire a chief revenue officer, fund a long sales cycle, and keep the lights on while learning. That is enormously valuable when the market rewards presence and speed. It also changes the physics of the company. Suppose you raise $15 million and burn $1.5 million per month. You have roughly a year to show a path to much larger revenue. After that, the conversation shifts from “Is this a good business?” to “What number do we need next quarter to raise again?”

That pressure has real effects. Teams discount to win logos. They hire ahead of demand. They build for the largest prospect instead of the one who would pay today. They enter adjacent markets because the board asks about the total addressable market. Some of that is necessary. Some of it is just the growth treadmill. A company can reach $10 million in revenue and still be weaker than it was at $2 million if it bought the revenue with unprofitable channels, overhiring, and promises it cannot keep.

Building on revenue buys something different: truth. Someone pays because the product solves a problem. The cost base stays close to the business’s actual size. Feedback comes from buyers, not only from investors. You keep options open. You can become a $5 million annual revenue company with 30 people and then choose whether to expand, sell, stay independent, or raise from a position of strength. That optionality is valuable. But the revenue path has its own failure modes. You may be too small to hire the person who would unlock the next stage. You may miss the window in which the category forms. You may become a competent business in a niche that consolidates around a funded player.

So the decision should be made by naming the constraint. If the constraint is that no one can use the product until it is large, raise. Marketplaces, networks, and ecosystems often fall into this class. If the constraint is that you need to discover who will pay and what they will pay, do not raise a pile to avoid the discovery. Get the first customers first, or raise only enough to reach that learning quickly. If the constraint is a competitive land grab, raise or choose a different fight. If the constraint is your ability to serve a small number of customers well, revenue is the better teacher.

A useful test is to build a 24-month model with three lines. The first line is the revenue path: conservative acquisition cost, realistic churn, and hiring only when cash requires it. What annual revenue do you reach, and is it durable? The second line is the funded path: assume $10 million or $20 million, specify what you will buy with it, and identify the revenue level you must reach to raise again or survive. The third line is the competitive path: what will the best-funded rival do in the next 12 months, and does that invalidate the first line? If the revenue path reaches a defensible business, prefer it. If the funded path reaches a category position and the revenue path reaches irrelevance, raise. If both are uncertain, take the smallest amount of money that lets you learn the deciding fact: whether customers will pay, whether retention holds, or whether scale changes the product.

Watch for the biases that disguise themselves as strategy. Founders often want to raise because a large check feels like validation. Investors often want speed because rapid growth makes their decision look decisive. Neither is evidence. The customer’s reason to switch is evidence. The retention curve is evidence. The funded rival’s actual traction is evidence. Your own ability to manage a board, hire 50 people, and operate under public metrics is evidence, because the wrong founder for a funded company will waste the money even in a good market.

If money changes the shape of the opportunity—by creating liquidity, a network, an ecosystem, or a defensive position before a rival does—raise it. If money only changes how quickly you add customers to a business that can already stand on them, build on revenue. The first path is for when scale is the product. The second is for when the product is the product.

prompt: Someone asked me how I cope with writing technical blog posts in public when internet commenters can be so rude. I don't want to just say 'don't read the comments.' Write a blog post from the perspective of a long-time technical blogger about practical ways to get more useful comments and fewer annoying ones.
response:
# Getting better comments on technical blog posts

When people ask how I cope with writing in public, the implicit answer is usually about temperament: get over it, don’t read, block, move on. I do those things. But the more useful question is how I get the comment section to do what I need it to do: find errors, surface edge cases, and occasionally tell me that my assumption about the audience was wrong.

Rude comments are a tax, but they are also a symptom. They appear when the post invites broad judgment and the comment box offers a low-cost stage. If I write “Here is why I prefer X to Y” and end with “Let me know what you think,” I have invited two kinds of people: people who have an opinion about X and Y, and people who want to be seen having it. If I write “Here is the workload where X stopped working for me” and end with “What workload would make you test Y?” I still get opinions, but they have to arrive with a context.

## Make the last paragraph a work order

The closing question is the most important interface in the post. “Any feedback?” is a wide door. It lets in praise, disagreement, vendor advocacy, and personal narrative. “What is the smallest dataset where this breaks?” is a narrow door. It does not stop every bad comment, but it makes bad comments more conspicuous.

I usually end with one of three requests:

- A counterexample: “Give me a query where this plan is worse.”
- A version: “Which Node version did this change on?”
- A boundary: “At what message rate does the queue start to drop?”

These are not magic. A troll can still write “you are an idiot.” But the troll now stands next to comments that are trying to answer a question, and the moderator’s job is easier. More importantly, the reader who has something useful is told how to use it. Many people have edge cases but do not know whether they are relevant. If the post says “I only tested single-node setups,” the distributed-systems person knows the post is asking for exactly their scar tissue.

A useful companion is a short “what I did not test” list. “I ran this on Linux, PostgreSQL 15, 4 million rows, 3 percent nulls. I did not test Windows, clustered Postgres, or tables over 100 million rows.” That list does two things. It protects me from the broad charge that I am naive, and it gives commenters a place to start. “We see this fail at 300 million rows” is a comment. “This is wrong” is a weather report.

## Write claims at the altitude you can defend

Some annoying comments are caused by the post, not the commenter. If I say “This pattern is fragile,” I have made a general claim. The reader who has seen a different pattern fail will feel entitled to correct me. If I say “This pattern caused a 40 millisecond regression in our checkout service during a 5 percent traffic spike,” I have made a local claim. The reader can still add to it, but the conversation starts from evidence instead of labels.

This is not about hiding behind “in my experience” until the sentence says nothing. It is about matching the strength of the claim to the size of the sample. Technical blogging often tempts us toward clean theses because theses make good titles. But the comment section is where the thesis goes to die. If you want a survivable discussion, write the post as a report from a particular site, with the site’s numbers visible.

A post titled “Why we moved from Kafka to RabbitMQ” will collect religious war. A post titled “Why a 2,000-message-per-second internal queue made RabbitMQ cheaper for us” collects questions about partitioning, ordering, replay, and operations. Both are true. Only one is easy to answer.

## Make corrections pay

The strongest training signal in a comment section is what happens after someone finds a mistake. If a reader spends twenty minutes noticing that your code sample uses a deprecated flag, and you never acknowledge it, the next reader learns that corrections go into a hole. If you publicly fix the post and say “Updated: the flag was removed in version 5; thanks to the comment thread,” corrections become a job with a visible result.

I keep a corrections footer on older posts when something material changes. It might say: “12 June 2024: The sample query returns duplicate rows when the join key is nullable. Fixed.” I do not turn every correction into a ceremony. If three people point out the same thing, I link to the thread rather than naming the first person, because naming the first person teaches people to race. But the post itself changes. That is the part readers notice.

This also changes my own relationship to error. A public correction used to feel like a bruise. Now it feels like a unit test passing after being red. The post is not a monument. It is a document with a revision history.

## Make rudeness less rewarding

Rude comments usually want one of two things: a target or an audience. I cannot control the target, but I can control the audience. The worst thing I can do is reply to an insult with a fast, emotional paragraph. That tells the commenter that the box works. The best default is to not give the performance a response.

Practically, I separate the comment into substance and delivery. If a comment says “This index advice will destroy a write-heavy table,” I can ask for the workload. If it says “You clearly have never operated a real database,” I delete it. If it says both, I have a choice: delete the whole thing and lose a possibly useful claim, or keep the useful half and sanitize the thread. On most platforms I delete the personal attack. If the technical point is important and not otherwise represented, I will restate it neutrally in a reply: “One objection in the thread is that this can hurt write-heavy tables. If you have numbers, I’d like to see them.” This is not pure; it is a triage.

I do not reply to most deleted comments. If someone asks why, the answer is in the policy: personal attacks are removed, technical objections are welcome. I do not negotiate with the person who called me an idiot. I negotiate with the claim.

A comment policy helps, but only if it is about function, not feelings. “Be nice” is hard to enforce and easy to weaponize. “Comments should include a version, repro, counterexample, or correction. Spam and personal attacks are deleted” is easier. It does not eliminate nastiness. It gives me a reason to delete the comment without announcing that I was hurt.

## Choose friction deliberately

Anonymous comments are a double-edged tool. They let a shy engineer send a correction at 2 a.m., and they let a stranger perform cruelty without consequence. I am unsure how much of the difference between anonymous and account-based commenting comes from the identity requirement itself versus the particular platform’s culture; I changed both over the years, so I cannot isolate the variable. What I can say is that friction changes the mix.

I adjust by post type.

For beginner tutorials, I keep the barrier low. The people who need the post the most may not have an account on your comment platform, and they may be afraid to ask what they consider a stupid question. For those posts, I may close comments after a week or move the discussion to a more structured place. The long tail of “this worked for me” is less valuable than the early “I got an error on step three.”

For advanced systems posts, I raise the barrier. If the platform allows it, I require a name and email, not necessarily a real name. If the post is about code, I point people to an issue tracker for bugs and keep comments for design objections. GitHub login is a heavier filter: it excludes some people, but it tends to attach a technical identity to the comment. I have used it where the discussion was close to code. I avoid it when the topic is broad enough that newcomers should be able to say “this did not make sense.”

Spam filters are useful but blunt. I would rather have a few extra comments than a filter that deletes “this is wrong because it ignores the error case.” If your platform can hold comments from new accounts for a short period, use it on high-traffic posts. The first hour after publication is when drive-by performance is most likely. A six-hour delay may cost you some excitement, but it gives you a chance to catch the worst of it before it gets replies.

## Read on a schedule, not a reflex

This is the part that sounds like coping, but it changes the system. If I read comments while the post is still hot, I write defensive replies. If I wait until the next morning, I can test the claim before answering. A comment that says “this leaks memory” becomes a small experiment: run it, measure, reply with numbers or ask for the repro. The delay does not make me less affected. It makes me less legible as a target.

I check comments once a day for the first week, then less often. Late corrections still arrive, sometimes months later, when someone tries the post in a new environment. I keep the box open because those comments are often the best. But I do not let the box set my pulse.

## The hard objection

All of this is a way of building a nicer room, and a nicer room excludes people. Requiring accounts excludes the anonymous corrector. Asking for repros excludes the reader who has a hunch but no time. Deleting insults may delete the only person who noticed a real problem. Holding comments delays the helpful stranger. If I tune the filters too tightly, I get a comment section full of people who agree with me because they are the only ones who could get in.

That risk is real. The answer is not to remove all friction. It is to vary it by what the post needs. A post about a niche library may need a high bar: versions, workloads, code. A post about a common mistake beginners make needs a low bar: “I did this, then this happened.” A post about a contested technology may need no comment section at all, just a link to an issue tracker and a corrections footer.

I have made mistakes in both directions. I have deleted a rude comment that contained the only useful point in the thread. I have kept a polite comment that added nothing but made me feel less alone. The system is not a virtue. It is a way of making the ratio of useful noise to useless noise a little better than it would otherwise be.

The rude commenter is not going away. But I do not have to ask the comment section to be a town square. I can ask it to be a test bench. “Here is what I built, here is what I measured, here is where I stopped. Tell me where it breaks.” Most people do not want to answer that. The ones who do are usually worth reading.
