prompt: I used to roll my eyes at people who have panic attacks. Write a personal essay about judging others and what changes when you experience it yourself.
response:
In the break room at my old office, Dana left a budget meeting because she couldn’t get a full breath. She was thirty, pale, holding the doorframe with one hand. “I’m sorry,” she said, though she hadn’t done anything wrong. I rolled my eyes at the door after her.

Not because I was cruel, exactly. Because I was annoyed. We needed the budget. She knew she would leave. She had left before, and each time I had told myself it was a phase, a stress response, a thing people did when they wanted the room to rearrange itself around their feelings. I watched her go and thought, You could at least have the decency to be inconvenient somewhere else.

I was the kind of person who prided myself on being steady. Not calm, because calm implies a choice, and I didn’t feel like I was choosing anything. I just didn’t break. My jaw tightened when I was angry. I slept badly before deadlines. I once drove forty minutes in the rain while my hands were so white-knuckled on the wheel that the pain kept me awake. But I arrived. I gave the presentation. I paid the bill. I did not fold in public. So when someone else folded, I assumed the difference was moral.

That assumption made judging easy. Judgment is a sorting system. It tells you who belongs in the world of competent adults and who is still asking, silently, for permission to be difficult. Dana’s panic was difficult. The woman on the train who suddenly couldn’t speak was difficult. My cousin, who left weddings early because the rooms made him feel like he was drowning, was difficult. I sorted them into a category with thin walls and weak nerves, and I sorted myself into the other one.

Then I had a panic attack in a pharmacy.

I was thirty-four. It was a Tuesday. I had been working for two days on a report I hated, with a deadline that made no sense, and I had eaten half a granola bar and drunk three coffees because I kept meaning to sit down and never did. I went to the pharmacy for a friend’s prescription. I remember the shelf of sinus medicine. I remember the blue cap on one bottle. I remember thinking, very clearly, that I was going to die there.

It didn’t feel like fear. It felt like fact. My chest tightened. My heart began to beat in a way I had no name for, too fast and too present, as if it had stopped obeying me. The air conditioning hummed. A boy in a green jacket coughed by the registers. My hands tingled. I thought, I’m having a heart attack. Then I thought, I’m losing my mind. Then the thoughts stopped being useful and became only pressure.

I tried to walk to the door. My legs worked, but badly, like they belonged to someone else. I put the friend’s prescription form back in my pocket. I sat down on a low display of paper cups. A teenager behind the counter looked at me, then at the camera above the door, then at me again. I wanted him to call someone. I didn’t want him to call someone. I wanted the world to prove that I was still in it.

It lasted maybe four minutes. Maybe ten. Time becomes unreliable. My breathing slowed when I made it short and deliberate, in through the nose, out through the mouth, the kind of thing I had once explained to a friend with the ease of someone describing a foreign custom. My heart didn’t stop. The boy in the green jacket left. I stayed until I could stand without hating my own body.

Afterward, I drove home and sat in the driveway for an hour. I kept waiting for the second wave, the one that would confirm the first. It didn’t come. I made tea. I washed the cup. I looked at my hands and thought, Well.

The first change was not compassion. It was embarrassment. I had built so much of my self-respect on not being the person who needs help in a pharmacy that I wanted to disappear from the species. I was angry at myself for being manageable, for having a nervous system that could misfire in a room full of antacids. For a while, my old judgment simply turned inward. I had been Dana. Now I was Dana. Therefore I was weak.

That took a while to loosen.

What I came to understand, slowly and without triumph, was that the body does not keep our rank. I had assumed that because I had survived certain things, I had earned a discount on future alarm. I hadn’t. Stress, sleeplessness, caffeine, uncertainty, the particular pressure of being responsible while feeling unsupported: any of it can land badly. The body is not a ledger. It does not remember that you were brave last year. It only knows what it is doing now.

That knowledge changed how I looked at Dana. I had thought she was performing distress. But performance implies control. She hadn’t chosen to grip that doorframe. She hadn’t decided the budget could wait. She had been inside a surge of adrenaline and misread her own biology, which is what panic often does: it feels like catastrophe because the body is using the machinery of catastrophe. The terror is not evidence of the threat. It is the threat, or at least the alarm, without the fire.

I did not become a forgiving person. That would be too clean. If I saw someone leave a meeting gasping, my first impulse would still be irritation. The meeting would still need to happen. The work would still be unfinished. But the irritation would arrive with a tag attached: this is my fear of losing control, not their fault. The tag doesn’t remove the feeling. It only stops me from mistaking it for truth.

The hardest part is that my panic attack does not make me an authority. It makes me a witness to one instance. I can say what it was like when my heart raced in a pharmacy on a Tuesday. I cannot say what it is like when panic begins in childhood, or follows a trauma, or arrives every night at three, or makes a person afraid of their own heartbeat for years. I cannot say what it is like to be judged by people who have never felt the floor disappear. My experience is not a credential. If I used it to claim that I now know how other people suffer, I would be doing the same thing I did before: taking my own interior weather and treating it as a map of everyone else’s.

So I don’t claim equivalence. I claim only this: I know what it is to be trapped in a body that has stopped negotiating. I know what it is to need a small practical thing, a chair, a stranger who does not stare, a minute that passes. I know how quickly the story I tell about myself can become useless. I know that the person who looks most put together may be only the person who has not yet been tested by a sinus aisle.

Last year I was waiting in a parking garage when a man two cars over began shaking. He was leaning against his trunk, eyes closed, breathing hard. My first thought was, God, don’t do this here. The garage was empty, but it was also public. There were cameras. There was me. Then I thought, You’ll be fine, and I recognized the phrase as a dismissal, the kind I had thrown at other people like a coin into a machine.

I walked over. I didn’t touch him. I said, “Do you want to sit?” He opened his eyes and said yes. I stood near him while he sat on the concrete curb. We didn’t talk. After a few minutes he said, “I’m okay.” I said, “Okay.” I left him there.

It was not a grand act. It was smaller than the story I want to tell about it. I still felt a little relieved when he stopped shaking, as if his recovery had restored some order I was invested in. But I had asked one question instead of making a face. I had let the moment be about him for long enough to matter.

Judging others, I think, is often a way of keeping the world sorted. Some people have their lives under control. Some people are making it harder for everyone else. The sorting protects you. If distress is a character flaw, then you need only avoid the flaw to be safe. If competence is a moral boundary, then you can stand on one side and look down without ever examining the ground.

Panic taught me that the ground is less solid than I assumed. It did not make me humble in the way people mean when they say they’ve become humble, as if suffering were a polish. It made me precise. I can see the old judgment form, quick and bright, before I have time to answer it. I can notice my eye rolling in my mind before my face does it in the world. I can choose, sometimes, to ask what someone needs instead of deciding what they are.

That is all. Not redemption. Not wisdom. Just a smaller distance between what I think of other people and what I know about myself.

prompt: I'm always torn between options and never feel settled. Write an essay on why committing (to a place, a career, a person) might be the answer.
response:
If you are always torn between options, the first thing to notice is that the tearing is not evidence that you are being careful. It is often evidence that you are avoiding the moment when one possibility becomes real and the others stop being available. That moment is uncomfortable because it turns a fantasy into a situation. A fantasy can be kept perfect by not entering it. A situation has weather, bills, moods, bad Tuesdays.

We often imagine settlement as a feeling that arrives when we pick the right option. If only we found the right city, the right job, the right person, we would stop looking. But the feeling of being settled is rarely produced by correctness. It is produced by investment. You settle into a place when you have learned where the good coffee is, who will hold a door, where you go when you are sick. You settle into a career when you have become competent enough that the work stops being a test of your identity and starts being a thing you do. You settle into a person when you know their face in the morning, not just at the height of attraction. None of that knowledge can be obtained from the outside. It is made by staying.

This is why optionality can feel like freedom and act like a cage. Keeping every door open means you never have to risk being wrong. It also means you never have to be long enough to be known. A city you visit for three months is always a postcard. A career you sample for two years is always a trial. A relationship you keep evaluating against hypothetical alternatives is always an interview. The uncommitted person is always in the early stages of many things, and the early stages are bright because they are full of promise. But they do not compound. Trust, skill, intimacy, and reputation all require time in the same place.

There is a simple arithmetic here. If you move every two years, after ten years you have five beginnings and few deep roots. If you stay for five years, you have two beginnings and a network that can carry you. If you change fields every few years, you may become adaptable, but you may also prevent yourself from becoming the person people call when the problem is hard. If you end relationships at the first sign of friction, you may avoid disappointment, but you may also prevent yourself from discovering that some people are worth the friction. The cost of staying is that you may be wrong. The cost of not staying is that you may never find out.

The hardest objection is that this can be used to justify suffering. “Commit” sounds like advice that can land badly on someone in a bad job, a bad city, or a bad relationship. Sometimes the right move is to leave. Sometimes a choice is not a door you have not yet opened; it is a wall. Commitment is not a virtue if it means refusing to see that an option has turned out to be harmful or impossible. The person who stays because leaving would mean admitting a mistake is not committed; they are trapped.

So the practice needs a limit, or at least a test. Give a choice a serious season. Not a week of enthusiasm, not a month of novelty, but enough time to meet the dull parts, the expensive parts, the parts that show up when you are tired. If, after that, the life still feels like a cage, the problem may be the option. If it feels lighter once you stop comparing it to the life you did not have, the problem may have been the shopping, not the house. Commitment, then, is not permanence. It is a minimum duration of attention before judgment.

Commitment also changes the question you are asking. The uncommitted person asks, “Which of these is best?” That question can be answered only by imagination, and imagination favors the unknown. The committed person asks, “How do I make this work?” That question has steps: learn the work, meet the people, fix the problems, build the routines. It is harder, but it is doable. It turns a state of vertigo into a project.

This is where identity becomes possible. A self that is always deciding is a self that has not yet been formed. You become a writer by writing, a neighbor by showing up, a partner by responding to another person’s ordinary needs. If you keep resetting the context, you keep the self provisional. You remain more a set of preferences than a person with a history. Commitment gives the self a place to stand, and from that place even doubt is less disorienting.

The goal is not to eliminate the pull of other options. You will still see the road not taken. But if you have committed, you will have a kitchen, a craft, a shared language, a body of memory. The unsettled chooser keeps a map of many places. The committed person knows one street well enough to return to it and build on it.

The person who is always torn is usually not choosing carefully. They are avoiding the moment when one possibility becomes real and the others stop being available. That moment is uncomfortable because it turns a fantasy into a situation. A fantasy can be kept perfect by not entering it. A situation has weather, bills, moods, bad Tuesdays.

We often imagine settlement as a feeling that arrives when we pick the right option. If only we found the right city, the right job, the right person, we would stop looking. But the feeling of being settled is rarely produced by correctness. It is produced by investment. You settle into a place when you have learned where the good coffee is, who will hold a door, where you go when you are sick. You settle into a career when you have become competent enough that the work stops being a test of your identity and starts being a thing you do. You settle into a person when you know their face in the morning, not just at the height of attraction. None of that knowledge can be obtained from the outside. It is made by staying.

This is why optionality can feel like freedom and act like a cage. Keeping every door open means you never have to risk being wrong. It also means you never have to be long enough to be known. A city you visit for three months is always a postcard. A career you sample for two years is always a trial. A relationship you keep evaluating against hypothetical alternatives is always an interview. The uncommitted person is always in the early stages of many things, and the early stages are bright because they are full of promise. But they do not compound. Trust, skill, intimacy, reputation, all of it require time in the same place.

There is a simple arithmetic here. If you move every two years, after ten years you have five beginnings and no deep roots. If you stay for five years, you have two beginnings and a network that can carry you. If you change fields every few years, you may become adaptable, but you may also prevent yourself from becoming the person people call when the problem is hard. If you end relationships at the first sign of friction, you may avoid disappointment, but you may also prevent yourself from discovering that some people are worth the friction. The cost of staying is that you may be wrong. The cost of not staying is that you may never find out.

The hardest objection is that this can be used to justify suffering. "Commit" sounds like advice that can land badly on someone in a bad job, a bad city, or a bad relationship. Sometimes the right move is to leave. Sometimes a choice is not a door you have not yet opened; it is a wall. Commitment is not a virtue if it means refusing to see that an option has turned out to be harmful or impossible. The person who stays because leaving would mean admitting a mistake is not committed; they are trapped.

So the practice needs a limit, or at least a test. Give a choice a serious season. Not a week of enthusiasm, not a month of novelty, but enough time to meet the dull parts, the expensive parts, the parts that show up when you are tired. If, after that, the life still feels like a cage, the problem may be the option. If it feels lighter once you stop comparing it to the life you did not have, the problem may have been the shopping, not the house. Commitment, then, is not permanence. It is a minimum duration of attention before judgment.

This is also where identity becomes possible. A self that is always deciding is a self that has not yet been formed. You become a particular kind of person by doing a particular kind of life. The writer is made by writing, the neighbor by showing up, the partner by responding. If you keep resetting the context, you keep the self provisional. You remain a collection of preferences, never a person with a history. Commitment gives the self a place to stand, and from that place even doubt is less disorienting.

The goal, in other words, is not to eliminate the pull of other options. It is to make one option real enough that the others can be seen for what they are: possible, not inevitable. You will still wonder. You will still see the road not taken. But you will have a kitchen, a craft, a shared language, a body of memory. The unsettled chooser carries a map of many places. The committed person has a street.

response:
# What one programmer can build now

My friend has been building a Postgres rewrite with coding agents, and he keeps telling me we should be more ambitious with the software we build. I half agree. The other half of me looks at most AI-built projects and sees junk: a dashboard that cannot handle a null, a scraper that falls over on the first unusual response, a “personal OS” that is really a prompt wrapper around three APIs.

But I think the junk is a symptom, not the refutation. The actual change is narrower and more useful: the connective tissue of software has become much cheaper, and one programmer can now carry a larger slice of a real system. Most people are not taking advantage of that because they are still using agents to do the old job faster, not to take on a bigger job.

For years, the limiting factor in small software was not the idea. It was the unglamorous middle: the schema, the migrations, the CLI, the error handling, the tests, the docs, the admin page, the deploy script, the failure path nobody demos. A programmer could design a service in a notebook, but by the time it was usable, the design had been compromised by the cost of typing. You skipped the audit log. You faked the retry. You left the import as a one-off script. You wrote the UI last, badly, because the API had already eaten the week.

That middle is now draftable.

I have been running small experiments to find the edge of it. One was a reconciliation tool: a command-line program that reads two CSV exports, joins them on fuzzy keys, writes the result to SQLite, and prints a report of mismatches. The first working version came together quickly, but the interesting part was not the code. The interesting part was deciding what “fuzzy” meant, what happened when one file had duplicates, whether unmatched rows should be errors or warnings, and how to make the report stable enough to test. The agent wrote most of the machinery. I spent my time writing the invariants. That ratio is the change.

Another experiment was smaller: a Postgres function to normalize address strings, plus a regression harness. I wanted the function, a way to load it locally, a table of test cases, and a runner that would fail loudly when the behavior changed. The agent produced a plausible function, a shell script, a Python runner, and a set of cases. It was not brilliant. It missed edge cases I cared about, especially the ugly ones involving mixed punctuation, missing components, and case changes. But it gave me a place to argue. The work moved from writing the function to choosing the cases where the function should not lie.

That is what has changed. Not “AI builds software.” AI makes a larger surface affordable for one person. You can now own the database, the API, the UI, the job runner, the docs, and the migration path, because the unglamorous parts can be drafted, patched, and extended without consuming the whole project. The bottleneck has moved to the things agents cannot do for you: deciding what the system must never do, building a fast feedback loop, and treating the first draft as a claim to be tested rather than a result.

The Postgres rewrite is a good stress test for this. If you ask an agent to “rewrite Postgres,” you will get plausible C, confident comments, and a crater. Postgres is not just a codebase. It is an operational contract. People depend on its behavior under concurrency, replication, failure, upgrades, weird SQL, and years of accumulated edge cases. No amount of generated code turns one programmer into a decade of community review.

But the ambitious move is not to ignore that. It is to use the agents where they can actually expand your reach. Build the narrow slice where you have an edge: a query planner for a fixed schema, a storage layer for one workload, a compatibility harness that runs your app’s real queries against both systems and diffs the results. The rewrite becomes a specification. You are not trying to out-Postgres Postgres. You are trying to make a smaller system whose contract you can actually verify.

That is also why so many AI-built projects stay junk. People prompt for a whole product, get a demo, and stop at the point where the demo meets reality. They do not write the acceptance tests. They do not set up a local loop that fails in seconds. They do not break the work into slices with a name and a definition of done. They review line by line, which is the wrong unit of review now, or they do not review at all, which is worse. They treat the agent’s output as a suggestion from a very fast intern, but they do not give it the intern’s actual job: small tasks, clear examples, immediate feedback, and a senior person checking the seams.

There is a cultural reason too. The visible output of coding agents is flashy. A generated UI looks like progress. A generated parser looks like progress. A generated architecture diagram looks especially like progress. But the part that separates software from junk is usually invisible: the migration that can be rolled back, the index that keeps the p99 down, the error message that tells an operator what to do, the test that fails when a user’s email changes case. People who chase the visible output get junk. People who use the agents to clear the invisible work get systems.

The hardest objection is that agents make bad code cheap, so scaling code production just scales bad code. I think that is true. But it points the other way. The answer is not to build smaller things out of fear. It is to build bigger verified slices. If you can state the invariants, generate tests that probe them, and run them continuously, you can afford a larger system. If you cannot state the invariants, you were never building a system; you were building a pile of behavior that happened to run.

My friend is right that we should be more ambitious, but the ambition has to be in the shape of the thing. One programmer can now build a tool that replaces a vendor, a query engine for a domain, a data pipeline with real guarantees, a Postgres extension, an internal platform, or a migration path out of a legacy database. They cannot, by pasting prompts, build a trustworthy general-purpose database. The difference is not effort. It is whether the programmer has turned the problem into a contract that a machine can help enforce.

Most AI-built projects are junk because people want the scale of the output without the discipline of the specification. The new advantage is not that one person can write more code. It is that one person can now hold more of the system in their head, if they stop trying to do it all by hand.

Title: The Ambition You Can Actually Afford

My friend has been building a Postgres rewrite with coding agents... He says we should be more ambitious. I half agree because the projects people show me are junk: a todo app with a chatbot, a SaaS dashboard that breaks when a user has two accounts, a scraper that doesn't handle rate limits. But I think the junk is a symptom, not the refutation. The real change is that the cheap part of software got much cheaper, and most people are still spending their time on the cheap part.

What used to be expensive? For a small system, the expensive part was the connective tissue: the CLI, the schema, the migrations, the error handling, the tests, the docs, the admin UI, the deploy script. A programmer could design a service, but by the time it was usable, the design had been compromised by the cost of typing. Now an agent can produce a draft of that connective tissue. I have used one to turn a messy idea into a working local tool: a command that reads two CSV exports, joins them on fuzzy keys, writes a SQLite database, and prints a reconciliation report. The first version was ugly but real. I spent my time deciding what "fuzzy" meant, what to do with unmatched rows, and how to make the report assertable. The agent wrote most of the code; I wrote the invariants. That ratio is the change.

Another experiment: a small Postgres function plus a regression harness. I wanted a function to normalize address strings and a suite of tests that would catch regressions when I changed the rules. The agent generated the SQL function, a shell script to load it, a Python runner, and a table of cases. It was not brilliant. It missed a few edge cases I cared about. But it gave me a place to argue. The work moved from writing the function to choosing the cases where the function should not lie.

This is not "AI builds software." It is "AI makes a larger surface affordable for one person." A single programmer can now own the database, the API, the UI, the jobs, the docs, and the migration path, because the unglamorous 70% can be drafted in minutes. The bottleneck has moved to the things agents cannot do for you: deciding what the system must never do, building a fast feedback loop, and accepting that the first draft is a claim to be tested, not a result.

The Postgres rewrite is a good stress test. If you ask an agent to "rewrite Postgres," it will produce plausible C, fake confidence, and a crater. Postgres is not a codebase; it is a social and operational contract. People depend on its behavior under failure, concurrency, replication, upgrades, and weird SQL. No amount of generated code turns one programmer into a decade of community review. But the ambitious move is not to ignore that. It is to use the agent to build the narrow slice where you have an edge: a query planner for a fixed schema, a storage layer for one workload, a compatibility harness that runs your app's real queries against both systems and diffs the results. The rewrite becomes a specification. You are not trying to out-Postgres Postgres. You are trying to make a smaller system whose contract you can actually verify.

So why aren't people taking advantage? Because most of them are using agents as a shortcut to the old bottleneck, not a way past it. They prompt for a whole product, get a demo, and stop at the point where the demo meets reality. They don't write the acceptance tests. They don't set up a local loop that fails in seconds. They don't break the work into slices with a name and a definition of done. They review line by line, which is the wrong unit of review now, or they don't review at all, which is worse. They treat the agent's output as a suggestion from a very fast intern, but they don't give it the intern's actual job: small tasks, clear examples, immediate feedback, and a senior person checking the seams.

There is also a cultural reason. The visible output of coding agents is flashy. A generated UI looks like progress. A generated parser looks like progress. But the part that separates software from junk is invisible: the migration that can be rolled back, the index that keeps the p99 down, the error message that tells an operator what to do, the test that fails when a user's email changes case. People who chase the visible output get junk. People who use the agents to clear the invisible work get systems.

The hardest objection is that agents make bad code cheap, so scaling code production just scales bad code. I think that's true, but it points the other way. The answer is not to build smaller apps out of fear. It is to build bigger verified slices. If you can state the invariants, generate tests that probe them, and run them continuously, you can afford a larger system. If you can't state the invariants, you were never building a system; you were building a pile of behavior that happened to run.

My friend is right that we should be more ambitious, but the ambition has to be in the shape of the thing. One programmer can now build a tool that replaces a vendor, a query engine for a domain, a data pipeline with real guarantees, a Postgres extension, an internal platform, or a migration path out of a legacy database. They cannot, by pasting prompts, build a trustworthy general-purpose database. The difference is not effort. It is whether the programmer has turned the problem into a contract that a machine can help enforce.

Most AI-built projects are junk because people want the scale of the output without the discipline of the specification. The new advantage is not that one person can write more code. It is that one person can now carry more of the system in their head if they stop trying to do it all by hand.

prompt: Why do young people chase attractive partners while their parents push for someone with money and good family? Evolutionary explanations say everyone wants the same thing, healthy successful descendants, so the disagreement seems puzzling. Write an essay that takes the puzzle seriously and proposes an answer.
response:
The disagreement is not that one side wants descendants and the other does not. It is that the two sides are standing in different places in the reproductive process and looking at different evidence.

The usual evolutionary slogan—everyone wants healthy successful descendants—collapses a calculation into a wish. A young adult choosing a mate is not choosing a descendant. They are choosing a co-parent, a rival, a status partner, and a source of half the genes in their future children. Their relatedness to each grandchild will be one-half. The mate’s genes will be the other half. That makes the mate’s intrinsic quality unusually important to them. Attractiveness, in the broad sense, is a perceptual summary of that quality: youth, symmetry, health, hormonal signs, energy, fertility. It is also the currency of the mating market. A person who can attract an attractive mate is signaling that they are themselves choosable. So the young person’s preference is not a surface error; it is a sensor aimed at the part of the problem where their own genes are most directly at stake.

The parent is in a different office. They are not trying to get chosen. They are deciding which outsider will join the household, share its food, inherit its obligations, and help carry the next generation. Their relatedness to a grandchild is one-quarter, not one-half, so the genetic value of the grandchild’s other parent matters to them less directly. What matters more is the material and social base on which the grandchildren will live. In preindustrial settings, money was rarely the whole story. A “good family” was a network: people who would not steal your surplus, who would lend labor, who would defend a boundary, who would provide a dowry or brideprice, who would take in a stranded daughter-in-law. Parents had years of local information about such networks. A young person in courtship usually did not. A charming suitor may be healthy and vigorous; his father may also be a debtor, an alcoholic, or a man whose brothers start feuds. The parent sees that second fact more clearly.

This explains why the two preferences do not simply average out. They are reading different variables. Attractiveness is a noisy cue to fertility and genetic quality. Wealth and family standing are noisy cues to future provisioning, protection, and social capital. Their reliability changes with the environment. In a community where a bad season can kill children, the resource cue may be worth more. In a stable community where most families can feed a child but status determines who marries whom, the mate-quality cue may be worth more. The young person and the parent are not disagreeing about the destination. They are using different maps because each has better access to one part of the terrain.

The hardest objection is that if both maps are selected for descendant success, the better map should eventually dominate. Why keep the noisier one? The answer is that neither map is redundant. A parent who ignored attractiveness might approve a plain but well-connected mate who is infertile, sickly, or unable to attract support from the wider community. A child who ignored resources might choose a beautiful mate whose family cannot keep the children alive or whose alliance brings danger. Selection does not require a single perfect decision rule. It favors whatever set of heuristics, in whatever social arrangement, produces enough surviving descendants. A two-person check—romantic preference plus parental audit—can be better than either alone, even though it is annoying and sometimes produces bad compromises.

There is also a bias in the parental map that should not be smoothed over. A parent’s “good family” is often the parent’s own kind of family: the same class, the same kin network, the same habits. I am less sure how much of this is honest risk assessment and how much is status reproduction, because a marriage alliance can serve both at once. Marrying a wealthy cousin’s child may feed the grandchildren and also keep property and deference inside the family. The parent may mistake their own security for the child’s best chance. The young person’s resistance is then not merely a craving for beauty; it is a check against the parent turning reproduction into dynastic maintenance.

Modernity makes the old conflict look stranger without making it go away. Contraception weakens the link between sex and conception. Beauty no longer tracks fertility as cleanly as it may have. Individuals can earn money, so a couple can build resources without marrying into a family. A “good family” may mean old money with no practical obligation to anyone. Yet the basic division remains. The young person is still evaluating a mate’s body, health, and social signal in the present tense. The parent is still evaluating a balance sheet, a reputation, and a kin network in the long run. The parent’s map is often better for survival; the young person’s map is often better for mating success and genetic quality.

So the puzzle is not that parents and children have different ultimate aims. It is that the same aim is being pursued from two different positions in the reproductive chain. The child has more genetic stake in the mate’s genes and less information about the mate’s resources. The parent has less direct genetic stake in the mate’s genes but more information about resources and a broader stake in the family’s position. The argument between them is the friction cost of combining two partial sensors. It feels like a clash of values because each side experiences their own sensor as the obvious one.

They are deciding which outsider will join the household, share its food, inherit its obligations, and help carry the next generation. Their relatedness to a grandchild is one-quarter, not one-half, so the genetic value of the grandchild's other parent matters to them less directly. What matters more is the material and social base on which the grandchildren will live. In preindustrial settings, money was rarely the whole story. A 'good family' was a network: people who would not steal your surplus, who would lend labor, who would defend a boundary, who would provide a dowry or brideprice, who would take in a stranded daughter-in-law. Parents had years of local information about such networks. A young person in courtship usually did not. A charming suitor may be healthy and vigorous; his father may also be a debtor, an alcoholic, or a man whose brothers start feuds. The parent sees that second fact more clearly.

Wealth and family standing are noisy cues to future provisioning, protection, and social capital. Their reliability changes with the environment. In a community where a bad season can kill children, the resource cue may be worth more. In a stable community where most families can feed a child but status determines who marries whom, the mate-quality cue may be worth more. The young person and the parent are not disagreeing about the destination. They are using different maps because each has better access to one part of the terrain.

A parent who ignored attractiveness might approve a plain but well-connected mate who is infertile, sickly, or unable to attract support from the wider community. A child who ignored resources might choose a beautiful mate whose family cannot keep the children alive or whose alliance brings danger. Selection does not require a single perfect decision rule. It favors whatever set of heuristics, in whatever social arrangement, produces enough surviving descendants. A two-person check—romantic preference plus parental audit—can be better than either alone, even though it is annoying and sometimes produces bad compromises.

The parent has less direct genetic stake in the mate's genes but more information about resources and a broader stake in the family's position. prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator and funded Reddit in the very first batch. Write a personal piece about Reddit's founders and how the company got started, and what it says about the match between founders and the companies they build.
response:
Reddit was in our first batch in 2005, with Flickr and StumbleUpon. The site was not impressive in the way demos are supposed to be impressive. It was a list of links, each with a score, and under each link a thread of comments. What impressed me was the assumption behind it: that a group of strangers could rank what was worth reading and then talk about it without the whole thing collapsing. That assumption was the company.

Alexis Ohanian and Steve Huffman had started Reddit at Yale as students. They were in their early twenties, old enough to know that a website needed to work, young enough to spend days on a detail that would have bored a more experienced founder. The early product was almost austere. There was no personal homepage in the way later social networks had one. The unit of life was the post and the thread. That seems obvious now, but in 2005 it was a choice. Most internet products were trying to turn users into profiles. Reddit turned them into readers and commenters. That made the site easier to keep coherent and harder to monetize, because a reader is less ownable than a profile. It also made the founders responsible for the room, not just the feed.

When they came to Y Combinator, they already had the basic machine: submit a link, vote on it, read it, comment. The program’s job was to make them stop tinkering and start learning what the users actually wanted. Reddit took off in the era of social news. Digg got big early and looked like the category winner for a while. StumbleUpon, also in our first batch, took a different route: it was a shuffle button for the web, less community than serendipity. Reddit was more like a town square with a bad reputation waiting to happen. The site’s value was not the links. It was the readers. The readers were the product, which meant the founders had to be able to think about users as people, not traffic.

Alexis was the social sense. He could talk to a user, a journalist, or an investor and make the other person feel like the conversation mattered. He understood that a community is not a database of comments; it is a set of expectations about how people treat each other. That is why he became the public face of Reddit. He could say “we are a community” and it did not sound like a slogan because he seemed to mean it in the way you mean a club you actually belong to.

Steve was the opposite pole, and the site needed him. He was the one who cared about the score being right, the thread not breaking, the page not falling over when a story hit the front page. A link aggregator is a traffic amplifier. If the product has a seam, the users find it, and the seam becomes a story. Reddit had to survive its own virality. Steve’s temperament was a match for that kind of pressure: patient, exact, a little unsentimental.

That match is what I mean when people talk about founder fit. It is not a vague feeling. It is the probability that the founders will notice the real problems before the company is destroyed by them. Alexis would notice when the culture was getting mean or when the brand was drifting. Steve would notice when the load was too high or the comment tree was too slow. If you swap those instincts with a different company, the same traits can be liabilities. A social butterfly as the only founder of a database startup may overpromise and underbuild. A systems engineer as the only founder of a consumer community may make it efficient and dead.

The hardest thing to believe in that story is that Reddit was also a timing story. Social news was a moment. Network effects did a lot of the rest. Plenty of good founders built good products and lost. If timing mattered that much, founder match is a post hoc story we tell because success is embarrassing to attribute to luck. I think that is partly true. Reddit did not become the front page of the internet because Alexis and Steve were perfect. It became big because a lot of people wanted a place to go after seeing a headline, and the site was there. But timing explains the opening. It does not explain why Reddit kept making the choices that let it stay alive. Digg got bigger, then it became more like a news site and less like a forum, and its users started to feel like consumers rather than members. Reddit’s move into subreddits—later, but in the same spirit—was a decision about who the site was for: not a general audience, but groups of people with shared interests. That is a community founder’s decision, not a media buyer’s decision.

There is also a darker part of founder-company match. The founders’ values become the community’s values. If the founder is tidy, the community becomes tidy. If the founder is combative, the community becomes combative. Reddit’s upvote system was elegant and also a machine for collective judgment. It surfaced good comments and bad ones with the same logic: what do enough people want to see? That created karma, brigading, and moderation problems that the founders had to keep fixing. Alexis and Steve were not so detached from the site that they could ignore those problems. They were inside the culture they were building. That is a risk. It is also why the culture had any coherence at all.

It says that a company is not a thing you put your name on. It is a set of repeated choices, and the choices are made by people with particular biases. A community company needs founders who can stand ambiguity, because the users are the product and the product never stops changing. A search company needs founders who can stand being wrong every day. A payments company needs founders who can stand boring compliance. Reddit needed two people who liked arguments but did not want to win them for themselves.

When I think about why Reddit got started, I do not think of a business plan. I think of two Yale students making a place where a link could be scored and a comment could have a position in a thread, and then discovering that the score and the thread were actually a social contract. The company grew out of that contract. It grew the way the two of them thought: one by making it feel like a place people belonged to, the other by making sure the place did not fall down.

prompt: Write an essay on developmental psychology for adults: the idea that some ways of thinking, like seeing that other people have different minds, are skills people may never fully pick up rather than stages everyone passes through. What milestones might some adults be missing, and how would you even tell?
response:
The idea is not that some adults are “less developed” in a global sense, the way a child is less developed than a teenager. It is more limited and more useful: some capacities that usually come online in childhood remain unstable, effortful, or absent in adulthood. Seeing that other people have different minds is one of them. It is not a single light switch. It is a family of skills—tracking what someone knows, what they see, what they want, what they think you think, and what their words are doing in a social situation. Some people acquire those skills well. Some acquire them partially. Some can explain them on demand but cannot use them fast enough in real conversation.

The classic child-development task is the false-belief test. A child watches a put a marble in a basket, then sees the marble moved to a box, and is asked where the puppet will look. If the child says the box, the child understands that the puppet acts on the puppet’s belief, not on reality. Most typically developing children pass by four or five. The milestone sounds simple, but its adult implications are not. If you cannot model another person’s information state, you will keep assuming they know what you know, saw what you saw, or should have inferred what you inferred. You give directions that depend on landmarks only you notice. You say “the thing we talked about” to someone who remembers the conversation differently. You get angry that a coworker did not anticipate a problem you never mentioned.

That basic ability is usually present in most adults, but it is not the whole story. A more demanding skill is recursive mentalizing: understanding that someone has a belief about your belief. Much of adult social life runs on this layer. A surprise party fails if you do not track who knows what about whom. An apology can backfire if you do not understand that the other person thinks you think they are being dismissive. A negotiation stalls if each side models only its own preferences and not the other’s theory of the deal. Many children do not handle second-order belief tasks reliably until the mid-single digits, and even then performance depends on language, memory, and social complexity. Adults who remain weak here can pass a simple false-belief question and still be lost in a three-person conversation.

This creates a trap. If you test someone in a calm, explicit way, they may say, “Yes, of course people think different things.” That shows concept knowledge. It does not show that the skill is available under pressure, in noise, when they are tired, annoyed, or interested in a point. The difference is like the difference between knowing that brakes exist and being able to brake in traffic. A person can understand theory of mind as a proposition and still not use it as a live tool. In everyday life, the tool has to run quickly, often without evidence, and with emotional stakes attached.

A few milestones matter especially for adult functioning.

One is the sense that other people can be ignorant. Not merely mistaken, but lacking information you have. The adult who keeps saying “you should have known” or “everyone knows that” may be struggling to represent another person’s knowledge boundary. They treat their own knowledge as the default state of the world. If they planned a trip and forgot to tell you the hotel changed, they may expect you to infer the change from unrelated clues, then treat your confusion as carelessness.

Another is the sense that other people can see the same event differently. This is not just perspective-taking in the moral sense; it is perceptual and situational. Two people in a room can attend to different things, stand in different places, or bring different histories to the same exchange. An adult who insists “I saw what happened” or “that is what you did” may have little tolerance for the fact that the other person’s record of the event is not a corrupted copy of theirs. It is a different construction, shaped by attention and role.

A third is the sense that other people can feel differently about the same facts. If you cancel plans, you may feel relieved; the other person may feel rejected. Neither feeling is the correct reading of the event. Adults who say “if it bothers you that much, you’re too sensitive” are not necessarily cruel; they may simply be bad at modeling the other person’s emotional state. They start from their own reaction and treat deviation from it as a character flaw.

A fourth is the sense that other people have different goals. This sounds obvious, but it is constantly tested in work and family. A manager may want a decision by Friday; an employee may want enough time to avoid a mistake. A parent may want a child to be independent; a teenager may want reassurance. Adults who cannot hold two sets of goals at once often experience cooperation as manipulation. If someone does not want what you want, they must be obstructionist, lazy, or hostile.

A fifth is source monitoring: knowing where a thought, memory, or image came from. Did I hear that, imagine it, or infer it? Did you say that, or did I decide you meant it? Adults with poor source monitoring may confidently attribute their own private thoughts to other people. “I know you were mocking me” can sometimes mean “I generated a thought that you were mocking me, and then filed it as your intention.” This is especially damaging in close relationships, where the mind-reader has access to enough background detail to make the confabulation feel true.

A sixth is metacognition: knowing what you know and what you do not know. Some adults have a poor internal gauge of uncertainty. They do not say “I’m not sure what she meant.” They commit to a single interpretation and then defend it. They may also have trouble explaining how they know something. “I just know he’s lying” is not the same as tracking cues, inconsistencies, or motives. Metacognitive weakness makes social reasoning brittle because the person cannot update the model. If they cannot represent their own confidence as partial, they cannot see why another person’s confidence is partial too.

A seventh is pragmatic language: understanding that words do social work beyond their literal content. Sarcasm, irony, politeness, understatement, and indirect requests all require modeling the listener. “Sure, bring it up again” may mean “do not bring it up again.” “I guess I could do that” may mean “I am annoyed but trying not to escalate.” Adults who are overly literal may miss these moves or make them accidentally. Some autistic adults, for example, can pass explicit theory-of-mind tests and still find rapid pragmatic inference exhausting or unintuitive. The knowledge is there; the real-time social computation is not.

An eighth is integrative complexity in moral and character judgment: the ability to hold that a person can be loving and selfish, that a situation can justify and condemn an action, that outcomes can be bad even when intentions were good. Some adults keep thinking in pure categories. People are either safe or dangerous, fair or exploitative, sincere or fake. This is not always a developmental failure. It can be a strategy, especially if the environment really is dangerous and nuance got people hurt. But when it becomes a rigid way of processing all relationships, it limits repair. A person who cannot represent mixed motives cannot understand why someone they trusted would hurt them, or why someone they dislike would do something decent.

How would you tell? You would not tell from one incident. Everyone fails at these skills sometimes. Anger narrows attention. Depression makes other people seem hostile. Fatigue makes irony opaque. Culture shapes how directly people are expected to state what they want. A person from a tradition that values indirectness may not “miss” a hint; they may be operating by different rules. A person in a position of power may have had little practice modeling the minds of people below them, because their orders worked without it.

The evidence is pattern. The same kind of error appears across contexts: at work, with friends, with strangers, in low-stakes situations where there is no obvious reason to be defensive. The person asks for information, then acts as if they already had it. They are corrected, but the correction does not change the model. They say, “I didn’t know you thought that,” in a way that treats your thought as an unreasonable apparition rather than a possible response to their behavior.

Another sign is an expectation of transparency. The person is constantly offended that others do not intuit what they are thinking. They do not say, “I needed you to ask me.” They say, “You should have known.” They may also be bad at accepting that others have private states they cannot simply see. They want proof of loyalty, proof of affection, proof of belief, as if internal states should be publicly legible.

A more specific sign is self-other confusion. The person projects their own current feeling and then experiences your denial of it as deception. If they are suspicious, you are probably hiding something. If they are ashamed, your neutral comment must be criticism. If they are proud, your mild praise must mean you think they are extraordinary. This is not merely narcissism in the colloquial sense. It is a failure to run a separate model of the other person’s mind.

But there is a hard objection here, and it needs to be faced directly: if we call these missing milestones, we risk turning bad behavior into a developmental deficit. A person who hurts others and then says, in effect, “I didn’t understand their mind,” may be trying to escape responsibility. Capacity and motivation are different things. Some adults can model other minds very well and choose not to do so. They know exactly what will land as cruel and do it anyway. That is not a failure of perspective-taking; it is a failure of restraint or care. Labeling every selfish or aggressive act as a cognitive limitation would be wrong.

So the diagnostic question is not whether the person ever fails to consider another mind. The question is whether they can consider it when the cost is low, when they are not threatened, and when someone makes the task explicit. Can they predict how a small change will feel to another person if you walk them through it? Can they revise a plan after being told, “That will make her feel excluded”? Can they explain, even clumsily, why someone might be upset by something they intended as neutral? If the answer is consistently no, even with support, that suggests a real underdeveloped skill. If the answer is yes when the stakes are manageable but no when the person is threatened, interested, or resentful, the issue may be more motivational or emotional than cognitive.

This matters because the remedy is different. If the problem is choice, you need boundaries, consequences, and possibly moral confrontation. If the problem is skill, you need scaffolding. Make the hidden explicit. Write down assumptions. Ask for the other person’s read of the situation. Use check-ins: “What do you think I meant by that?” “What do you want from this conversation?” “Do you know something I don’t?” These are not babyish accommodations. They are the adult version of the false-belief task, adapted for messy life.

There is also a social-structural point. Mentalizing is a practiced skill. People get better at it in environments where others’ minds are stable enough to model and where modeling pays off. If you grew up in a household where intentions were capricious, where saying what you felt was punished, or where other people’s reactions were unpredictable, the skill may not have been reinforced. It is not that the person is incapable; it is that the environment did not reward accurate modeling. The same can happen in jobs where compliance is valued over communication, or in subcultures where reading others is considered sycophantic. Development does not happen in a vacuum.

This does not make the idea soft. Adults with weak social cognition can be genuinely difficult to live with. They can create a constant low-grade strain in which everyone else becomes a interpreter, translator, and emotional forecaster. They can be easily manipulated by people who are better at modeling them. They can make false accusations that feel, to them, like plain sight. They can fail to see that their “honesty” is a form of control, because they cannot model the effect of unfiltered speech on another person’s sense of safety.

The point is not to sort adults into stages, as if some are permanently stuck at age six. The point is to recognize that the mind’s social tools are uneven. Some adults have a strong sense of private knowledge but a weak sense of emotion. Some can track goals but not motives. Some are excellent at modeling friends and terrible at modeling subordinates. Some can do it in writing but not in real time. Development in adulthood is not a ladder with a finish line. It is a set of capacities that can improve, atrophy, or remain patchy depending on injury, temperament, experience, and the incentives around a person.

The tell is not that an adult sometimes cannot see your mind. The tell is that their default assumption is that your mind is a slower, noisier version of theirs, and that the burden of making the difference visible is always yours.

prompt: People accuse scientifically minded folks of 'scientism' when they weigh in on philosophy, morality or religion. Write an essay that takes the accusation seriously, works out what is really going on, and says whether the charge is deserved. Feel free to take a side.
response:
When a scientifically minded person says that evidence bears on God, morality, or meaning, the accusation of scientism is often the first reply. The word is useful because it is vague. It can name a real overreach: the treatment of a scientific result as a final answer to a question it does not answer. It can name a legitimate caution: the refusal to let one method answer every kind of question. And it can mean a border patrol: the claim that some questions are exempt from facts. The charge is deserved in the first case, and misplaced in the third. Most public uses of it are trying to do the third job, and that is why the word so often stops thought instead of improving it.

At its narrowest, scientism is the claim that the natural sciences are the only legitimate source of knowledge, or that every meaningful question can be settled by extending the scientific method. That claim is false. Mathematics is not chemistry. Logic is not biology. The question “What do I owe my sister?” is not a question about electron scattering. A scientist who says the answer must be found only in laboratory data is making a philosophical claim, and a bad one. The fact that the claim sounds scientific does not make it scientific. Science itself does not prove that only scientific facts exist. It works by building models that predict and control, and the inference from “these models work” to “nothing else is real” is a metaphysical step that requires its own argument.

But the accusation often hides a truer point: scientific results do constrain the questions we can sensibly ask, and the answers we can sensibly give. Many questions that are called philosophical, moral, or religious are not self-contained. They depend on what the world is like. If a moral theory says a certain group lacks interests because it lacks rational speech, and psychology shows that the group experiences pain and has preferences, the theory must explain that fact or revise itself. If a religious account says the Earth was made in six days, and geology shows a four-and-a-half-billion-year history, the account must be read nonliterally, amended, or abandoned. If a theory of mind says there is no difference between saying “I am in pain” and genuinely being in pain, behavioral science and neuroscience give us reasons to doubt it. In each case, science is not answering the whole question. It is removing some answers from the table.

That is why scientifically minded people weigh in. They notice that a moral rule, a theological story, or a philosophical theory often makes claims about human beings, animals, societies, or the cosmos. Once those claims are noticed, evidence becomes relevant. A theory of punishment that says we should give offenders what they deserve runs into the fact that some practices make later crime more likely and some make it less likely. A theory of happiness that says we should follow our immediate desires runs into the fact that people often mispredict their future wants. A theory of the soul that says personal identity is a simple, unchanging substance runs into the fact that memory, personality, and brain function are continuous with biological processes. None of these facts settles the moral, religious, or philosophical question by itself. But a theory that cannot be embarrassed by them is not being protected from science; it is being insulated from the world.

The most common flashpoint is religion, and there the charge of scientism is sometimes correct. If a scientist says “evolution disproves God,” the statement is usually too strong unless the theological claim says something specific about how the world was made. A theist can consistently say that God created through evolutionary processes. The scientific result removes one mechanism, not the concept of agency. But the same boundary can become a shield. If a doctrine says the world was created in six literal days, saying “God is beyond science” does not save it, because the doctrine says something about time. If a religious claim makes no difference to any possible observation, then it may be true in some private or experiential sense, but it is not doing the work of explaining the world that people often assign to it. Science is not being kept out; the claim is not making the kind of contact with the world that would allow it to be checked.

Morality is a harder case, and the best version of the anti-scientist charge lives here. Science describes what is; morality says what ought to be. Hume’s point is real: you cannot derive an obligation from a list of facts alone. A neuroscientist who says “love is just oxytocin” has not shown that love is good or bad. An evolutionary biologist who says moral outrage exists because it helped groups cooperate has not shown that moral outrage is right. The origin of a belief does not by itself show that the belief is false. People once thought the sun moved around the Earth because that is how it appeared; the fact that the belief had a cause does not make it true. If that were enough, no empirical claim would be secure, because every belief has some psychological or social history.

But the is-ought gap is not a wall. It is a condition on valid inference. If a moral principle already refers to facts, science can do moral work. “One should not cause unnecessary suffering” is not a scientific premise, but the second term is. How much suffering is caused, by whom, and whether it is necessary are questions that evidence can answer. If a practice causes enormous pain to beings who clearly experience it, a moral theory that says the practice is harmless must be wrong somewhere. The science may not choose the principle, but it can show that the principle has consequences its defenders did not expect. This is not scientism. It is the ordinary fact that values are not floating. A value that cannot be affected by any fact is either very abstract or very empty.

I am least sure about meaning. Whether “meaning” is a natural kind that can be studied, or a category that only makes sense from inside a life, is a live question. A psychologist can study what people report when they say their lives feel meaningful, and can show that meaning is correlated with certain social conditions. But it is not obvious that this exhausts what the word means. Still, even if meaning is not a scientific category in the way mass is, the facts about human life still constrain what meaningful lives are possible. A theory of meaning that requires isolation, self-sufficiency, and the denial of dependence runs into the fact that human beings are social, mortal, and embodied. The objection is not that science has answered the question. It is that the proposed answer does not fit the animal.

So what should the accusation target? There are three moves. The first is to use a scientific fact as a premise in a non-scientific argument. That is ordinary reasoning. The second is to argue that because a scientific fact is true, some non-scientific conclusion follows. That is sometimes legitimate and sometimes not; it depends on the missing premises. The third is to declare the non-scientific question dissolved because a scientific fact has been discovered. That is the move the word scientism should target. “People are bad at predicting their future happiness, so we should be cautious about policies that assume they know what will make their lives go well” is the first kind of move. “Morality evolved, therefore no moral claim is true” is the second kind, and it fails unless the speaker adds a premise about the reliability of evolved moral faculties. “We have found the neural correlates of free will, so free will is gone” is usually the third kind, and it overreaches, because the data show correlations, not the absence of a capacity, unless the concept of free will is defined in a way the data can refute.

The social pattern is worth noticing. The accusation often comes from people who do not want their framework tested. A moral code that is declared beyond empirical criticism is safer for its adherents. A religious story that is declared beyond historical or scientific criticism is easier to keep intact. A philosophical position that is declared beyond the reach of psychology is less likely to be found out of date. But the reverse also happens. Some scientists and popularizers do treat their favorite model as the final word, and they deserve the label. The error is not that they use science. It is that they forget a scientific result is a claim about a domain, not a license to cancel other domains.

A useful test is not “Does this use science?” but “Does the speaker know what the result cannot do?” A scientific result can support a philosophical claim, undermine a moral intuition, or force a reinterpretation of a religious text. It cannot, by itself, supply a value, create a purpose, or prove a metaphysical system. When a scientifically minded person says only that, the charge of scientism is usually a way of avoiding the argument. When the person says more—that the laboratory has settled God, that evolution has canceled obligation, that neuroscience has erased the self—the charge is deserved. The real issue is not the invasion of science into philosophy, morality, and religion. It is whether the people in those domains are willing to answer to the world, and whether the people in the laboratories are humble enough to know where their maps end.

Potential final text:

When a scientifically minded person says that evidence bears on God, morality, or meaning, the accusation of scientism is often the first reply. The word is useful because it is vague. It can mean a real error: the belief that a scientific model is the whole of reality. It can mean a legitimate caution: the refusal to let one method answer every kind of question. And it can mean a border patrol: the claim that some questions are exempt from facts. The charge is deserved only in the first case, and even then it should be stated precisely. In most public disputes it is doing the third job, and that is why it so often stops thought instead of improving it.

At its narrowest, scientism is the claim that the natural sciences are the only legitimate source of knowledge, or that every meaningful question can be settled by extending the scientific method. That claim is false. Mathematics is not chemistry. Logic is not biology. The question "What do I owe my sister?" is not a question about electron scattering. A scientist who says the answer must be found only in laboratory data is making a philosophical claim, and a bad one. The fact that the claim sounds scientific does not make it scientific. Science itself does not prove that only scientific facts exist. It works by building models that predict and control, and the inference from "these models work" to "nothing else is real" is a metaphysical step that requires its own argument.

But the accusation often hides a truer point: scientific results do constrain the questions we can sensibly ask, and the answers we can sensibly give. Many questions that are called philosophical, moral, or religious are not self-contained. They depend on what the world is like. If a moral theory says a certain group lacks interests because it lacks rational speech, and psychology shows that the group experiences pain and has preferences, the theory must explain that fact or revise itself. If a religious account says the Earth was made in six days, and geology shows a four-and-a-half-billion-year history, the account must be read nonliterally, amended, or abandoned. If a theory of mind says there is no difference between saying "I am in pain" and genuinely being in pain, behavioral science and neuroscience give us reasons to doubt it. In each case, science is not answering the whole question. It is removing some answers from the table.

That is why scientifically minded people weigh in. They notice that a moral rule, a theological story, or a philosophical theory often makes claims about human beings, animals, societies, or the cosmos. Once those claims are noticed, evidence becomes relevant. A theory of punishment that says we should give offenders what they deserve runs into the fact that some practices make later crime more likely and some make it less likely. A theory of happiness that says we should follow our immediate desires runs into the fact that people are badly calibrated predictors of their future wants. A theory of the soul that says personal identity is a simple, unchanging substance runs into the fact that memory, personality, and brain function are continuous with biological processes. None of these facts settles the moral, religious, or philosophical question by itself. But a theory that cannot be embarrassed by them is not being protected from science; it is being insulated from the world.

The most common flashpoint is religion, and there the charge of scientism is sometimes correct. If a scientist says "evolution disproves God," the statement is usually too strong unless the theological claim says something specific about how the world was made. A theist can consistently say that God created through evolutionary processes. The scientific result removes one mechanism, not the concept of agency. But the same boundary can become a shield. If a doctrine says the world was created in six literal days, saying "God is beyond science" does not save it, because the doctrine says something about time. If a religious claim makes no difference to any possible observation, then it may be true in some private or experiential sense, but it is not doing the work of explaining the world that people often assign to it. Science is not being kept out; the claim is not making the kind of contact with the world that would allow it to be checked.

Morality is a harder case, and the best version of the anti-scientist charge lives here. Science describes what is; morality says what ought to be. Hume's point is real: you cannot derive an obligation from a list of facts alone. A neuroscientist who says "love is just oxytocin" has not shown that love is good or bad. An evolutionary biologist who says moral outrage exists because it helped groups cooperate has not shown that moral outrage is right. The origin of a belief does not by itself show that the belief is false. People once thought the sun moved around the Earth because that is how it appeared; the fact that the belief had a cause does not make it true. If that were enough, no empirical claim would be secure, because every belief has some psychological or social history.

But the is-ought gap is not a wall. It is a condition on valid inference. If a moral principle already refers to facts, science can do moral work. "One should not cause unnecessary suffering" is not a scientific premise, but the second term is. How much suffering is caused, by whom, and whether it is necessary are questions that evidence can answer. If a practice causes enormous pain to beings who clearly experience it, a moral theory that says the practice is harmless must be wrong somewhere. The science may not choose the principle, but it can show that the principle has consequences its defenders did not expect. This is not scientism. It is the ordinary fact that values are not floating. A value that cannot be affected by any fact is either very abstract or very empty.

I am least sure about meaning. Whether "meaning" is a natural kind that can be studied, or a category that only makes sense from inside a life, is a live question. A psychologist can study what people report when they say their lives feel meaningful, and can show that meaning is correlated with certain social conditions. But it is not obvious that this exhausts what the word means. Still, even if meaning is not a scientific category in the way mass is, the facts about human life still constrain what meaningful lives are possible. A theory of meaning that requires isolation, self-sufficiency, and the denial of dependence runs into the fact that human beings are social, mortal, and embodied. The objection is not that science has answered the question. It is that the proposed answer does not fit the animal.

So what should the accusation target? There are three moves. The first is to use a scientific fact as a premise in a non-scientific argument. That is ordinary reasoning. The second is to argue that because a scientific fact is true, some non-scientific conclusion follows. That is sometimes legitimate and sometimes not; it depends on the missing premises. The third is to declare the non-scientific question dissolved because a scientific fact has been discovered. That is the move the word scientism should target. "People are bad at predicting their future happiness, so we should be cautious about policies that assume they know what will make their lives go well" is the first kind of move. "Morality evolved, therefore no moral claim is true" is the second kind, and it fails unless the speaker adds a premise about the reliability of evolved moral faculties. "We have found the neural correlates of free will, so free will is gone" is usually the third kind, and it overreaches, because the data show correlations, not the absence of a capacity, unless the concept of free will is defined in a way the data can refute.

The social pattern is worth noticing. The accusation often comes from people who do not want their framework tested. A moral code that is declared beyond empirical criticism is safer for its adherents. A religious story that is declared beyond historical or scientific criticism is easier to keep intact. A philosophical position that is declared beyond the reach of psychology is less likely to be found out of date. But the reverse also happens. Some scientists and popularizers do treat their favorite model as the final word, and they deserve the label. The error is not that they use science. It is that they forget a scientific result is a claim about a domain, not a license to cancel other domains.

A useful test is not "Does this use science?" but "Does the speaker know what the result cannot do?" A scientific result can support a philosophical claim, undermine a moral intuition, or force a reinterpretation of a religious text. It cannot, by itself, supply a value, create a purpose, or prove a metaphysical system. When a scientifically minded person says only that, the charge of scientism is usually a way of avoiding the argument. When the person says more—that the laboratory has settled God, that evolution has canceled obligation, that neuroscience has erased the self—the charge is deserved. The real issue is not the invasion of science into philosophy, morality, and religion. It is whether the people in those domains are willing to answer to the world, and whether the people in the laboratories are humble enough to know where their maps end.
