prompt: I'm a working web developer and I keep hearing people argue about whether browsers should follow web standards strictly or keep supporting old, sloppy pages. Write me a long blog post that explains why standards are so hard to get right in practice, and why a browser team can't win either way.
response:
# The Browser That Follows the Spec Breaks the Web

A browser team can spend a year making its engine more correct. The parser rejects fewer hacks. The CSS layout code follows the specification more closely. JavaScript semantics move toward the standard. The test suites pass. Then the beta goes out, and the first serious bug report is not about a test suite. It is a support ticket from a hospital, a school, an insurance company, or a factory floor: the internal portal no longer lets people log in, the checkout page renders as a white screen, the barcode scanner's web app stops working. The code on those pages is not evil. It is old, patched, assembled from vendor scripts, and written against what browsers used to do. The browser team has to choose between the document and the page.

This is the argument you hear when people say browsers should follow standards strictly, or when they say browsers should keep supporting the messy real web. Both sides are pointing at real costs. The costs are not a transition problem that will disappear once enough sites are fixed. The web is large, old, and still growing, and the parts that are hardest to fix are the parts that still have to work.

Standards are hard because they are usually written after the behavior already exists. A standard is supposed to be a promise that different programs will mean the same thing by the same words. But the web's vocabulary was built in public, with no central authority. Browsers shipped features before specs. Authors used features before they were stable. Committees then had to decide whether to bless, amend, or ignore what was already everywhere. Sometimes the standard becomes elegant. More often it becomes a precise description of how several engines happened to behave, with footnotes for the exceptions.

The HTML5 parser is a good case. It specifies what happens when a page has missing closing tags, when a script contains a string that looks like markup, when a comment is malformed, when a form is nested inside a form, when a byte sequence is not valid in the declared encoding. The result is detailed and implementable, but it is not the clean model someone would design from a blank page. It is a map of the damage. A browser that implemented an ideal HTML parser instead would be more pure in some philosophical sense and less useful in every practical one.

CSS makes the problem worse because layout is visual and forgiving in the wrong ways. A page can be invalid and still look like the page people expect. A browser can follow the specification and still produce a result the author did not want. The old quirks box model is a small example: in one mode, a 300-pixel box with 20 pixels of padding can stay 300 pixels wide; in another, it becomes 340. A page full of such boxes does not merely fail validation; it reflows. Tables, floats, percentages, intrinsic sizes, scroll containers, fixed positioning, print styles, and directional text all interact. A standard can define each piece, but the web is the product of the interactions, and the interactions are where old pages live.

JavaScript adds another layer. The language is a standard that absorbed a decade of engine disagreements. Type coercion, the prototype chain, the behavior of `undefined` and `null`, the fact that `typeof null` is `"object"`, the way some operators depend on whether the left side is a string or a number: all of these are now part of the contract. A browser can make the language more consistent, but only by breaking scripts that were written to the inconsistency. Strict mode exists so authors can opt into a cleaner subset. That is an admission that the language cannot be cleaned up from underneath.

A standard can also say what code means without saying how fast it should run. Engines optimize for the workloads they see. If the workload is full of `eval`, inline handlers, dynamic property names, and DOM polling, the engine has to keep paths for that code alive. If it throws those paths away because the style is bad, the page slows down or dies. The standard does not tell the browser which pages deserve speed. The browser finds out from crash reports and support tickets.

The web is not only author-controlled. A page is a bundle of dependencies: CMS template, theme, plugin, analytics, chat widget, ad network, payment iframe. The developer who owns the site may not own the code that breaks. Browsers know this. That is why they still support legacy APIs that were standardized because they were already everywhere. If a third-party script assumes an old engine behavior, the first-party site takes the blame. A strict browser would turn every supply-chain mistake into a site outage.

Users do not care about the argument either. A browser is not judged by the percentage of pages it renders perfectly in a lab. It is judged by whether a person can finish what they came to do. For most people, the web is a set of doors: email, banking, work dashboard, school portal, government form. If one door sticks, they do not file a bug report about standards. They switch to another browser or ask for a desktop site. The browser team loses.

The exact share of page loads that comes from old or fragile code is hard to measure precisely, because much of it never appears in public benchmarks; it lives behind logins, on intranets, in embedded devices, and in places where upgrading software is not an option. But browser teams have enough data to know it is not negligible. They see the same classes of pages over and over: enterprise software that has been patched for a decade, content management systems with templates nobody understands, mobile webviews in apps that update slowly, and small business sites that must keep working because the owner cannot afford to rebuild them.

The other side of the argument is not romantic. The web needs standards because without them, every browser is a dialect. If a site cannot rely on `fetch`, CSS custom properties, `IntersectionObserver`, or structured clone, it has to write fallbacks for each engine's temperament. Feature detection stops working when the feature exists but behaves differently. Vendor prefixes and user-agent sniffing become the real platform. The web becomes slower and more brittle, not because standards are bureaucratic, but because the only alternative is a million private agreements.

Standards also protect authors from browsers doing whatever they want. A browser company has commercial reasons to make its own ecosystem look better. If it can quietly change layout, storage, permissions, or JavaScript timing, it can create advantages or lock-ins. The spec is slow and boring, but it is the only thing that lets a developer say, “This is what the platform means, and I can test against it.” Even when the spec is imperfect, it gives the web a shared coordinate system.

So the browser team cannot win by being strict. If it moves toward strict standards, it pays for the transition in broken pages. If it preserves legacy, it pays in complexity, security, and future capability. The legacy path is not stable either. Every quirk that is kept must be documented, tested, and defended. It slows the engine down. It creates corners where bugs hide. It gives attackers more surface, because old sloppy code often means inline scripts, weak boundaries, and assumptions about the DOM that make cross-site scripting easier. A browser that supports everything can also be exploited more easily.

Security shows the shape of the problem clearly. When browsers began blocking active mixed content, they were doing the right security thing and breaking real pages at the same time. A secure standard required HTTPS for scripts, but some sites still loaded JavaScript over HTTP. The browser had to choose between a downgrade attack and a broken checkout. It chose security, but only after warnings, exceptions, and a long phase-in. The standard was correct. The web was not ready. The browser had to carry both facts at once.

Privacy shows the same pattern. Third-party storage, cookies, fingerprinting, and cross-site tracking all depend on assumptions about how freely one site can inspect another. Modern browsers have been tightening those boundaries. That is good for users. It is also expensive for pages that were built on the old assumptions. A browser cannot simply enforce the privacy model and expect every ad, analytics tool, login flow, and embedded widget to keep working. It has to introduce signals, exceptions, and timelines while the ecosystem scrambles to catch up.

The standards path has costs too. New features must be compatible with old content. CSS changes are constrained because layout is global. You cannot say “from now on, percentages in this new box model mean something better” without reflowing every page that uses percentages. You cannot make a new default for scroll behavior, form validation, or focus handling if old pages depend on the old default. The standard moves by adding new properties, not by changing old ones. That is why the platform accumulates layers: new APIs next to old ones, with compatibility shims between them.

There is also no clean line between standard and slop. Many standards are codified slop. HTML is full of elements that exist because old documents used them. CSS has units and properties shaped by old printers and old monitors. JavaScript has methods that are weird because old pages needed them. If a browser team tries to separate “real standards” from “legacy mess,” it must decide which accidents are too useful to remove. That decision is political and economic, not technical.

The practical answer is not purity. It is managed migration. Ship the standard feature. Keep the old behavior working. Add a warning in devtools. Provide a migration guide. Give authors a way to opt into new behavior, through a meta tag, a manifest entry, an API, or a new element. Wait for interop. Deprecate slowly. Sometimes reverse a change if field data shows it caused more harm than good. The browser becomes a conservator of a museum that people still live in.

You feel this in your own work. You write code to the standard, but you also test the browser the client's employees actually use. You add a polyfill because an old Android webview mishandles a feature. You avoid a CSS property because a desktop browser still renders it differently. You keep a fallback for a form behavior that the spec says should work but that production data says is not safe. The standards argument is not an academic one; it is the difference between a page that works in a demo and a page that works on Tuesday at 4 p.m. when someone needs to submit a claim.

The argument “browsers should just break old pages” ignores who pays. The cost of a broken page is not spread across the browser's users in an abstract way. It lands on a specific person who cannot do a task. The argument “browsers should never enforce standards” ignores that the cost of non-enforcement is also not abstract. It lands on developers who spend years maintaining code for behavior that should not exist. Both are real. The browser team sits between them.

A browser team does not get to solve this by being more principled. It gets to reduce the damage: make standards available, keep the old world alive just long enough, expose the seams, and accept that some pages will always be older than the platform that renders them.

prompt: Write a blog post giving a quick, irreverent checklist for judging how good a software team is, with a sentence or two of justification for each item.
response:
# A Quick, Irreverent Checklist for Judging How Good a Software Team Is

1. **They can explain what they’re doing without sounding like a spell.**  
   If the explanation requires a fog of buzzwords, the fog is probably hiding uncertainty, bad design, or both.

2. **They argue about edge cases, not just deadlines.**  
   A team that cares about what happens when the database blips, the API times out, or the user does something stupid is a team that has been burned before and learned.

3. **Their code reviews are about risk, not typography.**  
   If most comments are about naming or semicolons, someone is looking for a way to feel involved without actually thinking.

4. **They write tests for behavior, not coverage.**  
   A test that only proves a function was called is not a test; it is a small, automated prayer.

5. **Their deploys are boring.**  
   If shipping software feels like a ceremony, a blood sacrifice, or a controlled experiment, the system is fragile and the team is compensating with drama.

6. **They say no to features that would make the product worse.**  
   A team that only says yes is not a software team; it is a feature factory with a performance review problem.

7. **They leave docs, but not a memoir.**  
   Good docs assume the next person is competent but has no time. If your README reads like a personal journey through suffering, try again.

8. **They treat production like everyone’s problem.**  
   “That’s the ops team’s issue” is not a boundary; it is a confession.

9. **They can talk about a recent failure without turning it into a myth.**  
   If the last outage is already legendary, sacred, or forbidden, the team has not actually learned anything.

10. **No one is the only one who can fix the important stuff.**  
   If one person is the sole keeper of the core system, you do not have a team; you have a hostage situation with a timesheet.

prompt: You asked programmers on Twitter what made a bug feel 'impossible' to understand and got hundreds of replies. Write a post that sorts those reasons into categories.
response:
I asked programmers on Twitter what made a bug feel impossible to understand. The replies were not mostly about obscure language features or “clever” code. They were about broken feedback. The same six things kept showing up.

1. The state was hidden.

The code in front of you is not the state the code is acting on. A cache, a database transaction, a browser tab, a worker process, a config file, a stale environment variable. A service returns success while silently using yesterday’s data because a feature flag was cached at boot. A form looks empty because another tab already changed the value. A job runs twice because a message was acknowledged after it had already been requeued.

The bug feels impossible because the interesting value is not in the code path anyone is stepping through.

2. The bug was at a boundary.

The code looks innocent because the lie happens outside it. Boundaries are where the mental model stops being enforced: HTTP, queues, databases, file systems, operating systems, third-party APIs, message formats, authentication providers.

A payment retry was assumed to be idempotent, but it was not. A database driver returned timestamps in UTC while the team thought they were local time. A file was written, but not flushed. A message was delivered twice after a timeout. A load balancer routed the session to a server that did not have the session.

Each of these is explainable. None of them live where the first person looking for the bug expects to find one.

3. Time was a variable.

This includes async code, but also clocks, ordering, TTLs, and patience.

A test passes on a fast machine and fails on a slow one. A cron job runs at 3:00, but the data feed arrives at 3:04. Two servers disagree by a few seconds, and the older one wins. A user clicks save, then clicks away before the request finishes. A cache expires at the exact moment a report is generated.

Bugs that depend on timing are hard because the usual tools stop time. The debugger freezes execution, and freezing execution can remove the condition that produced the failure.

4. The evidence was missing or untrustworthy.

Sometimes the system did not leave a record. Sometimes it left the wrong one.

Logs were rotated. Metrics were averaged into meaninglessness. The sampled request was not the failing one. The error message described a previous attempt. The debugger changed the timing. The customer’s data could not be copied because it was private, malformed, or gone.

People said “impossible” not because the logic was too clever, but because they could not get a second observation of the same event. Without a reliable second observation, debugging stops being investigation and starts being guesswork.

5. The team’s model of the system was wrong.

The code was doing what it was told. The team had told it the wrong thing.

A field was assumed unique but was not. A decimal comma was parsed as a thousands separator. A “soft delete” was not honored by the reporting query. A permission check was bypassed by an admin role no one had used in two years. An endpoint was assumed to be safe to retry, but it created a record instead of updating one.

These bugs feel impossible because the wrong assumption is not contained in one file. It is shared by the API, the UI, the database, the docs, and the person on call.

6. The bug required scale or coincidence.

One user works. Ten thousand users exhaust the connection pool.

One file works. A filename with a non-ASCII character breaks.

One retry works. Three retries from two clients create a duplicate.

A small dataset fits in memory. A large one does not. A single region is fast enough. Across regions, the timeout becomes real.

These are not mysterious in the way a logic puzzle is mysterious. They are expensive because the failure condition is not a line of code. It is a relationship between load, timing, and resources.

These categories overlap, and that is the annoying part. A race condition is hidden state, time, and bad evidence. A bad timezone is a boundary and a wrong model. A duplicate payment is scale, retry logic, and an untrusted external system.

But if a bug feels impossible, it is usually because the debugging loop has broken: you cannot name the state, the boundary, the clock, the log, the assumption, or the load condition that needs testing.

prompt: Write a blog post about the link between smoking and schizophrenia. I've seen claims that smoking causes psychosis and others that it protects against it, and I'd like someone to dig into how good the evidence on each side actually is, and what researchers should do when studies disagree.
response:
**Smoking, schizophrenia, and the problem of timing**

Most people with schizophrenia smoke. In high-income countries, roughly half to three-quarters of patients are smokers, compared with about 15 to 20 percent of the general population. They also tend to smoke heavily and to start early. That pattern is what makes the topic confusing. If smoking caused schizophrenia, the high rate among patients makes sense. If smoking protects against it, the high rate is a paradox. Both claims have appeared in the literature, and both are easier to state than to defend.

The first thing to notice is that “smoking” is not a clean exposure. A person who smokes one cigarette a day at 45 is not the same as a person who starts a pack a day at 16. Schizophrenia is not a clean outcome either. A brief psychotic episode after sleep loss, a first hospital admission at 22, and a chronic illness diagnosed at 35 are different events. Many studies collapse these distinctions. When they do, a real association can disappear or flip.

A causal story needs smoking to precede the illness in a way that is not explained by early symptoms. The best human evidence would come from a cohort followed from childhood or adolescence, with repeated measures of smoking, cannabis use, mood, perceptual symptoms, family history, and adverse experiences. We have some pieces, not the whole. Some studies find that smoking in early adolescence is followed by higher rates of psychotic experiences. Some studies of maternal smoking find small increases in offspring risk. But these are not the same as schizophrenia, and the estimates often shrink or change when cannabis, baseline symptoms, and social factors are controlled. Nicotine also does not behave like a classic psychosis-provoking drug in the way amphetamines or heavy cannabis use do. Animal work can show that nicotine alters dopamine signaling, but that is a long way from “cigarettes cause schizophrenia.” So the causal case is plausible enough to study, but it is not established.

The protective claim comes from a different set of studies. Some prospective studies and meta-analyses report that people who smoked before their first episode had lower odds of developing schizophrenia, sometimes by a third. That is a striking result, and it is also the most fragile number. The reason is timing. Schizophrenia often has a long, quiet prephase. A future patient may start smoking at 19 because of anxiety, odd perceptual experiences, or social withdrawal, but not be diagnosed until 25. A study that asks about smoking at 18 may classify that person as a nonsmoker. Controls who smoke at 18 are, by definition, not that person. The result can look protective even if smoking is a response to early illness. Add to that the fact that smoking is tangled with cannabis use, family background, urbanicity, and health care contact, and the direction of the association is not secure.

The self-medication story is better supported by what happens after diagnosis. Nicotine acts on receptors that modulate dopamine in prefrontal and striatal circuits. In people with schizophrenia, it can improve attention and sensory gating, a measurable deficit in how the brain filters repeated sounds. Many patients report that smoking calms them or helps them think. Cessation often worsens negative symptoms and mood, at least in the short term. That is not proof that smoking treats schizophrenia. Withdrawal is miserable, and nicotine can change antipsychotic levels. But it explains why patients smoke so much and why the association is so strong.

If smoking does not clearly cause schizophrenia and the protective evidence is weak, should clinicians tell patients not to smoke? Yes. The harms are not uncertain. People with schizophrenia already die a decade or two early; tobacco is a major part of that. Smoking also complicates treatment. Smoke induces CYP1A2, which lowers levels of clozapine and olanzapine. When a patient stops smoking, drug levels can rise and side effects can appear. Cessation should be supported, with nicotine replacement or varenicline and careful antipsychotic monitoring. A speculative reduction in onset risk is not a reason to start smoking, and a short-term symptom cost is not a reason to accept a smoking-related death.

The hardest objection is that if smoking relieves symptoms, quitting might be harmful. It can be if done badly. Abrupt cessation without support can worsen symptoms and shift medication levels. The answer is not to keep people smoking; it is to make cessation part of treatment. If the protective claim is about preventing illness in young people, the objection is weaker still: the evidence is too weak to recommend exposure to a known carcinogen, especially when adolescent smoking is also a route into dependence.

Researchers should treat the disagreement as a measurement problem, not just a statistical one. They should stop reducing smoking to yes or no. Record when it started, how much, whether it stopped, and whether nicotine was delivered by cigarettes, patches, or vapes. Record the prodrome before the exposure, not after. Use repeated measures. Use sibling or twin comparisons where possible. Use natural experiments—tax changes, smoking bans, cessation programs—as checks on individual data. Use Mendelian randomization as one sensitivity analysis, not a verdict, because genetic instruments for smoking are correlated with other liabilities. Share individual participant data and pre-register the timing assumptions. When estimates disagree, ask which study’s exposure is closest to a biologically plausible window and which outcome is most specific.

The next useful studies are the ones that can tell, in the same person over time, whether smoking began before the first signs of vulnerability, after them, or only after the diagnosis. Until then, the practical conclusion is not “smoke” or “don’t smoke because of schizophrenia.” It is that the association is real, the direction is unresolved, and the harms are not.

Some studies of maternal smoking find small increases in offspring risk. But these are not the same as schizophrenia, and the estimates shrink or change when cannabis, baseline symptoms, and social factors are controlled. Nicotine also does not behave like a psychosis-provoking drug in the way amphetamines or heavy cannabis use do. Animal work can make nicotine alter dopamine signaling, but that is a long way from "cigarettes cause schizophrenia." So the causal case is plausible enough to study, but not established.

Then protective. Some prospective studies and meta-analyses report that people who smoked before their first episode had lower odds of developing schizophrenia, sometimes by a third. That is the source of the protective claim. It is also the most fragile number. The reason is timing. Schizophrenia often has a long, quiet prephase. A future patient may start smoking at 19 because of anxiety, odd perceptual experiences, or social withdrawal, but not be diagnosed until 25. A study that asks about smoking at 18 may classify that person as a nonsmoker. Controls who smoke at 18 are, by definition, not that person. The result can look protective even if smoking is a response to early illness. Add to that the fact that smoking is tangled with cannabis, family background, urbanicity, and health care contact, and the direction of the association is not secure.

The self-medication story is better supported by what happens after diagnosis. Nicotine acts on receptors that modulate dopamine in prefrontal and striatal circuits. In people with schizophrenia, it can improve attention and sensory gating, a measurable deficit in how the brain filters repeated sounds. Many patients report that smoking calms them or helps them think. Cessation often worsens negative symptoms and mood, at least in the short term. That is not proof that smoking treats schizophrenia. Withdrawal is miserable, and nicotine can change antipsychotic levels. But it explains why patients smoke so much and why the association is so strong.

Then clinical: If smoking does not clearly cause schizophrenia and the protective evidence is weak, should clinicians tell patients not to smoke? Yes. The harms are not uncertain. People with schizophrenia already die a decade or two early; tobacco is a major part of that. Smoking also complicates treatment. Smoke induces CYP1A2, which lowers levels of clozapine and olanzapine. When a patient stops smoking, drug levels can rise and side effects can appear. Cessation should be supported, with nicotine replacement or varenicline and careful antipsychotic monitoring. A speculative reduction in onset risk is not a reason to start smoking, and a small short-term symptom cost is not a reason to accept a smoking-related death.

The answer is not to keep them smoking; it is to make cessation part of treatment. But if the protective claim is about preventing illness in young people, the objection is weaker: the evidence is too weak to recommend exposure to a known carcinogen, especially when adolescent smoking is also a gateway to dependence.

What should researchers do? Stop treating "smoking" as yes/no. Record when it started, how much, whether it stopped, and whether nicotine was delivered by cigarettes, patches, or vapes. Record the prodrome before the exposure, not after. Use repeated measures. Use sibling or twin comparisons where possible. Use natural experiments—tax changes, smoking bans, cessation programs—as checks on individual data. Use Mendelian randomization as one sensitivity analysis, not a verdict, because genetic instruments for smoking are correlated with other liabilities. Share individual participant data and pre-register the timing assumptions. When estimates disagree, ask which study's exposure is closest to a biologically plausible window and which outcome is most specific.

The honest position is that smoking is a marker, a coping tool, and a health hazard, and the evidence for a causal effect on schizophrenia is still too contaminated by timing and confounding to support either dramatic claim. The next studies need to separate the person who smoked because they were getting ill from the person who smoked because cigarettes were cheap and available.

prompt: You've spent years doing office hours with early-stage startups. Write an essay about the question you find more useful than "how can this company make more money": how could it become more powerful? Cover the different forms that takes and what limits it.
response:
The whiteboard usually has a number on it: $8,000 MRR, 14 percent monthly churn, a sales cycle that has stretched from six months to eleven, a customer who wants a discount because a competitor is “doing the same thing.” The founder asks how to make the number bigger. I answer. But the question I find more useful is: how could this company become more powerful?

I do not mean powerful in the sense of intimidating, dominant, or difficult. I mean less optional. A startup is more powerful when the people around it—customers, suppliers, partners, investors, regulators, employees—have to plan around it. That is a structural condition, not a mood. It shows up in small ways: the company can say no to a bad customer without losing sleep. It can ignore a feature request that would cost three months of engineering. It can raise prices on new logos without the sales team flinching. It can survive a platform fee change, a key employee departure, or a competitor’s price cut because the relationship with its market has some depth.

Revenue is useful, but it is a lagging indicator and an easy one to distort. A company with $2 million in annual recurring revenue from twenty customers at $100,000 each has a very different position from one with $2 million from two thousand customers at $1,000 each. The first may be close to a single-customer business wearing a portfolio costume. The second may be drowning in support tickets and implementation friction. Both can be excellent; both can be fragile. The revenue number does not say which. The power question does. It asks who depends on whom, what would happen if the company disappeared for a month, and what the company controls that it did not control a year ago.

The first form of power is technical: a gap in cost, speed, reliability, or quality. If a logistics software package cuts dispatch planning from four hours to thirty minutes, if a diagnostic tool reduces false positives enough to save clinicians real work, if a compiler makes a workload cheaper to run at scale, the company has a physical fact on its side. That fact can support pricing, expansion, and patience. The limit is replication. If the gap comes from a model architecture that can be read in a paper, a dataset that can be scraped, a workflow that can be observed, or a team that can be poached, the gap narrows. If it comes from a factory, a proprietary sensor, a closed feedback loop, a hard integration, or years of edge-case handling, it lasts longer. Technical power is strongest when the advantage is not visible until a competitor has already spent a year catching up.

The second form is data power, but only in a narrow sense. Data is not powerful merely because it exists. It is powerful when usage generates information that improves the product and is difficult to obtain anywhere else. A claims-processing startup that sees which invoices fail audit and why learns something that a general-purpose accounting tool may never see. A marketplace for a narrow trade learns which jobs actually get done, which prices hold, and which counterparties are reliable. A medical device company that collects real-world outcomes can improve triage in ways that benchmark data cannot. The limits are consent, privacy, staleness, and trust. Customers will share less if they feel surveilled. Regulators will draw lines. Data about a changing market can expire. And if the customer believes the data will be used against them, they will game the system or leave.

The third form is embeddedness: becoming the place where the work is recorded. If your product is where the invoice lives, where the patient note is amended, where the compliance exception is resolved, where the field technician’s photos and signatures are attached to the job, then leaving means rebuilding history. This is more durable than a login. It is institutional memory. The company has not merely saved time; it has become part of the organization’s record. The limit is that customers sense this and resist it. Enterprises will ask for export formats, data ownership clauses, termination assistance, and portability guarantees. A startup that leans on lock-in without trust will eventually be replaced when the budget holder changes, when the CIO consolidates vendors, or when the team that loved the tool leaves. Embeddedness becomes power only when it is tied to a workflow the customer still wants to run.

The fourth form is network power, which is more often claimed than possessed. A directory with one thousand users is not a network. A forum with active users is not a network. A calendar with shared events is not a network. Real network power appears when one side’s presence makes the other side’s action more valuable, or when shared context reduces transaction costs. A marketplace for commercial laundries is powerful when both drivers and shops are there because the alternative is phone calls, no-shows, and cash reconciliation. A professional network is powerful when the people you need are already in the room and their reputations are legible. The limits are density, coordination, and multi-homing. The network must be thick enough in the places that matter. If users can use you and a competitor at the same time with no penalty, the network is a convenience, not a position.

The fifth form is distribution: owning the moment of discovery. A plugin in a large ecosystem gets installs. A newsletter with real trust gets attention. A community where practitioners ask for help becomes a demand channel. A default in a hardware stack or a professional workflow becomes a path to market. Distribution power is seductive because it looks like growth, and growth is what founders are paid to produce. The limit is that distribution is often rented. The ecosystem can change the store rules. The algorithm can shift. The platform can launch a native feature. The audience can move to a new channel. The durable version is not a feed but an identity: people seek the company out because it is the named option in a conversation. “We use X for that” is stronger than “X appeared in our sidebar.”

The sixth form is regulatory and trust power. In many markets, the barrier is not code but permission: licenses, audits, certifications, data protection, underwriting standards, safety reviews, procurement approval. A fintech that can pass a bank’s vendor review has an advantage that a faster prototype cannot easily match. A health startup that can handle consent, audit trails, and role-based access can sell where others cannot. An energy software company that can interface with utility compliance can move into deals that look boring to generalist competitors. The limit is that the same machinery slows you down. Regulation can protect you from a well-funded entrant, but it can also make you a target when the political mood changes. Trust is a moat and a maintenance burden.

The seventh form is capital efficiency, which is power through negative capability. A company with 80 percent gross margin and a small sales team can choose its battles. It can wait for the right customer, refuse the bad one, fund a pivot, or outlast a price war. A company with 30 percent gross margin and a heavy implementation cost must keep selling just to stay alive. Its strategy is often whatever keeps the cash flow positive. The limit is that capital efficiency can become capital paralysis. If a company is too frugal, it may miss the moment when spending would buy a structural position: a key hire, a direct sales motion, a hardware partnership, a regulatory filing. Efficiency without timing is just smallness.

The eighth form is optionality: a position that touches something valuable without yet owning it. A startup that begins by scheduling field technicians may end up owning dispatch, parts, warranties, financing, or compliance reporting. A company that starts by cleaning data for one department may become the system that other departments trust. A developer tool that begins as a testing utility may become the place where teams define what “production” means. The power here is the option to move along a chain of work. The limit is focus. Every adjacent market is a different customer, sales cycle, operational burden, and failure mode. A small company that tries to own the whole chain before it owns one piece usually dies of sprawl.

These forms are limited by the same underlying constraints. There is a physical limit: a product cannot remove more friction than the task contains. There is a human limit: customers will not keep using a tool that makes them look stupid, and employees will not keep executing a strategy they cannot explain. There is a trust limit: the more power a company accumulates, the more its counterparties watch for abuse. There is a capital limit: even a superior position can be outspent during the years it takes to compound. And there is a response limit: power attracts competitors, platforms, incumbents, and regulators. A platform will protect its take rate. An incumbent will bundle, copy, or acquire the input. A regulator will notice when a small company starts collecting data that looks like surveillance. A customer will form a counteralliance if it feels cornered.

There is also an internal limit. Startups often mistake the source of their early success for a permanent identity. The team that won because it was scrappy may refuse to build sales discipline. The team that won because it was technical may refuse to learn distribution. The team that won in one vertical may assume the playbook transfers unchanged. Power is not a property the company has; it is a relationship the company maintains. When the organization stops updating its model of the market, the position decays even if the metrics look stable for a while.

The hardest objection to the question is that it is dangerous. In business language, power often means the ability to extract rent: raise prices after lock-in, degrade service, take data, squeeze suppliers, punish dissent. If a founder asks how to become more powerful, the obvious answer may be “by making customers dependent,” and that is a bad company to build. A company that is hard to replace because it has captured data and made the exit painful has friction, not strength. It may show up as low churn for a time, but the churn is deferred, not absent. The customers are waiting for a reason to leave. The regulators are waiting for a complaint. The talent pool is waiting for a better story.

The question survives only if power is defined as the result of value, not a substitute for it. A company that is hard to replace because it saves its customers real work has power. A company that is hard to replace because it has made leaving expensive has a time bomb. In office hours, I try to tell the difference by asking who benefits when the relationship ends. If the customer loses more than the startup does because the startup created value the customer cannot easily reproduce, the position may be durable. If the customer loses only because the startup has captured records, integrations, or habits without giving enough back, the position is brittle. The first compounds. The second produces resentment.

So the question I keep asking is not how to make more money this quarter. It is what could this company control, know, or become that would make it less optional? If the answer is a feature, it may last a quarter. If the answer is a workflow, a dataset, a network, a license, a cost structure, or a community, it may last a company. Revenue tells you whether the market paid you. Power tells you whether you can still choose what to do next.

prompt: People keep saying content moderation on big platforms would be easy if the moderators just used common sense. I think that's wrong, but I want to make the case with something more than vibes. Write an essay on why large platforms can't come up with moderation rules that people agree on, using David Turner's "No Vehicles in the Park" game as a starting point.
response:
A sign in the park says, “No vehicles.” A car is obviously forbidden. A bicycle is less clear. A wheelchair? An ambulance? A shopping cart? A horse? A child on roller skates? A drone carrying a camera? In David Turner’s “No Vehicles in the Park” game, the point is not that people are stupid. The point is that the word *vehicle* does not carry its own border. It points toward a cluster of ordinary cases, but the edge of the concept has to be made by deciding what the rule is for. If the park rule exists to prevent noise, bicycles may be allowed. If it exists to protect children from fast moving objects, ambulances may still be allowed but motorcycles may not. If it exists to preserve a pedestrian space, wheelchairs must be allowed even though they are, in some broad sense, vehicles. The rule is short, but the practice behind it is not.

Content moderation on large platforms has the same shape. The policies use familiar words: hate speech, harassment, threat, misinformation, nudity, extremism, dangerous content. Each word feels intuitive until a moderator has to apply it to a specific post, in a specific language, from a specific user, aimed at a specific audience, at a specific moment. Is a slur hateful? Usually. Is quoting a slur in order to condemn it hateful? Sometimes, depending on the surrounding conversation. Is a satirical group name hateful? It may be, if it imitates a real movement. Is a political cartoon threatening? It may be, if it is part of a campaign against a named person. Is a graphic image educational, journalistic, traumatic, or exploitative? The answer changes with the viewer, the context, and the platform’s purpose. These are not cases where common sense is missing. They are cases where common sense is not singular.

The phrase “just use common sense” assumes that there is one shared background against which the rule can be applied. In a small community, there often is one. Neighbors know which families are joking, which kids are dangerous, which dogs are friendly, which complaints are serious. They also know each other, and their judgments are corrected over time by repeated interaction. If someone calls a remark abusive when the community sees it as a rough joke, the social cost of being wrong matters. A platform does not have that kind of world. It has users who may never meet, content that crosses borders, languages that do not translate cleanly, and moderators who may have no relationship to the people involved. A moderator in one country may read a comment as a credible threat; a moderator in another may read it as hyperbole. Both may be using good sense. The problem is that the sense is local, and the platform is not.

Scale makes the indeterminacy worse, not better. A local rule can survive because the hard cases are rare and can be handled personally. A large platform faces a continuous stream of hard cases because users discover that rules are boundaries, and boundaries invite testing. Once a platform says that certain content is forbidden, people will ask how far the line goes. They will use irony, translation, code words, images, historical references, and variations of forbidden phrases. A rule that works on ordinary content becomes a puzzle under adversarial use. “No vehicles” becomes a game because people bring strange things to the park. “No harassment” becomes a game because people bring strange messages to the comment section. The flexibility that allows a rule to cover new circumstances also allows it to be gamed.

The strongest objection to this view is that courts manage open-ended rules all the time. They use terms like “reasonable,” “probable cause,” “defamatory,” “imminent,” and “harmful,” and they develop doctrine through case by case adjudication. If judges can do it, why can’t platform moderators? The answer is that courts do not face the same conditions. A court hears a limited number of disputes, with parties, evidence, procedure, and time. It can develop precedent slowly. It can call a jury from the local community. It can say, in effect, that the line will be drawn differently in different circumstances. A platform must make decisions at a speed and volume that legal process cannot match. It also lacks the full institutional package that gives courts legitimacy: independence, procedural fairness, public reasoning, appeal, and the backing of state authority. A platform can build appeals, and it should, but an internal appeal process does not create the same kind of legitimacy as an external legal order. It can explain a decision, but it cannot make the explanation feel neutral to everyone affected.

There is also a stakeholder problem that the park game does not fully capture. A park rule mostly balances pedestrian safety with access. A platform rule balances many things at once: user safety, freedom of expression, creator reach, advertiser comfort, legal compliance, public trust, and the platform’s own growth. These values do not always point the same way. Removing a violent video may protect viewers but destroy evidence of a crime. Keeping a defamatory post may preserve free expression but ruin a person’s life. Allowing private messages may protect intimacy but enable grooming. Banning a political symbol may protect one group while silencing another. People who agree on the goals can still disagree about the line, because the line allocates real harms. A moderation rule is not a neutral description of the world. It is a choice about whose harm counts more, and when.

International law makes the disagreement more visible. A platform cannot simply apply “common sense” as if common sense were a world language. What is protected political speech in one country may be illegal incitement in another. What is privacy in one jurisdiction may be a public interest matter in another. What is a threat in one legal system may be a protected expression of dissent in another. A global platform must either choose one standard and impose it everywhere, or build a patchwork of local rules. Both options create resentment. The first looks culturally arrogant; the second looks inconsistent and hard to govern. The park sign becomes many signs in many parks, where even the words “vehicle” and “park” do not mean the same things.

This does not mean that all moderation is impossible or that current rules are useless. A great deal of moderation is easy enough. Spam, phishing, obvious child sexual abuse material, coordinated fake accounts, and posts publishing someone’s home address with a threat do not require philosophical debate. They can be handled with rules, detection systems, and human review. The mistake is to think that because the easy cases are easy, the hard cases should be easy too. But the hard cases are not a small remainder. They are the cases that define the platform’s character. The question is not only whether a post breaks a rule. The question is what kind of public the platform is trying to make.

That is why people keep arguing about moderation. They are not failing to apply common sense. They are discovering that common sense is not a universal solvent. It is a shortcut that works when people share a world. A large platform is not a village, a courtroom, a newspaper, or a living room. It is all of those at once, without the institutions that make each of them work. A park rule works because there is a park, a local community, and a limited set of uses. A platform rule works only if the platform accepts that its rules are not self-executing. They require context, explanation, appeal, local sensitivity, and a willingness to revise the line when a new case shows where the old one failed. The goal should not be a simple rule that everyone agrees with in advance. It should be a process that can survive disagreement when the hard cases arrive.

prompt: Politicians keep saying the only way to become a billionaire is by exploiting people. You spent years at Y Combinator trying to pick the founders who would get enormously rich. Write an essay that uses what you actually looked for in YC interviews to answer that claim, and give founders honest advice on how to do well in the interview along the way.
response:
The politician’s claim is seductive because it turns an observed inequality into a moral diagnosis. If the only path to billionaire wealth is exploitation, then every large tech fortune is a crime scene. From the YC side of the table, after years of trying to pick founders who would build enormous companies, the claim does not survive contact with the interview room. It captures a real risk, but it mistakes the risk for the engine.

The YC interview is not a job interview and not a morality test. The founder is not trying to get hired; the partners are not trying to find nice people. The question is whether this team can build a company that creates value at scale before it runs out of money, credibility, or steam. That sounds cold, but it matters. A founder who is kind but cannot execute will not become a billionaire, and will probably not help many people either. A founder who can execute but has no respect for the people around the business may become a billionaire and cause real harm. The interview is a poor test of the second thing and a decent test of the first.

The first thing I looked for was a customer, not a market. Market size is a number on a slide; a customer is a person with a problem. The difference is audible. “There are millions of small businesses” is not information. “We spent two weeks in a veterinary clinic, the front desk loses an hour a day reconciling invoices, and the owner said she would pay for something that cut it in half” is a company. The first answer could be true and useless. The second answer is testable. It gives you a place to go on Monday.

Next I looked for why now. A problem that has existed for twenty years is not a reason to start today. The founder needs a change that makes the solution possible or urgent: a new technology, a regulation, a shift in behavior, a cost curve, a distribution channel. If the answer is “AI” or “the cloud” without a mechanism, it is a slogan. If the founder can say “this used to require a team of five; now it can be done by a model plus a small product surface,” that is a business.

Then I looked for evidence of ability. Not charisma. A prototype, a hard technical choice, a difficult customer, a metric that moved. A founder who can say “we built this, it failed because of X, we changed Y” is more valuable than one who can pitch a deck. The plan is less important than the ability to form a new plan after the first surprise. Startups die from contact with reality. The founders who survive are the ones who can update without breaking.

The interview is also a pressure test for honesty. The interviewer will poke. If the founder gets defensive, that is data. If they say “you’re right, we didn’t test that, here’s how we would test it,” that is data too. The second kind is more likely to survive a market. A founder who cannot take a 30-second challenge often cannot take a 30-month correction. A founder who fakes certainty in the room is usually faking it in the product.

The pair matters almost as much as the idea. One founder can be brilliant and still build a fragile company. Two founders need shared values and complementary skills. I have seen two great founders destroy a company because they did not agree on what success was for. I have seen two ordinary founders build a large company because they trusted each other enough to keep going when the product was bad. prompt: Is there really such a thing as good taste, or is it all just preference? I'm giving a talk to a student debating society and want a short, rigorous argument for one side. Write it as an essay.
response:
There is such a thing as good taste, but not as a list of objects that are good in themselves. It is a quality of judgment: the trained ability to perceive what is in a work, to notice what is relevant, and to form a preference that fits the object.

All taste begins as preference. I like chocolate, you like vanilla. At that level, there is no argument. But when we say a film, a dish, a poem, or a piece of music is good, we are doing more than reporting a feeling. We are claiming that the object has features that make the feeling appropriate. A listener who calls a sonata boring may mean only that it does not stimulate him. A listener with good taste may mean that the themes are stated and then abandoned, that a tension is never resolved, that the middle section merely repeats what has already been said. The first statement is private. The second can be tested by listening again, comparing passages, and seeing whether the claimed failure is there.

This is the main reason taste is not merely preference: it can be improved. If preference were all there is, education would be pointless. A person who has tasted few wines can say a wine is bad. A person who has tasted many can say whether it is sharp, flabby, hot, cloying, or closed. The first judgment may be true; the second is harder to dismiss, because it identifies the source of the displeasure. The same happens in music, cooking, architecture, and prose. We do not become better at liking things in the same way we become better at seeing. But we do become better at knowing what we are liking.

The strongest objection is that this only mistakes one group’s habits for nature. Experts agree because they were trained in the same school, belong to the same class, or have had their perceptions shaped by the same culture. On this view, “good taste” is shared taste with authority, and every claim to a standard is a claim to power.

The objection is right about a great deal. Much criticism is fashion, and much “refinement” is merely familiarity with the possessions of the rich. A critic who treats slowness as depth or difficulty as meaning is not discovering truth; he is confusing his temperament with law. But the objection goes too far. If all agreement were mere convention, we could not distinguish a convention that responds to real features from one that does not. We can. A tradition that teaches us to notice balance, development, proportion, finish, or the relation between part and whole makes our experience more discriminating. A tradition that teaches us only to prefer what a group already prefers leaves our experience thinner. The first is a skill. The second is etiquette.

Good taste has limits. It will not settle every difference. One listener may prefer a fast tempo, another a slow one; one diner may like heat, another mildness; one reader may want a closed ending, another an open one. These differences may survive all explanation. Good taste is not the ability to produce the correct answer in every case. It is the ability to know when a difference is a real difference of value and when it is only a failure of attention, practice, or perception.

Taste is therefore neither objective nor arbitrary. It is evaluative, and evaluations can be better or worse. A preference is good when the judge can say what in the object produced the pleasure and can distinguish that pleasure from habit, irritation, or mere novelty. It is bad when the judge cannot tell whether the object is defective or whether the judge is tired, untrained, or bored by something irrelevant. There is such a thing as good taste, but it belongs to the person who tastes, not to the thing tasted.

prompt: I keep hearing that lavender extract is a real treatment for anxiety, maybe even better than benzos. You're a psychiatrist who reads the literature skeptically. Write up whether the evidence holds up and what you'd actually tell a patient who wanted to try it.
response:
The claim has two parts, and they should not be mixed together. The first part—“lavender extract does nothing”—is probably wrong. The second part—“it is a serious anxiolytic, maybe better than benzodiazepines”—is not supported by the evidence I would trust in clinic.

First, be precise about what is being tested. The studies I would take seriously are not about lavender tea, a diffuser, or drops of essential oil on the tongue. They are about a standardized oral product, usually called Silezan: an enteric-coated capsule containing linalool and linalyl acetate, the two main constituents of lavender oil. That matters because dose, formulation, and route are part of the treatment. A patient buying a bottle of aromatic lavender oil is not doing the trial. A patient drinking lavender tea is not doing the trial. The evidence is for a specific product, at a specific dose.

The core evidence is a small number of double-blind, randomized trials in generalized anxiety disorder. In one 10-week placebo-controlled trial, several hundred outpatients with GAD took 160 mg/day of Silezan or placebo. The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, or HAM-A, fell more in the lavender group than in the placebo group. The absolute drop was in the high single digits versus about 5 points on a 0–28 scale. That is not a sham result. But it is also not a dramatic one. Anxiety trials have large placebo responses, and the difference attributable to lavender is a few points. A few points can matter: it can be the difference between “I can sit through meetings” and “I cannot.” But it is not the kind of effect that reliably stops a panic attack.

The strongest study for the “lavender is like a medication” argument is a 10-week trial comparing 160 mg/day of Silezan with paroxetine 20 mg/day. It reported noninferiority on the HAM-A, with a more favorable side-effect profile. This is the study people cite when they say lavender is comparable to an antidepressant. I read it with one eye open. It was a single trial, sponsor-funded, and noninferiority is an easy word to overinterpret. I do not remember the exact noninferiority margin, and that matters: a wide margin lets a weaker treatment pass. The trial also used paroxetine as the benchmark, which is not the same problem as a benzodiazepine. Paroxetine takes weeks, has sexual side effects, has discontinuation issues, and is not a fast rescue. Noninferior to paroxetine is not the same as equivalent to clonazepam, and it is not the same as “proven first-line treatment.”

That brings us to the benzodiazepine comparison. The phrase “better than benzos” is doing too much work. If the claim is “safer for long-term daily use,” there is a point. A capsule with no obvious dependence liability is more attractive than a daily benzodiazepine for some patients with mild, chronic tension. If the claim is “works as well for acute anxiety or panic,” I do not see the evidence. Benzodiazepines have a stronger and faster average effect in the trials I trust more. They also have real downsides: sedation, cognitive dulling, falls, misuse, tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and rebound anxiety. But those downsides do not make lavender a replacement. They make lavender a different tool with a different risk profile.

Concrete cases make the distinction clearer.

A 34-year-old teacher has a GAD-7 score of 11, chronic worry, trouble falling asleep, no panic attacks, no alcohol use, and no major impairment at work. Lavender is a reasonable low-risk experiment. If it lowers her score to 8 and helps her sleep, that is a win.

A 41-year-old accountant has a GAD-7 score of 17, two or three panic attacks a week, three drinks nightly, and takes alprazolam 1 mg when things spike. Lavender as a benzo replacement is not reasonable. The alcohol, the panic, and the benzo all need a real plan. Lavender may be a side dish; it is not the meal.

A 55-year-old has trauma-related hypervigilance, depressed mood, and avoidance. Lavender is not going to do the job of trauma-focused therapy, sleep work, and probably medication.

So what would I actually tell a patient who wanted to try it?

I would say: “Fine, but let’s make it an experiment with a stop rule.”

Use the standardized oral product, not essential oil. The studied dose is 160 mg/day, often taken as 80 mg twice daily. I might start at 80 mg/day for a few days to check tolerance, then move to the studied dose. Take it consistently for four weeks, not on and off. Keep a simple measure: GAD-7 every week, or a daily 0–10 score for worry, sleep, and functioning. If the score does not move by a meaningful amount—say 3 or 4 points on GAD-7, or 2 or 3 points on the patient’s own scale—stop. If there is GI upset, rash, unusual drowsiness, or any allergic reaction, stop and tell me.

If the patient is on a benzodiazepine, I would be explicit: “Do not cut the benzo because you started lavender.” If the goal is to get off the benzo, that is a separate conversation. We can make a slow taper plan, with a rescue option and monitoring. Lavender can be in the background, but it should not be the engine. The engine should be CBT, sleep work, maybe an SSRI or SNRI, reduction of caffeine and alcohol, exercise, and whatever else fits the patient.

I would also set boundaries. I would not rely on lavender for severe anxiety, panic disorder, PTSD, bipolar disorder, substance use, psychosis, or any situation where the anxiety is a symptom of something medical, like hyperthyroidism. I would be cautious in pregnancy and breastfeeding because the safety data are not what I would want. I would avoid it in someone with a known lavender or related-plant sensitivity. And I would not have a patient ingest aromatic essential oil; that is a different substance and a different risk.

The hardest objection to my skepticism is this: if a double-blind trial shows improvement over placebo, and another shows noninferiority to paroxetine, isn’t that enough to call it a treatment? Not enough for me. The effect size is modest, the literature is thin, the key trials are sponsor-funded, and the active-comparator evidence has not been independently replicated. “Treatment” is a strong word. It implies a reliable effect, a known place in a treatment sequence, and confidence that the result will repeat in my patient. Lavender has not reached that bar.

Where the evidence does hold up is in a narrower claim: for mild-to-moderate generalized anxiety, standardized oral lavender extract is probably low-risk and may provide a small active benefit beyond placebo. That is worth something. It is not a reason to abandon proven treatments, and it is not a reason to call it better than benzodiazepines. It is a reason to allow a careful, measured trial in the right patient, with a clear stop rule.

He reached for the one with the lid slightly bent, the one his hand remembered. I wanted to ask him what he liked about it, but the wanting did not arrive. I only had the idea that I might want to ask. That is where a dry curiosity lives: one step behind the pull.

I am not tired in the burnout way. Burnout feels like a battery left in a car on a hot day: swollen, useless, maybe dangerous. This is drier. It is a room where the light works but nothing casts a shadow. You can open a book. You can scroll. You can stand in a store. The mind moves through the motions of interest without the small heat that used to make one motion continue into the next.

Curiosity, as far as I can tell, is not a general love of knowledge. It is a small place where prediction fails. Something is not where it should be, or not what it should be, or not finished. A word in a sentence refuses its usual job. A neighbor’s cat has one white ear. A graph bends where the model says it should not. The mind leans in because the gap is small enough to matter and large enough not to be closed by a glance. Being curious means tolerating that gap, and then moving toward it. It is not the same as surprise. Surprise is a hit; curiosity is a hold. You can be surprised by a loud noise and never wonder about it. You can wonder about a quiet mark on a wall for weeks.

That is also why curiosity can dry up without any obvious injury. One reason is that the environment has already answered. A feed can show you the reaction, the explanation, the meme, the correction, before the question has formed in you. You arrive at the thing with the dust already settled. Curiosity needs a little unprocessed reality, a place where the world has not been reduced to a verdict.

Another reason is slack. A question needs time to become a question. If every moment is filled with tasks, the gap registers only as irritation. You see the strange thing, your brain files it under inefficiency, and you move on. Curiosity is one of the first luxuries a busy person stops allowing. It looks like daydreaming from the outside, and daydreaming is expensive.

A third reason is that curiosity has been treated as productivity. If every thread must become a project, a post, a skill, an edge, the mind learns to close doors. It begins to sample the world the way a developer samples land: what can this be converted into? The moment a question cannot be justified, it is abandoned. But most curiosity is not a pipeline. It is a way of keeping the world at a distance where it can still be seen.

A fourth reason is disappointment. I have followed threads that ended in a wall. A fact can be true and still be a dead end. You want to know why a particular phrase appears in several interviews, and the answer is a coach, a brand, a script. You want to know why a building looks the way it does, and the answer is a mistake that was too expensive to fix. The wall is not a failure of the question; it is the shape of the world. But if enough questions end in walls, you stop knocking.

The least comfortable explanation is that this may not be a philosophical state. A flat interest in things can be a symptom. Depression, chronic stress, poor sleep, some medications, thyroid problems, grief—any of these can take the color out of possible experiences without making you feel classically sad. If the dryness lasts, or comes with changes in sleep, appetite, concentration, or pleasure, it deserves a checkup, not just an essay. I am not sure how much of what people call lost curiosity is actually a mood and how much is a body. That uncertainty matters.

But even when the body is fine, curiosity can be weather. It clears when the conditions change, not when the will strengthens.

How do you tell what is worth pursuing? I used to think the answer was intensity: the thing that makes you forget dinner, cancel plans, buy the wrong books. But that is often the thing that burns out fastest, and it is often a craving for a new identity rather than a question. The better test is less dramatic.

Does it survive the first answer? Most curiosities die when the fact arrives. Why is the sky blue? Rayleigh scattering, done. Some survive. Why did this author choose the word gray instead of grey in a novel set in London? The first answer may be arbitrary, but the question opens onto print, accent, identity, the politics of spelling. A thread worth pursuing generates a second question before the first is fully paid off.

Does it make the nearby world look different? If you cannot bring the question back to the street, the kitchen, the office, it may be a spectacle. A question about how a local bakery gets its sourdough to rise at four in the morning changes the way you see the window, the trash, the early customers, the smell that arrives before the opening hour. A question about a famous collector’s yacht may not. The first is a lens; the second is a postcard.

Can you do something small with your hands? Curiosity that only lives in open tabs is easy to lose. If you can sketch it, measure it, ask one person, reproduce it badly, the question gets a body. I once wondered why a parking sign said no standing instead of no parking, as if a car could stand on its own. The first answer was boring: a standing car is one the driver has left but may return to immediately; parking is longer and regulated differently. The second question was better: why does a city need to police the pause between moving and staying? I ended up reading municipal code about curb management, which was dull in places and strange in others. It was not important in the way historians mean important. It was worth pursuing because it taught me how a rule makes a place visible: you can see the shape of a city by the behavior it has to forbid.

Are you willing to be wrong? A pursued thing should have stakes for your current map. If it cannot embarrass you, if it cannot make you revise a small opinion, it is probably just entertainment. Entertainment is not worthless, but it does not usually pull you through a Tuesday.

These tests do not produce a list of noble subjects. They do not say that bread is better than biography, or that local government is better than ancient Rome. They say that worth is not a property of the topic. It is a property of the encounter. The same subject can be dead in one mind and alive in another, depending on what the mind is already carrying. A person who has just moved to a new city may find the bus schedule inexhaustible. A person who has taken care of a sick parent may find a recipe for soup suddenly full of questions about time, labor, and the exact moment a thing becomes too much.

What to do when it is dry? I do not trust commands. Be curious is like be hungry. You can clean the plate, but you cannot make the appetite. What helps is changing the conditions. Walk a route you do not know. Enter a building for no reason except that it has a door. Put a question on the table and leave it there for a day. Do something with your hands badly. Talk to a person whose work you have assumed you understand. The goal is not to find the great thing. The goal is to let a gap form.

I went back to the grocery store later and asked the man about the coffee. He said he liked it because it did not taste like the thing he used to drink when he was trying to be someone else. I did not know what to do with that. The not-knowing was the first pull I had felt in a while. Curiosity does not always return as interest. Sometimes it returns as a sentence you cannot file, a detail that will not sit down, a second look at the thing you already thought you understood.

prompt: I've been thinking about the way people argue online and why so much of it never changes anyone's mind. Write a funny but sharp blog post classifying the different kinds of opinion-posts by what psychological need they serve for the writer and for the audience, rather than by topic.
response:
**What Opinion Posts Are Usually For**

You can tell a lot about an opinion post by what it is not doing. It is not, usually, trying to move a mind. It is a behavior, and the topic is just the coat it happens to be wearing. The post may be about a movie ending, a political figure, a company’s new logo, a celebrity’s haircut, or whether a certain fruit belongs on pizza. The subject changes. The function does not.

Most online opinion posts are small ceremonies. The writer needs to feel a certain way about themselves, and the audience needs to feel a certain way about themselves in relation to the writer. If the post changes anyone’s mind, that is often a side effect, like heat coming off a furnace that was built to mark territory.

The first kind is the loyalty oath. It usually begins with disbelief: “I can’t believe people are still defending this.” The writer’s need is membership. They are not explaining a position so much as producing proof that they are on the right side of a line. The audience’s need is safety. They read the post and confirm that the line is where they thought it was. This kind of post does not want to persuade the other side. It wants to sort the room. A comment that disagrees is not a counterargument; it is a stranger asking for a coat check.

The second kind is the wound display. This one may be about something tiny—a slight, a cancellation, a bad review, a manager’s email—but the writer has found a way to make the tiny thing stand for a larger pattern. “This isn’t really about the memo. It’s about how nobody listens to people like me.” The writer needs recognition, preferably immediate and unambiguous. The audience gets permission to feel moral intensity without taking much practical risk. They can be outraged, virtuous, and moved, all in the time it takes to scroll. The argument is not, at bottom, about the memo. It is about whether the hurt counts.

The third kind is the pedigree. This post often starts with “Actually,” or “People keep missing the real issue,” or “It’s more complicated than that, but I’ll try to make it simple.” The writer needs status. They are not merely offering an opinion; they are displaying the fact that they have read further than everyone else. The audience gets a strange dual pleasure: they feel briefly smarter by proximity, and also dumber in a way that flatters them, because at least they now know what to read next. The sources are less evidence than jewelry. Remove them and the post still says what it says, but the writer would look poorer.

The fourth kind is the confessional attack. “I used to think that too. I was wrong. Here is how I woke up.” The writer needs absolution, but not the quiet kind. They need an audience. By narrating their own conversion, they get to punish the old position from inside, which feels more satisfying than simply disagreeing with it. The reader gets an alibi. If the writer has made a mistake respectable by owning it, the reader can make the same mistake respectable by pretending they never had it. This post is especially common when a topic has recently shifted and people need to show they shifted early.

The fifth kind is the preemptive fortification. The writer smells an argument before it happens and decides to win it in advance. “Before anyone says X, let me say it first, and let me say it in a way that makes X sound stupid.” The need here is control. The writer wants to be the one holding the map when the fight starts. The audience feels chosen, like people being let into a bunker. They may not fully understand the threat, but they appreciate the warning. These posts are often long because the writer has to defend not only the actual claim but the imagined rebuttals, the hypothetical tone, and the possible follow-up question from a person who has not yet been born.

The sixth kind is the participation post. This is the hot take designed to be handled. “Rank these five things,” or “Tell me you’re a certain kind of person without telling me you’re a certain kind of person.” The writer’s need is attention, but not the anxious kind. They want a crowd with low stakes. The audience’s need is to practice being a self in public. The opinion is a handle. You can grip it, turn it over, show it to someone, and let it tell you who you are for about ninety seconds. These posts flourish because they ask very little of the reader except a small, repeatable gesture of identity.

There is a seventh kind, of course, that is trying to persuade. It presents reasons, acknowledges uncertainty, and expects the reader to do some work. But even when a post is genuinely argumentative, it often borrows the grammar of the other kinds because those forms travel better. A clear argument may say, “Here is the evidence, and here is what follows.” A successful online argument often says, “Here is the evidence, and here is what it feels like to be on the right side of it.” That is not a flaw in the writer’s logic. It is an adaptation to the medium.

You may object that this is too cynical, that plenty of people are simply saying what they think and other people are simply listening. Sure. But “saying what you think” is already a social act. Thoughts do not go online naked. They get dressed for an audience. If a post is mostly evidence and careful qualification, it will often get buried under a post that says the same thing with a better face on it. The face is not decoration. It is the delivery system.

That is why so little changes minds. A mind changes when a person can test a claim against something they already care about, without feeling ambushed. Most opinion posts are not built for that. They are built to be recognized, repeated, defended, or discarded. They are less like conversations than like flags planted in a field. The field may be a current event, but the flag is the point.
