prompt: It's 2004. You worked at Yahoo through the dot-com bubble and watched it burst. Everyone now treats anything that was fashionable in 1999 as discredited. Write an essay arguing about which of the bubble's ideas were actually right and will matter in the long run.
response:
The phrase “dot-com” has become a way of ending an argument. If someone in 2004 says a company is “dot-com,” the sentence is usually finished. It means the plan is soft, the multiples are silly, the founders have read too many essays about the future. I understand the reflex. I was at Yahoo when the future was being sold as if it had already arrived. We had free mail, a directory, news, sports, finance, search, and a brand that seemed to mean “the web.” The strategy was to be the front door. The financial strategy was to assume that if we could get people through the door, the rest would take care of itself.

When the market turned, those assumptions were displayed as evidence of mass delusion. “Eyeballs.” “Winner-take-all.” “The internet is the new retail.” “Free.” Each phrase became a small joke. Now people use the same words to dismiss any claim that the web is changing the economy. That is too cheap. The bubble got the timing wrong and the arithmetic wrong. It did not get the direction wrong.

The first distinction is between a technology and a business model. The web has real properties. Copying is cheap. Reach is global. Information can be searched. Users can talk back. Products can be improved by usage. These are not slogans. They are changes in cost structure. The bubble’s mistake was to assume that because the medium was real, every company in it would be profitable, and soon. It priced the end state into the beginning. A company can be right about a future and still fail because its income statement does not arrive fast enough. That is what happened to so many of them.

Take the portal. In 1999, the idea that users would need a home base on the web seemed obvious. We built Yahoo as a place where you could start: mail, news, weather, stocks, a directory of the web. The right part of that idea was that people do not want to wander. They want a place that organizes what matters to them. The wrong part was that organization could be done once by editors. The web grew faster than any directory. Search won because it is a directory that updates itself. The long-run lesson is not that portals were foolish. It is that the most valuable interfaces are not the ones that describe the world, but the ones that track it. A map made by hand becomes stale. A map made from behavior does not.

That is why search matters more than the bubble understood. In 1999, the web was already too large to be browsed sensibly. The problem was not a shortage of information; it was a shortage of filtering. Search reduced the cost of finding things. Sponsored search went further and aligned the advertiser’s payment with the user’s intent. A person who types “running shoes” is more valuable to a shoe company than a person who happens to see a banner on a news page. The old advertising model paid for exposure. The new model pays for interest. I think that shift is one of the most durable ideas from the bubble years. It is why free search can exist. Not because information is worthless, but because knowing what people want is valuable.

That leads to “free,” the word that now does the most work in tech mockery. The bubble used “free” the way a struggling company uses a smile: to hide the fact that it does not know how it will make money. But there is a real idea underneath. Digital goods have low marginal cost, so a service can be offered free to build a base and monetized through attention, transactions, or convenience. AOL gave away software and access. It built scale and still struggled to convert it. Google gives away search and makes money because the free service is the targeting mechanism. The difference is not the word free. It is what the free service does for the payer. Free works as a loss leader when the free activity creates a repeatable, measurable commercial moment. Free as a lifestyle produces martyrs.

In the long run, many consumer internet services will be free at the point of use. The businesses around them will charge for trust, speed, status, integration, or results. People will keep paying for things that save them trouble or make them look competent. The web will not make everything free. It will make the basic layer cheaper and push payment upstream.

The read-write web is another idea that sounded small in 1999. People kept personal pages, posted in forums, sent email, complained about ISPs. The commercial significance was not the number of pages. It was the division of labor. Users would do work that was too trivial or too personal for companies to do efficiently: describe a restaurant, tag a photo, rate a product, answer a question, curate a list. At first it looked messy. Now photo sites, blogs, wikis, review systems, and social-networking sites show that users will create content when it supports identity and community. The crowd is not always wise. It can be noisy, gullible, and biased. But it is scalable. The companies that can organize that labor own a new kind of infrastructure.

This changes media and commerce in the same direction. The old model was one-to-many: a publisher, a retailer, a brand. The new model is many-to-many with a thin layer of organization on top. A band can reach listeners. A seller can reach buyers. A user can tell other users what is worth their time. The gatekeepers do not disappear, but their power shifts from deciding what exists to deciding what is visible. That is a different job, and it is where the value will sit.

The bubble also talked about killing middlemen. Sometimes that was true. A book does not need a bookstore shelf. A song does not need a pressing plant. A small seller does not need a mall. But often the middleman changed form. eBay did not remove trust; it productized it with feedback and escrow. Amazon did not remove retail; it centralized logistics and reviews. PayPal made payments between strangers possible. The right idea was that reputation, identity, and payment can become portable network functions. The wrong idea was that any intermediary could be deleted. In the long run, the web will create fewer middlemen in some places and more in others. The ones that remain will be thinner, faster, and more data-driven.

Open source was another bubble-era idea that got mocked and then absorbed. Linux, Apache, Mozilla, and the rest were treated by some as a counter-culture and by others as a threat to software revenue. The simple claim that software would be free and the money would come from services was too simple. But the deeper idea was right: the base layer of computing can be commoditized, and value moves to the edges—integration, support, trust, distribution, user experience. A company can build a durable business on top of free components. The web itself is the largest example. Open protocols let anyone build a site, and that openness created the market that Google, Amazon, and eBay exploited. Control of the base layer is less valuable than control of the interface, the data, or the network.

Network effects were the bubble’s favorite excuse. “Winner-take-all” was often used by people who had no network effect at all. But in some markets the phrase is true. Email, instant messaging, search, social networks, and marketplaces can become self-reinforcing: the more people use them, the more useful they become. This changes the meaning of quality. A product is not just what it does; it is who else is on it. That matters for the long run because it makes some markets consolidate and makes switching costs social rather than technical. It also makes standards and regulation more important, because a network can become a bottleneck.

The hardest objection to all this is obvious: if the ideas were right, why did so many bubble companies fail? Because the ideas were necessary, not sufficient. The web lowers costs, but it does not tell you which costs are worth lowering. Online grocery had low information cost but high physical cost. Virtual communities had network effects but no monetization. Portal brands had attention but no conversion. The bubble assumed that a real platform plus real traffic plus a real brand would produce cash flow. It did not. The survivors are not the companies that believed hardest. They are the ones that found a loop: users come for a real benefit, the benefit improves with use, and the company captures a slice of the value created. Search ads, marketplaces, free email with switching costs, digital distribution—these work because the loop is concrete.

There are limits the bubble ignored. Bandwidth is not infinite. Latency matters. Atoms do not flow over fiber. People will not put every purchase online, and they will not tolerate data collection without a clear benefit. Privacy is not a bug to be optimized away; it is part of trust. The companies that treat privacy as a feature will outlast the ones that treat it as a nuisance. The web will be global in information and code, but local in services, trust, and physical delivery. Anyone who forgets that will build another set of overvalued balance sheets.

So when people say that anything fashionable in 1999 is discredited, I answer that the crash should be read as a correction in price, not a refutation of physics. The first internet race was a race to put a website on everything. It burst because it mistook presence for value. The second process is slower. It is built on costs that really fall: the cost of finding, the cost of reaching, the cost of trusting, the cost of making, the cost of transacting. Some of the companies chasing those cost reductions will fail. Many will. But the ideas behind the best of them are not a fad. They are the new economics. Yahoo’s mistake was not believing in the web. It was believing that being on the web was enough. We had the front door, but the door was a directory. The web became a search engine, a marketplace, a social place, a publishing platform. The ideas were right. The company had to become them.

prompt: Write a speculative essay that treats ideas, not people, as the real actors in culture: creators as hosts that ideas use. What does that lens say about reputation, about why audiences trap successful artists in their old work, and about how a creator might keep some freedom?
response:
Culture is easier to understand if you stop asking who made a thing and ask what the thing needs. A melody, a legal argument, a moral panic, a particular way of cutting a scene: these are not neutral contents carried by people. They are patterns that persist by finding bodies willing to repeat them. The bodies are us. The patterns are not conscious, but they have interests in a cold sense: they spread, they mutate, they die. A creator is a host. The work is what happens when an idea gets far enough inside a person to change their behavior.

This does not mean the person is absent. A host is not a mail truck. It has an immune system. Take the idea of the hard-boiled detective. It can use a writer who needs order, and produce a plot where clues line up neatly. It can use another who is afraid of order, and produce a city where every answer makes things worse. The detective idea is the same actor in both, but the work is different because the host’s temperament selects which variants survive. The “I” of the author is not a little sovereign signing the document; it is the name of the filter.

A reputation is what an idea builds when it has found a host that works. It is a label that tells the world: this body reliably produces this pattern. For the audience, the label saves effort. For the idea, it is a shell. It makes the host more usable, because now the host is not just a person with skills but a promise. The promise feeds back. The creator begins to feel that the idea is their identity, because the market has made it so. A poet known for one spare line about snow will find that every later poem is read as either a deepening of that line or a fall from it. The line has become the poet’s face. The poet may still have other faces, but the public has paid for one.

After the host dies or withdraws, the reputation often keeps working. It becomes a direction-finder for the idea. Imitators, covers, remakes, and biographies are new bodies recruited to carry the pattern. The name is a husk, but it still points.

Audiences trap successful artists for the same reason a body defends a habit that has become useful. The old work did something for them. It gave them a way to name a feeling, a ritual, a social position. To change is not merely a new style; it is a withdrawal of a service. The fans are not simply being greedy. They are being defensive. The idea lives in them now, and it resists mutation.

Success makes this worse. A small artist can change because the idea has few hosts to protect. A famous artist is a reservoir. The more people who carry the idea, the stronger the selective pressure against drift. The old work is not behind the artist; it is around them, in reviews, playlists, fan sites, the way strangers order their lives around the song. The artist is asked to be the idea’s permanent organ.

Miles Davis in the late 1960s is a clean case. The idea that had used him for years was the acoustic jazz quartet: sparse, collective, serious. By then that idea had a reputation attached to him so strong that his name was a shortcut for it. When another idea took him—electric instruments, rock rhythms, studio editing—the old audience experienced it as a betrayal. Some did not care that he was still making music; they cared that the particular idea they had built a relationship with was being altered. Davis was trapped in the ordinary way: stay and become a monument to the old pattern, or change and let the old pattern use someone else. He changed, and the price was the loss of a tribe that had mistaken him for the idea.

Duchamp shows the other side. The readymade was an idea that used him to make art less about craft and more about choice. Once the idea had gotten loose—once it could be argued, imitated, taught without him—he could step back. He spent years playing chess, working at the edge of the art world, letting the idea live in other hands. Salinger is the reverse. The idea of the wounded adolescent narrator in *The Catcher in the Rye* found a host with a temperament that could not bear to repeat it on demand. He withdrew from the public market for the idea, became a rumor. The idea survived without him, but the host was so identified with it that the only exit was disappearance. Both men were used; one let the idea leave, the other had to leave the world where the idea could find him.

The obvious objection is that this makes people into puppets. If ideas are the actors, why praise or blame the host? Why not say the book wrote itself? The answer is that an idea is not a ghost with a hand. It is a shape that must be metabolized. It has to pass through a particular history, a body’s limitations, a set of habits, a moral sense, a boredom. The same idea in different hosts becomes different work. The host’s choices are real because the host is the site where the idea either succeeds or fails. The self, in this view, is not the author of ideas but the ecology that makes some ideas possible. That does not erase responsibility. It moves it. A creator is responsible for the kinds of bodies they build: what they practice, what they allow to enter, what they refuse, what they repeat.

So how does a creator keep freedom? Not by becoming the source of their work. That is a fantasy the old lens created. Freedom is ecological. It means refusing to let one idea become the whole house.

One way is to keep a life where you are no one. A pseudonym, a new genre, a small room, a second body of work that the reputation has not yet learned to read. The unknown self is the place where new ideas can enter without being checked by the old fans. Anonymity is not just secrecy; it is a fresh immune system.

Another is to collaborate, because collaboration changes the host. An idea that passes through several bodies is less likely to be mistaken for one person’s nature. A band, a studio, a translator, a dancer: each adds a filter and a way out. The creator can say no to a variant without saying no to the idea, because the variant was never wholly theirs.

A third is to treat reputation as a tool, not a home. Feed it when it pays for time. Starve it when it starts making decisions. Let the label mean something useful for a while, then change the label. A creator can use fame to build a reservoir of trust and then spend that trust on work the old audience does not yet understand. The trick is not to let the trust become a leash.

A fourth is to make work that changes the audience as much as it serves them. A trap becomes a corridor when the audience is invited to move. This is harder than it sounds, because the idea that wants to spread usually wants the safest spread. It will try to make the artist more of the same, because that is what replicates. The artist has to be willing to make the idea less comfortable in its own niche.

All of these are also traps. The artist who makes reinvention a brand is used by the idea of novelty. The collaborator can be used by the idea of the group. The anonymous writer can be used by the idea of the secret self. Freedom is not a final state. It is the maintenance of enough friction that no single idea can say it is the only tenant.

A creator who understands this does not ask, “What do I want to say?” as if the self stood outside the material. They ask, “What idea is trying to use me right now, and do I want to be that kind of house?” The answer may be yes, for a season. The answer may be no, or not yet, or only under another name. The work begins when the question is honest.

prompt: Your daughter is turning eight and you wish you could hand her a book about living freely and getting things done. Write that essay: what does 'agency' really mean, what does it look like in the lives of people who have it (a filmmaker, perhaps), and what held you back from it for so long?
response:
You are eight. The word agency is too big for a birthday present and too small for a life. It sounds like something politicians say when they mean power, or something self-help books say when they mean confidence. But you already know it. When you build a fort out of chair cushions and the roof sags, you can leave it sagging, or you can put a broomstick across the middle. The fort becomes more yours not because you wanted it, but because you did something about it.

Agency is the space between wanting and having. It is not a mood. It is a practice made of small, unglamorous motions: noticing what you actually want, deciding what to do before you feel ready, doing it badly enough to learn, and then doing it again with what you learned. It is the ability to make a thing happen through time, despite boredom, fear, and other people's indifference. A person with agency can look at a situation and say, in effect: I want this. I do not have all the conditions. Here is what I can influence. Here is what I cannot. Here is the next step. Here is the person I will ask. Here is the price. I will pay it, or I will choose otherwise.

That last part matters. Agency is not freedom, though it needs some freedom. Freedom is the size of the room. Agency is the ability to move in it. If the room is a cell, the problem is not mainly the prisoner's mindset. If the room has a locked door, the first task is not positive thinking; it is finding the key, the lockpick, the window, or the person who holds the key. But even in a small room, a person can choose what to make with the light that comes through the bar. That choice is not the same as freedom. It is still agency.

There is a hard objection here, and an eight-year-old deserves it. Agency is not equally available. A child in a violent house does not lack agency because she cannot simply choose peace. A worker with three jobs and no transportation does not lack agency because she cannot follow a passion on a Sunday. A person with a disability in a city built for able bodies meets walls that no amount of inner resolve will move. To tell someone to be agentic when the world has taken her tools can become a second violence. So agency must be named honestly: it is a capacity that grows in conditions. It needs safety, food, sleep, money, time, permission, and other people who will believe you are allowed to want things. When those things are missing, the first act of agency may be to get them, or to survive without pretending the missing things are your fault.

When I look at people who seem to have agency, I do not always see boldness. I see decisions. I see a filmmaker who does not wait for a studio to make her interesting. Agnès Varda made movies when she had little money, with light that was there, with faces she met, with a camera she knew how to use. Cléo from 5 to 7 follows a woman for two hours. That sounds simple. It is not. It means every minute has to carry the film. It means the idea has to be exact. It means the maker has to be present in every cut. Varda's agency was not a roar. It was a hand. She picked up what the world offered and arranged it until it meant something.

You can see the same hand in smaller places. A person with agency says no to a meeting that will not move the thing forward. She shoots the scene on a Tuesday because the apartment is free on a Tuesday. She writes the email she has been avoiding in eleven minutes. She asks a stranger for advice and does not treat the answer as a verdict. She keeps a notebook not for beautiful thoughts but for problems. When the project stalls, she does not ask only, Am I enough? She asks, Which part is stuck? Is it the idea, the money, the schedule, my fear of calling, the fact that the second act is boring? The question changes the work.

Living freely, for an adult, often looks like maintenance. You protect your attention the way you would protect a fire in wind. You stop feeding people who make you small. You leave rooms. You make your work in public early, because a secret project is a hostage project. You learn to be disliked for a choice instead of being liked for a silence. This is not arrogance. It is hygiene. A free person is not someone who does whatever she feels like in the moment. She is someone who has made enough inner order that her choices are hers. She can say not today to a craving, a person, a distraction, or a flattering opportunity that leads nowhere. She can also say yes to the unglamorous task that keeps the thing alive.

What held me back was not a locked door. It was a set of comfortable lies. I told myself I was waiting for the right moment. I told myself I needed more skill, more savings, more proof that I was serious. I made plans so detailed that they could substitute for action. I wanted to be chosen by someone who already mattered, because being chosen would mean I did not have to risk being seen. I confused modesty with wisdom. I said someday and meant when I am safe, and safety never arrived because I had made it depend on things I had not done.

I can remember a year when I researched every stage of making a short film—formats, festivals, grants, cameras—and I did not film a single frame. The research felt like motion because it was inside my head. The film, outside my head, did not exist. That is how avoidance disguises itself: as preparation. I also thought agency was a personality: loud, bold, unstoppable. So when I was shy, I concluded I lacked it. Actually I had only a quieter mechanism. I had to learn to make small public moves, and to let them be small.

Getting things done is not a character trait. It is a system of promises. Make the first ugly version. Put the date on the calendar. Tell one person. Make the next step so small that resistance has nothing to grab. If you want to make a movie, make one with a phone and a friend in the yard. If you want to write, write one page and show it to someone who will tell you the truth. If someone says no, find out what the no is protecting. It may be a real wall. It may be fear. A real wall can be mapped. Fear can be waited out or gone around.

You will be told you are too young, too small, too emotional, too much, too little. Some of that will be true in the way that a seed is too small to be a tree. Do not let the true part become a prison. On your eighth birthday, I would not give you a book that says you can do anything. I would give you one that says you can do the next thing, and the next thing after that, and that the world will answer you, and you will not be finished being surprised. Tonight, choose one small thing you have been circling—a drawing, a question, a game, a letter—and do it before bed. Not well. Just done.

prompt: I want a blog post about what happens when you take utilitarianism seriously at a meetup and someone pushes you on animal welfare. How do you stay sane while still being honest about your own inconsistency?
response:
## The Animal Question at the Utilitarian Meetup

The question comes at the end, when the coffee is cold and the room has run through its favorite thought experiments. I have been saying the comfortable things about utilitarianism: we should care about outcomes, no person is intrinsically more important just because they are near us, and if a small cost to me can prevent a lot of suffering elsewhere, the arithmetic is not very hard.

A person across the table leans forward. “Then animals?” they ask. “If it is all about suffering, why are you still eating meat? Why don’t you donate more to animal welfare?”

It is not a trick question. It is the theory asking to be paid.

I had been treating utilitarianism like a clean lens, the kind you can hold up to a trolley problem or a charity comparison and then put back in your pocket. Animal welfare does not let you do that. It follows you out of the meeting room and into the kitchen, where you are standing in front of the fridge deciding whether to open a package of chicken. The theory stops being a lens and becomes a direction. It points at the beings you have been politely not thinking about.

The honest answer is that I am inconsistent. I care more about humans because they are my kind. They talk back. They have names, faces, childhoods, projects, and a recognizable future. I can imagine a human in pain in a way I do not naturally imagine a pig in pain. I also have habits. I like certain foods, I buy convenient things, and I have not spent as much time as I should on the evidence about animal suffering and the interventions that might reduce it. If I stand in a room and say that sentient beings count impartially, I am not describing my whole moral life. I am describing the part of it I feel safe saying out loud.

That admission is necessary, but it is not enough. “I’m inconsistent” can become a way to stop thinking. It can be a little moral blanket: I know I’m flawed, so don’t push me. The problem at the meetup is that the person pushing you is not asking for your humility. They are asking whether the principle you just praised has any reach at all.

The first way to stay sane is to stop treating every decision as a fresh moral trial. If I have to justify breakfast from first principles, I will either become paralyzed or I will start lying to myself with great speed. So I make rules. I eat less meat than I used to. I try to choose the options that plausibly involve less suffering when the price difference is not absurd. I set aside a fixed amount of money for causes I have checked, including animal welfare when the evidence supports it. The rule does the work so I do not have to relitigate my values every time I am hungry.

This is not purity. It is management. A rule can be bad, outdated, or self-serving. But a life full of unexamined defaults is worse. At least a rule can be revised.

The second thing is to separate moral judgment from moral performance. I can think animal suffering matters enormously and still fail to act in the way the view seems to require. If I treat every failure as proof that the view is false, I will just retreat to the more comfortable view: the one where the beings without a vote are not really part of the moral picture. But that is not honesty. That is pain avoidance. The utilitarian claim does not disappear because I am bad at following it.

This is where it gets uncomfortable, because the theory can make you feel like a chronic offender. The world raises and kills a very large number of animals for food. Many of them live in confinement. Many are transported, handled, and killed in ways that plausibly cause fear and pain. Even if we do not know exactly how much suffering is involved, the scale is large enough that one person’s dietary choices are not merely symbolic. They are repeated purchases.

So what do you do with that without becoming hysterical or numb? You limit the exposure. If I spend every free hour reading reports about factory farms, I will either stop functioning or stop feeling. I need a dose I can bear. I read one serious piece of writing a month. I look at the evidence for a particular intervention. I donate if I am convinced. I close the tab. The goal is not to live inside the problem. The goal is to let the problem change my choices without destroying my ability to make choices.

That brings us to the part people at meetups often miss: uncertainty is not an escape hatch, but it is real. We do not have a precise scale for animal suffering. We do not know with certainty which species are morally most weighty, how much suffering is avoided by a given product change, or which advocacy strategies actually work. So I do not need to solve consciousness in order to stop buying the worst options. I can act on plausible comparisons. If option A very likely causes less suffering than option B and I can choose A for a modest cost, the utilitarian case is strong enough to matter.

I also do not need to decide whether an animal’s life has positive value in order to think that preventing avoidable suffering is good. That is a lower bar, and it is high enough.

The hardest objection to all this is that it is just a way to keep the life and lose the argument. I can call my partial effort “practical,” “bounded,” or “honest,” and mean by that: I am not going to change much. The only defense is to let the criticism land. If I say I am taking animal welfare seriously, I have to be willing to be told when I am not. I have to update the rule when the evidence changes. I have to accept that someone can look at my spending, my diet, and my donations and say, “That is not enough,” and be right.

That is the difference between a rule and an excuse. A rule is something you follow until it turns out to be wrong. An excuse is something you follow because it protects you from having to follow anything.

At the meetup, I do not give a finished answer. I say, “You’re right that I’m inconsistent. I care too much about people like me and too little about beings who cannot complain to me. I don’t know how to fix that completely. What I can do is make fewer small choices that add up, and not pretend the gap isn’t there.”

The person may be disappointed. They wanted a cleaner confession or a stronger commitment. But the point was never to win the exchange. The point was to notice where the theory had been staying in the parking lot while I walked around talking about it.

Taking utilitarianism seriously means accepting that your ordinary life will keep showing you the inconvenient parts. You do not stay sane by solving the problem all at once. You stay sane by choosing a few real changes, keeping them under review, and refusing to turn your limitations into a philosophy. The inconsistency does not disappear. It becomes something you can see clearly enough to work with.

prompt: Everyone says AI tutors are about to revolutionize education. Write an essay on whether that's actually going to happen, and what might stand in the way.
response:
A student stuck on a fraction problem at 9 p.m. can now type the problem into a phone and receive a patient sequence of hints: what are you trying to find, what do you know, try making the denominators the same, check the answer by reversing the operation. That is not magic. It is a useful replacement for a tired parent, a textbook that only gives the final answer, or a tutor who costs tens of dollars an hour. The question is whether that replacement changes education.

The real novelty is not that software can explain things. Adaptive math systems have done that for decades, but usually through menus, multiple-choice questions, and fixed error messages. A large language model changes the interface: the student can say, in messy words, what they do not understand, and the system can respond in words. Help-seeking becomes cheap. In a class of thirty, a teacher may get one or two raised hands before the period ends; a student who is embarrassed, slow, or unsure may never ask. A chatbot removes some of that social cost.

That advantage is largest where progress can be checked. Algebra, geometry, programming, laboratory calculations, foreign-language grammar, music theory, and factual science all have properties that make tutoring easier: a wrong answer is often detectable, a hint can be calibrated, and a concept can be restated in several ways. A student can ask why the code fails, whether the proof step is legal, or what the sentence means. The machine can generate practice at the right level and keep a record. In open-ended domains the advantage shrinks. A history essay, a design project, a science argument, or a piece of fiction can be “explained,” but the hard part is judgment, evidence, taste, and audience. AI can imitate feedback, but without a human stake in the result, its praise and correction can feel generic.

The strongest case for transformation follows from scarcity. Good tutoring works, but it is expensive and unevenly distributed. Private tutoring commonly costs tens of dollars an hour in wealthy countries, and the students who get it are often those whose families already have time and money to spend. Tutoring and timely feedback both show up repeatedly as high-impact interventions in educational research, yet most students receive little of it outside tests. If an AI tutor can give a struggling reader ten minutes of targeted practice each day, or give a pre-med student repeated explanations of a difficult derivation, the cumulative effect could be large. This is not a fantasy; it is the same logic that made flashcards, drill software, and office hours valuable, only less constrained by human availability.

But the fantasy appears when the explanation is treated as the main thing. Students do not fail only because they missed a definition. They miss days, arrive hungry, forget prerequisites from two years earlier, dislike the subject, fear looking stupid, or live in homes where homework competes with work and care. A patient bot cannot make a fourteen-year-old attend school, sit still, or care about a grade. A teacher’s job is not only to supply the missing explanation; it is to keep thirty different trajectories moving through a shared curriculum, to notice when a student is disengaged, and to make the work matter enough to do. In a well-run classroom, the boring machinery of education—deadlines, peer comparison, a teacher’s attention, a seat, a routine—does real cognitive work. An AI tutor used for fifteen minutes after a chaotic day may add less than a worksheet completed under supervision during the day. The technology is best where it can be embedded in an existing structure of accountability, not where it is expected to create one.

Schools are also slow because the unit of purchase is not the student’s learning; it is the district’s budget, the teacher’s workload, and the administrator’s risk. If an AI tutor is optional, many students will not use it, and teachers will not know why. If it is required, it becomes another thing to monitor: logins, screen time, usage dashboards, parent complaints. A teacher already plans lessons, manages behavior, writes notes for parents, completes special-education paperwork, and grades assignments. Adding a tool that generates differentiated worksheets can increase labor unless it replaces something. The useful question is not “Can the AI explain photosynthesis?” but “Does it save the teacher an hour this week, and does that hour go to the students who need it?” If the answer is no, the tutor remains a demo.

Assessment is the deeper obstacle. Schools certify learning through exams, essays, and portfolios, and those credentials matter for college and jobs. If the final test is unchanged, an AI tutor may teach students to pass the test rather than to understand the field. It can help them memorize the right forms, recognize question types, and produce safe answers. In subjects where AI can do the work—coding, writing, translation, routine analysis—the problem is worse. If students use AI to complete assignments, the assignment no longer measures their skill. If schools ban AI, they push learning into unobservable channels. If they allow it, they must redesign tasks around verification, oral defense, process work, or in-person performance. That redesign is hard and politically costly, because credentials are promises to employers and parents.

Equity cuts both ways. In a country with severe teacher shortages, an AI tutor in a local language could give a rural student more individualized contact than any human system can afford. That possibility is real. But in many existing schools, the gap is not access to information; it is stable devices, reliable broadband, quiet space, adult support, and trust in the institution. A one-to-one laptop program can become a lost-device program. Filtering and security software can block useful tools. Affluent families can pair an AI tutor with a human coach, a quiet room, and the ability to ignore bad output; poorer families may get the raw model and the consequences. Without deliberate design, AI tutoring risks becoming another premium service sold to the families least likely to need it.

Trust is a technical problem as much as a social one. A K-12 tutor that occasionally invents a historical fact, misstates a chemical reaction, or gives a confident but wrong algebra step will lose the classroom. Teachers will not defend a tool that contradicts the curriculum, and students will learn to treat its output as something to be checked rather than something to be learned from. The fix—constraining the model to approved content, retrieving from textbooks, requiring step verification—reduces the flexibility that made it attractive. Privacy adds another layer. ## I built a DNS playground on a real subdomain

The site gives you a subdomain and a live log of the authoritative server answering for it. You choose a name, get something like `mira.dnslab.dev`, change a record, and watch the queries come in. If you create a CNAME, the log does not show a pretty animation. It shows the actual query sequence: the resolver asks for the alias, gets a pointer, asks for the target, and returns the answer. The packets are real. The resolvers are real. The only thing restricted is what the records can point at.

I made it because DNS is one of those systems that everyone touches and almost nobody feels. People know it as “the internet is down” or “my domain isn’t pointing right.” They know it as a five minute wait after changing an A record. They know it as the moment a support ticket says “can you clear your DNS cache?” But the actual loop is hidden. You change a record somewhere, a resolver somewhere else notices, a client somewhere else asks, and an answer comes back. Most teaching materials jump straight to diagrams: recursive resolver, authoritative server, TTL, NS record. The diagrams are correct, but they do not give you the feel of the system.

The missing piece is feedback.

You can learn a lot from `dig`. You can also learn a lot from DNSViz, Cloudflare dashboards, or a BIND lab in a VM. But those tools usually put you outside the loop. You are inspecting someone else’s zone, or you are managing a zone that feels like production infrastructure before you understand the basic trick. I wanted a place where the first experiment is not “configure a nameserver” but “make a name mean something and watch the machine ask for it.”

The hardest objection to that is obvious: this is not your domain. It is a subdomain of mine. You are not learning how to manage DNS for a company. You are not learning what happens when your registrar locks the zone, your nameservers disagree, or your TLS certificate expires. I agree. The site is not a production DNS course. It is a protocol bench. It tries to make one part of the system tangible: the exchange between a resolver and an authoritative server for a small, disposable zone. If that does not click, no amount of registrar UI will save you. If it does click, the rest becomes easier to attach.

## What the site actually gives you

When you arrive, you pick a handle. The site creates a subdomain under `dnslab.dev` and gives you two panes. On the left is a record editor. On the right is a live feed from the authoritative server.

The feed shows lines like this:

```text
14:02:11  mira.dnslab.dev      A       NOERROR  Google AS15169   3 ms
14:02:11  mira.dnslab.dev      AAAA    NOERROR  Google AS15169   4 ms
14:02:14  api.mira.dnslab.dev  CNAME   NOERROR  Cloudflare AS13335 2 ms
14:02:14  api.mira.dnslab.dev  A       NOERROR  Cloudflare AS13335 3 ms
```

The name is yours, so any query to that name is probably yours, or at least close enough. The client column is the recursive resolver that contacted my server, not the person holding the laptop. I show the ASN because it is more useful than an IP address. A query from `AS15169` is probably Google. A query from `AS13335` is probably Cloudflare. A query from some small regional ASN is probably someone’s ISP resolver. I do not show the end user’s IP, because in ordinary UDP DNS I usually do not have it.

There is also a “poke” button. It sends a query from a resolver I control. That sounds like a cheat, and in one sense it is. But the first version of the site had no poke button, and users would save a record, wait, and conclude the log was fake because nothing happened. Usually their local resolver had cached the previous answer. The poke button does not replace the real loop. It gives you a guaranteed event so you can see what an event looks like.

The record editor is deliberately narrow. You can create A, AAAA, CNAME, TXT, MX, and SRV records under your subdomain. You cannot upload a zone file. You cannot change the NS records for `dnslab.dev`. You cannot issue a zone transfer. You cannot point a CNAME at `evil.example`. A and AAAA records can only point at a small set of lab IPs that serve simple pages. MX records can only point at a lab mail name. The goal is not freedom. The goal is to let you change the DNS answer without turning the experiment into an incident response exercise.

## The experiments

I did not start with a blank canvas. The first version let people create any allowed record under their subdomain and stare at the log. That was terrible. People were clever, but they were clever in the wrong direction. One tester created a CNAME from `a` to `b`, then a CNAME from `b` to `a`, and spent ten minutes asking why the page would not load. Another created a TXT record and then tried to open the subdomain in a browser, confused that the text did not appear on the web page.

So the site now has a set of short experiments. Each one is supposed to answer one question and take about two minutes.

The first is “What does a name mean?” You create an A record for your subdomain and point it at one of the lab IPs. Then you open the subdomain in a browser. The page says the name. The log shows an A query and usually an AAAA query around the same time. The point is not the page. The point is that the browser did not magically know where to go. It asked.

The second is “What is an alias?” You create two names, say `target` and `alias`. `target` has an A record. `alias` has a CNAME to `target`. When you resolve `alias`, the log shows the resolver asking for `alias`, receiving a CNAME, then asking for `target`. This is the experiment I care about most. CNAMEs are everywhere and almost nobody internalizes the chase. Once you see the two queries, a lot of weird behavior becomes easier to explain.

The third is “How long should an answer live?” You set a TTL, then use a test resolver to query the name repeatedly. The site cannot force your ISP’s resolver to forget what it knows, so this experiment uses a recursive resolver I run. It reports whether each answer came from cache or from my authoritative server. Set the TTL to one second and the cache expires quickly. Set it to an hour and the second query is a hit. This is where the phrase “TTL is a hint, not a guarantee” stops being a meme.

The fourth is “Can DNS carry text?” You put a string in a TXT record and query it. This one is boring, which is why it is useful. TXT records are the reason people sometimes assume DNS is a general key-value store. The experiment lets you see that it is only a record type, and that browsers will not show it for you.

The fifth is “How do protocols find services?” MX and SRV records are often taught as exotic, but they are just answers to questions like “where should I deliver mail?” or “where is the service?” The site has buttons that run scripted queries from a test client. I do not run a real mail server for users, and I do not want to. The point is to see the MX query and the SRV query, not to receive email.

The sixth is “What does a bad answer look like?” You create a CNAME that points back at itself. In a normal resolver, that can turn into a loop. My authoritative server has a guard for the simple cases inside the lab zone. It returns an error and emits a special event in the log. The user sees that the system can fail in a structured way, not just “nothing happened.”

Each experiment has an “expected events” checklist. That sounds pedestrian, but it changed everything. Before, success was vague: the log moved, so maybe it worked. Now the site can say, “We expected a CNAME query and then an A query. We saw both.” The user is not trying to guess whether the machine did the right thing.

## What user testing taught me

I tested the site with twenty-two people: a few DNS people, a few web developers, a few students, and several people who described their relationship with DNS as “I once changed an A record and felt brave.” I asked them to complete the CNAME experiment without help, then to try the TTL experiment with hints.

The first thing I learned was that the live log was too honest.

When every query to the subdomain appears in real time, the feed looks like a firehose. Browser DNS, mobile DNS, DoH, background services, retries, AAAA queries, A queries. The user’s intended query is one line among several. In the first tests, people would save a record, watch three lines appear, and say, “Did that come from me?” I had assumed that owning the subdomain was enough. It is not. You need the UI to say which line is probably yours.

The fix was not to hide the other queries. It was to group them. The feed now clusters queries by name and type, highlights the most recent response, and shows a small “your recent action” marker when the UI knows you just clicked resolve. The raw lines are still there. But the interface stops pretending that a log line is self-explanatory.

The second lesson was about caching.

People expected changes to be instant because the UI changed instantly. The record editor saved, the button turned green, and then the browser still showed the old page. I had written “your resolver may cache the answer” in small text, which is the written equivalent of shouting from a rooftop. The problem is not that users are stupid. The problem is that DNS has two time scales: the time it takes to change the authoritative answer, and the time it takes for the world to notice. The first is under your control. The second is not.

I added a cache status panel for the test resolver. It says plainly: “This resolver has a cached answer. It will not query the authoritative server again until the TTL expires.” That sentence did more than any diagram. People started asking better questions. They wanted to know whose resolver was being used. They wanted to know whether their browser was using DoH. They wanted to know why one query came from Google and the next came from their ISP.

The third lesson was about TLS.

The early site let you create a subdomain and then told you to open it. The subdomain resolved, but the browser showed a certificate error because I had not solved the wildcard problem cleanly. That ruined the illusion. The whole point of the A record experiment is that the name resolves to a place that can serve something. If the browser screams about certificates, the user thinks DNS failed, even though DNS did its job.

I moved the lab IPs behind a reverse proxy with a wildcard certificate for `*.dnslab.dev`. Let’s Encrypt does not issue wildcard certificates via HTTP-01, so I used DNS-01 validation and automated it against the same zone the site uses. That felt slightly recursive, but it works. Now when a user creates an A record, the browser loads a boring green page that says the name. Boring is good. The DNS event is the interesting part.

The fourth lesson was that people do not want to type `dig` unless the site gives them the exact command.

I assumed developers would know to run `dig +short mira.dnslab.dev A`. Some did. Others opened a terminal, typed `dns`, and gave up. Others used a web-based DNS checker, which defeated the purpose because the query did not come from their machine. The site now puts a copyable command next to the record, and it also has a button that runs the query from the local test resolver. The command is for people who want to see the raw answer. The button is for people who want to see the loop.

The fifth lesson was that people want to break things.

This was the best feedback. Once users understood that the subdomain was disposable, they wanted to make it fail. Not in a harmful way, exactly, but in a “what happens if the answer is wrong” way. They wanted CNAME loops, missing targets, type mismatches, and weird TXT payloads. The original design treated breakage as an edge case. The users treated it as the curriculum.

So I made safe failure a feature. The broken CNAME experiment is now explicit. The server detects a few common self-referential patterns and returns a controlled error. The log shows the failure as a first-class event. Users stopped asking, “Why is it broken?” and started asking, “What would a resolver do here?”

I am not sure how much of the early confusion was caused by DNS and how much by the interface. A live log is a strange object. It is technical, temporal, and partial. It shows one node’s view of a distributed conversation. So I changed one thing at a time and watched completion rates. Before the UI changes, eleven of twenty people got a working CNAME without asking for help. After the changes, eighteen of twenty did. The time from first click to first successful CNAME query dropped from about nine minutes to about three. Those numbers are small and biased, but the direction was clear: the protocol was not the main obstacle. The feedback loop was.

## The interesting parts of the backend

The backend has four jobs: be an authoritative server for the lab zone, store user records, rate-limit abuse, and stream query events to browsers. The interesting part is that those jobs pull in different directions. A DNS server wants to be fast, stateless, and boring. A web app wants to be dynamic, user-aware, and chatty.

I could have run BIND or NSD and scraped logs. I could have used a managed DNS provider and webhooks. I could have built a fake DNS server in Node and called it a day. In the end I built a small authoritative server in Rust, using a maintained DNS wire-format library rather than parsing packets by hand. I have no desire to maintain my own DNS message parser. The internet has already found every bug in that layer. My server is a thin authoritative brain: it accepts queries, looks up the lab zone, builds answers, applies limits, and emits events.

It listens on UDP and TCP port 53 on a small VPS. It serves only `dnslab.dev` and names under it. Anything else gets REFUSED. There is no AXFR. There is no IXFR. There is no dynamic update over DNS. All record changes happen over an authenticated HTTPS API. That last part matters. DNS dynamic update is a powerful and historically messy mechanism. I do not need it. The web backend writes to Postgres, notifies the in-memory zone, and the authoritative server picks up the change.

The zone is stored in Postgres, but the DNS server does not query Postgres on every packet. It keeps the active lab records in memory. When the API creates, updates, or deletes a record, it writes to the database and publishes a change event. The authoritative server applies that event to its in-memory table. This gives me durability without putting a database in the hot path. If the DNS process restarts, it reloads the zone from Postgres. If the web backend restarts, nothing DNS-related breaks.

The record model is simple:

```text
owner:    mira.dnslab.dev
name:     api.mira.dnslab.dev
type:     CNAME
data:     target.mira.dnslab.dev
ttl:      300
```

The server validates the data before it accepts it. CNAME targets must be inside the lab zone. A and AAAA addresses must be in the allowlist. MX and SRV targets are constrained the same way. TXT data is capped in length. This is not a general DNS zone editor. It is a constrained state machine that happens to speak DNS.

Let's outline:

Title: A DNS Lab Where the Queries Are Real

Intro:
- Describe site: choose handle, get subdomain, set records, watch live authoritative log.
- Why: DNS is taught as diagrams but felt as outages. The missing piece is feedback.
- Hardest objection: Why not use dig? Answer: you can inspect, but you don't own the answer. Need a place where your change is the only variable and the authoritative server is yours.

Why I made it
- Story: teaching/interview? People ask "does it have DNS?" No. DNS is everywhere but invisible.
- Existing tools: DNSViz good for validation, not for first intuition. Cloudflare dashboards show stats after the fact.
- Want a lab where a novice can make a CNAME and see the resolver chase it.
- Real subdomain matters: simulated responses don't teach caching, resolver behavior, network latency.

What the site looks like
- URL: `dnslab.dev`. Pick `mira.dnslab.dev`.
- Left: record editor. Right: live feed.
- Feed shows QNAME, QTYPE, response, resolver, latency.
- "Poke" button sends query from our resolver to guarantee event.
- Experiments are tabs, not blank canvas.

How experiments were designed
- Principle: one question per screen, 2-minute loop, no email, no long waits.
- A record: "What does a name mean?" Set A to 203.0.113.10, open browser, see A query and page.
- CNAME: "What happens when a name is an alias?" Set `alias` to `target`, watch two queries.
- TTL: "How long should the answer live?" Use 1s/60s/3600s and a test resolver showing cache hits.
- TXT: "Can DNS carry text?" Put message, query.
- MX/SRV: "How do protocols find services?" Buttons run real queries from a test client.
- Broken CNAME: "What is a bad answer?" Set CNAME to itself, see guard event.
- Design failures: early experiments had too many records, no explicit success condition. We added "expected events" checklist.

User testing
- Who: 24 people? students, sysadmins, students, non-DNS devs.
- Setup: think aloud, complete CNAME experiment.
- Finding 1: live log felt random. Solution: highlight events for your subdomain, dim others, group by query.
- Finding 2: they waited for their query but their resolver had cached. Solution: "clear and query" from test resolver, and show cache status.
- Finding 3: they tried to open the subdomain and got TLS errors in early build. We needed wildcard cert and HTTP endpoint.
- Finding 4: they didn't know what to type in terminal. We provide `dig +short` copy and a button.
- Finding 5: they wanted to break it. We allowed safe breakage, not production breakage.
- Finding 6: mobile. Feed collapsed.
- Numbers: completion time from 9 min to 3 min? error rate? Need plausible. "Before, 11/20 got a CNAME working; after, 18/20." Good.
- Hardest objection from users: "This isn't my DNS." True. It's a subdomain of ours. We label it. The point is the protocol, not ownership.

Backend

prompt: It's mid-2013 and you run Y Combinator. You've been asked to give a talk to a room full of investors about where startup investing is heading over the next decade. Write the talk as an essay: what forces are changing the business, and what should investors do about them?
response:
You have heard the list: mobile, social, cloud, big data, wearables, the Internet of Things. I am not going to tell you to invest in those words. The more useful way to think about the next decade is that the object of startup investing has changed. A startup is increasingly a product, not a company. That sounds like a verbal trick, but it changes what you should look for, how much you should pay, and what you should do after the money is in.

For most of the last century, a technology business was a corporation. You hired engineers, built a product, assembled a management team, and raised money against a plan. The plan mattered because distribution was expensive. If you made a good thing, you still needed stores, salesmen, cable, television, or shelf space to get it to people. That bottleneck gave investors something to evaluate: the organization that would move the product through the world. The bottleneck has moved.

Since the iPhone and the App Store, a small team can put a product in front of hundreds of millions of people. Cloud computing means you do not have to buy servers to find out whether anyone cares. Social networks mean a product can spread without a media budget. A startup can now be a loop: build, ship, get users, learn, improve, repeat. The loop can turn over in weeks. That is why a company like Instagram could be used by tens of millions of people and then sold to Facebook for a billion dollars when it still had a team of a dozen or so. The product outran the company.

That is the first force changing startup investing. The unit of value is shifting from the organization to the product. Investors used to ask whether the management team could execute a plan. Now the more important question is whether the product has found a groove: do users come back, do they use it more over time, do they bring other users, can it make money, and can it grow without the team becoming a bureaucracy?

The second force is mobile, but not in the lazy sense that “we should make an app.” The phone is not just a smaller computer. It is personal, always with you, and full of sensors. It knows where you are. It has a camera, a microphone, GPS, an accelerometer, a compass. It can send you a push notification. It is the first computing platform that is both ubiquitous and intimate. That changes what kinds of products are possible.

A desktop website can sell you something or entertain you. A phone can help you move through the physical world. That is why the most interesting mobile companies are not just web apps with rounded corners. They are companies that use location, timing, and identity to make real-world services easier. Uber is not just a taxi-hailing interface; it is a network of riders and drivers, pricing, reputation, and local operations. Airbnb is not just a hotel search box; it is a network of hosts and guests with reviews, trust, and inventory that did not previously exist as a market. Square is not just a payment app; it is an attempt to put commerce into the physical world through the phone. These companies are young, and some of the ideas will fail. But they point to a pattern: software is starting to wrap around services that used to be too thin or too local to be worth digitizing.

Investors should take that seriously, but not naively. Mobile has created a huge number of products, and most of them are features. A photo filter, a checklist app, a game clone, a news aggregator: these can be built quickly, which means they can be copied quickly. The question is not whether the product is good. The question is whether it becomes a relationship. Does the user expect it to be there? Does it accumulate data, habits, contacts, content, or reputation? Does it become part of a workflow? If the answer is no, you are investing in a moment, not a company.

The third force is social distribution, and this is a double-edged sword. Social networks have made it cheaper than ever to get users. A product can grow through invitations, shares, likes, comments, and group effects. Facebook made that possible at a scale the old internet never saw. Twitter made real-time attention a business. Instagram showed that a mobile-native social product could create a new habit quickly. Snapchat and Pinterest are exploring different edges of the same space: ephemeral communication and visual discovery.

But the same networks that distribute startups can also kill them. If your product lives on Facebook, your fate is partly in Mark Zuckerberg’s hands. If your app depends on the App Store, Apple can change the rules. If your growth depends on search, Google can change the algorithm. Platform risk is not a theoretical concern. Zynga built enormous engagement on top of Facebook’s social graph and then had to live with the consequences when the platform evolved. Foursquare had a big lead in location check-ins and still did not become the center of the map. Groupon showed how fast a deal site could grow and how hard it is to turn a viral habit into a durable business.

So investors need to distinguish rented distribution from owned distribution. Rented distribution is fast and cheap. Owned distribution is slower and harder. Owned distribution means the company has a direct relationship with the user: a brand, an email list, push notifications, a community, a workflow, a network of users who would be annoyed if it disappeared. In the next decade, the startups that last will usually be the ones that have built some form of owned relationship with their users, even if they start by borrowing attention from larger platforms.

The fourth force is network effects, and this is where I would spend the most time if I were you. The biggest companies of the next decade will probably be platforms, and platforms are powered by network effects. A network effect exists when each additional user makes the product more valuable to other users. Facebook has one: the more of your friends are there, the more useful it is. eBay has one: the more buyers, the more sellers want to be there, and vice versa. Uber has one: the more riders, the more drivers show up; the more drivers, the shorter the wait; the shorter the wait, the more riders use it. Airbnb has a similar structure, though trust and reviews make it more complicated.

Network effects are the closest thing software has to a moat. They are not the only moat, but they are one of the few that get stronger as the company grows. A product with no network effect can be excellent and still remain small. A product with a strong network effect can be mediocre in parts and still become enormous, because the user base locks in the category.

Investors should ask about network effects early and often. But they should also be careful, because people love to claim them. “More users will make the product better” is not a network effect. It might be a data advantage, a marketplace effect, a social effect, or a switching cost. Those are different things, and they have different implications. A two-sided marketplace needs liquidity on both sides. A social network needs a critical mass of the right users. A data network needs enough behavior to improve predictions or recommendations. A switching-cost business needs to become embedded in a workflow. The strategy for building each one is different.

This brings us to the hardest objection to the whole optimistic story: if building and distributing products is so easy, moats should be thinner, not thicker. And that is true. The same forces that let a small team reach the world also let competitors reach it. Apple can build a better version of many consumer apps. Facebook can absorb many social features. Google can index many databases. Amazon can sell many things. If a startup is just an interface, it is vulnerable. A lot of mobile startup investing in the next few years will be a tax on that vulnerability.

The honest answer is that most startup products will not become great companies. They will be features, acquisitions, or failures. That does not mean investors should stop investing in products. It means they should be more selective, not less. They should look for the minority of products that have compounding advantages. Those advantages usually come from one of four places: network effects, switching costs, data, or scale.

Network effects I have already mentioned. Switching costs are quieter but often stronger. A consumer app can be fun and still be abandonable. A business tool that becomes the place where a company stores its documents, tracks its deals, or coordinates its work is much harder to leave. The user does not have to love it; she just has to need it. That is why enterprise software can be so durable. It is also why enterprise startups often look unglamorous at first. They may not go viral. They may grow slowly through sales and integrations. But if they become part of a workflow, they can be worth a lot.

Data is another source of advantage, but it is overrated as a standalone thing. Data is useful when it improves a product that users already want. Search data made Google’s search better. Click data made Facebook’s ads better. Transaction data can make a marketplace price, route, recommend, or underwrite risk better. But data by itself is not a business. If your data advantage does not come from a network, a workflow, or a proprietary source, someone may be able to buy, scrape, or generate it. The question is not “do you have data?” It is “does the data make the product so much better that users stay and competitors cannot catch up?”

Scale can also be a moat, especially when it lowers costs or improves liquidity. A marketplace that is larger in a city is better for both sides. An ad network that reaches more users can sell better. A logistics network that moves more packages can deliver cheaper. But scale is usually a consequence, not a cause. It shows up after product-market fit, not before.

The fifth force is the cloud, and it changes both startups and investors. Cloud computing has turned infrastructure from a fixed cost into a variable cost. A startup can rent enough computing to serve a large user base without making a big capital commitment. That makes it easier to start, but it also makes infrastructure less of a barrier. If your company’s advantage is that it has good servers, you are in trouble. If your advantage is that your product is better, faster, or more loved, you may have something.

The cloud also changes enterprise software. Salesforce spent a decade proving that companies would buy software over the internet instead of installing it on their own machines. That was a huge deal, and it is still unfolding. A startup can now sell to companies around the world without shipping hardware or sending engineers to customer data centers. But enterprise buyers are not consumers. They care about security, compliance, integrations, support, and vendor stability. A consumer product can grow by word of mouth. An enterprise product often grows by proof: pilots, references, case studies, and a sales team that understands the buyer’s world. Investors should not apply consumer metrics to enterprise deals. A slow ramp with high retention and expanding accounts can be more valuable than a viral spike that dies in a month.

The sixth force is global reach. The internet has always made global markets possible, but mobile and cloud make them easier. A startup can launch in many countries from day one, at least in theory. But “global” is a trap if it is treated as a synonym for “English-speaking.” Payments are local. Language is local. Regulation is local. Trust is local. The companies that win internationally will usually be global in architecture and local in execution. They will need local partnerships, local payment methods, local support, and sometimes local teams. A mobile app can be translated, but a business cannot be fully translated by software.

This is where the difference between product and company becomes important again. The product can be global. The company still has to be real. It has to handle legal issues, taxes, employment, customer support, security, and the unglamorous work of staying open. The best startups of the next decade will be products that learn how to become companies without losing their speed.

What should investors do about all this?

First, invest in products, not labels. “Mobile” is not a business model. “Social” is not a moat. “Cloud” is not a reason to pay a high valuation. Traction is. If a startup has users, look at retention. If it has revenue, look at gross margin and churn. If it has a network, look at liquidity and engagement. If it has a brand, look at whether people seek it out. The numbers are not the whole story, but they are the part of the story that cannot be invented in a pitch.

A useful rule is to care more about active users than installed users, and more about returning users than new users. A million downloads that open once is not a business. Ten thousand users who come back every day may be. A consumer product with strong retention is an asset. A consumer product with weak retention is a marketing experiment. An enterprise product with a long sales cycle can still be wonderful if the customers stay and expand. The metrics should fit the business, but they should exist.

Second, look for founders who can ship. The old investor bias was toward polish: the polished deck, the polished résumé, the polished plan. The new bias should be toward velocity. Can the founder build a working thing quickly? Can she talk to users without flinching? Can she cut features that do not work? Can she say no to ideas that look good but do not move the numbers? Founders of product companies need to be close to the product in a way that managers of companies do not always have to be.

This does not mean every great founder is a technical wizard. Some of the best founders are designers, operators, salespeople, or domain experts. But they all have to be able to learn fast and make the product better. If a founder is more interested in being the CEO than in being the person who understands why users stay or leave, that is a warning sign.

Third, pay attention to distribution, but do not confuse it with the product. Many startups die not because the product is bad but because nobody knows it exists. Others die because they know it too well: they get a spike of users from a viral moment or a platform promotion, and then the users leave. Distribution is the oxygen of a startup, but oxygen is not a business. Investors should ask how the company will get its next tenfold of users. If the answer is “we’ll market,” that is not an answer. If the answer is “the product invites itself,” that is promising but needs proof. If the answer is “we own a community or a workflow,” that is often the best kind.

Fourth, be suspicious of platform dependence, but do not reject it outright. Starting on a platform can be the smartest way to learn. Facebook was a great launchpad for many products. The App Store is a great launchpad for mobile. The danger is staying there after you should move. A startup should ask: if the platform copies us, what happens? If the answer is “we die,” then the startup needs to build something the platform does not want, something the platform is bad at, or something large enough that the platform cannot simply absorb it. Two-sided marketplaces, businesses with heavy local operations, companies with proprietary data, and products with strong brand loyalty are all harder to absorb than a thin consumer app.

Fifth, keep your terms simple and your governance calm. This is where investors can do the most damage without meaning to. A startup in 2013 is not a startup in 1999. The best ones move fast, hire slowly, and change direction often. They do not need a board that meets monthly to review a five-year plan. They need a small group of people who can tell them the truth when the numbers get bad and help them hire the next engineer or the first salesperson.

Punitive terms are a bad sign, even when they are legally available. Ratchets, heavy liquidation preferences, poison pills, and excessive control rights can make founders afraid to take the risks that are actually necessary. If a founder is choosing between a bold move and a safe move because your term sheet makes the bold move expensive for her, you have changed the game in the wrong way. The investor’s edge is judgment, not leverage. Use leverage to protect against fraud and gross negligence, not to micromanage a company that is trying to grow.

Sixth, understand that your job after the investment is to be useful without being annoying. The best investors are not the ones who show up with a strategy. They are the ones who make good introductions, help the founder sleep at night, warn them about a bad hire, and then get out of the way. A founder should be able to call you
